{三十六度|さんじゅうろくど}{五分|ごぶ} = 36.5 degrees ({分|ぶ} is a tenth of a degree here);
{原因|げんいん} = cause (lesson 26); {痛|いた}み{止|ど}め = painkiller; {頼|たの}む = to ask (N4);
{怒|おこ}る = to get angry (N4).

## Reading: an email to an old friend

An email between friends, in polite です/ます style.

> {真理|まり}さん
>
> お{元気|げんき}ですか。{先日|せんじつ}は、わざわざお{見舞|みま}いの{電話|でんわ}をありがとうございました。
>
> {実|じつ}は{先月|せんげつ}、{会社|かいしゃ}のけんこうしんだんで、「もう{少|すこ}し{体重|たいじゅう}を{減|へ}らしたほうがいいですね」と{言|い}われました。{自分|じぶん}ではまだ{若|わか}いつもりだったので、ショックでした。{去年|きょねん}より{五|ご}キロも{増|ふ}えていたんです。
>
> それから、{毎朝|まいあさ}{駅|えき}まで{歩|ある}くことにしました。バスに{乗|の}ろうとしたときも、「これも{運動|うんどう}だ」と{思|おも}って、{乗|の}らないで{歩|ある}くことがあります。{食事|しょくじ}も、なるべく{野菜|やさい}を{多|おお}くして、{夜|よる}は{満腹|まんぷく}になるまで{食|た}べないようにしています。
>
> でも、{一番|いちばん}{難|むずか}しいのは{寝不足|ねぶそく}です。{早|はや}く{寝|ね}るつもりでも、ついスマホを{見|み}てしまいます。{先週|せんしゅう}は{妻|つま}に「もう{寝|ね}たら？」と{言|い}われて、{寝|ね}たふりをしながら、ふとんの{中|なか}でゲームをしていました。すぐに{見|み}つかって、{笑|わら}われてしまいました。
>
> {医者|いしゃ}には「{無理|むり}をしないで、{続|つづ}けることが{大切|たいせつ}です」と{言|い}われました。{来月|らいげつ}、もう{一度|いちど}けんさを{受|う}ける{予定|よてい}です。
>
> {真理|まり}さんも、お{体|からだ}に{気|き}をつけてください。
>
> {健二|けんじ}

お{見舞|みま}い = asking after someone who is ill; けんこうしんだん = a health check (one kanji is
outside N3); つい = without meaning to; {無理|むり} = overdoing it
(N4, now in kanji).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. Why was Kenji shocked by the health check? — He still thought of himself as young
   ({若|わか}いつもりだった), but he was told to lose some weight.
2. What does he sometimes do when he's about to get on the bus? — He thinks "this is exercise
   too" and walks instead.
3. What did he do when his wife told him to go to sleep? — He pretended to be asleep
   ({寝|ね}たふり) and played a game under the covers.
4. What did the doctor say matters most? — Not overdoing it and keeping it up.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Dear Mari,

How are you? Thank you for taking the trouble to phone the other day to ask how I was.

Actually, at my company health check last month I was told, "You should lose a bit more
weight." I still thought of myself as young, so it was a shock. I'd put on as much as five kilos since
last year.

Since then I've decided to walk to the station every morning. Even when I'm about to get on
a bus, I sometimes think "this is exercise too" and walk instead. With meals, I eat
as many vegetables as I can and try not to eat until I'm full in the evening.

But the hardest thing is lack of sleep. Even when I mean to go to bed early, I end up looking
at my phone. Last week my wife said, "Why don't you go to sleep?", so I pretended to be asleep
and played a game under the covers. She found out straight away and laughed at me.

The doctor told me, "Don't overdo it; what matters is keeping it up." I'm due for another
check-up next month.

Please look after yourself too, Mari.

Kenji

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{頭|あたま:3}が{痛|いた:2}いんです。
= I've got a headache.
{昨日|きのう}から{熱|ねつ:2}があります。
= I've had a temperature since yesterday.
{大|おお}きく{息|いき:1}を{吸|す:0}ってください。
= Please take a deep breath.
なるべく{歩|ある:2}くようにしています。
= I try to walk as much as possible.
{今|いま}の{話|はなし:3}は、{聞|き}かなかったことにします。
= I'll pretend I didn't hear that.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{私|わたし}は{医者|いしゃ}に{行|い}こうとしません. 〜ようとしない is mostly about other people. For
  yourself: {行|い}きたくないです, {行|い}くつもりはありません.
- ×{病気|びょうき}ふりをする. A noun takes の: {病気|びょうき}のふり. A な-adjective takes な:
  {元気|げんき}なふり.
- {飲|の}んだつもり (thought I'd taken it) and {飲|の}むつもりだった (meant to take it) are different
  stories: the first one you got wrong, the second one you didn't do.
- {食|た}べることにした is "decided to eat"; {食|た}べたことにした is "treated it as eaten".
- わざと for kindness: ×わざと{来|き}てくれてありがとう. The trouble someone took is わざわざ.
- {寝|ね}る vs {眠|ねむ}る: you {寝|ね}る (go to bed) and then, with luck, {眠|ねむ}る (fall asleep).

## Key points

- 〜ようとしたとき / ところに: just as I was about to, something happened.
- 〜ようとしない: (someone) won't, refuses to.
- 〜つもりで: with the intention of, as if. 〜たつもり: thought I had. 〜つもりだった: meant to.
- 〜ふりをする: pretend (plain form, な-adj. + な, noun + の).
- 〜たことにする / 〜なかったことにする: treat it as having (not) happened.
- なるべく (as much as possible), わざと (on purpose), わざわざ (going to the trouble).
- New kanji: 身 背 腹 歯 息 吸 痛 疲 眠 寝 健 康 満.

This is the end of module 1. The reference sheet "Time and change" collects the module's time
patterns. The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when
you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Natural speech: intonation, fillers and aizuchi
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Real conversations don't sound like textbook dialogues. People's voices go up and down to ask
or to agree, they say えーと and あのう while they think, the listener keeps saying はい and
うん, and common phrases get squashed in fast speech. The JLPT N3 listening section is "at near
natural speed", so this honors lesson is about recognising all of that, and using a little of
it yourself.

It builds on N4 lesson 05h1, which taught pitch accent: the high and low inside each word.
This lesson is about **[[intonation]]**, the rise and fall over a whole phrase, which carries the
speaker's attitude.

About the listening here: the speak blocks and listening questions use your device's voice,
which reads the words correctly but often flattens the rises and falls, so read the arrows as
well as listening. Recordings of native speakers, or Japanese TV and podcasts, are the best way
to hear the real thing.

## Rising and falling

In casual speech, the same words can be a question or a statement. The difference is only the
end of the phrase: rising (↑) asks, falling or level (↓) states.

| Words | Rising ↑ | Falling ↓ |
|---|---|---|
| そう | そう？ — Really? Is that so? | そう。 — I see. / Yes, that's right. |
| いい | いい？ — Is it OK? May I? | いい。 — It's fine. (or: No thanks.) |
| {行|い}く | {行|い}く？ — Are you going? Shall we go? | {行|い}く。 — I'm going. |
| {本当|ほんとう} | ほんと？ — Really? | ほんと。 — It's true. |
| {食|た}べない | {食|た}べない？ — Won't you eat? Want some? | {食|た}べない。 — I'm not eating. |

The negative question with a rise is a common, friendly offer: コーヒー、{飲|の}まない？↑ (fancy a
coffee?). With a fall, the same words are a refusal.

### じゃない: question or statement?

〜じゃない has two jobs, and intonation tells them apart:

- {学生|がくせい}じゃない。↓ — He isn't a student. (a plain negative)
- いいじゃない？↑ — Isn't it nice? It's nice, isn't it! (asking for agreement; said with a rise,
  or level and drawn out)

In the second use, people often say じゃん (lesson 25) instead: いいじゃん.

### ね and よ

The sentence-final particles carry intonation too. ね with a rise asks the listener to agree
(いい{天気|てんき}ですね↑, lovely weather, isn't it?); a long, level ねえ shares a
feeling (きれいだねえ, isn't it beautiful). よ with a fall gives information firmly; a rising
よ↑ can sound pushy or surprised. These are tendencies, not rules: speakers vary, and lesson 25
returns to the particles.

### Keep the word accent

Intonation goes on top of each word's pitch accent; it doesn't erase it. In {雨|あめ:1}？ (rain?)
the word still falls after its first **[[mora]]**, あ, and the question rise comes on the end. That's why a question can
sound like a fall followed by a quick rise.

## Fillers: えーと, あのう, まあ, なんか, その

A **[[filler]]** fills the silence while you think. Every language has them, and using the Japanese ones
(instead of English "um") makes you sound much more natural.

| Filler | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| えーと / ええと | searching for a word or a number | えーと、{三時|さんじ}だったかな。 — Let me see, was it three? |
| あのう / あの | opening, getting attention, hesitating politely | あのう、すみません。 — Um, excuse me. |
| まあ | "well, sort of": softening, not going into detail | まあ、なんとかなるよ。 — Well, it'll work out somehow. |
| なんか | "like, kind of": vague, casual | なんか、{眠|ねむ}いんだよね。 — I'm kind of sleepy. |
| その | "that, um": looking for the next word | その、{言|い}いにくいんですが…… — Um, this is hard to say, but… |

Some notes:

- えーと is the thinking filler. It's fine in polite speech, but too many sound unprepared.
- あのう before a request or a question is polite and gentle: it warns the listener that
  something is coming. Drawn out (あのー), it shows hesitation.
- まあ often comes before an answer you don't want to make too strong: 「{仕事|しごと}、どう？」
  「まあまあかな。」 (How's work? So-so.)
- なんか is very common among young people, at the start of almost any sentence. It's casual:
  avoid it in a job interview. (Lesson 20 teaches なんか as a grammar word, "something like".)
- その as a filler is said quickly and without pointing at anything.

## Aizuchi: the listener's part

In a Japanese conversation the listener isn't silent. They keep sending short signals, called
**[[aizuchi]]** (あいづち), to show they're following: はい, ええ, うん, へえ, なるほど. A speaker who
hears nothing will often stop and ask {聞|き}いてる？ (are you listening?).

| Aizuchi | Style | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| はい / ええ | polite | yes, I'm listening (ええ is softer) |
| うん | casual | yeah, uh-huh |
| そうですか / そう | polite / casual | I see |
| そうなんですか / そうなんだ | polite / casual | oh, is that so? (new information) |
| へえ | both | oh really? wow (surprise, interest) |
| なるほど | both | I see, that makes sense |
| そうですね / そうだね | polite / casual | yes, that's right (agreeing) |
| {確|たし}かに | both | true, that's right |
| さすが | both | that's (just like) you! impressive! |

Three things to know:

- **Aizuchi aren't agreement.** はい and うん mean "I'm following", not "yes, I agree". A
  business partner who says はい、はい all through your proposal may still turn it down.
- **They come often.** In conversation, listeners give one at most pauses; on the phone, where
  there's no nodding, even more. Silence on the phone can sound as if the line has gone dead or
  the listener disapproves.
- **Nodding counts.** Face to face, a small nod (うなずく, to nod) does the same job.

Use なるほど carefully with people above you: some speakers feel it sounds as if you're judging
whether they make sense. そうなんですか and はい are safe everywhere.

## Fast speech: what to listen for

In everyday speech, some common sequences shrink. You know several from N4. You don't need to
say these, but you'll hear them all the time.

| Careful | Fast | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜ています | 〜てます | {待|ま}ってます (I'm waiting) |
| 〜ている | 〜てる | {知|し}ってる？ (do you know?) |
| すみません | すいません | すいません、ちょっと… |
| 〜という | 〜って | {田中|たなか}って{人|ひと} (someone called Tanaka) |
| 〜と{言|い}った | 〜って{言|い}った / 〜って | {来|く}るって (he said he's coming) |
| 〜のです / 〜のだ | 〜んです / 〜んだ | {行|い}くんです |
| 〜ではない | 〜じゃない | {学生|がくせい}じゃない |
| 〜てしまう | 〜ちゃう / 〜じゃう | {忘|わす}れちゃった |
| 〜ておく | 〜とく / 〜どく | {買|か}っとく (I'll buy it in advance) |
| 〜なければ | 〜なきゃ | {行|い}かなきゃ (I have to go) |
| ところ | とこ | {今|いま}{行|い}くとこ (I'm just leaving) |
| {分|わ}からない | {分|わ}かんない | |
| やはり | やっぱり | |

すいません is so common that many people say it in polite speech too, but in writing and formal
speech use すみません.

## Listening practice

Listen to each line, then read it. Notice where the voice rises.

```speak
そう？
= Really? (rising)
そう。
= I see. (falling)
コーヒー、{飲|の}まない？
= Fancy a coffee? (rising)
えーと、{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}だったと{思|おも}います。
= Let me see, I think it was in front of the station.
あのう、ちょっとよろしいですか。
= Um, do you have a moment?
へえ、そうなんですか。
= Oh, really?
なるほど。
= I see, that makes sense.
```

## Dialogue: on the phone

Aoi is telling her friend Ren about a new job. Listen to how often Ren gives aizuchi. (Casual:
friends. The device voice may not produce the rises; the arrows show them.)

```dialogue
# On the phone
あおい: もしもし、れん？{今|いま}、ちょっといい？
= Hello, Ren? Have you got a minute?
れん: うん、いいよ。どうしたの？
= Yeah, sure. What's up?
あおい: あのね、{実|じつ}は{来月|らいげつ}から{新|あたら}しい{会社|かいしゃ}で{働|はたら}くことになったんだ。
= Well, actually, I'm going to start working at a new company next month.
れん: へえ、そうなんだ！どこ？
= Oh, really! Where?
あおい: えーと、{駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くの、デザインの{会社|かいしゃ}。
= Um, a design company near the station.
れん: うん、うん。
= Uh-huh.
あおい: {給料|きゅうりょう}はまあ、{前|まえ}とあんまり{変|か}わらないんだけど、{家|いえ}から{近|ちか}いし……
= The pay's, well, not that different from before, but it's close to home, and…
れん: なるほどね。それ、{大事|だいじ}だよね。
= I see. That matters, doesn't it.
あおい: でしょ？↑ なんか、{毎日|まいにち}{一時間|いちじかん}も{電車|でんしゃ}に{乗|の}るの、もう{疲|つか}れちゃって。
= Right? I'm kind of tired of riding the train for an hour every day.
れん: {分|わ}かる。さすが、あおい。ちゃんと{考|かんが}えてるね。
= I know what you mean. That's you all over, Aoi: you've thought it through.
あおい: ほんと？↑ ありがとう。
= Really? Thanks.
```

{給料|きゅうりょう} = pay (lesson 11); {大事|だいじ} = important (N4); でしょ？ is a casual でしょう with a
rise, "right?". Count Ren's aizuchi: うん, へえ, そうなんだ, うん、うん, なるほどね, {分|わ}かる.

## Reading: a column on listening

A short column from a magazine for learners, in polite style.

> {日本語|にほんご}で{話|はな}していると、{相手|あいて}が「はい、はい」「うん、うん」とよく{言|い}います。{初|はじ}めて{日本|にほん}に{来|き}たころ、{私|わたし}はそれを「{賛成|さんせい}です」という{意味|いみ}だと{思|おも}っていました。でも、そうではありません。あいづちは「{聞|き}いていますよ」という{合図|あいず}です。{電話|でんわ}で{私|わたし}が{何|なに}も{言|い}わずに{聞|き}いていたら、{友|とも}だちに「もしもし？{聞|き}いてる？」と{何度|なんど}も{言|い}われました。{今|いま}は{私|わたし}も、{話|はなし}を{聞|き}きながら「へえ」や「そうなんですか」を{使|つか}うようにしています。

{相手|あいて} = the other person; {賛成|さんせい} = agreement (lesson 28); {合図|あいず} = a signal;
〜ずに = without (lesson 10).

## Key points

- Rising intonation asks (そう？↑), falling or level states (そう。↓). A rising negative is often an
  invitation: {飲|の}まない？↑.
- Intonation goes on top of word accent; it doesn't replace it.
- Fillers: えーと (thinking), あのう (polite opening), まあ (softening), なんか (casual "like"),
  その (looking for a word).
- **[[Aizuchi]]** (はい, ええ, うん, へえ, そうなんですか, なるほど) mean "I'm listening", not "I agree", and
  they come often, especially on the phone.
- Fast speech: 〜てます, すいません, 〜って, 〜ちゃう, 〜とく, 〜なきゃ, とこ, {分|わ}かんない.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Hot springs and public baths
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Getting into a big bath of hot water with strangers is one of the most Japanese experiences
there is, and one of the most relaxing, once you know the rules. This honors lesson covers the
neighbourhood public bath and the hot spring: what each one is, how a visit works step by step,
the manners everyone expects, the notices you'll read on the wall, and the one rule that varies
a lot from place to place: tattoos.

Two words first. A neighbourhood public bath is a せんとう (its first kanji is outside N3), and a
hot spring is an {温泉|おんせん}. The second kanji of {温泉|おんせん}, {泉|いずみ} (spring), is outside N3, so
you'll see it here only with furigana, for recognition; your vocabulary card is the carried
word おんせん from N5.

## せんとう and {温泉|おんせん}

| | せんとう | {温泉|おんせん} |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | a public bath in town, heated tap or well water | a bath of water that comes from the ground |
| Where | in neighbourhoods, often near stations | in hot-spring towns, hotels and spas |
| Price | set by each prefecture: a little over 500 yen in Tokyo in the mid-2020s | anything from a few hundred yen to the price of a hotel stay |
| Why people go | a big bath after work, chatting with neighbours | the water itself, the views, a weekend away |

Under Japanese law, water counts as an {温泉|おんせん} if it comes out of the ground at 25°C or
more, or contains certain minerals. Many places have outdoor baths, ろてんぶろ, and some hotels
have private baths you can book for your family: {貸|か}し{切|き}り (reserved).

The number of せんとう has fallen a long way since most homes got their own baths, but in big
cities many still open every afternoon, and some have been rebuilt with saunas and cafés.

## A visit, step by step

1. Take off your shoes at the entrance and put them in the shoe locker, げたばこ.
2. Pay. Old せんとう have a {番台|ばんだい}, a raised seat where the attendant sits between the men's
   and women's sides; newer ones have a front desk or a ticket machine. Towels, soap and shampoo
   are often for sale or rent.
3. Go through the right curtain: {男湯|おとこゆ} (men's bath) or {女湯|おんなゆ} (women's bath). The
   curtains (のれん) often have the kanji {男|おとこ} or {女|おんな}, and many are blue for men and
   red for women, but read the kanji: some places swap the sides on different days.
4. In the changing room, だついじょ, put your clothes in a locker or basket. Take only a small
   towel into the bathroom.
5. Before you get in, pour hot water over yourself: かけ{湯|ゆ}. Then wash your whole body at the
   washing area, sitting on a stool, and rinse off all the soap.
6. Now get into the bath, {湯船|ゆぶね}, slowly. The water is often 40 to 42°C.
7. Before you go back to the changing room, wipe yourself down with your small towel so you don't
   drip on the floor.

Afterwards, drink some water. A cold bottle of milk after the bath is a well-known custom, and
many せんとう sell it.

## Manners

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| wash before you get in | wash or use soap in the bath itself |
| keep your towel out of the water (on your head or by the side) | put your towel in the bath |
| tie up long hair | let your hair hang in the water |
| get in quietly | swim, dive or splash |
| take a break if you feel hot | stay in until you feel faint |

If you stay in too long you can feel dizzy and hot in the face: that's のぼせる (to feel faint from
the heat). Get out, sit down and drink water. People who have been drinking alcohol shouldn't
take a hot bath at all.

## Tattoos

Many hot-spring hotels, spas and gyms refuse people with tattoos (いれずみ, or タトゥー), because
tattoos were long linked with crime gangs. Neighbourhood せんとう are often more relaxed. The
rules vary a great deal: some places welcome everyone, some let you in if you cover a small
tattoo with a sticker, and some say no to any tattoo. In recent years more places have relaxed
their rules for visitors from abroad, but don't count on it: read the notice or ask before you
pay.

## Reading the notices

Notices in baths use patterns you know: 〜てください, 〜ないでください, and ご〜ください ("please
do", very polite). Two new ones are common on signs: お{断|ことわ}り, "not allowed" (literally "we
must refuse"), and ごえんりょください, "please refrain from".

> **お{客様|きゃくさま}へのお{願|ねが}い**
>
> ・{湯船|ゆぶね}に{入|はい}る{前|まえ}に、かけ{湯|ゆ}をして、{体|からだ}を{洗|あら}ってください。
>
> ・タオルは{湯船|ゆぶね}に{入|い}れないでください。
>
> ・{長|なが}い{髪|かみ}は{結|むす}んでください。
>
> ・{湯船|ゆぶね}の{中|なか}で{泳|およ}いだり、{体|からだ}を{洗|あら}ったりしないでください。
>
> ・お{酒|さけ}を{飲|の}んだ{方|かた}のにゅうよくは、お{断|ことわ}りします。
>
> ・いれずみ（タトゥー）のある{方|かた}は、ごえんりょください。
>
> ・だついじょに{戻|もど}る{前|まえ}に、{体|からだ}をよくふいてください。
>
> ・{小学生|しょうがくせい}{以下|いか}のお{子様|こさま}は、{大人|おとな}と{一緒|いっしょ}に{入|はい}ってください。
>
> ゆっくりお{楽|たの}しみください。　さくら{湯|ゆ}

Read it once for the general sense, then again for the details: it's the kind of notice the JLPT
calls information retrieval. にゅうよく is "bathing" (its second kanji is outside N3), ふく is
"to wipe" (N4), and お{子様|こさま} is a polite word for children. さくら{湯|ゆ} is the bath's name:
many せんとう are called 〜{湯|ゆ}.

## Dialogue: a first visit

Yuki grew up abroad and has never been to a せんとう. Her friend Haruto takes her to the one near
his flat. (Casual: friends.)

```dialogue
# At the entrance
はると: ここだよ。{入|い}り{口|ぐち}で{靴|くつ}をぬいで、げたばこに{入|い}れてね。
= Here it is. Take your shoes off at the entrance and put them in the shoe locker.
ゆき: うん。お{金|かね}はどこで{払|はら}うの？
= OK. Where do I pay?
はると: あそこのフロントで。タオルを{持|も}ってないなら、{借|か}りられるよ。
= At the front desk over there. If you haven't got a towel, you can rent one.
ゆき: {持|も}ってきた。……あ、{赤|あか}いのれんが{女湯|おんなゆ}？
= I brought one. …Oh, is the red curtain the women's bath?
はると: {今日|きょう}はね。でも、{曜日|ようび}で{変|か}わるから、{字|じ}を{見|み}たほうがいいよ。
= Today it is. But it changes with the day of the week, so you'd better look at the kanji.
ゆき: {分|わ}かった。{入|はい}る{前|まえ}に{体|からだ}を{洗|あら}うんだよね？
= Got it. I wash before I get in, right?
はると: そう。かけ{湯|ゆ}をして、{洗|あら}ってから{湯船|ゆぶね}に{入|はい}るの。タオルはお{湯|ゆ}に{入|い}れないでね。
= Yes. Pour some water over yourself, wash, and then get in the bath. Don't put your towel in the water.
ゆき: {頭|あたま}の{上|うえ}にのせればいい？
= Can I put it on my head?
はると: うん、みんなそうしてる。あと、{熱|あつ}いから、{長|なが}く{入|はい}りすぎないように。のぼせちゃうよ。
= Yeah, everyone does that. And it's hot, so don't stay in too long. You'll get light-headed.
ゆき: {気|き}をつける。じゃあ、{一時間後|いちじかんご}にここでね。
= I'll be careful. See you here in an hour, then.
はると: {出|で}たら、{冷|つめ}たいぎゅうにゅうを{飲|の}もう。
= When you come out, let's have some cold milk.
```

フロント = front desk; {字|じ} = written characters (N4); のせる = to put on top (the verb you met as {乗|の}せる in lesson 2, written here in kana because
its usual kanji for this sense is outside N3).

## Key points

- A せんとう is a neighbourhood public bath; an {温泉|おんせん} ({泉|いずみ} is outside N3) uses water from the
  ground, by law at least 25°C or with certain minerals.
- Order: shoes in the げたばこ, pay, the right curtain ({男湯|おとこゆ} / {女湯|おんなゆ}), undress in the
  だついじょ, かけ{湯|ゆ}, wash, then the {湯船|ゆぶね}; wipe yourself before going back.
- No towels or soap in the bath, hair tied up, no swimming; get out before you のぼせる.
- Tattoo rules (いれずみ, タトゥー) vary a lot: many hot-spring hotels refuse them, many せんとう don't.
  Check first.
- Signs: 〜ないでください, ご〜ください, お{断|ことわ}り (not allowed), ごえんりょください (please refrain).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Thanks to and because of: おかげで, せいで, ことから
topics: おかげで and せいで
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 was about time: when things happen and how they change. Module 2 is about *why*:
reasons, conclusions, and what you should or shouldn't do. This first lesson gives you the words
for causes that Japanese speakers choose by how they feel about the result.

You already have から and ので (N5, N4) and the て form as a soft "because". They give a reason
and say nothing about whether the result is good or bad. N3 adds reasons with an attitude:

{雨|あめ}がやんだおかげで、{花火|はなび}が{見|み}られた。 — Thanks to the rain stopping, we could see the fireworks.
{雨|あめ}のせいで、{花火|はなび}が{中止|ちゅうし}になった。 — Because of the rain, the fireworks were cancelled.
{大雨|おおあめ}のため、{電車|でんしゃ}が{止|と}まっています。 — Owing to heavy rain, trains are stopped. (an announcement)

Then two patterns for reasoning from evidence: 〜ことから (from the fact that…) and 〜{結果|けっか}
(as a result of…). The theme is the weather and the natural world: snow and sun, wind and
typhoons, leaves and grass, and what happens when the weather turns dangerous.

The new words in this module's lessons are written with kanji wherever all their kanji are on the
course list, and so are the words you met in kana in N5 and N4 ({雪|ゆき}, {晴|は}れる, {言葉|ことば}
in this lesson). The grammar words stay in kana: おかげ, せい, ため, こと, わけ, もの.

## Thanks to: 〜おかげで

おかげ is "the favour of, the help of". 〜おかげで introduces a cause that gave a *good*
result, and the speaker is grateful for it. It joins like a noun: plain form of a verb or
い-adjective, な-adjective + な, noun + の.

| Before it | Example |
|---|---|
| verb (plain, often past) | {早|はや}く{出|で}たおかげで |
| い-adjective | {天気|てんき}がよかったおかげで |
| な-adjective + な | {道|みち}が{静|しず}かなおかげで |
| noun + の | {先生|せんせい}のおかげで |

{晴|は}れたおかげで、せんたくものがすぐかわいた。 — Thanks to the sunny weather, the washing dried quickly.

{友|とも}だちが{手伝|てつだ}ってくれたおかげで、{雪|ゆき}かきが{早|はや}く{終|お}わりました。 — Thanks to my friend's help, the snow shovelling was over quickly.
{天気予報|てんきよほう}を{見|み}ていたおかげで、かさを{持|も}って{出|で}かけられました。 — Because I'd checked the forecast, I could go out with an umbrella.
{山田|やまだ}さんのおかげです。 — It's thanks to you, Ms Yamada. (おかげです at the end of a sentence)

The second half states a result that happened or a state that holds; it isn't a request, an
invitation or what you intend to do. ×{晴|は}れたおかげで、{出|で}かけましょう doesn't work: say
{晴|は}れたから、{出|で}かけましょう.

### Ironic おかげで

Said about a bad result, おかげで sounds sarcastic, "thanks a lot":
{弟|おとうと}が{窓|まど}を{開|あ}けたままにしたおかげで、{部屋|へや}が{雪|ゆき}だらけだよ。 (My brother left the
window open, so thanks to him the room is full of snow; 〜だらけ, covered in, is lesson 16's.) It's a
tone of voice, not a separate
rule, and it's mostly casual.

The set phrase おかげさまで (N4) is the polite answer to お{元気|げんき}ですか and the like: "I'm well,
thanks to you (all)". It doesn't need a reason in front of it.

## Because of (it's its fault): 〜せいで, 〜せいか

せい is "fault, blame". 〜せいで introduces a cause that led to a *bad* result. It joins
exactly like おかげで.

{台風|たいふう}のせいで、{旅行|りょこう}が{中止|ちゅうし}になりました。 — Because of the typhoon, the trip was called off.
{寒|さむ}さのせいで、{池|いけ}の{水|みず}がこおっている。 — The pond has frozen because of the cold.
{昨日|きのう}{雨|あめ}にぬれたせいで、かぜをひいたみたいです。 — I seem to have caught a cold because I got soaked in the rain yesterday.

- 〜せいだ / 〜せいです ends a sentence: {頭|あたま}が{痛|いた}いのは{寝不足|ねぶそく}のせいだ (My headache is
  down to lack of sleep).
- 〜せいか is "maybe because": the speaker isn't sure of the cause. It's also used when the
  result isn't clearly bad: {気温|きおん}が{上|あ}がったせいか、さくらが{早|はや}くさいた。 (Perhaps
  because it got warmer, the cherry blossoms came out early.)
- 〜のせいにする is "to blame (it) on": {失敗|しっぱい}を{天気|てんき}のせいにする (blame a failure
  on the weather). {失敗|しっぱい} (failure) is glossed here.

おかげで and せいで are the speaker's judgement. The same fact can take either, depending on how
you see it:

{雪|ゆき}が{降|ふ}ったおかげで、スキーができた。 — Thanks to the snow, we could ski.
{雪|ゆき}が{降|ふ}ったせいで、バスが{遅|おく}れた。 — Because of the snow, the bus was late.

Like おかげで, せいで reports a result. A wish, a plan or a request after it is wrong:
×{雨|あめ}のせいで、{家|いえ}にいてください. Use から or ので for those:
{雨|あめ}なので、{家|いえ}にいてください.

## Because (formal): 〜ため(に)

In N4 you learned ため(に) for *purpose*: {健康|けんこう}のために{歩|ある}く (walk for your
health). The same ため also gives a *cause*, in a formal, neutral voice: announcements, the
news, notices and written reports. Its connections are the same as おかげで (noun + の, な-adjective
+ な, plain verb and adjective forms).

{大雪|おおゆき}のため、{本日|ほんじつ}は{休校|きゅうこう}です。 — Owing to heavy snow, the school is closed today. ({休校|きゅうこう} = school closure)
{強風|きょうふう}のため、{電車|でんしゃ}が{遅|おく}れております。 — Trains are running late because of strong winds. (an announcement: 〜ております is polite; lesson 24)
じこがあったため、{道|みち}がじゅうたいしていた。 — Because there had been an accident, the road was jammed.

How to tell the two ため apart:

| | Purpose ため | Cause ため |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | in order to | because of |
| Before ため | dictionary form of an action someone chooses to do; noun + の | past forms, states, things nobody chooses; noun + の |
| Example | {合格|ごうかく}するために{勉強|べんきょう}する | {勉強|べんきょう}しなかったために{落|お}ちた |
| Translation | study in order to pass | failed because (I) didn't study |

A noun can go either way, so context decides: {雪|ゆき}のために{道具|どうぐ}を{買|か}った would most
naturally be "bought tools for the snow (to deal with it)", while {雪|ゆき}のために{遅|おく}れた is
"was late because of the snow". In speech, a plain から or ので is usually more natural; cause ため
sounds like a notice.

## From the fact that: 〜ことから

〜ことから gives the evidence or the observed fact that something follows from. It's common in
explanations and writing. Before it: the plain form of a verb or い-adjective; a な-adjective +
な (or である); a noun + である.

{道|みち}がぬれていることから、{夜|よる}の{間|あいだ}に{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}ったと{分|わ}かる。 — From the fact that the road is wet, you can tell it rained in the night.
{煙|けむり}が{出|で}ていることから、{火事|かじ}だと{思|おも}われた。 — Since smoke was coming out, people thought it was a fire.

Its best-known use is how something got its name: 〜ことから、〜と{呼|よ}ばれている / 〜という
{名前|なまえ}がついた.

{冬|ふゆ}になると{雪|ゆき}が{多|おお}いことから、この{町|まち}は「{雪国|ゆきぐに}」と{呼|よ}ばれている。 — Because it gets so much snow in winter, this town is called "snow country".
{秋|あき}に{葉|は}が{赤|あか}くなることから、この{山|やま}は「{赤山|あかやま}」と{名付|なづ}けられた。 — The mountain was named "Red Mountain" because its leaves turn red in autumn.

The word for "origin (of a name)" is {由来|ゆらい}: {地名|ちめい}の{由来|ゆらい} (the origin of a place
name; {地名|ちめい} is glossed here).

Use ことから for reasoning and names, not for everyday reasons: ×{疲|つか}れたことから、{早|はや}く{寝|ね}た
sounds odd; say {疲|つか}れたので、{早|はや}く{寝|ね}た.

## As a result of: 〜{結果|けっか}

{結果|けっか} (result, N4's けっか, now in kanji) follows a verb in the た form or a noun + の. It
says what came out of an action or a process, often after effort or investigation, and the second
half is the outcome.

{毎日|まいにち}{水|みず}をやった{結果|けっか}、{草花|くさばな}が{元気|げんき}になった。 — As a result of watering them every day, the flowers recovered.
{調|しら}べた{結果|けっか}、ていでんの{原因|げんいん}は{強風|きょうふう}だと{分|わ}かりました。 — Investigation showed that the cause of the power cut was the strong wind.
{話|はな}し{合|あ}いの{結果|けっか}、{旅行|りょこう}は{来月|らいげつ}にのびた。 — After a discussion, the trip was put off until next month.

{原因|げんいん} (cause) is a lesson 26 word; ていでん (power cut) is new here; のびる (to be put off)
is a gloss.

## Choosing a "because"

| Pattern | Feeling about the result | Style | After it: request, plan, opinion? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜から | none | everyday, direct | yes |
| 〜ので | none | softer, polite | yes (polite requests) |
| 〜て | none | casual link; feelings and things you can't control | no |
| 〜ため(に) | none | formal, written, announcements | only a polite request in a notice: {雨|あめ}のため、{足元|あしもと}にご{注意|ちゅうい}ください |
| 〜おかげで | good (grateful); ironic for bad | all styles | no: a result |
| 〜せいで | bad (blame) | all styles | no: a result |
| 〜せいか | maybe this is why | all styles | no |
| 〜ことから | reasoning from a fact; names | explanations, writing | no |
| 〜によって | neutral cause in writing: {台風|たいふう}によって{木|き}が{倒|たお}れた | written | no (lesson 13 teaches によって fully) |

A quick test: if you can add "thank goodness", use おかげで; if you can add "unfortunately", せいで;
if it sounds like a train announcement, ため.

## Weather and nature words

The words for this lesson cover the sky, the seasons and what grows. Some you know in kana now take
kanji: {雪|ゆき}, {晴|は}れ, {晴|は}れる. A few kanji you'd expect aren't on the N3 list, so their words
stay in kana: きり (fog), にじ (rainbow), えだ (branch), さく (to bloom), かれる (to wither), こおる
(to freeze), こうずい (flood).

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| sun and sky | {太陽|たいよう}, {日差|ひざ}し, {晴天|せいてん}, {日|ひ}の{出|で}, {夕日|ゆうひ}, にじ |
| the weather | {気候|きこう} (climate), {天候|てんこう} (weather, formal), {陽気|ようき} (the weather of a season), {小雨|こさめ}, にわか{雨|あめ}, {雨上|あめあ}がり, {水|みず}たまり, きり |
| wind and snow | {風|かぜ}が{吹|ふ}く, {強風|きょうふう}, {大雪|おおゆき}, {吹雪|ふぶき}, {雪|ゆき}が{積|つ}もる, {雪|ゆき}かき, {雪|ゆき}だるま, {雪国|ゆきぐに} |
| heat and cold | {真夏|まなつ}, {真冬|まふゆ}, {暑|あつ}さ, {寒|さむ}さ, {最高気温|さいこうきおん}, {最低気温|さいていきおん}, こおる |
| plants | {草|くさ}, {葉|は}, {葉|は}っぱ, {落|お}ち{葉|ば}, {草花|くさばな}, しょくぶつ, えだ, さく, {散|ち}る, かれる, {地面|じめん}, {石|いし} |
| when weather turns bad | {予報|よほう}, {注意報|ちゅういほう} (advisory), {警報|けいほう} (warning), {害|がい}, ひがい, {水害|すいがい}, さいがい, こうずい, どしゃくずれ, {川|かわ}があふれる, ていでん, {木|き}が{倒|たお}れる, {流|なが}れる / {流|なが}す, {煙|けむり} |

Three pairs to notice:

- {倒|たお}れる (to fall over, of a tree, a person, a bike) and {倒|たお}す (to knock down) are an
  intransitive and transitive pair, like N4's {落|お}ちる and {落|お}とす. So are {流|なが}れる (to flow,
  be washed away) and {流|なが}す (to let flow, wash away).
- {注意報|ちゅういほう} and {警報|けいほう} are the two levels you hear on Japanese weather reports:
  an advisory and a more serious warning.
- {害|がい} is harm in general ({体|からだ}に{害|がい}がある, harmful to the body); ひがい is the damage
  a disaster or crime does ({台風|たいふう}のひがい). Its first kanji is outside the N3 list, so it
  stays in kana.

えいきょう (influence, effect; in kana for the same reason): {台風|たいふう}のえいきょうで、
{飛行機|ひこうき}が{飛|と}ばなかった (because of the typhoon, the plane didn't fly). 〜のえいきょうで is a
neutral "because of" that news reports use a lot.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: the sky and the weather, plants and stone, and four verbs of things falling,
flowing and burning.

### The sky and the weather

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 雪 | snow | セツ | ゆき | 11 | {雪|ゆき}, {大雪|おおゆき}, {雪国|ゆきぐに}, {吹雪|ふぶき} (special) |
| 晴 | clear (weather) | セイ | は(れる) | 12 | {晴|は}れ, {晴|は}れる, {晴天|せいてん} |
| 吹 | blow | スイ | ふ(く) | 7 | {吹|ふ}く, {吹雪|ふぶき} (special) |
| 候 | climate; season | コウ | — | 10 | {気候|きこう}, {天候|てんこう} |
| 陽 | sun; positive | ヨウ | — | 12 | {太陽|たいよう}, {陽気|ようき} |

- {雪|ゆき} and {晴|は}れ, {晴|は}れる were N5 and N4 words in kana; write them with kanji from now on.
- {吹雪|ふぶき} (a snowstorm) is a special reading of the whole word: neither kanji is read that way
  elsewhere.
- {吹|ふ}く isn't ふく "to wipe" (N4) or {服|ふく} (clothes): same sound, different words.

### Plants and stone

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 草 | grass | ソウ | くさ | 9 | {草|くさ}, {草花|くさばな} |
| 葉 | leaf | ヨウ | は (ば) | 12 | {葉|は}, {葉|は}っぱ, {落|お}ち{葉|ば}, {言葉|ことば} |
| 石 | stone | セキ | いし | 5 | {石|いし} |

- 葉 lets you write N5's ことば: {言葉|ことば}, "words" (literally "leaves of speech"). は becomes ば
  in {落|お}ち{葉|ば} and {言葉|ことば}.
- 石's on'yomi セキ comes in later words; at N3 you'll mostly read it いし.

### Harm, and things that fall, flow and burn

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 害 | harm | ガイ | — | 10 | {害|がい}, {水害|すいがい} |
| 倒 | fall over | トウ | たお(れる), たお(す) | 10 | {倒|たお}れる, {倒|たお}す, {面倒|めんどう} |
| 流 | flow | リュウ | なが(れる), なが(す) | 10 | {流|なが}れる, {流|なが}す, {流|なが}れ, {交流|こうりゅう} (exchange, lesson 13) |
| 落 | fall | ラク | お(ちる), お(とす) | 12 | {落|お}ちる, {落|お}とす, {落|お}ち{葉|ば}, {落|お}とし{物|もの} |
| 煙 | smoke | エン | けむり | 13 | {煙|けむり} |

- Carried words you can now write: {面倒|めんどう} (troublesome, N4), {落|お}ちる, {落|お}とす (N4) and
  {落|お}とし{物|もの} (N5).
- きんえん (no smoking) uses 煙, but its first kanji isn't on the N3 list, so it stays in kana.

Memory notes (my own pictures, not the kanji's history):

- 雪 starts with 雨 (rain) and has a hand-like shape under it: rain you can hold in your hand.
- 晴 is 日 (sun) beside 青 (blue): sun and blue sky.
- 吹 is 口 (mouth) beside 欠 (a person yawning, mouth open): blowing.
- 草, 葉 and 落 all have the grass radical (three short strokes) on top: grass, a leaf, and
  leaves falling.
- 倒 is the person radical beside 到 (to arrive, lesson 14): a person who's arrived at the ground.
- 流 starts with the three dots of the water radical: water flowing away.
- 煙 has 火 (fire) on the left: what rises from a fire.
- 陽 has the hill radical on the left: the sun over the hill.

```trace
雪晴吹候陽草葉石害倒流落煙
```

## Dialogue: after the typhoon

Two neighbours, Kōta and Emi, meet in the street the morning after a typhoon. They're the same
age and talk casually.

```dialogue
# The morning after
こうた: おはよう。{昨日|きのう}の{夜|よる}、すごい{風|かぜ}だったね。
= Morning. Wasn't the wind something last night?
えみ: ほんとに。{風|かぜ}の{音|おと}のせいで、{全然|ぜんぜん}{寝|ね}られなかったよ。
= Really. The noise of the wind kept me awake all night.
こうた: うちもだよ。{見|み}て、あそこの{木|き}が{倒|たお}れてる。
= Same here. Look, that tree over there has come down.
えみ: わあ、{大|おお}きい{木|き}なのに。{車|くるま}に{当|あ}たらなくてよかった。
= Wow, and it's such a big tree. Lucky it didn't hit a car.
こうた: {駅|えき}のほうはだいじょうぶかな。{電車|でんしゃ}、{動|うご}いてる？
= I wonder if it's OK near the station. Are the trains running?
えみ: さっきアプリで{見|み}たら、{強風|きょうふう}のため{運転|うんてん}を{見合|みあ}わせています、って。
= I checked the app just now and it said "services suspended owing to strong winds".
こうた: そうか…。でも、{雨|あめ}はもうやんだね。{予報|よほう}より{早|はや}く{行|い}ったおかげで、{川|かわ}もあふれなかったし。
= I see… But the rain's stopped, anyway. The typhoon moved on sooner than forecast, so the river didn't flood either.
えみ: うん、ていでんもなかったし。{去年|きょねん}のはひどかったよね。
= Yeah, and no power cut. Last year's was awful, wasn't it.
こうた: {去年|きょねん}は{三日|みっか}も{電気|でんき}が{来|こ}なかった。れいぞうこの{中|なか}が{全部|ぜんぶ}だめになって…
= Last year we had no electricity for three days. Everything in the fridge went off…
えみ: そうそう。だから{今回|こんかい}は{前|まえ}の{日|ひ}に{水|みず}と{電池|でんち}を{買|か}っておいたんだ。
= Right. That's why this time I bought water and batteries the day before.
こうた: えらいね。ぼくは{何|なに}もしなかった。{運|うん}がよかっただけだよ。
= Good for you. I didn't do anything. I was just lucky.
えみ: じゃあ、{今日|きょう}は{落|お}ち{葉|ば}とえだのかたづけ、{手伝|てつだ}ってよ。
= Then help me clear up the leaves and branches today.
```

{見合|みあ}わせる (to suspend, put off) is a word you'll hear in train announcements; {当|あ}たる is
"to hit"; {運|うん} is luck (N4); かたづけ is the noun of N4's かたづける (to tidy up). Notice the three
causes: せいで for the lost sleep, ため in the app's formal notice, おかげで for the luck with the
river.

## Reading: a blog from snow country

A blog post by someone who moved to a snowy town. Blogs are usually written in the plain だ style,
as this one is.

> {雪国|ゆきぐに}に{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}して{三年|さんねん}になる。{東京|とうきょう}に{住|す}んでいたころは、{雪|ゆき}が{降|ふ}るとうれしくて、{子供|こども}のように{外|そと}に{出|で}て{雪|ゆき}だるまを{作|つく}ったりしていた。しかし、ここでは{雪|ゆき}は{遊|あそ}びではない。{一晩|ひとばん}で{一|いち}メートルも{積|つ}もる{日|ひ}があるので、{朝|あさ}はまず{雪|ゆき}かきから{始|はじ}まる。
>
> {今年|ことし}の{冬|ふゆ}は{特|とく}に{大雪|おおゆき}が{多|おお}かった。{一月|いちがつ}には{吹雪|ふぶき}のせいで{道|みち}が{見|み}えなくなり、{三日間|みっかかん}{家|いえ}から{出|で}られなかった。やねの{雪|ゆき}が{落|お}ちて、となりの{家|いえ}の{窓|まど}が{割|わ}れたこともある。{寒|さむ}さのせいか、{体調|たいちょう}をくずす{人|ひと}も{多|おお}かった。
>
> それでも、この{町|まち}が{好|す}きだ。{近所|きんじょ}の{人|ひと}たちが{雪|ゆき}かきを{手伝|てつだ}ってくれたおかげで、{一人|ひとり}でもなんとか{冬|ふゆ}を{過|す}ごせた。それに、{雪|ゆき}がとけたあとの{春|はる}は{本当|ほんとう}にきれいだ。{山|やま}の{雪|ゆき}が{川|かわ}に{流|なが}れて、{田|た}んぼに{水|みず}が{入|はい}る。{草|くさ}や{花|はな}がいっせいに{出|で}てくる。{長|なが}い{冬|ふゆ}があるおかげで、{春|はる}がいっそううれしく{感|かん}じられるのだろう。
>
> ところで、この{町|まち}の{名前|なまえ}は「{白石|しろいし}」という。{昔|むかし}、{川|かわ}に{白|しろ}い{石|いし}が{多|おお}かったことから、この{名前|なまえ}がついたそうだ。{冬|ふゆ}には{町|まち}{全体|ぜんたい}が{白|しろ}くなるので、{今|いま}では{雪|ゆき}の{町|まち}にぴったりの{名前|なまえ}だと{思|おも}っている。

やね = roof; {体調|たいちょう}をくずす = to get ill (lesson 5 has {体調|たいちょう});
とける = to melt; いっせいに = all at once; ぴったり = just right; いっそう = all the more.

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What did the writer do when it snowed in Tokyo? — Went outside like a child and made snowmen.
2. Why couldn't the writer leave the house for three days in January? — Because of a snowstorm
   ({吹雪|ふぶき}のせいで): the roads couldn't be seen.
3. How did the writer get through the winter alone? — Thanks to neighbours who helped with the
   snow shovelling (おかげで).
4. Where does the town's name come from? — From the many white stones in the river long ago
   (〜ことから).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

It's three years since I moved to snow country. When I lived in Tokyo, I was so happy when it
snowed that I'd go outside like a child and make snowmen. Here, though, snow isn't a game. Some
days a metre falls in one night, so every morning starts with clearing snow.

This winter there was a lot of heavy snow. In January, a snowstorm meant you couldn't see the
road, and I couldn't leave the house for three days. Snow once fell off a roof and broke the
window of the house next door. Perhaps because of the cold, a lot of people got ill, too.

Even so, I love this town. Thanks to the neighbours helping me shovel snow, I managed to get
through the winter on my own. And spring, after the snow melts, is really beautiful. The snow
from the mountains runs into the rivers, and water goes into the rice fields. Grass and flowers
come up all at once. I suppose it's thanks to the long winter that spring feels all the more
welcome.

By the way, this town is called Shiroishi, "White Stone". Apparently it got the name because there
used to be lots of white stones in the river. In winter the whole town turns white, so these days
I think it's the perfect name for a snowy town.

</details>

## Pronunciation: は, は and は

{葉|は:0} (leaf) is flat: a particle after it stays high, {葉|は:0}が. {歯|は:1} (tooth, N5) falls
after its only mora, so a particle after it is low, {歯|は:1}が. The topic particle は has no accent of
its own. Say them with が after each and you'll hear the difference.

```speak
{雪|ゆき}のせいで、バスが{遅|おく}れました。
= The bus was late because of the snow.
{晴|は}れたおかげで、{山|やま}がよく{見|み}えました。
= Thanks to the clear weather, we could see the mountains well.
{強風|きょうふう}のため、{運転|うんてん}を{見合|みあ}わせております。
= Owing to strong winds, services are suspended.
{葉|は:0}が{落|お}ちる。
= Leaves fall.
{歯|は:1}が{痛|いた}い。
= My tooth hurts.
```

## Common mistakes

- A wish, plan or request after おかげで or せいで: ×{雨|あめ}のせいで、{明日|あした}{行|い}きましょう.
  They report results; use から or ので.
- せいで for a good result: ×{先生|せんせい}のせいで{合格|ごうかく}できました blames the teacher for
  your success. Use おかげで.
- Forgetting の or な: ×{台風|たいふう}せいで, ×{静|しず}かおかげで. A noun takes の
  ({台風|たいふう}のせいで), a な-adjective な ({静|しず}かなおかげで).
- Cause ため in everyday chat: {寒|さむ}いため、セーターを{着|き}た sounds like a report. To a friend,
  {寒|さむ}いから or {寒|さむ}かったので.
- 〜{結果|けっか} after a dictionary form: ×{調|しら}べる{結果|けっか}. Use the た form:
  {調|しら}べた{結果|けっか}.
- Writing {葉|は} for the particle は, or {吹|ふ}く for ふく "to wipe": they're different words that
  sound the same.

## Key points

- 〜おかげで: a cause with a good result (grateful); ironic with a bad one. N の / な / plain form.
- 〜せいで: a cause with a bad result (blame); 〜せいか: maybe because; 〜のせいにする: blame on.
- 〜ため(に) as "because": formal and written; past forms and states before it. Purpose ため takes
  the dictionary form of a chosen action.
- 〜ことから: reasoning from a fact, and how something got its name ({由来|ゆらい}).
- 〜た{結果|けっか} / N の{結果|けっか}: as a result of.
- おかげで, せいで, ことから and {結果|けっか} don't take a request, an invitation or a plan after
  them; から and ので do. In notices, ため can take a polite request (〜のため、ご{注意|ちゅうい}ください).
- New kanji: 雪 晴 吹 候 陽 草 葉 石 害 倒 流 落 煙. Write {雪|ゆき}, {晴|は}れる, {言葉|ことば},
  {面倒|めんどう}, {落|お}ちる, {落|お}とす with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: That's why, not that, no way: わけ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 6 gave causes: おかげで, せいで, ため. This lesson is about the conclusions you draw from
them. One small noun does most of the work: わけ, "reason, the way things add up". With it you
can say "so that's why", "it's not that…", "there's no way…" and "I can't (because it wouldn't be
right)".

「{田中|たなか}さんは{十年|じゅうねん}フランスに{住|す}んでいたんですよ。」「それでフランス{語|ご}が{上手|じょうず}なわけですね。」 — "Mr Tanaka lived in France for ten years." "So that's why his French is so good."
{高|たか}い{店|みせ}がいつもおいしいわけではない。 — It's not that expensive restaurants are always good.
こんな{値段|ねだん}で{新品|しんぴん}が{買|か}えるわけがない。 — There's no way you can buy a new one at this price.
{借|か}りたお{金|かね}だから、{返|かえ}さないわけにはいかない。 — It's borrowed money, so I can't not pay it back.

The theme is money in daily life: prices, household spending, banks, paying and saving. Several
words you know in kana now get kanji: {払|はら}う, {支払|しはら}う, {値段|ねだん}, {商品|しょうひん},
{経験|けいけん}, {資料|しりょう}.

わけ is a formal noun, so it's written in kana, like こと and ため. It joins like a noun:

| Before わけ | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, plain form | {行|い}く / {行|い}った / {行|い}かない わけ |
| い-adjective | {高|たか}い / {高|たか}かった わけ |
| な-adjective + な | {便利|べんり}な わけ |
| noun + な, or + という | {学生|がくせい}な わけ, {学生|がくせい}という わけ |

## So that's why / which means: 〜わけだ

〜わけだ has two closely related jobs.

1. You hear a fact and it explains something you'd noticed: "so that's why". It often follows
   それで or だから.

   「{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}に{大|おお}きいスーパーができたんだよ。」「だから{最近|さいきん}、{近所|きんじょ}の{店|みせ}にお{客|きゃく}さんが{少|すく}ないわけだ。」 — "A big supermarket's opened in front of the station." "So that's why the shops round here have had so few customers."
   {今月|こんげつ}は{四回|よんかい}も{外食|がいしょく}した。お{金|かね}が{足|た}りなくなるわけだ。 — I've eaten out four times this month. No wonder I'm short of money.

2. You work out a conclusion from what you know: "which means", "so it follows that".

   {一日|いちにち}{五百円|ごひゃくえん}ためれば、{一年|いちねん}で{十八万円|じゅうはちまんえん}{以上|いじょう}になるわけだ。 — If you save 500 yen a day, that comes to over 180,000 yen a year.
   {値段|ねだん}は{同|おな}じで{量|りょう}が{減|へ}ったのだから、{実際|じっさい}には{値上|ねあ}がりしたわけです。 — The price is the same but there's less in the pack, so in fact the price has gone up.

{外食|がいしょく} (eating out) is glossed here; {実際|じっさい} (in fact) is lesson 22's word.

〜というわけだ sums up a story: "so that's how it is".
{電車|でんしゃ}が{止|と}まって、タクシーに{乗|の}るしかなかった。それで{交通費|こうつうひ}が{三千円|さんぜんえん}もかかったというわけ。
(The trains stopped and I had to take a taxi. So that's how my fare came to 3,000 yen.) In casual
speech the sentence can end in わけ without だ. 〜しかなかった (had no choice but) is lesson 10's
grammar.

### わけだ and はずだ

N4's はずだ is an expectation ("it should be so"); わけだ is a conclusion or an explanation ("so it
is so"). Compare:

にもつは{昨日|きのう}{送|おく}ったから、{今日|きょう}{着|つ}くはずだ。 — I sent the parcel yesterday, so it should arrive today. (You don't know yet.)
{昨日|きのう}{送|おく}ったにもつがもう{着|つ}いた。{速達|そくたつ}だから{早|はや}いわけだ。 — The parcel I sent yesterday has already arrived. It went express; that's why it was so quick. (You're explaining a fact.)

For an expectation you can't check yet, as in the first sentence, use はずだ. はずだ also has a
"no wonder" use when you discover the reason for something: {寒|さむ}いはずだ。{窓|まど}が{開|あ}いている
(no wonder it's cold: the window's open). So in "so that's why" sentences you'll hear both;
わけだ is the more common choice when the reason comes from what someone has just told you.
{速達|そくたつ} (express post) is a gloss.

## It's not that…: 〜わけではない, 〜わけでもない

〜わけではない (casual: わけじゃない) denies a conclusion the listener might draw. It softens: "it's
not (exactly) that…".

お{金|かね}がないわけではないが、{高|たか}いものは{買|か}わないことにしている。 — It's not that I have no money; I just make a point of not buying expensive things.
「カード、{使|つか}わないの？」「きらいなわけじゃないけど、{現金|げんきん}のほうが{安心|あんしん}なんだ。」 — "Don't you use cards?" "It's not that I dislike them, but I feel safer with cash."

〜わけでもない adds "nor": the listener has guessed another reason, and you deny that too.

「{安|やす}かったから{買|か}ったの？」「{安|やす}かったわけでもないけど、{色|いろ}が{気|き}に{入|い}ったんだ。」 — "Did you buy it because it was cheap?" "It wasn't cheap either, really; I just liked the colour."

### Partial negation

With words for "all" or "always", わけではない gives **[[partial negation]]**: not all, not always. It
denies the whole, not each part.

| Sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {全部|ぜんぶ}{分|わ}かるわけではない。 | I don't understand all of it. (I understand some.) |
| {全部|ぜんぶ}は{分|わ}からない。 | the same: は after {全部|ぜんぶ} also makes it partial |
| {全然|ぜんぜん}{分|わ}からない。 | I don't understand any of it. (total) |
| {高|たか}いものがいつもいいわけではない。 | Expensive things aren't always good. (Sometimes they are.) |
| {日本人|にほんじん}がみんな{現金|げんきん}を{使|つか}うわけではない。 | Not every Japanese person uses cash. |

This is how you avoid overgeneralizing, which matters in essays and opinions (lesson 28). Lesson 8
adds 〜とは{限|かぎ}らない and {必|かなら}ずしも, which work in the same way.

## There's no way: 〜わけがない

〜わけがない (casual わけない) is a strong denial: "there's no way that…", "it can't possibly be".

{学生|がくせい}のアルバイト{代|だい}で、そんな{高|たか}い{車|くるま}が{買|か}えるわけがない。 — There's no way a student could buy such an expensive car on part-time wages.
「{明日|あした}までに{十万円|じゅうまんえん}{用意|ようい}できる？」「できるわけないよ！」 — "Can you get 100,000 yen together by tomorrow?" "No way!"

アルバイト{代|だい} (pay from a part-time job) is a gloss. Note: as an い-adjective, わけない
also means "easy" (そんなの、わけないよ: that's nothing, it's easy). Context tells them apart.

### わけがない and はずがない

N4's はずがない also means "it can't be". They often overlap:
{田中|たなか}さんが{約束|やくそく}を{忘|わす}れるはずがない / わけがない (Mr Tanaka would never forget a
promise). The differences:

- はずがない reasons from what you know or expect; わけがない sounds more emotional and more
  spoken.
- For your own will, use わけがない: あんな{高|たか}い{店|みせ}、{二度|にど}と{行|い}くわけがない (I'm
  never going to that pricey place again). With はずがない it would sound as if you were predicting
  your own behaviour from evidence, which most speakers find odd.
- For the positive, they part ways completely: はずだ is "should be" (expectation), わけだ is "so
  that's why / which means" (above).

## Can't (it wouldn't be right): 〜わけにはいかない

The potential ({行|い}けない) says you're unable. 〜わけにはいかない says you could, but you can't
allow yourself to, for social, moral or practical reasons. The verb before it is in the dictionary
form.

{明日|あした}は{大事|だいじ}な{会議|かいぎ}があるから、{休|やす}むわけにはいかない。 — I've got an important meeting tomorrow, so I can't take the day off.
{店|みせ}の{人|ひと}が{間違|まちが}えて、おつりを{多|おお}くくれた。もらうわけにはいかないので、{返|かえ}した。 — The shop assistant gave me too much change by mistake. I couldn't keep it, so I gave it back.

With the ない form, 〜ないわけにはいかない is "I can't not…", so "I have to", out of obligation:

{部長|ぶちょう}にさそわれたら、{行|い}かないわけにはいかない。 — If the department head invites you, you can't not go. (さそう = to invite)

Polite: 〜わけにはいきません. In conversation it's usually about yourself or your side. About
someone else you'd normally add how you know: {田中|たなか}さんは{休|やす}むわけにはいかないらしい (it seems
Mr Tanaka can't take the day off). Stories use it freely for their characters.

## For some reason: どういうわけか

どういうわけか (literally "by what reason?") is a set phrase: "for some reason (I can't explain)".

どういうわけか、{今月|こんげつ}はお{金|かね}が{余|あま}った。 — For some reason I had money left over this month.

And わけ on its own is "the reason": わけを{話|はな}す (explain why), いいわけ (an excuse, N4).

## Money words

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| prices | {値段|ねだん}, {値上|ねあ}げ / {値下|ねさ}げ (a shop raises or lowers it), {値上|ねあ}がり / {値下|ねさ}がり (it goes up or down), ぶっか (prices in general), {景気|けいき} (the economy, business) |
| spending | {費用|ひよう}, {生活費|せいかつひ}, {食費|しょくひ}, {光熱費|こうねつひ} (gas and electricity), {交通費|こうつうひ}, {会費|かいひ}, {家計|かけい}, {支出|ししゅつ}, {収入|しゅうにゅう}, {赤字|あかじ} / {黒字|くろじ} |
| paying | {支払|しはら}い, {払|はら}い{込|こ}む, ふりこむ (by bank transfer), {分割払|ぶんかつばら}い, {手数料|てすうりょう}, レシート, りょうしゅうしょ (receipt for expenses), せいきゅうしょ (bill, invoice), キャッシュレス, {電子|でんし}マネー, クレジットカード |
| banks and cash | {口座|こうざ}, {残高|ざんだか}, {引|ひ}き{出|だ}す, あんしょうばんごう (PIN), {現金|げんきん}, こぜに (coins), おさつ (notes), {借金|しゃっきん} |
| saving and wasting | ためる, せつやく, むだ, むだづかい, {使|つか}い{道|みち}, よさん, よゆう, {余|あま}る, {余計|よけい} |
| rich and poor | {財産|ざいさん}, {富|とみ}, {金持|かねも}ち, {貧|まず}しい, びんぼう, そん (a loss), もうかる (to make a profit), {資金|しきん} |
| shops and trade | {商店|しょうてん}, {商売|しょうばい}, {経済|けいざい}, {経済的|けいざいてき}, {個人|こじん}, 〜{個|こ}, ぜいきん, しょうひぜい, {消費|しょうひ}, わりかん |

Notes:

- {値上|ねあ}げ / {値下|ねさ}げ are what a seller does ({店|みせ}が{値下|ねさ}げした); {値上|ねあ}がり / {値下|ねさ}がり
  is what prices do by themselves ({野菜|やさい}が{値上|ねあ}がりした). It's the transitive and
  intransitive pattern of {上|あ}げる / {上|あ}がる.
- {経済的|けいざいてき} means both "economic" and "economical": {経済的|けいざいてき}な{車|くるま} is a car
  that's cheap to run.
- {個人|こじん} is "an individual": {個人|こじん}の{口座|こうざ} (a personal account).
- Many money words have kanji outside N3 and stay in kana: ぶっか, ぜいきん, せつやく, よさん, こぜに,
  おさつ, ためる, わりかん (splitting the bill). In print you'll see them with kanji.
- {現金|げんきん} (N4's げんきん) and {口座|こうざ} (N4's こうざ) are now written in kanji: their
  N3 kanji were taught in lessons 4 and 2.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji: paying and spending, wealth, and trade.

### Paying and spending

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 払 | pay | — | はら(う) | 5 | {払|はら}う, {支払|しはら}う, {支払|しはら}い, {払|はら}い{込|こ}む |
| 費 | cost, expense | ヒ | — | 12 | {費用|ひよう}, {交通費|こうつうひ}, {生活費|せいかつひ}, {消費|しょうひ} |
| 値 | price, value | チ | ね | 10 | {値段|ねだん}, {値上|ねあ}げ, {値下|ねさ}がり, {数値|すうち} (a figure) |
| 収 | take in, collect | シュウ | — | 4 | {収入|しゅうにゅう}, {収集|しゅうしゅう} (collection, lesson 9) |
| 余 | too much, left over | ヨ | あま(る) | 7 | {余|あま}る, {余計|よけい} |

- {払|はら}う and {支払|しはら}う (N4) are now written with kanji. 払's on'yomi is rare; learn it by
  its kun'yomi.
- 値 is ね in price words; チ in {数値|すうち}.

### Wealth

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 財 | wealth, property | ザイ | — | 10 | {財産|ざいさん} |
| 富 | rich, wealth | フ | と(む), とみ | 12 | {富|とみ} |
| 貧 | poor | ヒン | まず(しい) | 11 | {貧|まず}しい |
| 資 | resources, capital | シ | — | 13 | {資金|しきん}, {資料|しりょう}, {資格|しかく} (qualification, lesson 8) |

- 財, 貧 and 資 all contain the "shell" shape (an eye-like box on two legs): shells were once
  money, so it marks money words.
- {資料|しりょう} (N4's しりょう: documents, materials) can now be written with kanji.
- さいふ (wallet) has 財 too, but its second kanji isn't on the list: write it in kana.

### Trade and the economy

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 済 | settle, finish | サイ | す(む) | 11 | {経済|けいざい}, {済|す}む (lesson 8) |
| 経 | pass through; manage | ケイ | — | 11 | {経済|けいざい}, {経験|けいけん} |
| 商 | trade | ショウ | — | 11 | {商店|しょうてん}, {商売|しょうばい}, {商品|しょうひん} |
| 個 | individual; counter | コ | — | 10 | {個人|こじん}, 〜{個|こ} |

- {経験|けいけん} (N5) and {商品|しょうひん} (N4) can now be written with kanji. しょうてんがい keeps
  kana: its last kanji is outside N3.
- 〜{個|こ} counts small, separate things: {三個|さんこ} (three), {何個|なんこ} (how many). It's a
  common alternative to {三|みっ}つ, especially above ten.
- 済 changes to ザイ after ケイ: {経済|けいざい}.

Memory notes:

- 払 is a hand (the left part) pushing away a small thing (ム): paying it out.
- 費 has a twisting shape over the shell (money): money that slips away.
- 値 is a person (the left part) and 直 (straight, lesson 16): what a person straightforwardly
  pays, the price.
- 富 has a roof on top over a full storehouse: a rich house.
- 貧 is 分 (divide, N4) over the shell (money): money divided up until there's little left.
- 余 is a roof with too much under it: left over.
- 個 is a person beside a box with 古 (old, N5) inside: one solid, separate person, an
  individual.

```trace
払費値財富貧収資済経商個余
```

## Dialogue: this month's bills

Yūta and Saki share a flat. Yūta has just opened the electricity bill. (Casual speech.)

```dialogue
# The electricity bill
ゆうた: ねえ、{今月|こんげつ}の{電気代|でんきだい}、{見|み}た？{一万二千円|いちまんにせんえん}だって。
= Hey, did you see this month's electricity bill? It's 12,000 yen.
さき: えっ、そんなに？…あ、そうか。{毎晩|まいばん}エアコンをつけたまま{寝|ね}てたからね。
= What, that much? …Oh, I see. We slept with the air conditioner on every night.
ゆうた: それで{高|たか}いわけだ。
= So that's why it's so high.
さき: でも、{全部|ぜんぶ}エアコンのせいってわけでもないよ。{電気|でんき}の{料金|りょうきん}も{値上|ねあ}がりしてるらしいし。
= But it's not all down to the air conditioner, either. Apparently electricity prices have gone up too.
ゆうた: そっか。じゃあ、{今月|こんげつ}は{少|すこ}しせつやくしないとね。{外食|がいしょく}も{減|へ}らそうか。
= I see. Then we'd better economize a bit this month. Shall we eat out less too?
さき: うん。でも{金曜日|きんようび}の{飲|の}み{会|かい}は{行|い}かないわけにはいかないんだよね。{部長|ぶちょう}の{送別会|そうべつかい}だから。
= Yeah. But I can't not go to Friday's drinks. It's the department head's farewell party.
ゆうた: それは{行|い}かなきゃね。{会費|かいひ}はいくら？
= You've got to go to that. How much is it?
さき: {一人|ひとり}{五千円|ごせんえん}。
= Five thousand yen each.
ゆうた: {五千円|ごせんえん}か…。まあ、{毎週|まいしゅう}{行|い}くわけじゃないし、いいか。
= Five thousand… Well, it's not as if you go every week. Fine.
さき: それより、ゆうたが{毎朝|まいあさ}コンビニで{買|か}うコーヒー。{一杯|いっぱい}{二百円|にひゃくえん}でも、{一|いっ}か{月|げつ}で{六千円|ろくせんえん}だよ。
= What about the coffee you buy at the convenience store every morning? Even at 200 yen a cup, that's 6,000 a month.
ゆうた: え、そんなに？{毎日|まいにち}{二百円|にひゃくえん}なら、{三十日|さんじゅうにち}で{六千円|ろくせんえん}…ほんとだ。{一年|いちねん}で{七万円|ななまんえん}{以上|いじょう}{使|つか}ってるわけか。
= Really? 200 a day for thirty days is 6,000… You're right. So I'm spending over 70,000 a year.
さき: でしょ？うちでいれて{持|も}っていけばいいじゃない。
= See? Why not make it at home and take it with you?
ゆうた: でも、{朝|あさ}はそんな{時間|じかん}、あるわけないよ。
= But there's no way I've got time for that in the mornings.
さき: {十分|じゅっぷん}{早|はや}く{起|お}きればいいでしょ。
= Just get up ten minutes earlier.
```

{減|へ}らす = to cut down (transitive partner of N4's へる); {送別会|そうべつかい} = a farewell party;
{会費|かいひ} here is the fee for the party; いれる = to make (coffee or tea). Count the kinds of
わけ: an explanation ({高|たか}いわけだ), a partial denial (わけでもない, わけじゃない), an obligation
({行|い}かないわけにはいかない), a conclusion ({使|つか}ってるわけか), and an impossibility (あるわけない).

## Reading: a money advice column

A reader's question and the answer, from the money page of a magazine (です/ます style).

> 「{毎月|まいつき}、{給料日|きゅうりょうび}の{前|まえ}になるとお{金|かね}がなくなります。むだづかいをしているわけではないのですが…。どうすればいいでしょうか。」（{会社員|かいしゃいん}、{二十六歳|にじゅうろくさい}）
>
> むだづかいをしていないのにお{金|かね}が{足|た}りないということは、{何|なに}にいくら{使|つか}っているのか、{自分|じぶん}でも{分|わ}かっていないわけです。まず{一|いっ}か{月|げつ}、レシートを{全部|ぜんぶ}{取|と}っておいて、{支出|ししゅつ}を{書|か}き{出|だ}してみてください。{食費|しょくひ}、{交通費|こうつうひ}、{光熱費|こうねつひ}、スマホの{料金|りょうきん}…。{一回|いっかい}の{支払|しはら}いは{小|ちい}さくても、{合計|ごうけい}すると、{思|おも}ったより{大|おお}きな{数字|すうじ}になっているはずです。
>
> キャッシュレスは{便利|べんり}ですが、お{金|かね}を{使|つか}った{感覚|かんかく}が{少|すく}ないので、{気|き}をつけましょう。{現金|げんきん}がいいというわけではありません。アプリで{残高|ざんだか}をこまめに{確|たし}かめればいいのです。
>
> {次|つぎ}に、{給料|きゅうりょう}が{入|はい}ったら、すぐに{一万円|いちまんえん}でもいいので、{別|べつ}の{口座|こうざ}に{入|い}れてください。{残|のこ}ったお{金|かね}で{生活|せいかつ}すれば、{自然|しぜん}にお{金|かね}がたまるわけです。
>
> ただし、{全部|ぜんぶ}がまんする{必要|ひつよう}はありません。{楽|たの}しみにお{金|かね}を{使|つか}うのは{悪|わる}いことではないのですから。

こまめに = often and carefully; {感覚|かんかく} = the feeling (lesson 10's word); {数字|すうじ} =
figure (lesson 4).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What is the reader's problem? — Money runs out every month before payday, though they don't
   think they waste it.
2. According to the writer, why is the money running short? — The reader doesn't know what they
   spend how much on (〜わけです).
3. Does the writer say cash is better than cashless payment? — No: {現金|げんきん}がいいというわけではありません.
   Checking the balance often in the app is enough.
4. What should the reader do on payday? — Put some money, even 10,000 yen, into a separate
   account straight away.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"Every month, just before payday, my money runs out. It's not that I'm wasting it… What should I
do?" (Office worker, 26)

If you're not wasting money and still don't have enough, it means that even you don't know what
you're spending how much on. First, for one month, keep every receipt and try writing out what
you spend. Food, travel, gas and electricity, your phone… Each payment may be small, but when you
add them up, I expect they come to a bigger figure than you thought.

Cashless payment is convenient, but you don't feel you're spending money, so be careful. That
isn't to say cash is better. You just need to check your balance in the app regularly.

Next, as soon as your salary comes in, put some of it, even 10,000 yen, into a separate account.
If you live on what's left, you'll find the money builds up by itself.

But you don't need to give up everything. Spending money on things you enjoy isn't a bad thing,
after all.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
それで{高|たか}いわけですね。
= So that's why it's expensive.
{全部|ぜんぶ}{分|わ}かるわけではありません。
= It's not that I understand all of it.
そんなこと、できるわけがないよ。
= There's no way I can do that.
{明日|あした}は{休|やす}むわけにはいきません。
= I can't take tomorrow off.
どういうわけか、{今月|こんげつ}はお{金|かね}が{余|あま}りました。
= For some reason I had money left over this month.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{学生|がくせい}のわけだ for "so he's a student". わけ after a noun takes な or という:
  {学生|がくせい}なわけだ, {学生|がくせい}というわけだ. ({学生|がくせい}のわけ would be "the student's
  reason".)
- Mixing up わけではない and わけがない. わけではない softens ("it's not that…"); わけがない denies
  strongly ("no way").
- Using 〜わけにはいかない for inability: ×{足|あし}が{痛|いた}くて、{歩|ある}くわけにはいかない.
  If you physically can't, use the potential: {歩|ある}けない.
- ×{行|い}かないわけにはいかないだ, ×{行|い}くわけにはいかないです for a plain or polite end. The
  endings are 〜わけにはいかない (plain) and 〜わけにはいきません (polite).
- わけだ for a plain expectation. "It should be fine tomorrow (I expect so)" is
  {明日|あした}は{晴|は}れるはずだ; {晴|は}れるわけだ presents it as a conclusion you've just worked out.
- {値上|ねあ}げ and {値上|ねあ}がり: a shop does {値上|ねあ}げ; prices do {値上|ねあ}がり.

## Key points

- わけ is a formal noun in kana; it joins like a noun (な or という after a noun).
- 〜わけだ: so that's why (an explanation); which means (a conclusion). はずだ is mainly an
  expectation (it should be so).
- 〜というわけだ: so that's how it is (summing up).
- 〜わけではない / 〜わけでもない: it's not that…; with {全部|ぜんぶ}, いつも, みんな it's partial
  negation (not all, not always).
- 〜わけがない (casual わけない): no way; more emotional than はずがない, and the one for your own
  refusal.
- 〜わけにはいかない: can't, for social or moral reasons; 〜ないわけにはいかない: have to.
- どういうわけか: for some reason.
- New kanji: 払 費 値 財 富 貧 収 資 済 経 商 個 余. Write {払|はら}う, {支払|しはら}う, {値段|ねだん},
  {商品|しょうひん}, {経験|けいけん}, {資料|しりょう} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: No need and not necessarily: ことはない, とはかぎらない, てすむ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 7 ended with partial negation, 〜わけではない: "it's not that…". This lesson adds more ways
to soften and limit what you say, and to reassure people: "there's no need", "not necessarily",
"I could, I suppose", "it only took…".

{心配|しんぱい}することはありませんよ。 — There's no need to worry.
{高|たか}いものがいいものだとは{限|かぎ}らない。 — Expensive things aren't necessarily good.
{行|い}けないことはないけど、ちょっと{遠|とお}いね。 — I could go, I suppose, but it's a bit far.
ネットで{申|もう}し{込|こ}めたので、{窓口|まどぐち}に{行|い}かないで{済|す}んだ。 — I could apply online, so I didn't have to go to the counter.

You'll need these exactly where Japan is most formal: forms, deadlines, documents and the people
at the counter who process them. The theme is applications and procedures: signing up, documents
and ID, confirming, deadlines and online forms. (The city office words, such as
{転入|てんにゅう} and {生年月日|せいねんがっぴ}, are N4's.)

## There's no need: 〜ことはない

The dictionary form + ことはない says there's no need to do something, usually to reassure someone
or to tell them not to bother.

{心配|しんぱい}することはないよ。{書類|しょるい}は{来週|らいしゅう}{出|だ}してもだいじょうぶだって。 — There's no need to worry. They said the documents can go in next week.
わざわざ{市役所|しやくしょ}に{行|い}くことはありません。この{手続|てつづ}きはネットでできます。 — You don't need to go all the way to the city office. You can do this procedure online.
そんなに{急|いそ}ぐことはないですよ。{期限|きげん}はまだ{先|さき}ですから。 — There's no need to rush. The deadline's still a while off.

- Compare N4's 〜なくてもいい (you don't have to). ことはない adds "there's no reason to, so don't
  worry". The formal, neutral version is 〜{必要|ひつよう}はない / 〜{必要|ひつよう}はありません, which
  is safer with someone above you and in notices: {写真|しゃしん}を{用意|ようい}する{必要|ひつよう}はありません.
- Don't confuse it with the た form + ことはない, "have never" (N5): {申|もう}し{込|こ}んだことはない is
  "I've never applied". With the dictionary form it's "no need": {申|もう}し{込|こ}むことはない.

## I could, I suppose: 〜ないことはない, 〜ないこともない

Two negatives make a weak, hesitant positive: "it's not that it isn't…", so "it's possible, but…".
It's a polite way to agree without enthusiasm.

「{今日中|きょうじゅう}に{出|だ}せますか。」「{出|だ}せないことはないですが、ちょっと{急|いそ}がないと…。」 — "Can you hand it in today?" "It's not impossible, but I'd have to hurry…"
この{料理|りょうり}、{食|た}べられないこともないけど、{少|すこ}しからいね。 — I can eat this, I suppose, but it's a bit spicy.
「この{書|か}き{方|かた}で{分|わ}かる？」「{分|わ}からないことはないけど、もう{少|すこ}し{短|みじか}いほうがいいかな。」 — "Does this wording make sense?" "It's not that it doesn't, but it'd be better a bit shorter."

ないこともない is a little softer than ないことはない. Both usually go on with けど or が and a
"but".

## Not necessarily: 〜とは{限|かぎ}らない, {必|かなら}ずしも

〜とは{限|かぎ}らない (literally "it isn't limited to being…") is "not necessarily, not always". It
follows the plain form; after a noun or な-adjective, だ is optional.

{安|やす}い{店|みせ}がいつも{安|やす}いとは{限|かぎ}らない。 — A cheap shop isn't always cheap.
{日本人|にほんじん}だからといって、けいごが{上手|じょうず}だとは{限|かぎ}らない。 — Being Japanese doesn't necessarily make you good at keigo.
{申|もう}し{込|こ}んでも、{必|かなら}ず{入|はい}れるとは{限|かぎ}りません。{定員|ていいん}より{多|おお}ければ、ちゅうせんになります。 — Applying doesn't guarantee you a place. If there are more applicants than places, there'll be a draw.

〜だからといって (just because…) and ちゅうせん (a draw, a lottery) are glosses.

{必|かなら}ずしも (N5's かならず + しも) adds "necessarily" and needs a negative later in the sentence:
〜とは{限|かぎ}らない, 〜わけではない, or a plain 〜ない.

{高|たか}い{薬|くすり}が{必|かなら}ずしもよくきくわけではない。 — Expensive medicine doesn't necessarily work better. (きく = to work, of medicine)
{必|かなら}ずしも{全部|ぜんぶ}{書|か}く{必要|ひつよう}はない。 — You don't necessarily have to fill it all in.

Like わけではない, these are partial negation: they deny "always" or "all", not the whole idea.

## Not particularly: {別|べつ}に〜ない (review)

{別|べつ}に (N4) + a negative is "not particularly": {別|べつ}に{問題|もんだい}はありません (there's no
particular problem). As a one-word answer, {別|べつ}に。 can sound cold, "not really, whatever"; add
something: {別|べつ}に、だいじょうぶです.

## It only took…: 〜て{済|す}む, 〜ないで{済|す}む, 〜ずに{済|す}む

{済|す}む is "to be settled, to be over". After a て form it means a matter was settled with less
than you feared: "it only took…", "I got away with…".

{電話|でんわ}{一本|いっぽん}で{済|す}みました。 — It only took one phone call.
{書類|しょるい}に{不備|ふび}がなかったので、{一回|いっかい}{行|い}くだけで{済|す}んだ。 — The documents had nothing missing, so one visit was enough.
{五千円|ごせんえん}で{済|す}んでよかった。 — I'm glad it only cost 5,000 yen.

With a negative, it's what you were spared: "didn't have to after all".

ネットで{予約|よやく}したので、ならばないで{済|す}んだ。 — I'd booked online, so I didn't have to queue.
{早|はや}めに{確認|かくにん}したおかげで、{書|か}き{直|なお}さずに{済|す}んだ。 — Thanks to checking early, I didn't have to rewrite it.

〜ずに is a written-style 〜ないで: {書|か}き{直|なお}さないで = {書|か}き{直|なお}さずに. Lesson 10 teaches
it properly. {不備|ふび} is something missing or wrong in a form; ならぶ (to queue, N4) is in kana
because its kanji is outside the list.

The transitive partner is {済|す}ませる (to get something done): {手続|てつづ}きを{済|す}ませてから
{入|はい}ってください (please go in after you've finished the procedure). And すむ "to live" (N5) is a
different word: same sound, different kanji in print.

## I did, but…: 〜ことは〜が / 〜けど

Say the verb (or adjective) twice, joined by ことは, and add が or けど: "I did…, but". It admits
something and then limits it.

{申|もう}し{込|こ}んだことは{申|もう}し{込|こ}んだけど、まだ{返事|へんじ}が{来|こ}ない。 — I did apply, but I haven't heard back yet.
{高|たか}いことは{高|たか}いが、それだけのことはある。 — It is expensive, but it's worth it.
{読|よ}めることは{読|よ}めるんですが、{意味|いみ}がよく{分|わ}かりません。 — I can read it, all right, but I don't really understand it.

The two halves use the same word, and the first is the plain form.

## You don't have to: 〜なくてもいい (review)

N4's 〜なくてもいい / 〜なくてもかまわない is the neutral "you don't have to". Choose by what you
want to add:

| Pattern | Says | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜なくてもいい | not required | {写真|しゃしん}は{出|だ}さなくてもいいです |
| 〜ことはない | no need, don't worry | {心配|しんぱい}することはない |
| 〜{必要|ひつよう}はない | not required (formal, notices) | はんこを{持|も}ってくる{必要|ひつよう}はありません |
| 〜ないことはない | possible, but reluctant | {行|い}けないことはない |
| 〜とは{限|かぎ}らない | not necessarily | {必|かなら}ず{通|とお}るとは{限|かぎ}らない |
| 〜て{済|す}む / 〜ないで{済|す}む | only took / spared | {電話|でんわ}で{済|す}んだ, ならばないで{済|す}んだ |

## Forms and procedures

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| applying | {申|もう}し{込|こ}む, {申|もう}し{込|こ}み (N4), {申込書|もうしこみしょ}, しんせい (to the authorities), {受|う}け{付|つ}ける, {申|もう}し{出|で}る, おうぼ (for a job or a prize), {求人|きゅうじん}, {資格|しかく}, じょうけん |
| filling in | {記入|きにゅう}する (N4), らん (a box on a form), しめい (full name), ねんれい, こくせき, れんらくさき, {日付|ひづけ}, {記号|きごう}, ていせい (correcting), {不備|ふび} |
| ID and documents | {本人確認|ほんにんかくにん}, みぶんしょうめいしょ, {在留|ざいりゅう}カード, パスワード, {正式|せいしき}, {送付|そうふ}, ていしゅつ, {再発行|さいはっこう} |
| deadlines and limits | {期限|きげん}, {期限切|きげんぎ}れ, えんちょう, {限度|げんど}, {限定|げんてい}, {限|かぎ}る, {限|かぎ}り, {事前|じぜん} |
| checking and deciding | {確認|かくにん}する, チェックする, {確実|かくじつ}, {正確|せいかく}, {確定|かくてい}, {決定|けってい}, きょか, {認|みと}める, {同意|どうい}する, ちゅうせん, ゆうこう |
| being a member | {会員|かいいん}, {入会|にゅうかい}, {退会|たいかい}, とうろく, キャンセル, じゅんばん |
| need and importance | {要|い}る, {不要|ふよう}, {要点|ようてん}, {要求|ようきゅう}, {求|もと}める, {重要|じゅうよう}, {主要|しゅよう}, {困難|こんなん}, {必|かなら}ずしも, {済|す}む, {済|す}ませる |

Notes:

- {要|い}る (to need) is a group 1 verb that looks like group 2: {要|い}らない, {要|い}ります. It isn't
  いる "to be" (group 2): {要|い}りますか (is it needed?) vs いますか (is anyone there?). It's mostly
  spoken; notices say {必要|ひつよう}です / {不要|ふよう}です.
- {限|かぎ}る is also group 1: {限|かぎ}らない, {限|かぎ}ります. {限|かぎ}り is "as long as, as far as":
  {時間|じかん}の{許|ゆる}す{限|かぎ}り (as long as time allows).
- {正確|せいかく} (accurate, exact) and lesson 16's {性格|せいかく} (personality) sound the same.
- {資格|しかく} is a qualification or eligibility: {申|もう}し{込|こ}む{資格|しかく}がある (be eligible
  to apply).
- Many form words have off-list kanji and stay in kana here: しんせい, きょか, ていしゅつ, とうろく,
  しめい, らん, ゆうこう (valid). Forms in Japan print them in kanji, so learn to recognize
  them by their shapes as you meet them.

A typical form looks like this:

| らん | {記入例|きにゅうれい} (example) |
|---|---|
| しめい (フリガナ) | {山田|やまだ}{花子|はなこ} (ヤマダ ハナコ) |
| {生年月日|せいねんがっぴ} | 2001{年|ねん}4{月|がつ}10{日|か} |
| {住所|じゅうしょ} | {東京都|とうきょうと}… |
| れんらくさき | 090-XXXX-XXXX |
| ごきぼうのコース (the course you want) | □ {午前|ごぜん} □ {午後|ごご} ({当|あ}てはまるものにチェック: tick the one that applies) |

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for applying, checking and needing. Several of them let you write N5 and N4 words
in kanji at last: {申|もう}し{込|こ}み, {記入|きにゅう}する, {日記|にっき}, {記事|きじ}, {番号|ばんごう},
{信号|しんごう}, {必要|ひつよう}, {必|かなら}ず, {確|たし}か, {確|たし}かめる, {予定|よてい}, {定員|ていいん},
{困|こま}る, {許|ゆる}す.

### Applying and allowing

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 申 | say (humble); apply | シン | もう(す) | 5 | {申|もう}し{込|こ}む, {申込書|もうしこみしょ}, {申|もう}し{出|で}る |
| 込 | go into; be crowded | — | こ(む), こ(める) | 5 | {申|もう}し{込|こ}む, {払|はら}い{込|こ}む |
| 許 | permit | キョ | ゆる(す) | 11 | {許|ゆる}す |
| 認 | recognize, admit | ニン | みと(める) | 14 | {認|みと}める, {確認|かくにん} |
| 求 | request, seek | キュウ | もと(める) | 7 | {求|もと}める, {要求|ようきゅう}, {求人|きゅうじん} |

- 申 is the kanji of the humble verb もうす (N4), but this course keeps もうす and もうします in
  kana, as N4 did, like the other keigo verbs. In {申|もう}し{込|こ}む the kanji is always written.
- 込 is a kanji made in Japan, with no on'yomi. Its verb こむ is "to go in" in compounds and "to be
  crowded" on its own ({電車|でんしゃ}が{込|こ}む is also written with another kanji in print).
- {許|ゆる}す (N4's ゆるす) can now be written with kanji. Its common compound きょか (permission)
  needs a kanji outside N3, so it stays in kana.

### Sure and fixed

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 確 | certain | カク | たし(か), たし(かめる) | 15 | {確認|かくにん}, {確|たし}か, {確|たし}かめる, {確実|かくじつ}, {正確|せいかく} |
| 定 | fix, decide | テイ | さだ(める) | 8 | {予定|よてい}, {決定|けってい}, {定員|ていいん}, {限定|げんてい} |
| 記 | write down | キ | しる(す) | 10 | {記入|きにゅう}, {記号|きごう}, {日記|にっき}, {記事|きじ} |
| 号 | number; sign | ゴウ | — | 5 | {番号|ばんごう}, {記号|きごう}, {信号|しんごう} |

- {確|たし}か (N4: "if I remember rightly") and {確|たし}かめる (N4: to make sure) share the kun'yomi
  たし. 確 is カク in compounds.
- 定 is テイ in most words; さだめる (to lay down, as a rule) is mostly written.
- 号 is the "number" of {番号|ばんごう} and {信号|しんごう} (traffic light): N5 words you can now
  write in kanji.

### Need and limits

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 要 | need; main point | ヨウ | い(る) | 9 | {必要|ひつよう}, {重要|じゅうよう}, {要|い}る, {不要|ふよう}, {要点|ようてん} |
| 必 | certainly, must | ヒツ | かなら(ず) | 5 | {必要|ひつよう}, {必|かなら}ず, {必|かなら}ずしも |
| 限 | limit | ゲン | かぎ(る) | 9 | {限|かぎ}る, {限度|げんど}, {期限|きげん}, {限定|げんてい} |
| 困 | be troubled | コン | こま(る) | 7 | {困|こま}る, {困難|こんなん} |

- {必要|ひつよう} (N4), {必|かなら}ず (N5) and {困|こま}る (N5) are now written with kanji.
- 必 is ヒツ before よう; in {必|かなら}ず it's read with its kun'yomi.

Memory notes:

- 申 is a box with a line straight through it: words that go straight through, said out loud.
- 込 is 入 (enter) on the "moving" shape that runs along the bottom: moving in.
- 許 is 言 (words, N4) beside 午 (noon, N5): someone at noon saying "go ahead".
- 認 is 言 (words) beside a heart under a blade: words you accept even though they hurt, to admit.
- 確 starts with 石 (stone, lesson 6): as sure as stone.
- 定 is a roof over a foot that has stopped: something settled in place.
- 記 is 言 (words) and a shape like a coiled string: words tied down, written.
- 必 is 心 (heart) with a stroke cutting through it: something that cuts to the heart, a must.
- 困 is 木 (tree) shut in a box: a tree with no room to grow, in trouble.
- 限 has the hill shape on the left: a hill where you have to stop, a limit.

```trace
申込許認確定記号要必求限困
```

## Dialogue: joining the city pool

Lin, who lives in Japan, wants to join the pool at the city sports centre. Mr Mori is at the
reception desk. (Polite speech; the staff member uses a little keigo.)

```dialogue
# At the sports centre
リン: すみません、プールの{会員|かいいん}になりたいんですが、{申|もう}し{込|こ}みはこちらでいいですか。
= Excuse me, I'd like to become a member of the pool. Do I apply here?
もり: はい、こちらで{受|う}け{付|つ}けております。この{申込書|もうしこみしょ}にご{記入|きにゅう}ください。
= Yes, we take applications here. Please fill in this form.
リン: {名前|なまえ}はローマ{字|じ}でもいいですか。
= Can I write my name in the Roman alphabet?
もり: はい。ただ、カタカナの{読|よ}み{方|かた}も{書|か}いてください。それから、{本人確認|ほんにんかくにん}のため、{在留|ざいりゅう}カードを{見|み}せていただけますか。
= Yes. But please write how it's read in katakana too. And to confirm your identity, could I see your residence card?
リン: はい、どうぞ。あ、{先月|せんげつ}{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}したばかりなんですが、{住所|じゅうしょ}はだいじょうぶでしょうか。
= Here you are. Oh, I only moved last month. Will the address be OK?
もり: カードのうらに{新|あたら}しい{住所|じゅうしょ}が{書|か}いてあれば、{問題|もんだい}ありません。…はい、{確認|かくにん}できました。
= If the new address is written on the back of the card, there's no problem. …Yes, that's confirmed.
リン: よかった。{写真|しゃしん}も{要|い}りますか。
= Good. Do you need a photo too?
もり: いいえ、{写真|しゃしん}を{用意|ようい}していただく{必要|ひつよう}はありません。こちらでとりますので。
= No, there's no need to bring a photo. We'll take one here.
リン: {会費|かいひ}は{毎月|まいつき}ここで{払|はら}うんですか。
= Do I pay the fee here every month?
もり: {月|つき}の{会費|かいひ}は、{口座|こうざ}からの{引|ひ}き{落|お}としになります。{現金|げんきん}で{払|はら}えないこともないんですが、{毎月|まいつき}{窓口|まどぐち}に{来|こ}ないといけないので…。
= The monthly fee is taken from your bank account. You could pay in cash, I suppose, but then you'd have to come to the counter every month…
リン: じゃあ、{口座|こうざ}にします。いつから{使|つか}えますか。
= Then I'll use my account. When can I start?
もり: {明日|あした}から{使|つか}えます。ただ、{初|はじ}めての{方|かた}は{説明会|せつめいかい}に{出|で}ていただくことになっています。
= From tomorrow. But first-time members are required to attend an information session.
リン: {説明会|せつめいかい}って、{水着|みずぎ}も{持|も}ってこないといけませんか。
= For the session, do I need to bring a swimsuit too?
もり: いえ、{水着|みずぎ}を{持|も}ってくることはありませんよ。{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}ぐらい{話|はなし}を{聞|き}くだけですから。
= No, there's no need to bring a swimsuit. You just listen to a talk for about thirty minutes.
リン: そうですか。それなら{一回|いっかい}で{済|す}みますね。
= I see. Then it'll only take one visit.
```

{受|う}け{付|つ}けております is the polite form of {受|う}け{付|つ}けています (〜ております: lesson 24);
{引|ひ}き{落|お}とし = an automatic debit; {説明会|せつめいかい} = an information session; うら = the
back. The staff member uses {必要|ひつよう}はありません to a customer and ことはありません once the talk is
friendlier.

## Reading: a library notice

A notice from a city library's website (です/ます style, as notices are).

> {市立図書館|しりつとしょかん}：{利用|りよう}カードの{申|もう}し{込|こ}みについて
>
> {図書館|としょかん}で{本|ほん}を{借|か}りるには、{利用|りよう}カードが{必要|ひつよう}です。{市内|しない}に{住|す}んでいる{方|かた}、または{市内|しない}の{会社|かいしゃ}や{学校|がっこう}に{通|かよ}っている{方|かた}なら、どなたでも{申|もう}し{込|こ}めます。
>
> {申|もう}し{込|こ}みは、{一階|いっかい}の{受付|うけつけ}で{受|う}け{付|つ}けています。{申込書|もうしこみしょ}に{名前|なまえ}、{住所|じゅうしょ}、{電話番号|でんわばんごう}を{記入|きにゅう}し、{住所|じゅうしょ}の{確認|かくにん}できるもの（{在留|ざいりゅう}カード、マイナンバーカードなど）を{見|み}せてください。{写真|しゃしん}を{用意|ようい}する{必要|ひつよう}はありません。
>
> ホームページから{事前|じぜん}に{申|もう}し{込|こ}むこともできます。その{場合|ばあい}も、カードを{受|う}け{取|と}るときに{一度|いちど}{受付|うけつけ}に{来|き}ていただきますが、{申込書|もうしこみしょ}を{書|か}かずに{済|す}みます。
>
> カードはゆうこうきげんが{三年|さんねん}です。{期限|きげん}が{切|き}れても、カードを{新|あたら}しく{作|つく}ることはありません。{受付|うけつけ}で{住所|じゅうしょ}を{確認|かくにん}すれば、そのまま{使|つか}えます。カードをなくした{場合|ばあい}は、すぐに{受付|うけつけ}にお{知|し}らせください。{再発行|さいはっこう}には{二百円|にひゃくえん}かかります。
>
> また、{本|ほん}の{予約|よやく}はネットでもできますが、{予約|よやく}してもすぐに{借|か}りられるとは{限|かぎ}りません。{人気|にんき}のある{本|ほん}は、{数|すう}か{月|げつ}{待|ま}つこともあります。

{市立|しりつ} = city-run; {利用|りよう} = use (lesson 28's word); {市内|しない} = in the city; {期限|きげん}が
{切|き}れる = to expire; {数|すう}か{月|げつ} = several months.

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. Who can get a card? — Anyone who lives in the city, or who works or studies there.
2. Do you need a photo? — No: {写真|しゃしん}を{用意|ようい}する{必要|ひつよう}はありません.
3. What's the advantage of applying online first? — You don't have to fill in the paper form
   ({書|か}かずに{済|す}みます), though you still go to the desk once to collect the card.
4. If you reserve a popular book, can you borrow it straight away? — Not necessarily: it can take
   several months (すぐに{借|か}りられるとは{限|かぎ}りません).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

City library: applying for a library card

To borrow books from the library, you need a library card. Anyone who lives in the city, or who
goes to a company or school in the city, can apply.

Applications are taken at the reception desk on the ground floor. Fill in your name, address and
phone number on the application form and show something that confirms your address (a residence
card, a My Number card, etc.). There's no need to bring a photo.

You can also apply in advance on our website. In that case you'll still need to come to the desk
once to collect your card, but you won't have to fill in the form.

The card is valid for three years. Even when it expires, you don't need to have a new one made: if
we confirm your address at the desk, you can keep using it. If you lose your card, please tell the
desk at once. A replacement costs 200 yen.

You can also reserve books online, but reserving a book doesn't necessarily mean you can borrow it
straight away. For popular books you may have to wait several months.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{心配|しんぱい}することはありませんよ。
= There's no need to worry.
{行|い}けないことはないですけど…。
= I could go, I suppose, but…
{高|たか}ければいいとは{限|かぎ}りません。
= Expensive doesn't necessarily mean good.
{電話|でんわ}で{済|す}みました。
= A phone call was enough.
{申|もう}し{込|こ}んだことは{申|もう}し{込|こ}んだんですが…。
= I did apply, but…
```

## Common mistakes

- The た form for "no need": ×{心配|しんぱい}したことはない means "I've never worried". Use the
  dictionary form: {心配|しんぱい}することはない.
- {必|かなら}ずしも without a negative: ×{必|かなら}ずしもいい. It needs 〜とは{限|かぎ}らない,
  〜わけではない or 〜ない later in the sentence.
- Answering a request with 〜ないことはない when you mean a clear yes: it sounds reluctant. If you're
  happy to, say はい、できます.
- ×{限|かぎ}れない, ×{要|い}れない: {限|かぎ}る and {要|い}る are group 1 verbs: {限|かぎ}らない,
  {要|い}らない.
- 〜て{済|す}む with a long or bad outcome: it's for "it only took / it was only…". ×{三時間|さんじかん}も
  {待|ま}って{済|す}んだ contradicts itself (も stresses that it was a lot).
- Writing {済|す}む for すむ "to live": {東京|とうきょう}に{住|す}む, not ×{済|す}む.

## Key points

- Dictionary form + ことはない: there's no need (reassuring). Formal: 〜{必要|ひつよう}はない.
- 〜ないことはない / 〜ないこともない: it's possible, I suppose (hesitant yes).
- 〜とは{限|かぎ}らない: not necessarily; {必|かなら}ずしも〜ない adds "necessarily". Like
  わけではない, these are partial negation.
- 〜て{済|す}む: it only took…; 〜ないで{済|す}む / 〜ずに{済|す}む: didn't have to after all.
- A ことは A が / けど: I do A, but…
- {要|い}る and {限|かぎ}る are group 1 verbs.
- New kanji: 申 込 許 認 確 定 記 号 要 必 求 限 困. Write {申|もう}し{込|こ}み, {記入|きにゅう},
  {番号|ばんごう}, {必要|ひつよう}, {必|かなら}ず, {確|たし}か, {予定|よてい}, {困|こま}る, {許|ゆる}す with kanji
  from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Should and the way things are: べきだ, ものだ, ことだ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 6 to 8 gave reasons and conclusions. This lesson is about judgements: what people should
do, what's expected, and what's simply the way things are. Endings like these, which show the
speaker's attitude to what they're saying (sure, unsure, approving, obliged), are called
**[[modality]]**. You've used several since N5: 〜でしょう, 〜なければならない, 〜たほうがいい, 〜はずだ.
N3 adds three that are about right and wrong:

{電車|でんしゃ}では、お{年寄|としよ}りに{席|せき}をゆずるべきだ。 — On trains you should give up your seat to elderly people.
{人|ひと}の{話|はなし}は{最後|さいご}まで{聞|き}くものだ。 — You're supposed to hear people out to the end.
{日本語|にほんご}が{上手|じょうず}になりたければ、たくさん{話|はな}すことだ。 — If you want to get good at Japanese, the thing to do is speak a lot.

The theme is manners and public behaviour: trains, phones, rubbish, queues and noise, what's
polite and what's rude. Several N5 and N4 words can now be written with kanji: {守|まも}る,
{違|ちが}う, {間違|まちが}える, {静|しず}か, {恥|は}ずかしい, {失礼|しつれい}, お{礼|れい}, {迷|まよ}う,
{留守|るす}.

## Should: 〜べきだ

べき follows the dictionary form of a verb. It gives the speaker's judgement of what's right:
"should, ought to".

| Verb | べき form |
|---|---|
| {守|まも}る | {守|まも}るべきだ |
| {話|はな}す | {話|はな}すべきだ |
| する | するべきだ, or すべきだ (more formal) |
| {来|く}る | {来|く}るべきだ |
| noun / な-adjective | 〜であるべきだ: {静|しず}かであるべきだ (should be quiet) |

{約束|やくそく}は{守|まも}るべきだ。 — Promises should be kept.
{悪|わる}いことをしたら、すぐにあやまるべきです。 — If you've done something wrong, you should apologize at once.
もっと{早|はや}く{相談|そうだん}すべきだった。 — I should have asked for advice sooner.

- The negative is べきではない (casual べきじゃない): {電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}で{大声|おおごえ}で{話|はな}す
  べきではない. You can't put ない before べき: ×{話|はな}さないべきだ.
- Past: べきだった (should have: regret or criticism), べきではなかった (shouldn't have).
- Before a noun, べき + noun is "that should be…": {今|いま}するべきこと (what needs doing now).

べき is strong. Said to someone's face, especially someone above you, it sounds like a lecture:
×{部長|ぶちょう}、{休|やす}むべきですよ. To advise a person, use 〜たほうがいい, or something softer
still: {少|すこ}し{休|やす}んだほうがいいかもしれませんね. べき is at home in opinions, essays and
statements about people in general.

べき is about what's right, not what's required. For a rule or a law, use N4's 〜なければならない:

{電車|でんしゃ}に{乗|の}るには、きっぷを{買|か}わなければならない。 — To get on a train, you have to buy a ticket. (a rule)
{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}では、まわりの{人|ひと}のことを{考|かんが}えるべきだ。 — On the train you should think about the people around you. (a judgement)

## That's how it is, that's what you do: 〜ものだ
