もの here is the abstract "thing" (so it's in kana), and 〜ものだ presents something as the
natural way of the world. It follows the plain form (な-adjective + な). It has three uses.

### 1. General truths

{人|ひと}は{変|か}わるものだ。 — People change. (That's how people are.)
{子供|こども}は{泣|な}くものです。 — Children cry. (It's what children do; don't worry.)
{時間|じかん}がたつのは{早|はや}いものですね。 — Doesn't time fly.

The last one is a common feeling-filled use: "how…!" about something that's always true.

### 2. What's expected: social norms

Said about behaviour, ものだ is "you're supposed to, it's what one does", and ものではない is "you
just don't". It sounds like a parent or an elder: the voice of common sense.

{目上|めうえ}の{人|ひと}には、けいごを{使|つか}うものだ。 — You use keigo with your superiors.
{人|ひと}の{悪口|わるぐち}を{言|い}うものではない。 — You shouldn't speak ill of people.
{食|た}べながら{歩|ある}くものじゃないよ。 — You don't eat while walking. (casual: ものじゃない)

べき and ものだ often overlap. べき is the speaker's own judgement ("I think it's right");
ものだ presents a rule everyone is supposed to know ("that's just how it is").

### 3. 〜たものだ: used to (looking back)

With the た form, ものだ remembers something you often did in the past, with feeling:

{子供|こども}のころは、よくこの{川|かわ}で{泳|およ}いだものだ。 — When I was a child, I used to swim in this river a lot.
{学生|がくせい}のときは、{朝|あさ}まで{友|とも}だちと{話|はな}したものです。 — When I was a student, we'd talk until morning.

It's for repeated actions over a period, not a single event: ×{去年|きょねん}、{一度|いちど}{京都|きょうと}に
{行|い}ったものだ.

In casual speech, もの often shortens to もん: そういうもんだよ (that's how it goes).

## The thing to do: 〜ことだ

〜ことだ gives advice: "the best thing is to…, you should…". It follows the dictionary form or the
ない form. It's usually said by someone older or more experienced, to people in general or to a
junior, and is common in advice columns.

かぜを{早|はや}く{治|なお}したければ、よく{寝|ね}ることだ。 — If you want to get over a cold quickly, the thing to do is sleep well.
{分|わ}からないときは、えんりょしないで{聞|き}くことです。 — When you don't understand, the thing to do is ask without holding back.
{人|ひと}の{悪口|わるぐち}は{言|い}わないことだ。 — Best not to speak ill of others.

To a superior, 〜ことだ sounds as if you were teaching them; use 〜たほうがいいと{思|おも}います, or
ask a question instead.

## Choosing between them

| Pattern | Voice | Typical use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜べきだ | my judgement: it's right | opinions, essays, criticism | ルールは{守|まも}るべきだ |
| 〜ものだ / ものではない | common sense: that's how it is | general truths, social norms, an elder's reminder | {夜|よる}は{静|しず}かにするものだ |
| 〜たものだ | memory | things you used to do | よく{遊|あそ}んだものだ |
| 〜ことだ | advice from experience | advice columns, seniors to juniors | {毎日|まいにち}{続|つづ}けることだ |
| 〜たほうがいい | friendly advice (N4) | to friends, colleagues | {早|はや}く{寝|ね}たほうがいいよ |
| 〜なければならない | a requirement (N4) | rules, laws, duties | きっぷを{買|か}わなければならない |

## Rules and habits: 〜ことになっている, 〜ことにしている (review)

From N4: 〜ことになる / 〜ことにする are "it's been decided" / "I've decided". With 〜ている they
describe a standing rule or a personal habit:

このマンションでは、ごみは{朝|あさ}{八時|はちじ}までに{出|だ}すことになっている。 — In this building, rubbish has to be put out by 8 a.m. (a rule others set)
{私|わたし}は、{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}では{電話|でんわ}に{出|で}ないことにしている。 — I make it a rule not to answer the phone on trains. (my own rule)

Notices often say 〜ことになっています: politely stating a rule without saying who made it.

## Never: {決|けっ}して〜ない

{決|けっ}して (lesson 28 adds it to your list) + a negative is a strong "never, by no means". It
belongs in promises, warnings and writing.

このことは{決|けっ}して{忘|わす}れません。 — I'll never forget this.
{非常口|ひじょうぐち}の{前|まえ}には、{決|けっ}して{物|もの}を{置|お}かないでください。 — Never leave anything in front of the emergency exit.

It needs the negative: ×{決|けっ}していい. In everyday speech, {絶対|ぜったい}(に)〜ない (N5) is more common.

In Japan, many people think that talking on the phone on a train breaks the rules of manners. On
trains there's an announcement: "Please set your phone to silent mode and refrain from making

When I was a child, my grandmother would often say, "On a train, you keep quiet." When I made a

But a friend from abroad was puzzled: "Talking with your friends is louder than talking on the
phone, so why is it only the phone that's not allowed?" Now that I think about it, she's right.
One theory says that phone calls are disliked because you can't hear the other person, so you
only understand half of what's said, and that bothers you all the more.

## Common mistakes

- ×{言|い}わないべきだ. The negative is べきではない: {言|い}うべきではない.
- べき to a superior's face: ×{先生|せんせい}、{休|やす}むべきです sounds like an order. Say
  {少|すこ}し{休|やす}まれたほうが…, or simply お{休|やす}みください.
- べき for a rule: ×{図書館|としょかん}では{本|ほん}を{返|かえ}すべきだ is an opinion. If it's a rule, say
  {返|かえ}さなければならない or {返|かえ}すことになっている.
- 〜たものだ for one event: ×{昨日|きのう}、{映画|えいが}を{見|み}たものだ. It's for things you used to
  do regularly.
- ことだ for your own plans: ×{明日|あした}から{毎日|まいにち}{走|はし}ることだ means "the thing to do
  is run". For a decision, use N4's ことにする: {走|はし}ることにした.
- {決|けっ}して without a negative: ×{決|けっ}してします.

## Key points

- Modality is the speaker's attitude in a sentence's ending: sure, unsure, approving, obliged.
- 〜べきだ: should (the speaker's judgement); する → するべき / すべき; negative べきではない; past
  べきだった. Strong: avoid it to superiors.
- 〜ものだ: that's how things are (general truths); what one is expected to do (social norms);
  〜ものではない: one shouldn't; 〜たものだ: used to (nostalgic).
- 〜ことだ: the thing to do is… (advice from experience).
- 〜ことになっている: a rule; 〜ことにしている: my own rule or habit.
- {決|けっ}して〜ない: never.
- New kanji: 礼 規 制 法 守 違 反 恥 静 常 識 非 迷. Write {守|まも}る, {違|ちが}う, {間違|まちが}える,
  {静|しず}か, {恥|は}ずかしい, {失礼|しつれい}, {迷|まよ}う, {留守|るす} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Without, no choice, can't help: ずに, しかない, てしょうがない
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson closes the module with feelings: how strongly you feel something, what you can't help
doing, and what you have no choice about.

{何|なに}も{言|い}わずに{帰|かえ}ってしまった。 — He went home without saying anything.
{終電|しゅうでん}がないから、{歩|ある}いて{帰|かえ}るしかない。 — There's no last train, so I have no choice but to walk home.
{明日|あした}の{旅行|りょこう}が{楽|たの}しみでしょうがない。 — I'm so looking forward to tomorrow's trip I can hardly stand it.
その{話|はなし}を{聞|き}いて、{笑|わら}わずにはいられなかった。 — When I heard that story, I couldn't help laughing.

First comes a new verb form, the **[[ず form]]**, a written-style partner of the ない form that you
met in passing in lessons 8 and 9. The theme is emotions: joy, anger, fear, sadness,
embarrassment, worry, stress and being moved. (Personality is lesson 16's theme; love is lesson
17's.) Many feeling words you know in kana now take kanji: {悲|かな}しい, {喜|よろこ}ぶ, {怒|おこ}る,
{怖|こわ}い, {笑|わら}う, {泣|な}く, {残念|ざんねん}, {欲|ほ}しい, and the everyday お{願|ねが}いします.

## The ず form

Take the ない form and replace ない with ず:

| Dictionary form | ない form | ず form |
|---|---|---|
| {食|た}べる | {食|た}べない | {食|た}べず |
| {見|み}る | {見|み}ない | {見|み}ず |
| {行|い}く | {行|い}かない | {行|い}かず |
| {言|い}う | {言|い}わない | {言|い}わず |
| {待|ま}つ | {待|ま}たない | {待|ま}たず |
| {分|わ}かる | {分|わ}からない | {分|わ}からず |
| する | しない | せず (not ×しず) |
| {来|く}る | {来|こ}ない | {来|こ}ず |

The only irregular one is する → せず, and with it every する verb: {勉強|べんきょう}せず,
{心配|しんぱい}せず. ある has no everyday ず form (its old form あらず survives only in set phrases).
The ず form isn't one of your conjugation drill forms: you'll practise it in sentences instead.

### 〜ずに: without doing

〜ずに means the same as 〜ないで, "without doing" or "instead of doing", and sounds a little more
formal or written.

{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べずに{家|いえ}を{出|で}た。 — I left the house without eating breakfast.
かさを{持|も}たずに{出|で}かけて、{雨|あめ}にぬれた。 — I went out without an umbrella and got soaked.
{何|なに}も{言|い}わずに、{部屋|へや}を{出|で}ていった。 — She walked out of the room without a word.
{会議|かいぎ}には{行|い}かずに、{資料|しりょう}だけ{送|おく}りました。 — Instead of going to the meeting, I just sent the documents.

### 〜ず、: and not, so not (in writing)

On its own, ず links two clauses the way 〜なくて (or 〜ないで) does: "not A, and B" or "because not A,
B". This is mostly written or formal speech.

{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}らず、{水|みず}が{足|た}りなくなっている。 — There's been no rain, and water is running short.
{答|こた}えが{分|わ}からず、{困|こま}ってしまった。 — I didn't know the answer and was stuck.

### Set phrases with ず

You'll meet ず in words where it's frozen:

| Phrase | Literally | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {思|おも}わず | without thinking | involuntarily, before I knew it |
| {相変|あいか}わらず | without changing | as always, as ever |
| とりあえず | without (time to) do more | for now, for the time being |
| {必|かなら}ず (N5) | | without fail |

{思|おも}わず{笑|わら}ってしまった。 — I burst out laughing before I could stop myself.
{相変|あいか}わらず{忙|いそが}しそうですね。 — You look as busy as ever.
とりあえず、ビールをください。 — A beer to start with, please.

### ず, ないで and なくて

| Use | 〜ずに / 〜ず | 〜ないで | 〜なくて |
|---|---|---|---|
| without doing: {食|た}べずに{出|で}た | ✓ (a bit formal) | ✓ | ✗ |
| instead of: {行|い}かずに{家|いえ}にいた | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ |
| cause: {分|わ}からなくて{困|こま}った | ✓ in writing: {分|わ}からず{困|こま}った | rarely | ✓ (everyday) |
| request: {行|い}かないでください | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ |

So: 〜ないで is the everyday "without", 〜なくて the everyday cause, and ず can do both jobs in a
more formal voice, but never a request: ×{行|い}かずにください.

## No choice but: 〜しかない

The dictionary form + しかない is "there's nothing for it but to…". You've weighed the options
and only one is left.

{終電|しゅうでん}がないから、タクシーで{帰|かえ}るしかない。 — There's no last train, so I'll have to take a taxi.
{自分|じぶん}で{決|き}めたことだから、やるしかない。 — I decided it myself, so I just have to do it.
もう{一度|いちど}あやまるしかないと{思|おも}う。 — I think the only thing for it is to apologize again.

It's the same しか as N4's しか〜ない (only): {千円|せんえん}しかない is "I've only got 1,000 yen", and
{待|ま}つしかない is literally "there's only waiting". The polite form is 〜しかありません.

## Unbearably: 〜てしょうがない, 〜てしかたがない

The て form of a feeling or sensation + しょうがない / しかたがない says it's so strong you can't do
anything about it: "terribly, unbearably, I can't stop…". しかたがない ({仕方|しかた}がない) is slightly more
formal; しょうがない is its everyday form.

{試験|しけん}の{結果|けっか}が{気|き}になってしょうがない。 — I can't stop thinking about the exam results.
{今日|きょう}は{朝|あさ}から{眠|ねむ}くてしかたがない。 — I've been dreadfully sleepy since this morning.
{合格|ごうかく}できて、うれしくてしょうがないです。 — I passed, and I'm so happy I don't know what to do with myself.

- It's for feelings and sensations (うれしい, {悲|かな}しい, {心配|しんぱい}, {眠|ねむ}い, {痛|いた}い,
  {気|き}になる), not for facts: ×この{部屋|へや}は{広|ひろ}くてしょうがない sounds odd.
- It's about your own feelings. For someone else, add a word for how you know:
  {妹|いもうと}は{旅行|りょこう}が{楽|たの}しみでしょうがないようだ (my sister seems to be desperately
  looking forward to the trip).
- In writing and in N2 you'll also see 〜てたまらない, which is similar.

On its own, しかたがない / しょうがない is "it can't be helped": {雨|あめ}ならしょうがないね (if it's
raining, there's nothing we can do).

## Can't help it: 〜ずにはいられない

The ず form + にはいられない is "can't help doing": the feeling is too strong to hold back. It's a
little written; in speech, 〜ないではいられない is also heard.

その{話|はなし}を{聞|き}いて、{泣|な}かずにはいられなかった。 — When I heard that story, I couldn't help crying.
{困|こま}っている{人|ひと}を{見|み}ると、{声|こえ}をかけずにはいられない。 — When I see someone in trouble, I can't help speaking to them.
{悪|わる}いと{分|わ}かっていても、あまいものを{食|た}べずにはいられない。 — Even though I know it's bad for me, I can't resist sweet things.

With する: せずにはいられない: {心配|しんぱい}せずにはいられない (I can't help worrying).

Compare: 〜てしょうがない is about a feeling (it's unbearable); 〜ずにはいられない is about an action the
feeling pushes you to (you can't stop yourself doing it).

## No way to: 〜ようがない

The ます stem + ようがない says there's no means of doing something: "there's no way to…". Here よう
is a noun meaning "way, means".

{住所|じゅうしょ}が{分|わ}からないので、{手紙|てがみ}の{出|だ}しようがない。 — I don't know her address, so there's no way to send her a letter.
こんなにこわれていたら、{直|なお}しようがありません。 — When it's this badly broken, there's no way to fix it.
{気持|きも}ちは{言葉|ことば}では{言|い}い{表|あらわ}しようがない。 — There's no way to put my feelings into words.

With する verbs, both {説明|せつめい}しようがない and {説明|せつめい}のしようがない are used (there's no way to explain).

## To recognize: 〜てもしかたがない, 〜ている{場合|ばあい}じゃない

Two more patterns to understand when you hear them:

- 〜てもしかたがない: "it's no use…": {今|いま}さら{心配|しんぱい}してもしかたがない
  (there's no point worrying now). {今|いま}さら = now, at this late stage.
- 〜ている{場合|ばあい}じゃない: "this is no time for…": {寝|ね}ている{場合|ばあい}じゃない！{明日|あした}は
  {試験|しけん}だ (This is no time to be sleeping! The exam's tomorrow).

## Emotion words

| Feeling | Words |
|---|---|
| joy and satisfaction | {喜|よろこ}び, {楽|たの}しむ, {満足|まんぞく} (lesson 5), ほっとする, {笑顔|えがお}, {笑|わら}い, {笑|わら}い{声|ごえ}, {感動|かんどう}, {感心|かんしん}する |
| sadness and disappointment | {悲|かな}しみ, {悲|かな}しむ, {落|お}ち{込|こ}む, がっかりする, {失望|しつぼう}, なみだ, {泣|な}き{声|ごえ}, {情|なさ}けない, くやしい |
| anger | {怒|いか}り, {怒鳴|どな}る, {腹|はら}が{立|た}つ, {頭|あたま}にくる, いらいらする, {不満|ふまん} |
| fear and worry | {恐|おそ}れる, {恐|おそ}ろしい, {怖|こわ}がる, {恐怖|きょうふ}, きんちょうする, {念|ねん}のため |
| surprise and embarrassment | おどろく, ショック, てれる, {苦笑|にがわら}い |
| feeling for others | {同情|どうじょう}, きのどく, かわいそう, うらやましい, はげます, かんしゃ |
| wanting and hoping | {欲|よく}, {食欲|しょくよく}, {望|のぞ}む, {望|のぞ}み, {願|ねが}う, {願|ねが}い, きぼう |
| feelings in general | {感情|かんじょう}, {感|かん}じる, {感|かん}じ, {感覚|かんかく}, {表情|ひょうじょう}, きげん, {平気|へいき}, {落|お}ち{着|つ}く, {立|た}ち{直|なお}る, なつかしい |
| phrases | {仕方|しかた}がない, しょうがない, {思|おも}わず, {相変|あいか}わらず, とりあえず |

Notes:

- {怒|おこ}る (N4) and {怒|いか}り share a kanji but not a reading: the verb is usually おこる in speech;
  {怒|いか}り is the noun "anger" (its verb いかる is written style).
- {腹|はら}が{立|た}つ and {頭|あたま}にくる both mean "to get angry": {腹|はら}が{立|た}つ is neutral,
  {頭|あたま}にくる is casual.
- {怖|こわ}い (N4) is how *you* feel; {怖|こわ}がる is how someone else shows fear, like N4's 〜がる:
  {妹|いもうと}は{犬|いぬ}を{怖|こわ}がる (my sister is scared of dogs).
- {恐|おそ}ろしい is stronger and more serious than {怖|こわ}い: {恐|おそ}ろしい{事件|じけん} (a
  terrible incident).
- {感心|かんしん}する is to be impressed by someone's effort or behaviour, usually by someone
  you're above or equal to. It sounds the same as lesson 12's {関心|かんしん} (interest).
- {感|かん}じ (feeling, impression: いい{感|かん}じ) sounds like N4's {漢字|かんじ}.
- きげん (mood) has a kanji outside N3; it sounds like lesson 8's {期限|きげん} (deadline). In speech,
  {期限|きげん} falls after the first mora, きげん (mood) is flat.
- {念|ねん}のため is "just in case, to be on the safe side": {念|ねん}のため、もう{一度|いちど}{確認|かくにん}します.
- {平気|へいき} is "fine, not bothered": {寒|さむ}くても{平気|へいき}です.
- The verbs {喜|よろこ}ぶ and {悲|かな}しむ describe what people show; for your own feelings now, the
  adjectives うれしい and {悲|かな}しい are more natural.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for feelings, from joy to fear, and for hoping and wanting.

### Feeling

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 感 | feel | カン | — | 13 | {感|かん}じる, {感情|かんじょう}, {感動|かんどう}, {感心|かんしん}, {感想|かんそう} (lesson 20) |
| 情 | feeling; circumstances | ジョウ | なさ(け) | 11 | {感情|かんじょう}, {表情|ひょうじょう}, {同情|どうじょう}, {情|なさ}けない, {情報|じょうほう} |
| 念 | thought, wish | ネン | — | 8 | {残念|ざんねん}, {念|ねん}のため |

- {情報|じょうほう} (information, N4) and {残念|ざんねん} (N5) can now be written in kanji.
- 感 is on'yomi only, even in the verb {感|かん}じる: {感|かん} + じる.

### Joy and sadness

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 喜 | joy | キ | よろこ(ぶ) | 12 | {喜|よろこ}ぶ, {喜|よろこ}び |
| 笑 | laugh, smile | ショウ | わら(う), え(む) | 10 | {笑|わら}う, {笑|わら}い, {笑顔|えがお}, {苦笑|にがわら}い |
| 悲 | sad | ヒ | かな(しい), かな(しむ) | 12 | {悲|かな}しい, {悲|かな}しむ, {悲|かな}しみ |
| 泣 | cry | キュウ | な(く) | 8 | {泣|な}く, {泣|な}き{声|ごえ} |

- {喜|よろこ}ぶ (N4), {笑|わら}う, {悲|かな}しい and {泣|な}く (N4 and N5) can now be written in kanji.
- 笑 is え in {笑顔|えがお} (a smiling face; 顔 is N4's).
- {泣|な}く (to cry) and lesson 20's {鳴|な}く (an animal's cry; a bird's song) sound the same.

### Anger and fear

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 怒 | anger | ド | おこ(る), いか(る) | 9 | {怒|おこ}る, {怒|いか}り, {怒鳴|どな}る |
| 怖 | fear | フ | こわ(い) | 8 | {怖|こわ}い, {怖|こわ}がる, {恐怖|きょうふ} |
| 恐 | fear, dread | キョウ | おそ(れる), おそ(ろしい) | 10 | {恐|おそ}れる, {恐|おそ}ろしい, {恐怖|きょうふ} |

- {怒|おこ}る and {怖|こわ}い (N4) can now be written in kanji.
- 怒 is ド in {怒鳴|どな}る (to yell), with 鳴 (lesson 20).

### Hoping and wanting

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 望 | hope, wish | ボウ | のぞ(む) | 11 | {望|のぞ}む, {望|のぞ}み, {失望|しつぼう} |
| 願 | ask, wish | ガン | ねが(う) | 19 | {願|ねが}う, {願|ねが}い, お{願|ねが}いします |
| 欲 | desire | ヨク | ほ(しい) | 11 | {欲|よく}, {食欲|しょくよく}, {欲|ほ}しい |

- お{願|ねが}いします (N5) can now be written with kanji, and so can {欲|ほ}しい (N5) as a main word:
  {新|あたら}しいかばんが{欲|ほ}しい. After a て form, ほしい stays in kana: {来|き}てほしい.
- きぼう (hope) needs a kanji outside N3, so it stays in kana.

Memory notes:

- 感, 念, 恐 and 悲 all have 心 (heart) at the bottom, and 情 and 怖 have its narrow side form on the
  left: feeling words.
- 感 is 心 under a shape like a weapon and a mouth: when your heart is struck, you feel.
- 念 is 今 (now, N5) over 心: what's in your heart now, a thought.
- 喜 is a drum on a stand over 口 (mouth): drumming and singing for joy.
- 笑 has the bamboo shape on top, bending in the wind like someone doubled up laughing.
- 泣 is water (three dots) beside 立 (stand, N5): standing in tears.
- 怒 is 女 (woman, N5) and a hand over 心 (heart): a heart held down until it boils over.
- 望 has 月 (moon) in it: gazing at the moon and wishing.
- 願 ends in the "head" shape that also ends 頭 and 顔 (N4): bowing your head to ask.
- 欲 is a valley shape beside a yawning mouth: a mouth as wide as a valley, wanting everything.

```trace
感情悲喜怒怖恐笑泣念望願欲
```

## Dialogue: bad news

Mei has just heard she didn't get the job she wanted most. Her friend Riku calls round. (Casual
speech between friends.)

```dialogue
# After the interview
りく: どうしたの？{元気|げんき}ないね。
= What's up? You seem down.
めい: {一番|いちばん}{入|はい}りたかった{会社|かいしゃ}、だめだった。
= I didn't get into the company I wanted most.
りく: そうか…。それは{落|お}ち{込|こ}むよね。
= Oh… No wonder you're down.
めい: めんせつできんちょうしちゃって、{言|い}いたいことが{全然|ぜんぜん}{言|い}えなかったんだ。{思|おも}い{出|だ}すと、{恥|は}ずかしくてしょうがない。
= I got so nervous in the interview, I couldn't say any of what I wanted to. When I remember it, I'm so embarrassed I can't bear it.
りく: でも、{終|お}わったことを{今|いま}さら{考|かんが}えてもしかたがないよ。
= But there's no point thinking about it now it's over.
めい: {分|わ}かってるけど、{考|かんが}えずにはいられないの。{親|おや}にもなんて{言|い}えばいいか…。
= I know, but I can't help it. And I don't know what to tell my parents…
りく: {正直|しょうじき}に{言|い}うしかないんじゃない？きっと{分|わ}かってくれるよ。
= Isn't the only thing to just tell them honestly? I'm sure they'll understand.
めい: そうだね。…ありがとう。りくに{話|はな}したら、{少|すこ}し{落|お}ち{着|つ}いた。
= You're right. …Thanks. Talking to you has calmed me down a bit.
りく: よかった。{他|ほか}にも{受|う}けてる{会社|かいしゃ}、あるんでしょ？
= Good. You've applied to other companies too, haven't you?
めい: うん、{二|ふた}つ。{一|ひと}つは{来週|らいしゅう}めんせつ。
= Yeah, two. One has its interview next week.
りく: じゃあ、{落|お}ち{込|こ}んでる{場合|ばあい}じゃないよ。めんせつの{練習|れんしゅう}、{手伝|てつだ}おうか？
= Then this is no time to be moping. Shall I help you practise for the interview?
めい: ほんと？うれしい！じゃあ、とりあえず{今日|きょう}は、{何|なに}かおいしいもの{食|た}べに{行|い}こう。
= Really? That'd be great! Then for now, let's go and eat something nice today.
りく: いいね。{悲|かな}しいときは、{食|た}べるしかない。
= Sounds good. When you're sad, there's nothing for it but to eat.
```

めんせつ = job interview (N4); {正直|しょうじき}に = honestly (lesson 16's word); {今|いま}さら = now,
at this late stage. The last line is a joke: 〜しかない used about something pleasant.

## Reading: a short story

A short story, written, as stories usually are, in the plain past.

> {引|ひ}っ{越|こ}しのじゅんびをしていたとき、{押|お}し{入|い}れのおくから{古|ふる}い{箱|はこ}が{出|で}てきた。{開|あ}けてみると、{手紙|てがみ}が{何通|なんつう}も{入|はい}っていた。{十年前|じゅうねんまえ}に{亡|な}くなった{祖母|そぼ}からの{手紙|てがみ}だった。
>
> {大学|だいがく}に{入|はい}って{一人|ひとり}で{暮|く}らし{始|はじ}めたころ、{私|わたし}は{毎日|まいにち}さびしくてしかたがなかった。{友|とも}だちもなかなかできず、{電話|でんわ}で{母|はは}に{泣|な}き{言|ごと}を{言|い}ったこともある。そんなとき、{祖母|そぼ}はいつも{短|みじか}い{手紙|てがみ}を{送|おく}ってくれた。
>
> 「{元気|げんき}ですか。さびしいのは、がんばっているからです。{無理|むり}をせず、{自分|じぶん}のペースで{行|い}きなさい。」
>
> {読|よ}みながら、{思|おも}わず{笑|わら}ってしまった。{祖母|そぼ}の{字|じ}は{相変|あいか}わらず{大|おお}きくて、{少|すこ}しゆがんでいる。でも、{読|よ}んでいるうちに、だんだん{目|め}が{熱|あつ}くなってきて、{泣|な}かずにはいられなかった。
>
> あのころは、{祖母|そぼ}の{手紙|てがみ}が{来|く}るのがうれしくてしょうがなかった。それなのに、{私|わたし}は{一度|いちど}もちゃんとお{礼|れい}を{言|い}わなかった。{今|いま}となっては、もう{伝|つた}えようがない。
>
> {手紙|てがみ}を{箱|はこ}に{戻|もど}して、{新|あたら}しい{部屋|へや}に{持|も}っていくことにした。{言|い}えなかったお{礼|れい}は、{私|わたし}がこれから{元気|げんき}に{暮|く}らすことで{返|かえ}すしかない。そう{思|おも}うと、{少|すこ}し{気持|きも}ちが{軽|かる}くなった。

じゅんび = preparations (N4); {押|お}し{入|い}れ = a futon cupboard (N5's おしいれ); おく = the back
(of a cupboard); {何通|なんつう} = how many letters (〜{通|つう} counts letters); {泣|な}き{言|ごと} = a complaint, a
moan; ゆがむ = to be crooked; {今|いま}となっては = now (that it's too late); {戻|もど}す = to put back
(lesson 21's word); {暮|く}らす = to live (lesson 23's word).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What did the writer find, and who were the letters from? — An old box of letters from her
   grandmother, who died ten years ago.
2. How did the writer feel in her first year at university? — Terribly lonely
   (さびしくてしかたがなかった).
3. Why did she cry as she read? — The letters moved her; she couldn't hold back the tears
   ({泣|な}かずにはいられなかった).
4. How does she decide to repay her grandmother? — By living well from now on (the only way left,
   since she can no longer thank her).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

While I was getting ready to move, an old box turned up from the back of the futon cupboard. When
I opened it, there were a lot of letters inside. They were from my grandmother, who died ten years
ago.

When I'd started university and was living alone, I was terribly lonely every day. I couldn't
make friends easily, and I even moaned to my mother on the phone. At times like that, my
grandmother always sent me a short letter.

"How are you? You're lonely because you're trying hard. Don't overdo it; go at your own pace."

As I read, I laughed before I could stop myself. Her handwriting was as big as ever, and a little
crooked. But as I went on reading, my eyes slowly grew hot, and I couldn't help crying.

Back then, I'd been so happy every time one of her letters came. And yet I never once thanked her
properly. Now there's no way to tell her.

I put the letters back in the box and decided to take them to my new room. The thanks I never
said, I can only repay by living well from now on. Thinking that, I felt a little lighter.

</details>

## Pronunciation: きげん and {期限|きげん}

The two きげん are told apart by pitch: {期限|きげん:1} (deadline) falls after the first mora;
[きげん:0] (mood) is flat. A particle after {期限|きげん:1} is low; after [きげん:0] it stays high.

```speak
{思|おも}わず{笑|わら}ってしまいました。
= I laughed before I could stop myself.
{歩|ある}いて{帰|かえ}るしかありません。
= I have no choice but to walk home.
{明日|あした}が{楽|たの}しみでしょうがないです。
= I'm so looking forward to tomorrow.
{泣|な}かずにはいられませんでした。
= I couldn't help crying.
{今|いま}さら{心配|しんぱい}してもしかたがありません。
= There's no point worrying now.
{住所|じゅうしょ}が{分|わ}からないので、{手紙|てがみ}の{出|だ}しようがありません。
= I don't know the address, so there's no way to send a letter.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×しずに. The ず form of する is せず: {勉強|べんきょう}せずに, {心配|しんぱい}せずにはいられない.
- ×{来|き}ず. {来|く}る becomes {来|こ}ず, like {来|こ}ない.
- A request with ず: ×{忘|わす}れずにください. Use 〜ないでください. (〜ずに can come before a request
  verb, though: {忘|わす}れずに{持|も}ってきてください, please don't forget to bring it.)
- 〜てしょうがない for facts or other people's feelings: ×{山|やま}が{高|たか}くてしょうがない;
  ×{田中|たなか}さんはうれしくてしょうがない. It's for your own feelings and sensations; for others
  add ようだ or らしい.
- 〜しかない with a ない form: ×{行|い}かないしかない. しかない follows the dictionary form:
  {行|い}くしかない.
- 〜ようがない with the dictionary form: ×{直|なお}すようがない. Use the ます stem:
  {直|なお}しようがない.
- Writing ほしい after a て form in kanji: it stays in kana as an auxiliary: {手伝|てつだ}ってほしい.

## Key points

- The ず form: ない → ず ({食|た}べず, {行|い}かず); する → せず; {来|く}る → {来|こ}ず. It isn't a
  drill form.
- 〜ずに = 〜ないで (without; instead of), more formal; 〜ず、 links clauses in writing; set phrases:
  {思|おも}わず, {相変|あいか}わらず, とりあえず.
- Dictionary form + しかない: no choice but to.
- て form + しょうがない / しかたがない: unbearably (your own feelings and sensations).
- ず form + にはいられない: can't help doing.
- ます stem + ようがない: there's no way to.
- To recognize: 〜てもしかたがない (no use), 〜ている{場合|ばあい}じゃない (no time for).
- New kanji: 感 情 悲 喜 怒 怖 恐 笑 泣 念 望 願 欲. Write {悲|かな}しい, {喜|よろこ}ぶ, {怒|おこ}る,
  {怖|こわ}い, {笑|わら}う, {泣|な}く, {残念|ざんねん}, {情報|じょうほう}, {欲|ほ}しい, お{願|ねが}いします with
  kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The neighbourhood and volunteering
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 9 was about the rules of public life; lesson 8 about forms and signing up. This honors
lesson puts them together in the place where many people in Japan meet both: their neighbourhood.
You'll read about the residents' association, the clipboard of notices that goes from door to
door, clean-up days, disaster drills and volunteering, and you'll read a real-looking notice and
answer it.

Customs differ a lot from town to town, between city flats and older houses, and they're
changing. Take what follows as a common pattern, not a rule for everywhere.

## The residents' association: {町内会|ちょうないかい} and {自治会|じちかい}

Most neighbourhoods have a residents' association. In older town areas it's often called
{町内会|ちょうないかい} (the association of a {町|ちょう}, a block of streets); in newer housing it's
often {自治会|じちかい} ("self-government association"). They do much the same things:

- keep the rubbish collection points clean, often with a rota of households;
- pass round notices from the town hall and the police;
- run clean-up days, summer festivals and children's events;
- organize disaster drills and check on elderly residents;
- look after street lights and the {集会所|しゅうかいじょ} (the neighbourhood meeting hall).

Joining is voluntary, though in many places most households join. There's usually a small
membership fee ({会費|かいひ}), often a few hundred yen a month; amounts vary. Jobs such as
{会長|かいちょう} (chair) or はんちょう (the head of a small group of houses) often go round in turn.

{当番|とうばん} is a turn of duty: ごみ{置|お}き{場|ば}の{当番|とうばん} (your turn to look after the
rubbish point), そうじ{当番|とうばん} (cleaning duty). A sign or a card often moves from door to door
to show whose turn it is.

## The clipboard: かいらんばん

かいらんばん (written with kanji outside the N3 list, so in kana here) is a folder or clipboard of
notices that each household reads, signs or stamps, and passes on to the next house. It might
hold the dates of the next clean-up, a festival programme, a warning about phone scams or a list
of who has paid the fee.

The manners are simple and follow lesson 9's ものだ: you read it and pass it on quickly, usually
within a day or two, by putting it in the next house's postbox or handing it over. Keeping it for
a week is the classic way to annoy the neighbours. In many places かいらんばん now also come by
email or through an app, and some associations have stopped them.

{読|よ}んだら、すぐに{次|つぎ}の{家|いえ}に{回|まわ}すものです。 — Once you've read it, you're supposed to pass it on straight away.

## Clean-up days and the ごみ{置|お}き{場|ば}

Many associations hold a clean-up day once or twice a year, often early on a Sunday morning:
residents pull weeds, sweep the streets, clear drains and pick up litter in the park.
{草|くさ}を{取|と}る (to pull weeds) and {落|お}ち{葉|ば}を{集|あつ}める (to gather fallen leaves) come from
lesson 6.

Whether you have to take part depends on the neighbourhood. You don't always have to; if you
can't come, it's polite to say so in advance, and in some places households that don't come are
asked to pay a small amount instead. Ask a neighbour: {参加|さんか}しないといけないとは{限|かぎ}らない
けど、{来|こ}られないときは{一言|ひとこと}{言|い}ったほうがいい (you don't necessarily have to go, but it's
better to say a word when you can't come). {参加|さんか} (taking part) is lesson 23's word.

## Disaster drills: ぼうさいくんれん

ぼうさい (disaster prevention) and くんれん (training, a drill) both need kanji outside N3, so
they're in kana here. A ぼうさいくんれん might practise:

- walking to the evacuation site (N4's ひなん{場所|ばしょ}) along the local route;
- using a fire extinguisher, or the stretchers and tools kept in the neighbourhood store;
- checking which households have elderly or disabled members who may need help.

September 1st is ぼうさいの{日|ひ} (Disaster Prevention Day), the anniversary of the 1923 Great
Kantō earthquake, and many drills are held around then; others are in spring or autumn. The
emergency words themselves (じしん, ひなん, つなみ) are N4's.

## Volunteering: ボランティア

ボランティア means both a volunteer and voluntary work: ボランティアをする (to volunteer),
ボランティアに{参加|さんか}する (to take part as a volunteer). Common local kinds are reading to
children at the library, helping at festivals, teaching Japanese to residents from abroad,
patrolling school routes and, after a disaster, clearing mud and helping in shelters. Many towns
have a volunteer centre that matches people with places that need help.

Signing up uses lesson 8's words: {申|もう}し{込|こ}む, {申込書|もうしこみしょ}, {期限|きげん},
{事前|じぜん}に, and often 〜{必要|ひつよう}はありません or 〜とは{限|かぎ}りません in the notice.

## Reading: a notice in the かいらんばん

A notice from a residents' association, as it might appear in the clipboard (です/ます style).

> {町内|ちょうない}そうじのお{知|し}らせ
>
> {住民|じゅうみん}の{皆様|みなさま}へ
>
> {今年|ことし}も{秋|あき}の{町内|ちょうない}そうじを{行|おこな}います。{公園|こうえん}や{道|みち}の{落|お}ち{葉|ば}、ごみを{集|あつ}め、{草|くさ}を{取|と}ります。{一時間|いちじかん}ほどで{終|お}わる{予定|よてい}です。
>
> {日時|にちじ}：{十一月|じゅういちがつ}{十日|とおか}（{日|にち}）{午前|ごぜん}{八時|はちじ}から（{雨|あめ}の{場合|ばあい}は{十七日|じゅうしちにち}）
>
> {集合|しゅうごう}：{第二公園|だいにこうえん}の{入口|いりぐち}
>
> {持|も}ち{物|もの}：ぐんて（{作業用|さぎょうよう}の{手|て}ぶくろ）、{飲|の}み{物|もの}
>
> ごみぶくろと{道具|どうぐ}は{町内会|ちょうないかい}で{用意|ようい}しますので、{持|も}ってくる{必要|ひつよう}はありません。{参加|さんか}できる{方|かた}は、{十一月|じゅういちがつ}{五日|いつか}までに、このお{知|し}らせの{下|した}の{表|ひょう}にお{名前|なまえ}と{人数|にんずう}を{書|か}いて、かいらんばんを{次|つぎ}のお{宅|たく}に{回|まわ}してください。{当日|とうじつ}の{参加|さんか}もかまいません。
>
> {小学生|しょうがくせい}のお{子|こ}さんは、{大人|おとな}と{一緒|いっしょ}に{参加|さんか}してください。{参加|さんか}できない{方|かた}も、{家|いえ}の{前|まえ}の{道|みち}をきれいにしていただけると{助|たす}かります。
>
> なお、{今年|ことし}から{町内会|ちょうないかい}のお{知|し}らせはメールでも{送|おく}っています。メールで{受|う}け{取|と}りたい{方|かた}は、{会長|かいちょう}の{山本|やまもと}までお{知|し}らせください。
>
> {本町|ほんちょう}{町内会|ちょうないかい}・{会長|かいちょう}{山本|やまもと}

{日時|にちじ} = date and time; {集合|しゅうごう} = meeting point; ぐんて = cotton work gloves;
{作業用|さぎょうよう} = for work; {人数|にんずう} = number of people; お{宅|たく} = house (polite; lesson 24's
word); {当日|とうじつ} = on the day; かまいません = that's fine; なお = also, please note (in notices).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What should you bring? — Work gloves and something to drink; bags and tools are provided.
2. How do you say you'll come? — Write your name and the number of people in the table on the
   notice by 5 November, then pass the clipboard on. You can also just turn up on the day.
3. If it rains on the 10th, what happens? — The clean-up moves to the 17th.
4. What's new this year? — Notices are also sent by email; tell Mr Yamamoto if you want them.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Notice of the neighbourhood clean-up

To all residents

As every year, we're holding the autumn neighbourhood clean-up. We'll collect fallen leaves and
litter in the park and on the roads, and pull weeds. It should be over in about an hour.

Date and time: Sunday 10 November, from 8 a.m. (if it rains, the 17th)

Meeting point: the entrance to the Second Park

What to bring: work gloves, something to drink

The association will provide rubbish bags and tools, so you don't need to bring them. If you can
take part, please write your name and the number of people in the table at the bottom of this
notice by 5 November, and pass the clipboard on to the next house. You're also welcome to join on
the day.

Primary-school children should take part with an adult. If you can't take part, we'd be grateful
if you could tidy the road in front of your house.

Please also note that from this year, the association's notices are also sent by email. If you'd
like to receive them by email, please let Yamamoto, the chair, know.

Honmachi Residents' Association, Yamamoto (chair)

</details>

## Dialogue: the clipboard

Sam has just moved into a house. His neighbour Mr Kimura rings the bell holding a clipboard.
(Polite speech.)

```dialogue
# At the door
きむら: こんにちは。となりの{木村|きむら}です。かいらんばんを{持|も}ってきました。
= Hello. I'm Kimura from next door. I've brought the clipboard.
サム: あ、ありがとうございます。かいらんばん…ですか。
= Oh, thank you. A… clipboard?
きむら: {町内会|ちょうないかい}のお{知|し}らせです。{読|よ}んだら、ここにはんこかサインをして、{次|つぎ}のお{宅|たく}に{回|まわ}してください。
= It's notices from the residents' association. When you've read them, put your seal or signature here and pass it on to the next house.
サム: {次|つぎ}はどちらですか。
= Which house is next?
きむら: {向|む}かいの{石田|いしだ}さんです。{一日|いちにち}か{二日|ふつか}で{回|まわ}すものなので、あまり{長|なが}く{置|お}いておかないでくださいね。
= The Ishidas opposite. You're supposed to pass it on within a day or two, so please don't hang on to it too long.
サム: {分|わ}かりました。この{町内|ちょうない}そうじというのは、{必|かなら}ず{出|で}なければいけませんか。
= I see. This neighbourhood clean-up: do I have to go?
きむら: {必|かなら}ず{出|で}なければいけないわけではありませんよ。でも、{新|あたら}しく{来|き}た{方|かた}は、{一度|いちど}{出|で}ておくと{近所|きんじょ}の{人|ひと}の{顔|かお}が{分|わ}かっていいですよ。
= You don't absolutely have to. But for someone new, if you go once you'll get to know the neighbours' faces, which is nice.
サム: そうですね。じゃあ、{出|で}てみます。ぐんては{買|か}わないといけませんか。
= True. Then I'll give it a try. Do I need to buy work gloves?
きむら: {百円|ひゃくえん}ショップで{売|う}っていますよ。{私|わたし}のを{貸|か}してもいいですけど。
= They sell them at the 100-yen shop. Or I can lend you mine.
サム: ありがとうございます。{町内会|ちょうないかい}の{会費|かいひ}は、どうやって{払|はら}えばいいですか。
= Thank you. How do I pay the association fee?
きむら: {年|ねん}に{一回|いっかい}、はんちょうが{集|あつ}めに{来|き}ます。{今年|ことし}は{私|わたし}がはんちょうなので、また{来|き}ますね。
= The group leader comes round to collect it once a year. This year I'm the group leader, so I'll come again.
サム: よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
= Thank you very much.
```

はんこ = a personal seal (N5); {向|む}かい = opposite (lesson 14's kanji); {百円|ひゃくえん}ショップ = a
100-yen shop. Mr Kimura uses lesson 9's ものです for the custom, and lesson 7's わけではありません to
say the clean-up isn't compulsory.

## Words for the neighbourhood

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {町内会|ちょうないかい}, {自治会|じちかい} | residents' association |
| {住民|じゅうみん} | resident(s) of an area |
| ちいき | area, region; the local community |
| かいらんばん | clipboard of notices passed from house to house |
| {当番|とうばん} | one's turn of duty; the person on duty |
| {集会所|しゅうかいじょ} | neighbourhood meeting hall |
| ぼうさい, くんれん | disaster prevention; training, a drill |
| ボランティア | volunteer; voluntary work |

ちいき has a kanji outside N3. You'll see it constantly in notices: ちいきの{住民|じゅうみん}
(local residents), ちいきのボランティア.

## Key points

- {町内会|ちょうないかい} / {自治会|じちかい}: residents' associations; joining is voluntary, small fees,
  jobs in turn. Customs vary by place.
- かいらんばん: read it, sign or stamp it, pass it on within a day or two (〜ものだ).
- {当番|とうばん}: whose turn it is, for the rubbish point or cleaning.
- Clean-up days and ぼうさいくんれん (often around 1 September, ぼうさいの{日|ひ}).
- ボランティア: local volunteering; signing up uses lesson 8's words and grammar.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Pets
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japan has a great many pet dogs and cats, and a lot of rules and customs around them: which flats
allow them, what owners must do by law, how to walk a dog without annoying the neighbours, and how
to behave at a cat café. This honors lesson covers them, and uses lesson 9's べき and ものだ for pet
manners. (Wild and farm animals are lesson 26's theme; N4 taught {動物|どうぶつ}, {犬|いぬ}, ペット and
かう, to keep an animal.)

Laws and local rules change, and they vary by city. The facts below are the general picture;
always check your own city's website.

## Finding a flat: ペット{可|か}

Many rented flats don't allow pets at all. In listings and on agents' websites, look for:

| Listing says | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ペット{可|か} | pets allowed |
| ペット{相談|そうだん} | pets negotiable: ask first |
| ペット{不可|ふか} | no pets |
| {犬|いぬ}・{猫|ねこ}{一|いっ}ぴきまで | one dog or cat only |

{可|か} (allowed) is outside the N3 list, but you'll see it on every listing, so it's shown here
with furigana. ペット{可|か} flats often ask for a larger deposit or a cleaning fee when
you leave, and some limit the size or number of animals. Keeping a pet secretly in a no-pets flat
is a breach of the contract and can end it, so ask before you sign. {相談|そうだん} (asking for
advice) is N4's そうだん.

## The law: registering a dog

In Japan, dog owners are required to register their dog with the city or town they live in, once
in the dog's life, and to have it vaccinated against rabies every year. The city gives two small
tags (one for registration, one for the year's injection) to put on the dog's collar. Owners
usually register soon after they get the dog; spring is the usual season for the rabies
injection, often at group sessions in parks. Since June 2022, dogs and cats sold by breeders and pet
shops must be microchipped, and in cities that take part in a joint scheme the chip's registration
also counts as the city registration. The details (deadlines, fees, where to go) differ from city to city.

Cats don't have to be registered, but many cities advise keeping them indoors.

## The vet: じゅうい

A vet is じゅうい (its first kanji is outside N3) and an animal hospital is {動物|どうぶつ}{病院|びょういん}.
There's no public health insurance for pets, so treatment can be expensive; many owners buy
private pet insurance, ペット{保険|ほけん}. You'll hear:

- ワクチン: a vaccine (for dogs and cats, several diseases besides rabies);
- えさ: pet food (for people, {食|た}べ{物|もの}); {人|ひと}の{食|た}べ{物|もの}をえさにするべきではない
  (you shouldn't feed it human food);
- しつけ: training an animal (and bringing up a child well): トイレのしつけ (house-training).

## Walking a dog: the manners

Dog-walking manners are a favourite topic of neighbourhood notices. The usual points:

- Always use a リード (lead). In most parks and streets, letting a dog off the lead isn't allowed.
- Pick up the ふん (droppings) in a bag and take it home.
- Many owners carry a bottle of water and rinse away the urine where their dog has gone.
- Don't let the dog bark at night or jump up at people; keep it close on narrow pavements.

People explain these rules with lesson 9's grammar:

ふんは{必|かなら}ず{持|も}ち{帰|かえ}るべきだ。 — You should always take the droppings home.
{散歩|さんぽ}のときは、リードを{短|みじか}く{持|も}つものです。 — When you walk a dog, you're supposed to hold the lead short.
{犬|いぬ}をかうなら、まず{近所|きんじょ}のルールを{知|し}ることだ。 — If you're going to keep a dog, the first thing to do is learn the local rules.

{散歩|さんぽ} (N5's さんぽ) is now written with kanji (its first kanji is lesson 27's). {鳴|な}き{声|ごえ} is an
animal's cry: {犬|いぬ}の{鳴|な}き{声|ごえ}がうるさいと、{近所|きんじょ}から{苦情|くじょう}が{来|く}ることもある (if
the barking's loud, neighbours sometimes complain). It's written with the kanji of {鳴|な}く (lesson 20), not
lesson 10's {泣|な}く, which is for people crying.

## Reading: the rules at a cat café

{猫|ねこ}カフェ, where you pay by the hour to spend time with resident cats, have been around in Japan
since the 2000s (the first is usually said to have opened in Taiwan, in 1998) and are common in
cities. This is the
kind of card you're handed at the door.

> ご{来店|らいてん}の{皆様|みなさま}へ：{店内|てんない}でのお{願|ねが}い
>
> {一|いち}、{入|はい}る{前|まえ}に、{手|て}を{洗|あら}ってください。
>
> {二|に}、{寝|ね}ている{猫|ねこ}は{起|お}こさないでください。{猫|ねこ}は{一日|いちにち}の{半分|はんぶん}{以上|いじょう}{寝|ね}ています。
>
> {三|さん}、{猫|ねこ}を{抱|だ}いたり、{追|お}いかけたりしないでください。{猫|ねこ}のほうから{来|く}るのを{待|ま}つものです。
>
> {四|よん}、{写真|しゃしん}はとってもかまいませんが、フラッシュは{使|つか}わないでください。
>
> {五|ご}、{猫|ねこ}に{人|ひと}の{食|た}べ{物|もの}をあげないでください。{店|みせ}で{売|う}っているおやつは{一回|いっかい}だけあげられます。
>
> {六|ろく}、{小学生|しょうがくせい}{以下|いか}のお{子様|こさま}は、{大人|おとな}の{方|かた}と{一緒|いっしょ}にご{利用|りよう}ください。
>
> {猫|ねこ}の{体調|たいちょう}によって、{会|あ}えない{猫|ねこ}がいることもあります。ご{理解|りかい}ください。

{来店|らいてん} = coming to the shop; {店内|てんない} = in the shop; {抱|だ}く = to hold in your arms (lesson
17's word); おやつ = a snack, a treat; {体調|たいちょう} = health, condition (lesson 5); ご{理解|りかい}
ください = we ask for your understanding.

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What must you do before going in? — Wash your hands.
2. Why shouldn't you wake the cats? — They sleep more than half the day.
3. What's the right way to make friends with a cat here? — Wait for it to come to you
   ({来|く}るのを{待|ま}つものです), without picking it up or chasing it.
4. Can you give the cats food? — Not human food; you can give the treats sold in the shop, once.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

To all our visitors: requests inside the café

1. Please wash your hands before you go in.
2. Please don't wake sleeping cats. Cats sleep for more than half the day.
3. Please don't pick the cats up or chase them. The thing to do is wait for them to come to you.
4. You're welcome to take photos, but please don't use a flash.
5. Please don't give the cats human food. You can give them the treats sold in the shop, once.
6. Children of primary-school age and under should visit with an adult.

Depending on how they're feeling, some cats may not be available. Thank you for your
understanding.

</details>

## Dialogue: a new dog

Haruto has just got a puppy. His colleague Ms Nakamura has had dogs all her life. (Polite speech
between colleagues.)

```dialogue
# At lunch
はると: {中村|なかむら}さん、{先週|せんしゅう}、{子犬|こいぬ}をかい{始|はじ}めたんです。
= Ms Nakamura, I got a puppy last week.
なかむら: わあ、いいですね！{名前|なまえ}は？
= Oh, lovely! What's her name?
はると: モモです。でも、{夜|よる}、{鳴|な}き{声|ごえ}が{大|おお}きくて、{近所|きんじょ}にめいわくをかけていないか{心配|しんぱい}で…。
= Momo. But she whines loudly at night, and I'm worried she's bothering the neighbours…
なかむら: {子犬|こいぬ}はさびしいと{鳴|な}くものですよ。{少|すこ}しずつ{慣|な}れますから。
= Puppies cry when they're lonely; that's what they do. She'll get used to it bit by bit.
はると: そうですか。それから、{市役所|しやくしょ}に{行|い}かないといけないって{聞|き}いたんですが…。
= I see. And I heard I have to go to the city office…
なかむら: ええ、{犬|いぬ}は{市|し}にとうろくすることになっているんです。{毎年|まいとし}、{春|はる}にはワクチンも{受|う}けさせないといけません。
= Yes, dogs have to be registered with the city. And every spring you have to get her vaccinated.
はると: {毎年|まいとし}ですか。{知|し}らなかった…。
= Every year? I didn't know…
なかむら: {動物|どうぶつ}{病院|びょういん}でもできますよ。いいじゅういを{一人|ひとり}{知|し}っておくと、{安心|あんしん}です。
= You can do it at an animal hospital too. It's reassuring to know one good vet.
はると: {散歩|さんぽ}はいつから{行|い}けますか。
= When can I start taking her for walks?
なかむら: それもじゅういに{聞|き}くことですね。{行|い}くようになったら、ふんを{取|と}るふくろと{水|みず}は{必|かなら}ず{持|も}っていくものですよ。
= That's something to ask the vet too. Once you start, you always take bags for the droppings and some water.
はると: {水|みず}も{要|い}るんですか。
= Water too?
なかむら: おしっこの{後|あと}に{流|なが}すんです。{家|いえ}の{前|まえ}でされたら、だれでもいやですからね。
= You rinse away the pee. Nobody likes it done in front of their house.
はると: なるほど。しつけも{大変|たいへん}そうですね。
= I see. Training her looks like hard work.
なかむら: {最初|さいしょ}の{一年|いちねん}が{大事|だいじ}ですよ。でも、{楽|たの}しいですよ。
= The first year's the important one. But it's fun.
```

{子犬|こいぬ} = puppy; {受|う}けさせる = to have (an animal) receive (a causative); おしっこ = pee
(casual); されたら = if it's done (to you: N4's passive of trouble). Ms Nakamura uses ものだ for
what dogs and owners do, ことになっている for the rule, and ことだ for advice.

## Words

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| じゅうい | vet |
| かいぬし | owner (of an animal) |
| えさ | pet food; animal feed |
| リード | lead, leash |
| {鳴|な}き{声|ごえ} | an animal's cry (barking, mewing, birdsong) |
| {猫|ねこ}カフェ | cat café |
| しつけ | training (an animal); discipline (of a child) |
| ワクチン | vaccine |

{猫|ねこ} (N5's ねこ) is written with lesson 26's kanji. じゅうい and かいぬし have kanji outside N3.

## Key points

- Flats: ペット{可|か} (allowed; {可|か} is outside N3), ペット{相談|そうだん} (ask), ペット{不可|ふか} (not
  allowed).
- Dogs must be registered with the city once and vaccinated against rabies every year; details
  vary by city. Pets have no public health insurance.
- Walking manners: always a リード, take the ふん home, rinse with water, keep the noise down
  (〜べきだ, 〜ものだ).
- Cat cafés: wash your hands, don't wake, hold or chase the cats, no flash, no human food.
- {鳴|な}き{声|ごえ} is for animals; {泣|な}き{声|ごえ} (lesson 10) is for people.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Roles and viewpoints: として, にとって, に対して
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 2 was about reasons and judgements. Module 3 is about the phrases that make Japanese
sound grown-up: the ones you meet in newspapers, at work, in essays and in the JLPT's reading
texts. として (as), にとって (for), に{対|たい}して (towards), について (about), によって (depending
on), に{比|くら}べて (compared with) and their relatives each look like several words, but they
work as one. They're called **[[compound particles]]**: a **[[particle]]** and a verb form (usually a
て form) that have fused into a single unit. You already know two of them from N4: について (about)
and によると (according to).

{父|ちち}は{医師|いし}として{三十年|さんじゅうねん}{働|はたら}いてきました。 — My father has worked as a doctor for thirty years.
{子供|こども}がいる{社員|しゃいん}にとって、{在宅勤務|ざいたくきんむ}はありがたいです。 — For employees with children, working from home is a real help.
{課長|かちょう}は{新|あたら}しい{社員|しゃいん}に{対|たい}して、いつもていねいに{説明|せつめい}します。 — The section chief always explains things carefully to new employees.

This lesson's three answer three different questions: in what role? (として), from whose point
of view? (にとって) and towards whom? (に{対|たい}して). The theme is work: jobs, positions in a
company, responsibility, pay, commuting and changing jobs.

A note on spelling, which this module repeats for each phrase: として and にとって are written in
kana; に{対|たい}して is written with its kanji, because 対する still means "to face".

## 〜として: as, in the role of

Noun + として says in what role, position or capacity someone acts, or what something is used
as or seen as.

{私|わたし}は{会社|かいしゃ}の{代表|だいひょう}として{会議|かいぎ}に{出|で}ました。 — I attended the meeting as the company's representative.
この{部屋|へや}は{今|いま}、{事務所|じむしょ}として{使|つか}っています。 — We use this room as an office now.
{京都|きょうと}は{古|ふる}い{寺|てら}の{町|まち}として{有名|ゆうめい}です。 — Kyoto is famous as a city of old temples.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{留学生|りゅうがくせい}として{日本|にほん}に{来|き}て、そのまま{日本|にほん}の{会社|かいしゃ}に{勤|つと}めています。 — She came to Japan as an international student and has worked for a Japanese company ever since.

English often says "as" or "for" here, and both translate として. For a role, Japanese
doesn't normally use で: ×{医師|いし}で{働|はたら}く sounds wrong; it's {医師|いし}として{働|はたら}く. (With a
place, で is right: {病院|びょういん}で{働|はたら}く, to work at a hospital. A type of employment
also takes で: アルバイトで{働|はたら}く, to work part-time.)

### 〜としては, 〜としても, 〜としての

- 〜としては puts the role up as a topic: "as far as … is concerned", "speaking as…". It often
  gives the official position of a person or group.
  {会社|かいしゃ}としては、{今年|ことし}{新|あたら}しい{人|ひと}を{入|い}れる{予定|よてい}はありません。 —
  As a company, we have no plans to take on new people this year.
  {私|わたし}としては、もう{少|すこ}し{待|ま}ったほうがいいと{思|おも}います。 — Speaking for myself, I
  think we'd better wait a little longer.
- 〜としても adds "also as" (も: too): {彼|かれ}は{医師|いし}としても、{作家|さっか}としても{有名|ゆうめい}です。
  — He's famous both as a doctor and as a writer.
- 〜としての + noun describes the noun: {社会人|しゃかいじん}としての{責任|せきにん} (the responsibility of
  a working adult, literally "responsibility as a working adult"), {医師|いし}としての{経験|けいけん}
  (experience as a doctor). The の is needed: ×{社会人|しゃかいじん}として{責任|せきにん}.

To recognize: {一人|ひとり}として〜ない means "not a single person": {一人|ひとり}として{遅|おく}れた{人|ひと}は
いなかった (not one person was late). It's emphatic and a little literary.

## 〜にとって: for, from the point of view of

Noun + にとって says from whose point of view a judgement is made. What follows is an evaluation:
{大切|たいせつ}だ, {大事|だいじ}だ, {難|むずか}しい, ありがたい, {便利|べんり}だ, {問題|もんだい}だ, {意味|いみ}が
ある and the like.

{私|わたし}にとって、{仕事|しごと}は{生活|せいかつ}の{一部|いちぶ}です。 — For me, work is a part of life.
{外国人|がいこくじん}にとって、けいごは{難|むずか}しいです。 — For foreigners, honorific language is difficult.
{給料日|きゅうりょうび}は、{会社員|かいしゃいん}にとって{一番|いちばん}うれしい{日|ひ}かもしれません。 — Payday may be the happiest day for office workers.
この{制度|せいど}は、{働|はたら}く{親|おや}にとって{役|やく}に{立|た}ちます。 — This system is useful for working parents.

({一部|いちぶ} = a part; けいご = honorific language, written in kana here because one of its
kanji is outside N3; {制度|せいど} = a system, lesson 9.)

What にとって can't do is introduce an action done for someone. "For (the benefit of)" is
のために, and the person you do something to or give something to takes に:

| You mean | Say | Not |
|---|---|---|
| I made a cake for my mother. | {母|はは}のためにケーキを{作|つく}りました。 | ×{母|はは}にとってケーキを{作|つく}りました。 |
| I explained it to the customer. | {客|きゃく}に{説明|せつめい}しました。 | ×{客|きゃく}にとって{説明|せつめい}しました。 |
| This job is hard for me. | この{仕事|しごと}は{私|わたし}にとって{大変|たいへん}です。 | |

In conversation, 〜には often does the same job: {私|わたし}には{難|むずか}しすぎます (it's too hard for
me). And some adjectives take に by themselves: {体|からだ}にいい (good for your health),
{若者|わかもの}に{人気|にんき}がある (popular with young people).

にとっては and にとっても work as you'd expect (for X at least; for X too), and にとっての + noun
describes a noun: {私|わたし}にとっての{幸|しあわ}せ (happiness as I see it).

### として or にとって?

Both translate "for" or "as" now and then, but they answer different questions.

| | として | にとって |
|---|---|---|
| Asks | in what role? | from whose point of view? |
| What follows | anything: an action, a state, a judgement | a judgement |
| Example | {親|おや}として{心配|しんぱい}です (as a parent, I worry) | {親|おや}にとって{子供|こども}は{一番|いちばん}{大切|たいせつ}です (to parents, children matter most) |

The two meet in a pair that's easy to mix up:

{私|わたし}としては、{転職|てんしょく}しないほうがいいと{思|おも}います。 — Personally, I think it's better not to change jobs. (my position, my opinion)
{私|わたし}にとっては、{給料|きゅうりょう}より{時間|じかん}のほうが{大事|だいじ}です。 — For me, time matters more than salary. (what it means to me)

## 〜に対して: towards, to; in contrast

に{対|たい}して has two main jobs.

### 1. The target of an attitude or action

Noun + に{対|たい}して marks who or what an attitude, a feeling, words or an action are aimed at.
It's often with verbs and adjectives of attitude: きびしい (strict; its kanji is outside N3),
ていねいだ, {失礼|しつれい}だ, {意見|いけん}を{言|い}う, {答|こた}える.

{課長|かちょう}は{部下|ぶか}に{対|たい}してきびしいですが、{自分|じぶん}に{対|たい}してはもっときびしいです。 — The section chief is strict with his staff, but even stricter with himself.
{会社|かいしゃ}の{決定|けってい}に{対|たい}して、{多|おお}くの{社員|しゃいん}が{意見|いけん}を{言|い}いました。 — Many employees spoke up about the company's decision.
お{客様|きゃくさま}の{質問|しつもん}に{対|たい}して、すぐに{答|こた}えられませんでした。 — I couldn't answer the customer's question straight away.

({決定|けってい} = decision, lesson 8; お{客様|きゃくさま} = customer, lesson 24.)

For plain giving and telling, に alone is the normal choice: {友|とも}だちに{本|ほん}を{貸|か}した (I lent
a friend a book), not ×{友|とも}だちに{対|たい}して{本|ほん}を{貸|か}した. に{対|たい}して is for an attitude
towards someone, or for a reply or reaction to something, and it's more formal.

### 2. Contrast: A のに対して, B

Plain form + のに{対|たい}して (or noun + に{対|たい}して) sets two facts side by side: "whereas",
"while". It's common in reports and explanations.

{兄|あに}が{会社員|かいしゃいん}なのに{対|たい}して、{弟|おとうと}は{職人|しょくにん}です。 — My older brother is an office worker, whereas my younger brother is a craftsman.
{東京|とうきょう}{本社|ほんしゃ}は{残業|ざんぎょう}が{多|おお}いのに{対|たい}して、{名古屋|なごや}{支社|ししゃ}はほとんどありません。 — The Tokyo head office has a lot of overtime, while the Nagoya branch has almost none.

Nouns and な-adjectives take な: {会社員|かいしゃいん}なのに{対|たい}して (in writing also 〜である
のに{対|たい}して). Don't confuse this with N4's のに (although): のに{対|たい}して only compares, with no
surprise or complaint.

One more use to recognize, in statistics: {社員|しゃいん}{三人|さんにん}に{対|たい}して{一人|ひとり} (one
for every three employees: a ratio).

### に対する + noun

Before a noun, に{対|たい}して becomes に{対|たい}する: {仕事|しごと}に{対|たい}する{考|かんが}え{方|かた} (one's
attitude to work), {客|きゃく}に{対|たい}する{言葉|ことば}づかい (the way you speak to customers). に{対|たい}しての
+ noun also exists and means the same.

### にとって or に対して?

にとって is about a judgement seen from someone's side; に{対|たい}して is about what's aimed at
someone. If an action follows, it can't be にとって:

{課長|かちょう}は{部下|ぶか}に{対|たい}して、いつもていねいに{話|はな}します。 — The section chief always speaks politely to his staff. (×{部下|ぶか}にとって{話|はな}します)
{部下|ぶか}にとって、{話|はな}しやすいじょうしはありがたいです。 — For staff, a boss who is easy to talk to is a blessing. (×{部下|ぶか}に{対|たい}して、ありがたいです)

## Noun-modifying forms

A compound particle ending in て can't go straight before a noun. It takes a
**[[noun-modifying form]]** instead. There are two patterns:

| Compound particle | Before a noun | Example |
|---|---|---|
| として | としての | {社会人|しゃかいじん}としての{責任|せきにん} (the responsibility of a working adult) |
| にとって | にとっての | {私|わたし}にとっての{幸|しあわ}せ (happiness as I see it) |
| に{対|たい}して | に{対|たい}する (に{対|たい}しての) | {仕事|しごと}に{対|たい}する{考|かんが}え{方|かた} (one's attitude to work) |
| について (lesson 12) | についての | {仕事|しごと}についての{質問|しつもん} (questions about the job) |
| に{関|かん}して (lesson 12) | に{関|かん}する (に{関|かん}しての) | {給料|きゅうりょう}に{関|かん}する{資料|しりょう} (documents on pay) |
| によって (lesson 13) | による | {人|ひと}による{違|ちが}い (differences from person to person) |

Most compound particles just add の to the て form. The ones built on a verb that keeps its own
meaning ({対|たい}する, {関|かん}する, よる) usually use that verb's dictionary form, which sounds more formal;
for に{対|たい}して and に{関|かん}して the の form is also heard, while ×によっての is rare. The
reference sheet "Formal phrases" lists every one in this module.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for the working world. Only the readings you meet at N3 are listed.

### Working

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 職 | job, post | ショク | | 18 | {職業|しょくぎょう} (occupation), {職場|しょくば} (workplace), {職員|しょくいん} (staff member), {退職|たいしょく}, {転職|てんしょく} |
| 勤 | work for, serve | キン | つと(める) | 12 | {勤|つと}める, {通勤|つうきん} (commuting), {勤務|きんむ}, {出勤|しゅっきん}, {勤|つと}め{先|さき} (workplace) |
| 務 | duty, task | ム | つと(める) | 11 | {事務|じむ} (office work), {事務所|じむしょ}, {業務|ぎょうむ} (business, tasks), {公務員|こうむいん} |
| 労 | labour, toil | ロウ | | 7 | {労働|ろうどう} (labour), {労働者|ろうどうしゃ} (worker), {苦労|くろう} (hardship) |
| 給 | pay, supply | キュウ | | 12 | {給料|きゅうりょう}, {給料日|きゅうりょうび} (payday), {時給|じきゅう} (hourly pay), {月給|げっきゅう}, {給食|きゅうしょく} (school lunch) |

### Roles and responsibility

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 任 | entrust; duty | ニン | まか(せる) | 6 | {任|まか}せる (to leave to someone), {責任|せきにん} |
| 責 | blame; duty | セキ | せ(める) | 11 | {責任|せきにん} (responsibility), {責任者|せきにんしゃ}, {責|せ}める (to blame) |
| 役 | role, use | ヤク | | 7 | {役|やく} (a role), {役割|やくわり}, {役|やく}に{立|た}つ, {役員|やくいん}, {役所|やくしょ}, {市役所|しやくしょ} |
| 係 | person in charge; connection | ケイ | かかり (がかり) | 9 | {係|かかり}, {係長|かかりちょう} (subsection chief), {関係|かんけい} (relation, lesson 12) |

### The company

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 部 | part; department | ブ | | 11 | {部|ぶ} (department), {部長|ぶちょう}, {部下|ぶか}, {部分|ぶぶん} (part), {全部|ぜんぶ}, {部屋|へや} |
| 課 | section; lesson | カ | | 15 | {課|か} (section), {課長|かちょう}, {課題|かだい} (assignment, lesson 12), {第一課|だいいっか} (Lesson 1 of a textbook) |

### Leaving

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 退 | withdraw, leave | タイ | | 9 | {退職|たいしょく} (retiring, leaving a job), {退社|たいしゃ}, {早退|そうたい} (leaving early), {退職金|たいしょくきん} |
| 辞 | resign; words | ジ | や(める) | 13 | {辞職|じしょく} (resignation), {辞|や}める (to quit a job), {辞書|じしょ} |

Carried words you can now write with kanji: {勤|つと}める, {給料|きゅうりょう}, {部長|ぶちょう}, {部下|ぶか},
{全部|ぜんぶ}, {係|かかり}, {市役所|しやくしょ}, {辞書|じしょ}, and {部屋|へや}, a special reading: 屋 is
the や of {本屋|ほんや}, but 部 is never read へ anywhere else, so learn {部屋|へや} as a whole word.

Notes:

- {勤|つと}める and {務|つと}める are the same word つとめる (N5) written two ways. {勤|つと}める is "to work for (a
  company)": {銀行|ぎんこう}に{勤|つと}める. {務|つと}める is "to serve as, to fill a role":
  {代表|だいひょう}を{務|つと}める (to act as the representative). A third spelling, {努|つと}める (to
  make an effort), belongs to lesson 28's kanji.
- {辞|や}める is N4's やめる when it means quitting a job or a post: {会社|かいしゃ}を{辞|や}める. For giving
  up a habit, write やめる: たばこをやめる.
- {退職|たいしょく} is the general word for leaving a job (including retiring at {定年|ていねん}); {辞職|じしょく} is
  formal, for resigning from a post, as in the news. {退社|たいしゃ} means both "leaving the office for
  the day" and "leaving the company"; context decides.
- 係 is かかり on its own, but がかり after another word: {安全係|あんぜんがかり} (the person in charge of
  safety). This is the same sound change as こえ → ごえ in N4.

Memory notes (hooks, not etymology):

- 勤 and 務 both have 力 (strength) on the right or at the bottom: you work with your strength. 労
  has it too, under a little crown of sparks: work so hard the sparks fly.
- 職: an ear (耳) on the left, then a sound (音) and a spear: a craftsperson who listens to the
  tool.
- 給: the thread radical on the left and 合 (to fit together): what keeps your life sewn together, your
  pay.
- 任 is a person (the thin form of 人, on the left) carrying a load; 責 has a shell, old money, at the bottom: money you owe,
  a duty.
- 役 starts with the "going" radical, a doubled person: someone going out to do their part.
- 係: a person (the thin 人 again) next to a hanging thread: the person tied to the job.
- 課 is words (言) and fruit (果): the fruit of your words, your assignment.
- 退 sits on the "moving" radical (⻌): moving back, leaving. 辞 has a tongue on the left: words,
  and resigning with a few last words.

```trace
職勤務労給任責役係部課退辞
```

## Dialogue: thinking of changing jobs

Haruka and Daisuke were at university together and meet for coffee. (Casual: old friends.)

```dialogue
# At a café
はるか: だいすけ、{最近|さいきん}{元気|げんき}ないね。{仕事|しごと}、{忙|いそが}しいの？
= Daisuke, you haven't seemed yourself lately. Is work busy?
だいすけ: うん…。{実|じつ}は、{転職|てんしょく}しようかと{思|おも}ってるんだ。
= Yeah... Actually, I'm thinking of changing jobs.
はるか: えっ、{本当|ほんとう}に？ {今|いま}の{会社|かいしゃ}、{給料|きゅうりょう}がいいって{言|い}ってたじゃない。
= What, really? You said your company paid well, didn't you?
だいすけ: {給料|きゅうりょう}はね。でも、{去年|きょねん}{係長|かかりちょう}になってから、{毎晩|まいばん}{十時|じゅうじ}まで{残業|ざんぎょう}なんだよ。{係長|かかりちょう}として{責任|せきにん}があるから、{先|さき}に{帰|かえ}れないし。
= The pay, yes. But since I became a subsection chief last year, I've been doing overtime till ten every night. As subsection chief I've got responsibilities, so I can't leave first.
はるか: そっか。{課長|かちょう}は{何|なん}て{言|い}ってるの？
= I see. What does your section chief say?
だいすけ: {課長|かちょう}は{部下|ぶか}に{対|たい}してはいい{人|ひと}なんだけど、{大事|だいじ}な{仕事|しごと}を{全部|ぜんぶ}ぼくに{任|まか}せるんだ。
= He's nice to his staff, but he leaves all the important work to me.
はるか: それは{大変|たいへん}だね。でも、だいすけにとって、{一番|いちばん}{大事|だいじ}なのは{何|なに}？ お{金|かね}？ {時間|じかん}？
= That's tough. But for you, what matters most? Money? Time?
だいすけ: {前|まえ}はお{金|かね}だと{思|おも}ってた。でも{今|いま}は、{家族|かぞく}との{時間|じかん}かな。{子供|こども}もまだ{小|ちい}さいし。
= I used to think it was money. But now I'd say time with my family. The kids are still small.
はるか: じゃあ、{在宅勤務|ざいたくきんむ}ができる{会社|かいしゃ}はどう？ うちの{会社|かいしゃ}は{週|しゅう}に{三日|みっか}、{家|いえ}で{働|はたら}けるよ。
= Then how about a company where you can work from home? At mine you can work from home three days a week.
だいすけ: いいなあ。でも、{今|いま}の{会社|かいしゃ}に{対|たい}して、もうしわけない{気持|きも}ちもあるんだよね。
= Sounds great. But I also feel bad towards my current company.
はるか: {会社|かいしゃ}としては{困|こま}るかもしれないけど、だいすけの{人生|じんせい}だよ。{一度|いちど}、うちの{会社|かいしゃ}の{話|はなし}を{聞|き}きに{来|き}たら？
= The company might not like it, but it's your life. Why not come and hear about my company once?
だいすけ: うん、そうしてみる。ありがとう。
= Yeah, I'll do that. Thanks.
```

そっか = casual そうか (I see); じゃない with a rising tone = "didn't you?"; もうしわけない = to feel
sorry, to feel bad (one kanji is outside N3); 〜たら？ = why don't you…? (N4). Daisuke says ぼく,
in kana as in lesson 1. Notice where the compound particles go: {係長|かかりちょう}として (his role),
{部下|ぶか}に{対|たい}しては (the target of the boss's attitude, with は for contrast: nice to his staff,
but…), だいすけにとって (whose values), {会社|かいしゃ}としては (the company's position).

## Reading: an interview in a company newsletter

A page from a factory's newsletter, in its series "{仕事|しごと}の{話|はなし}" (talking about work). It's
in polite です/ます style, as interviews usually are.

> ――{木村|きむら}さんは、どんなお{仕事|しごと}をしていますか。
>
> {工場|こうじょう}の{安全|あんぜん}の{責任者|せきにんしゃ}として{働|はたら}いています。{大|おお}きなきかいを{使|つか}う{職場|しょくば}なので、じこが{起|お}きないように、{毎日|まいにち}{工場|こうじょう}の{中|なか}を{見|み}て{回|まわ}っています。
>
> ――この{仕事|しごと}を{始|はじ}めたきっかけは{何|なん}ですか。
>
> {十年前|じゅうねんまえ}までは、{本社|ほんしゃ}で{事務|じむ}の{仕事|しごと}をしていました。ある{日|ひ}、{工場|こうじょう}で{働|はたら}いていた{友人|ゆうじん}が、ひどいけがをしたんです。そのとき、{働|はたら}く{人|ひと}にとって{一番|いちばん}{大切|たいせつ}なのは{安全|あんぜん}な{職場|しょくば}だと{思|おも}いました。それで、{工場|こうじょう}に{転勤|てんきん}させてほしいと、{自分|じぶん}から{会社|かいしゃ}に{頼|たの}みました。
>
> ――{大変|たいへん}なことは{何|なん}ですか。
>
> {注意|ちゅうい}することです。{年上|としうえ}の{職人|しょくにん}さんに{対|たい}して「その{使|つか}い{方|かた}は{危|あぶ}ないですよ」と{言|い}うのは、{今|いま}でもきんちょうします。でも、{責任者|せきにんしゃ}としての{役割|やくわり}がありますから、{相手|あいて}がだれでも、{言|い}うべきことは{言|い}います。
>
> ――{最後|さいご}に、{今年|ことし}{社会人|しゃかいじん}になる{人|ひと}に{一言|ひとこと}お{願|ねが}いします。
>
> {給料|きゅうりょう}も{大事|だいじ}ですが、「{自分|じぶん}にとって{意味|いみ}のある{仕事|しごと}は{何|なに}か」を{一度|いちど}{考|かんが}えてみてください。{私|わたし}としては、{人|ひと}の{役|やく}に{立|た}っていると{感|かん}じられる{仕事|しごと}が、{一番|いちばん}{長|なが}く{続|つづ}けられると{思|おも}います。

きかい = machine and じこ = accident (N4, one kanji each is outside N3);
{見|み}て{回|まわ}る = to go round checking; きっかけ = what started something, the trigger; ひどい =
terrible; きんちょうする = to get nervous (kanji outside N3); {言|い}うべきこと = what should be said
(lesson 9); {年上|としうえ} = older (lesson 1).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What is Mr Kimura's job now? — He's in charge of safety at the factory: he walks round it
   every day so that accidents don't happen.
2. Why did he move from the head office to the factory? — A friend who worked at the factory was
   badly hurt, and he felt that a safe workplace matters most to workers, so he asked for the
   transfer himself.
3. What does he still find hard? — Warning older craftsmen that what they're doing is
   dangerous; it still makes him nervous.
4. What advice does he give new workers? — Pay matters, but think about which work is
   meaningful to you; he believes work where you feel useful to people is the work you can keep
   doing longest.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

— Mr Kimura, what kind of work do you do?

I work as the person responsible for safety at the factory. It's a workplace that uses big
machines, so I go round the factory every day checking, so that there are no accidents.

— What made you start this job?

Until ten years ago I did office work at the head office. One day a friend who worked at the
factory was badly injured. That's when I thought that what matters most to people at work is a
safe workplace. So I asked the company myself to transfer me to the factory.

— What's hard about it?

Giving warnings. Even now I get nervous saying to an older craftsman, "That's a dangerous way
to use it." But I have a role as the person in charge, so whoever it is, I say what needs to be
said.

— Finally, a word for people starting work this year, please.

Pay is important too, but please think once about what work is meaningful to you. Speaking for
myself, I think work where you can feel you're useful to people is the work you can keep doing
longest.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{社会人|しゃかいじん}としての{責任|せきにん:0}があります。
= I have responsibilities as a working adult.
{私|わたし}にとって、{家族|かぞく}が{一番|いちばん}{大切|たいせつ:0}です。
= For me, my family matters most.
お{客様|きゃくさま}に{対|たい}しては、ていねいに{話|はな}しましょう。
= Let's speak politely to customers.
この{仕事|しごと}は{私|わたし}に{任|まか}せてください。
= Please leave this job to me.
{来月|らいげつ}から{名古屋|なごや}{支社|ししゃ}に{転勤|てんきん:0}することになりました。
= I'm being transferred to the Nagoya branch from next month.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{医師|いし}で{働|はたら}く. A role takes として: {医師|いし}として{働|はたら}く.
- ×{社会人|しゃかいじん}として{責任|せきにん}. Before a noun, add の: {社会人|しゃかいじん}としての{責任|せきにん}.
- ×{母|はは}にとってケーキを{作|つく}った. にとって is followed by a judgement, not an action done for
  someone: {母|はは}のためにケーキを{作|つく}った.
- ×{私|わたし}に{対|たい}して、この{仕事|しごと}は{大事|だいじ}だ. A judgement from your point of view is
  にとって: {私|わたし}にとって、この{仕事|しごと}は{大事|だいじ}だ.
- ×{兄|あに}は{会社員|かいしゃいん}のに{対|たい}して. Nouns and な-adjectives need な: {会社員|かいしゃいん}なのに{対|たい}して.
- Spelling: this course writes として and にとって in kana and に{対|たい}して with its kanji.

## Key points

- Compound particles are particle + verb form units that work like one particle: として,
  にとって, に{対|たい}して (and について, によって later in the module).
- 〜として: as, in the role of. 〜としては: speaking as, X's position; 〜としても: also as;
  〜としての + noun.
- 〜にとって: for, from X's point of view, followed by a judgement ({大切|たいせつ}だ, {難|むずか}しい, ありがたい).
  "For the benefit of" is のために.
- 〜に{対|たい}して: towards (the target of an attitude, words or a reaction); A のに{対|たい}して B:
  whereas. Before a noun: に{対|たい}する.
- Noun-modifying forms: としての, にとっての, に{対|たい}する, についての, に{関|かん}する, による.
- {勤|つと}める (work for) and {務|つと}める (serve as) are one word; {辞|や}める is quitting a job.
- New kanji: 職 勤 務 労 給 任 責 役 係 部 課 退 辞.

The reference sheet "Formal phrases" collects this module's compound particles. The words from
this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: About and centred on: について, に関して, を中心に, をはじめ, において
topics: について and に関して
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 11 gave roles and viewpoints. This lesson gives the phrases that say what a text, a talk
or a piece of research is about, what it centres on, which example leads the list, and where
it takes place. They're the vocabulary of papers, presentations, notices and reports, so the
theme is university life and research: subjects, seminars, surveys, data and essays.

この{論文|ろんぶん}は、{留学生|りゅうがくせい}の{生活|せいかつ}について{書|か}かれています。 — This paper is about the lives of international students.
{試験|しけん}に{関|かん}する{質問|しつもん}は、メールでお{願|ねが}いします。 — Please send questions about the exam by email.
このじゅぎょうでは、{会話|かいわ}を{中心|ちゅうしん}に{勉強|べんきょう}します。 — In this class we'll focus mainly on conversation.
{学長|がくちょう}をはじめ、{多|おお}くの{先生|せんせい}が{参加|さんか}しました。 — Many teachers took part, the university president among them.
{発表|はっぴょう}は{第一|だいいち}{会議室|かいぎしつ}において{行|おこな}われます。 — The presentations will be held in Meeting Room 1.

Spelling, as promised in lesson 11: について and において in kana; に{関|かん}して and
を{中心|ちゅうしん}に with their kanji; をはじめ usually in kana.

## 〜について: about (review and new forms)

You met について in N4: noun + について + a verb of speaking, thinking, writing, asking or
researching.

{日本|にほん}の{歴史|れきし}について{調|しら}べています。 — I'm researching Japanese history.
しょうらいのことについて、{親|おや}と{話|はな}しました。 — I talked with my parents about my future. (しょうらい: one kanji outside N3)

New at N3 are its three other forms:

- についての + noun: {留学生|りゅうがくせい}の{生活|せいかつ}についてのアンケート (a questionnaire about
  international students' lives). This is lesson 11's noun-modifying form.
- については makes it a contrastive topic: "as for…": {費用|ひよう}については、{後|あと}で{説明|せつめい}
  します (as for the costs, I'll explain later).
- についても: "about … too": この{点|てん}についても{考|かんが}えてください (please think
  about this point too).

## 〜に関して, 〜に関する: concerning, regarding

に{関|かん}して means much the same as について, but it's more formal, so it suits notices, reports,
emails and announcements. Before a noun it becomes に{関|かん}する.

この{件|けん}に{関|かん}して、{何|なに}かご{質問|しつもん}はありますか。 — Do you have any questions concerning this matter?
{試験|しけん}の{内容|ないよう}に{関|かん}しては、{来週|らいしゅう}のじゅぎょうで{説明|せつめい}します。 — As for what the exam covers, I'll explain in next week's class.
{日本|にほん}の{教育|きょういく}に{関|かん}する{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでいます。 — I'm reading a book on Japanese education.

({件|けん} = a matter, a case, lesson 19.)

### について or に関して?

In most written sentences you can swap them. The differences are of tone and focus:

| | について | に{関|かん}して |
|---|---|---|
| Style | everyday and written | formal, written, announcements |
| Focus | the topic itself | the topic and what's related to it |
| Before a noun | についての | に{関|かん}する |
| In chat | natural: {映画|えいが}について{話|はな}そう | stiff: ×{映画|えいが}に{関|かん}して{話|はな}そうよ |

に{関|かん}する is very common in titles and headings: {留学|りゅうがく}に{関|かん}するお{知|し}らせ (a notice
about studying abroad), {働|はたら}き{方|かた}に{関|かん}するちょうさ (a survey on ways of working).
ちょうさ (a survey, an investigation) is written in kana here because one of its kanji is outside
N3.

## 〜を中心に: centred on, mainly

Noun + を{中心|ちゅうしん}に(して) says what's at the centre: of a place, a group, an activity or a
topic. It often translates "mainly", "focusing on" or "around".

{駅|えき}を{中心|ちゅうしん}に、{店|みせ}や{会社|かいしゃ}が{集|あつ}まっています。 — Shops and offices are gathered around the station.
このゲームは{若者|わかもの}を{中心|ちゅうしん}に{人気|にんき}があります。 — This game is popular, mainly among young people.
{今日|きょう}のこうぎは、{前回|ぜんかい}のふくしゅうを{中心|ちゅうしん}に{進|すす}めます。 — Today's lecture will focus mainly on reviewing last time.

(こうぎ = a lecture and ふくしゅう = review: both stay in kana because they have kanji outside
N3.)

Other forms:

- を{中心|ちゅうしん}として is a more formal を{中心|ちゅうしん}に.
- を{中心|ちゅうしん}とした / を{中心|ちゅうしん}とする + noun: {東京|とうきょう}を{中心|ちゅうしん}とした
  {関東|かんとう}{地方|ちほう} (the Kanto region, centred on Tokyo).
- が{中心|ちゅうしん}だ for a plain statement: じゅぎょうは{会話|かいわ}が{中心|ちゅうしん}です (the
  class is mainly conversation).

## 〜をはじめ: starting with, including

Noun + をはじめ(として) names the best-known or most important member of a group, then the
group: "A and others", "A, B and many more", "not least A". What follows is plural: {多|おお}くの,
いろいろな, たくさんの, {全国|ぜんこく}の, 〜など.

{学長|がくちょう}をはじめ、{多|おお}くの{先生|せんせい}が{卒業式|そつぎょうしき}に{出席|しゅっせき}しました。 — Many teachers, led by the university president, attended the graduation ceremony.
{東京|とうきょう}の{大学|だいがく}をはじめ、{全国|ぜんこく}の{大学|だいがく}で{同|おな}じちょうさが{行|おこな}われた。 — The same survey was carried out at universities around the country, starting with those in Tokyo.
{日本|にほん}には、すしをはじめ、{世界|せかい}で{人気|にんき}がある{料理|りょうり}がたくさんあります。 — Japan has many dishes that are popular around the world, sushi first among them.

Before a noun: をはじめとする: {京都|きょうと}をはじめとする{古|ふる}い{町|まち} (old cities such as Kyoto).
It isn't for a single item on its own: ×{田中|たなか}さんをはじめ、{来|き}ました needs a group after
it ({田中|たなか}さんをはじめ、{研究室|けんきゅうしつ}の{全員|ぜんいん}が{来|き}ました, everyone from the lab came, Ms
Tanaka included). The kanji 始め is possible (をはじめ comes from はじめる, to start), but kana is
the common choice.

## 〜において, 〜における: in, at (formal)

において is a formal で: in or at a place, a time, a situation or a field. It belongs to writing,
speeches and announcements; in conversation, use で. Before a noun it becomes における.

{入学式|にゅうがくしき}は、{四月|しがつ}{三日|みっか}に{大|だい}ホールにおいて{行|おこな}われます。 — The entrance ceremony will be held in the main hall on 3 April.
{現代|げんだい}の{社会|しゃかい}において、インターネットは{欠|か}かせないものだ。 — In modern society, the internet is something we can't do without.
この{分野|ぶんや}における{研究|けんきゅう}は、まだ{少|すく}ない。 — There is still little research in this field.

({欠|か}かせない = indispensable, lesson 18's kanji.)

において doesn't replace every で. It isn't for the place of an everyday action
(×{家|いえ}において{昼|ひる}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べた sounds comic) or for means and materials (with a pen, in
English: ペンで, {英語|えいご}で). It suits events, fields and periods.

## The five side by side

| Phrase | Meaning | Before a noun | Style | Spelling |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| について | about | についての | everyday + written | kana |
| に{関|かん}して | concerning | に{関|かん}する | formal | kanji |
| を{中心|ちゅうしん}に | centred on, mainly | を{中心|ちゅうしん}とした / とする | neutral | kanji |
| をはじめ | starting with, including | をはじめとする | written-ish | kana |
| において | in, at | における | formal, written | kana |

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for study and research. Only the readings you meet at N3 are listed.

### Thinking it through

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 論 | argue; theory | ロン | | 15 | {論文|ろんぶん} (paper, thesis), {理論|りろん} (theory), {卒論|そつろん} (graduation thesis), {結論|けつろん} (conclusion, lesson 28) |
| 調 | investigate; tune | チョウ | しら(べる) | 15 | {調|しら}べる, {調|しら}べ{物|もの} (looking things up), {調子|ちょうし}, {強調|きょうちょう} (emphasis) |
| 解 | untie, solve | カイ | と(く), と(ける) | 13 | {解|と}く (to solve), {解|と}ける (to be solved), {解決|かいけつ}, {解説|かいせつ}, {理解|りかい}, {解答|かいとう} |
| 例 | example | レイ | たと(えば) | 8 | {例|れい}, {例|たと}えば, {例文|れいぶん}, {例外|れいがい} (exception) |

### Fields of study

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 科 | department, branch of study | カ | | 9 | {科学|かがく} (science), {科目|かもく} (subject), {学科|がっか} (department), {科学者|かがくしゃ} |
| 術 | art, skill | ジュツ | | 11 | {美術|びじゅつ} (fine art), {美術館|びじゅつかん}, {手術|しゅじゅつ} (operation) |

### Showing

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 表 | surface; show; table | ヒョウ | おもて, あらわ(す) | 8 | {表|ひょう} (a table, a chart), {表|あらわ}す, {表現|ひょうげん}, {発表|はっぴょう}, {代表|だいひょう}, {表|おもて} (front) |
| 示 | show, point to | ジ | しめ(す) | 5 | {示|しめ}す (to show, to indicate), {指示|しじ} (instructions, lesson 29) |

### Order, links and contents

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 第 | ordinal prefix | ダイ | | 11 | {第一|だいいち} (first, number one), {第二|だいに}, {第一課|だいいっか} |
| 関 | connection; barrier | カン | | 14 | {関係|かんけい}, {関心|かんしん} (interest), {関連|かんれん}, {関東|かんとう}, {関西|かんさい} |
| 参 | take part; refer | サン | | 8 | {参考|さんこう} (reference), {参考書|さんこうしょ} (study guide), {参加|さんか} (taking part, lesson 23) |
| 内 | inside | ナイ | うち | 4 | {内容|ないよう} (contents), {国内|こくない} (domestic, lesson 13), {以内|いない} (within), {内側|うちがわ} |
| 容 | contain; form | ヨウ | | 10 | {内容|ないよう}, {美容院|びよういん} (hair salon, lesson 16) |

Carried words you can now write with kanji: {調|しら}べる, {調子|ちょうし}, {発表|はっぴょう}, {美術館|びじゅつかん},
{関西|かんさい}, and, with kanji from other N3 lessons, {必要|ひつよう}, {歴史|れきし} and {図書館|としょかん}. One
carried word stays in kana: まいる, the humble "come, go", follows the course rule for keigo
verbs even though 参 is now on the list.

Notes:

- 表 has three faces: ヒョウ in {表|ひょう} (a table of figures) and {発表|はっぴょう}; あらわ(す) in
  {表|あらわ}す (to express, to stand for); おもて in {表|おもて} (the front, the surface, the outside:
  {紙|かみ}の{表|おもて}, the front of the sheet).
- {解|と}く (transitive: you solve it) and {解|と}ける (intransitive: it gets solved) are a pair like
  N4's {開|あ}ける / {開|あ}く. {問題|もんだい}が{解|と}けた is "I managed to solve the problem" (literally,
  the problem got solved).
- 第 + number makes ordinals in writing: {第一|だいいち}, {第三回|だいさんかい} (the third time, the third
  session). In speech you'll also hear {一番目|いちばんめ}.
- {内|うち} as "inside" is formal or written ({内側|うちがわ}, the inside; がわ is lesson 13's {側|がわ}).
  The formal noun うち of 〜うちに (lesson 1) stays in kana.
- {解答|かいとう} is the answer to a test question; {回答|かいとう} is a reply to a survey or an enquiry.
  They sound the same; the kanji tell them apart.

Memory notes (hooks, not etymology):

- 論, 調 and 課 (lesson 11) all start with 言 (words): research is mostly words.
- 解: a horn on the left, a knife at the top right and a cow (牛) below it: cutting a cow
  apart, piece by piece, to see how it works.
- 科: a stalk of grain on the left and a measuring ladle on the right: sorting things into kinds, the
  branches of study.
- 術 is 行 (to go) with a sprouting plant in the middle: a skill that grows as you go.
- 示 is an altar: a sign shown to the gods. 表 hides the shape of a robe with a mark on it: what shows on
  the outside.
- 第 has bamboo on top (like 答 and 笑): numbered slips of bamboo in order.
- 関 is a gate (門) with something tied across it: a checkpoint, a connection.
- 内 is a person going in under a roof: inside. 容 has a roof and a valley under it: room to
  hold things, contents.

```trace
論調解例科術表示第関参内容
```

## Dialogue: preparing a presentation

Mao and Ryo are third-year students in the same seminar. They're in the library. (Casual:
classmates.)

```dialogue
# In the library
まお: りょうくん、{来週|らいしゅう}のゼミの{発表|はっぴょう}、テーマ{決|き}まった？
= Ryo, have you decided on a topic for next week's seminar presentation?
りょう: うん。{留学生|りゅうがくせい}のアルバイトについて{調|しら}べることにした。
= Yeah. I've decided to look into part-time work among international students.
まお: {面白|おもしろ}そう。データはあるの？
= Sounds interesting. Do you have any data?
りょう: {大学|だいがく}の{国際課|こくさいか}が{去年|きょねん}アンケートをしてて、その{結果|けっか}を{使|つか}わせてもらえることになったんだ。
= The university's international office did a questionnaire last year, and they've said I can use the results.
まお: いいね。どんな{内容|ないよう}？
= Nice. What's in it?
りょう: アルバイトの{時間|じかん}とか{時給|じきゅう}とか、{仕事|しごと}と{勉強|べんきょう}の{関係|かんけい}に{関|かん}する{質問|しつもん}が{中心|ちゅうしん}だよ。
= Mostly questions about hours and hourly pay and how work relates to study.
まお: {留学生|りゅうがくせい}って、{働|はたら}ける{時間|じかん}に{決|き}まりがあるよね。{確|たし}か{週|しゅう}に{二十八時間|にじゅうはちじかん}だっけ。
= International students have a limit on the hours they can work, don't they? Twenty-eight a week, was it?
りょう: そう。その{点|てん}についても、{先生|せんせい}が{参考|さんこう}になる{資料|しりょう}を{教|おし}えてくれた。
= That's right. Our professor told me about some useful materials on that point too.
まお: {私|わたし}はまだ{全然|ぜんぜん}…。{日本|にほん}の{食文化|しょくぶんか}をテーマにしたいんだけど、{広|ひろ}すぎて。
= I haven't got anywhere yet... I want to do Japanese food culture, but it's too broad.
りょう: じゃあ、{一|ひと}つの{地方|ちほう}を{中心|ちゅうしん}にしたら？ {例|たと}えば、{関西|かんさい}とか。
= Then why not centre it on one region? Kansai, for example.
まお: なるほど。{関西|かんさい}のこなもんをはじめ、{地方|ちほう}の{料理|りょうり}を{比|くら}べるのもいいかも。ありがとう！
= Good idea. Comparing regional dishes, starting with Kansai's flour-based foods, could work. Thanks!
```

{国際課|こくさいか} = the international office (its words are in lessons 11 and 13); 〜っけ = "was it?"
when you're trying to remember (lesson 17); こなもん = Kansai's word for dishes made with flour
batter, like okonomiyaki and takoyaki (lesson 25h1 is about Kansai speech). The limit Mao
mentions is the usual rule for students with a student visa, who also need permission to work
(in term time; it can change, so check the immigration website before relying on it).

## Reading: a campus newspaper article

From a university newspaper, in the plain だ style of news articles.

> {北山|きたやま}{大学|だいがく}は{先月|せんげつ}、{学生|がくせい}のアルバイトに{関|かん}するちょうさの{結果|けっか}を{発表|はっぴょう}した。ちょうさは{今年|ことし}の{五月|ごがつ}に{行|おこな}われ、{学部|がくぶ}の{学生|がくせい}を{中心|ちゅうしん}に、{約|やく}{二千人|にせんにん}が{回答|かいとう}した。
>
> {結果|けっか}によると、アルバイトをしている{学生|がくせい}は{全体|ぜんたい}の{七割|ななわり}だった。{働|はたら}く{理由|りゆう}についての{質問|しつもん}では、「{生活費|せいかつひ}のため」が{最|もっと}も{多|おお}く、「{社会|しゃかい}{経験|けいけん}のため」が{二番目|にばんめ}だった。{仕事|しごと}の{種類|しゅるい}を{見|み}ると、{飲食店|いんしょくてん}が{一番|いちばん}{多|おお}く、コンビニやスーパーをはじめとする{店|みせ}の{仕事|しごと}、{子供|こども}に{勉強|べんきょう}を{教|おし}える{仕事|しごと}が{続|つづ}いた。{時給|じきゅう}は{千百円|せんひゃくえん}から{千三百円|せんさんびゃくえん}ぐらいという{答|こた}えが{多|おお}かった。しかし、{週|しゅう}に{二十時間|にじゅうじかん}{以上|いじょう}{働|はたら}いている{学生|がくせい}の{半分|はんぶん}{近|ちか}くが、「じゅぎょうの{課題|かだい}をする{時間|じかん}が{足|た}りない」と{答|こた}えている。
>
> この{結果|けっか}について、{教育学部|きょういくがくぶ}の{山下|やました}きょうじゅは「アルバイトは{社会|しゃかい}を{知|し}るいい{機会|きかい}だが、{学生|がくせい}にとって{一番|いちばん}{大切|たいせつ}なのは{学|まな}ぶことだ。{大学|だいがく}としても、しょうがくきんをはじめ、{学生|がくせい}を{支|ささ}える{制度|せいど}を{増|ふ}やす{必要|ひつよう}がある」と{話|はな}している。
>
> {大学|だいがく}は、この{結果|けっか}を{参考|さんこう}に、{来年|らいねん}から{学生|がくせい}{生活|せいかつ}に{関|かん}する{相談|そうだん}の{窓口|まどぐち}を{増|ふ}やすことにしている。

{全体|ぜんたい} = the whole (lesson 4); {飲食店|いんしょくてん} = places to eat and drink; 〜{割|わり} = tenths, so {七割|ななわり} = 70% (lesson 4);
{最|もっと}も = most (lesson 14); {半分|はんぶん}{近|ちか}く = nearly half; {機会|きかい} = an opportunity;
きょうじゅ = professor and しょうがくきん = scholarship (kanji outside N3); {支|ささ}える = to support
(lesson 22); {相談|そうだん} = consultation (N4); {窓口|まどぐち} = a service counter (lesson 27's kanji).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. Who answered the survey? — About 2,000 students, mainly undergraduates
   ({学部|がくぶ}の{学生|がくせい}を{中心|ちゅうしん}に).
2. What was the most common reason for working? — Living costs ({生活費|せいかつひ}のため).
3. What problem did students working 20 hours or more a week report? — Nearly half said they
   didn't have enough time for their coursework.
4. What does Professor Yamashita say the university should do? — Increase the systems that
   support students, scholarships first among them.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Last month Kitayama University announced the results of a survey on students' part-time work.
The survey was carried out in May this year, and about 2,000 people answered, mainly
undergraduates.

According to the results, 70% of all students have a part-time job. In the question about why
they work, "for living costs" was the most common answer, and "for experience of the working
world" came second. By type of work, restaurants and cafés came first, followed by work in
shops such as convenience stores and supermarkets, and teaching children. Most said their
hourly pay was between about 1,100 and 1,300 yen. However, nearly half of the students who work twenty hours or more a week
answered that they don't have enough time to do their coursework.

On these results, Professor Yamashita of the Faculty of Education says, "Part-time work is a
good opportunity to get to know society, but for students the most important thing is
