lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 11 was about having a job. This honors lesson is about getting one the way many
Japanese students do: しゅうかつ, short for しゅうしょく{活動|かつどう} ("job-hunting activities"). One of
its kanji is outside N3, so it's written in kana here. You'll see how the process usually runs,
the documents and steps it uses, and how lesson 11's として and にとって turn up in interview
answers.

Everything about dates in this lesson describes the usual pattern in the mid-2020s. The rules
are guidelines, they've changed several times, and companies don't all follow them, so check
current information if you're job hunting yourself.

## Hiring new graduates all at once

Many Japanese companies, especially large ones, hire {新卒|しんそつ} (new graduates) as a group
once a year. Students hunt in their final year or so of university, receive an offer, finish
their studies, and start work together on 1 April, often with weeks of company training. Mid-
career hiring ({転職|てんしょく}, lesson 11) is common too and has been growing, but the {新卒|しんそつ}
route is still the big one.

## The usual calendar

The government asks companies to follow a timetable for students graduating in March. Roughly:

| When | What happens |
|---|---|
| Third-year summer and winter | インターンシップ (internships, often only a day or a few days) |
| 1 March of the third year | Companies start public recruiting: {説明会|せつめいかい} (information sessions) and sign-ups |
| From around March | エントリーシート, written tests, group discussions |
| 1 June of the fourth year | Formal selection (interviews) starts |
| 1 October of the fourth year | Formal offers: {内定|ないてい}; many companies hold a {内定式|ないていしき} (offer ceremony) |

In practice many companies, and many students, start earlier, and informal offers often come
well before October. Students apply to a lot of companies: dozens is not unusual.

## The steps and their words

- エントリー: signing up with a company, usually on its website or on a job-hunting site, to
  show interest and get information. The verb is エントリーする, or the Japanese word
  おうぼする (to apply; its kanji are outside N3).
- {説明会|せつめいかい}: an information session where a company explains its work, often online.
- エントリーシート (ES for short): the company's own application form, with questions such as
  {学生時代|がくせいじだい}に{力|ちから}を{入|い}れたこと (what you put most effort into as a student) and
  しぼう{動機|どうき} (why you want to join). しぼう means "your choice, what you hope for":
  {第一|だいいち}しぼう is your first choice.
- りれきしょ: a CV on a standard form: name, photo, education ({学歴|がくれき}), {資格|しかく}
  (qualifications, lesson 8) and a short self-introduction. Some companies still like it
  handwritten, but typed and online versions are now common.
- Written tests: general ability and personality tests; many companies use a commercial one.
- めんせつ (N4: the interview): often several rounds, from group interviews to a final one
  with senior staff.
- {内定|ないてい}: an informal job offer. A student who has one says {内定|ないてい}をもらった.
- さいよう: hiring, being hired (its kanji are outside N3): さいようされる (to be hired).

Many students wear a plain dark suit, the リクルートスーツ, for sessions and interviews, though
some companies now say casual clothes are fine.

## Interview language

Interviews use the polite language of N4's keigo lessons. Two words to know:

- おんしゃ, "your company", used in speech. In writing (an ES, an email) the word is きしゃ. Both
  have kanji outside N3.
- {私|わたし} is read わたくし in very formal speech.

Lesson 11's phrases are everywhere:

{大学|だいがく}では、サークルのリーダーとして、{五十人|ごじゅうにん}のメンバーをまとめました。 — At university I led a fifty-member club as its leader.
{私|わたし}にとって、{働|はたら}くことは{人|ひと}の{役|やく}に{立|た}つことです。 — For me, working means being useful to people.
{留学|りゅうがく}の{経験|けいけん}を、おんしゃの{海外|かいがい}の{仕事|しごと}に{生|い}かしたいと{思|おも}います。 — I'd like to put my experience of studying abroad to use in your company's overseas work.

(サークル = a university club; まとめる = to bring together, to lead; {生|い}かす = to make use of.)

## Dialogue: a practice interview

Sota is a fourth-year student. His university's careers office is giving him a practice
interview. (Formal: an interview.)

```dialogue
# Practice interview
めんせつかん: それでは、じこしょうかいをお{願|ねが}いします。
= Well then, please introduce yourself.
そうた: はい。{北山|きたやま}{大学|だいがく}{経済学部|けいざいがくぶ}{四年|よねん}の{木下|きのした}そうたともうします。{本日|ほんじつ}はよろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。
= Yes. My name is Sota Kinoshita, a fourth-year student in the Faculty of Economics at Kitayama University. Thank you for seeing me today.
めんせつかん: {学生時代|がくせいじだい}に{一番|いちばん}{力|ちから}を{入|い}れたことは{何|なん}ですか。
= What did you put the most effort into as a student?
そうた: {国際交流|こくさいこうりゅう}のサークルです。{三年生|さんねんせい}のときは{代表|だいひょう}として、{留学生|りゅうがくせい}と{地元|じもと}の{人|ひと}たちの{交流|こうりゅう}イベントを{十回|じっかい}{開|ひら}きました。
= An international exchange club. In my third year, as its representative, I organized ten events for international students and local people to meet.
めんせつかん: {大変|たいへん}だったことは{何|なん}ですか。
= What was difficult?
そうた: {国|くに}によって{考|かんが}え{方|かた}が{違|ちが}うので、みんなの{意見|いけん}をまとめるのに{苦労|くろう}しました。でも、{一人一人|ひとりひとり}の{話|はなし}をよく{聞|き}くことの{大切|たいせつ}さを{学|まな}びました。
= Ways of thinking differ from country to country, so bringing everyone's opinions together was hard. But I learned how important it is to listen carefully to each person.
めんせつかん: なぜ{当社|とうしゃ}をしぼうしたのですか。
= Why did you choose our company?
そうた: {説明会|せつめいかい}で、おんしゃは{若|わか}い{社員|しゃいん}にも{海外|かいがい}の{仕事|しごと}を{任|まか}せているとうかがいました。サークルでの{経験|けいけん}を{生|い}かして、{世界|せかい}の{人|ひと}とつながる{仕事|しごと}がしたいと{考|かんが}えています。
= At the information session I heard that your company gives overseas work even to young staff. I'd like to use my club experience in work that connects me with people around the world.
めんせつかん: では、あなたにとって、{働|はたら}くとはどういうことですか。
= Then, what does working mean to you?
そうた: {私|わたし}にとって{働|はたら}くことは、{自分|じぶん}の{力|ちから}で{人|ひと}の{役|やく}に{立|た}つことです。
= For me, working means being useful to people through my own abilities.
めんせつかん: {分|わ}かりました。{最後|さいご}に、{何|なに}か{質問|しつもん}はありますか。
= I see. Finally, do you have any questions?
そうた: はい。{入社|にゅうしゃ}してから{最初|さいしょ}の{一年|いちねん}は、どのような{仕事|しごと}をすることが{多|おお}いでしょうか。
= Yes. In the first year after joining, what kind of work do people usually do?
めんせつかん: いい{質問|しつもん}ですね。{本番|ほんばん}でもその{調子|ちょうし}でがんばってください。
= Good question. Keep that up in the real interview.
```

めんせつかん = interviewer (in kana: one kanji is outside N3); {本日|ほんじつ} = today (formal);
もうします = humble "am called" (N4 keigo, in kana by the course rule); {当社|とうしゃ} = our company,
said by its own staff (lesson 22's kanji); うかがう = humble "hear" (N4); {生|い}かす = to make
use of; つながる = to connect; 〜とは = "is", in a definition (lesson 23); {本番|ほんばん} = the real
thing. Sota answers with として (his role), によって (lesson 13) and にとって (his view), and calls
the company おんしゃ while the interviewer says {当社|とうしゃ}.

## Reading: an information-session notice

A notice on a company's recruiting page. The company is made up for this course.

> {会社|かいしゃ}{説明会|せつめいかい}のお{知|し}らせ
>
> ミナト{商事|しょうじ}では、{来年|らいねん}{三月|さんがつ}に{大学|だいがく}を{卒業|そつぎょう}する{予定|よてい}の{方|かた}のために、{会社|かいしゃ}{説明会|せつめいかい}を{行|おこな}います。
>
> {日時|にちじ}：{三月|さんがつ}{五日|いつか}（{水|すい}）{午後|ごご}{二時|にじ}～{四時|よじ}
>
> {場所|ばしょ}：オンライン（{参加|さんか}の{方法|ほうほう}は、エントリーした{方|かた}にメールでお{知|し}らせします）
>
> {内容|ないよう}：{仕事|しごと}の{説明|せつめい}、{若手|わかて}{社員|しゃいん}との{座談会|ざだんかい}
>
> ※ {服|ふく}は{自由|じゆう}です。
>
> ※ エントリーシートは、この{説明会|せつめいかい}に{参加|さんか}した{方|かた}だけが{出|だ}すことができます。

{日時|にちじ} = date and time; {若手|わかて} = young (staff); {座談会|ざだんかい} = an informal talk, a
round-table; ※ marks a note.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Company information session

Minato Trading is holding a company information session for people who expect to graduate from
university next March.

Date and time: Wednesday 5 March, 2–4 pm

Place: online (we'll email details of how to join to people who have signed up)

Contents: an explanation of the work; a round-table talk with young employees

Note: you may wear what you like.

Note: only people who have attended this information session can submit an entry sheet.

</details>

## Common mistakes

- Calling the company you're applying to おんしゃ in writing. In an ES or an email, it's きしゃ;
  おんしゃ is for speech.
- ×{会社|かいしゃ}にとって{働|はたら}きたい. にとって needs a judgement after it; for "I want to work at
  your company", say おんしゃで{働|はたら}きたい.
- ×サークルのリーダーで、{五十人|ごじゅうにん}をまとめました is understandable but loose; the role is
  として: サークルのリーダーとして.

## Key points

- しゅうかつ: job hunting, often for {新卒|しんそつ} (new graduates) hired together to start in April.
- The usual steps: エントリー, {説明会|せつめいかい}, エントリーシート and りれきしょ, tests,
  several めんせつ, then {内定|ないてい} (an offer). Dates follow a guideline (March, June,
  October) that many companies don't keep to, and the rules change.
- おんしゃ in speech, きしゃ in writing; the company says {当社|とうしゃ}.
- として (your role), にとって (your view) and によって are interview staples.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Proverbs and four-character compounds
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japanese speakers often sum up a situation with a ことわざ (a proverb) or a よじじゅくご (a
four-character compound; one of its kanji is outside N3, so it's in kana). You'll hear them in
conversation, on TV and in essays, and the common ones turn up in reading texts. Using
one at the right moment sounds natural and a little playful. This lesson takes six well-known
ones: what they say word for word, what they mean, when people use them, and the nearest
English.

## Two kinds

- A ことわざ is a short saying, often a whole sentence, and sometimes in old grammar:
  {急|いそ}がば{回|まわ}れ, {石|いし}の{上|うえ}にも{三年|さんねん}.
- A よじじゅくご packs an idea into four kanji, mostly read in on'yomi: {一石二鳥|いっせきにちょう},
  {十人十色|じゅうにんといろ}. Many come from old Chinese writing; some were made in Japan; one of this
  lesson's is often said to come from English.

Both are written with kanji where the kanji are on the list, and in kana where they aren't:
{花|はな}よりだんご keeps だんご (dumplings) in kana because one of its kanji is outside N3.

## Six to know

### {一石二鳥|いっせきにちょう}: one stone, two birds

Getting two good results from one action. English has the same picture: "to kill two birds
with one stone", and the Japanese is often said to have been made from that English saying.

{自転車|じてんしゃ}で{通勤|つうきん}すれば、{運動|うんどう}にもなるし、{交通費|こうつうひ}もかからない。{一石二鳥|いっせきにちょう}だね。 — If you cycle to work, you get exercise and pay no fares. Two birds with one stone.

({交通費|こうつうひ} = travel costs, lesson 7.)

### {十人十色|じゅうにんといろ}: ten people, ten colours

Everyone has their own tastes and ideas. English: "to each their own", "different strokes for
different folks". Note the reading: {十人|じゅうにん} is じゅうにん, but {十色|といろ} is といろ, with the native
readings と (ten) and いろ (colour).

{好|この}みは{十人十色|じゅうにんといろ}だから、プレゼントを{選|えら}ぶのは{難|むずか}しい。 — Everyone's tastes are different, so choosing presents is hard.

({好|この}み = taste, preference.)

### {七転|ななころ}び{八起|やお}き: fall seven times, get up eight

However often you fail, you get up and try again. English: "fall seven times, stand up eight";
"if at first you don't succeed, try, try again". {転|ころ}ぶ is N4's "fall over"; {起|お}きる is
"get up".

{試験|しけん}に{三回|さんかい}{落|お}ちたけど、{七転|ななころ}び{八起|やお}きだ。{来年|らいねん}こそ{合格|ごうかく}する。 — I've failed the exam three times, but fall seven times, get up eight. Next year I'll pass for sure.

### {急|いそ}がば{回|まわ}れ: if you're in a hurry, go round

The safe, sure way is faster in the end than a risky short cut. English: "more haste, less
speed"; "slow and steady wins the race". The grammar is old: いそがば is classical Japanese for
"if you hurry" (today: {急|いそ}げば), and {回|まわ}れ is the imperative of {回|まわ}る (N4).

{近道|ちかみち}は{危|あぶ}ない{道|みち}だから、{急|いそ}がば{回|まわ}れで、{大|おお}きい{道|みち}を{行|い}こう。 — The short cut is a dangerous road, so more haste, less speed: let's take the main road.

({近道|ちかみち} = a short cut.)

### {石|いし}の{上|うえ}にも{三年|さんねん}: even on a stone, three years

Sit on a cold stone for three years and even it gets warm: patience and perseverance pay off.
English: "perseverance prevails"; "Rome wasn't built in a day" is close. It's often said to
someone new in a job who wants to quit too soon.

{仕事|しごと}が{合|あ}わないと{思|おも}っても、{石|いし}の{上|うえ}にも{三年|さんねん}って{言|い}うでしょう。もう{少|すこ}しがんばってみたら？ — Even if you feel the job doesn't suit you, they say perseverance pays off, don't they? Why not hang in there a bit longer?

### {花|はな}よりだんご: dumplings rather than flowers

Preferring what's useful (or tasty) to what's merely beautiful. It's said with a smile about
people at a cherry-blossom party who care more about the food than the blossoms, and about
anyone who chooses the practical over the pretty. There's no exact English equivalent;
"substance over style" is near.

うちの{子供|こども}たちは、{花見|はなみ}に{行|い}っても{食|た}べてばかりで、まさに{花|はな}よりだんごだ。 — When my kids go to see the cherry blossoms, all they do is eat. Dumplings over flowers, exactly.

## Using them in conversation

A proverb usually comes at the end of a thought, to sum it up. Useful frames:

| Frame | Example | Feel |
|---|---|---|
| 〜って{言|い}うでしょう / 〜って{言|い}うじゃない | {急|いそ}がば{回|まわ}れって{言|い}うでしょう | as they say (casual) |
| 〜と{言|い}いますね | {十人十色|じゅうにんといろ}と{言|い}いますね | as they say (polite) |
| まさに〜だ | まさに{一石二鳥|いっせきにちょう}だ | it's exactly… |
| それこそ〜だ | それこそ{七転|ななころ}び{八起|やお}きだね | that's just what … means (lesson 15's こそ) |

One caution: a proverb can sound like a lecture. Among friends that's fine; with someone senior
to you, it's safer to use one about yourself than about them.

## Dialogue: a new job

Mika started at a company in April. In June she meets Ms Okada, who joined three years earlier.
(Mika is polite to her senior; Ms Okada speaks casually.)

```dialogue
# In the break room
おかだ: みかさん、{最近|さいきん}どう？ {仕事|しごと}には{慣|な}れた？
= Mika, how's it going? Have you got used to the work?
みか: それが…。{失敗|しっぱい}ばかりで、もう{辞|や}めたいと{思|おも}うこともあるんです。
= Well... I keep making mistakes, and sometimes I feel like quitting.
おかだ: {私|わたし}も{一年目|いちねんめ}はそうだったよ。でも、{石|いし}の{上|うえ}にも{三年|さんねん}って{言|い}うでしょう。
= I was the same in my first year. But they say "three years even on a stone", don't they?
みか: {三年|さんねん}もですか。
= Three whole years?
おかだ: {三年|さんねん}は{例|たと}えだけどね。{失敗|しっぱい}しても、また{立|た}ち{上|あ}がればいいの。{七転|ななころ}び{八起|やお}きだよ。
= The three years is just a figure of speech. Even if you make mistakes, you just have to get back up. Fall seven times, get up eight.
みか: そうですね。{早|はや}く{仕事|しごと}を{覚|おぼ}えたくて、{急|いそ}ぎすぎていたかもしれません。
= You're right. I wanted to learn the job quickly, so maybe I was rushing too much.
おかだ: それこそ{急|いそ}がば{回|まわ}れだね。{一|ひと}つずつ{確|たし}かめながらやれば、{結局|けっきょく}{早|はや}く{覚|おぼ}えられるよ。
= That's just it: more haste, less speed. If you go one step at a time and check as you go, you'll learn it faster in the end.
みか: ありがとうございます。{少|すこ}し{元気|げんき}が{出|で}ました。
= Thank you. I feel a bit better.
おかだ: よかった。じゃあ、{今日|きょう}の{帰|かえ}りにケーキでも{食|た}べに{行|い}こうか。{元気|げんき}も{出|で}るし、おいしいし、{一石二鳥|いっせきにちょう}でしょう？
= Good. Then shall we go for some cake on the way home today? It'll cheer you up and it's delicious: two birds with one stone, right?
```

{一年目|いちねんめ} = the first year; {例|たと}え = a figure of speech, an example; {立|た}ち{上|あ}がる =
to stand up; {覚|おぼ}える = to learn (N5; lesson 18's kanji); {確|たし}かめる = to check (lesson 8's
kanji); {結局|けっきょく} = in the end (lesson 28).

## Reading: proverb of the week

A short column from a learners' newsletter. It's in polite です/ます style.

> {今週|こんしゅう}のことわざは「{花|はな}よりだんご」です。{春|はる}になると、{日本|にほん}では{多|おお}くの{人|ひと}が{公園|こうえん}で{花見|はなみ}をします。でも、さくらを{見|み}るより、おべんとうを{食|た}べたり、{友|とも}だちと{話|はな}したりするほうが{楽|たの}しいという{人|ひと}も{少|すく}なくありません。そんな{人|ひと}のことを「{花|はな}よりだんご」と{言|い}います。「きれいなものより、お{腹|なか}がいっぱいになるもののほうがいい」という{意味|いみ}です。{悪|わる}い{意味|いみ}で{使|つか}うこともありますが、たいていは{笑|わら}いながら{言|い}います。みなさんは、{花|はな}とだんご、どちらを{選|えら}びますか。

おべんとう = a packed lunch (N4; one of its kanji is outside N3); {少|すく}なくありません = there are
quite a few; たいてい = usually.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

This week's proverb is "dumplings rather than flowers". When spring comes, many people in Japan
go to the park to view the cherry blossoms. But quite a few people say that eating their packed
lunch and talking with friends is more fun than looking at the blossoms. People like that are
described as "dumplings rather than flowers". It means "something that fills your stomach is
better than something pretty". It's sometimes used in a bad sense, but it's usually said with a
laugh. Which would you choose: the flowers or the dumplings?

</details>

## Key points

- ことわざ (proverbs) and よじじゅくご (four-kanji compounds) sum up a situation; they usually
  come at the end of a thought: 〜って{言|い}うでしょう, まさに〜だ, それこそ〜だ.
- {一石二鳥|いっせきにちょう}: two benefits from one action. {十人十色|じゅうにんといろ}: everyone is different
  (note といろ). {七転|ななころ}び{八起|やお}き: never give up. {急|いそ}がば{回|まわ}れ: the sure way is faster
  in the end. {石|いし}の{上|うえ}にも{三年|さんねん}: perseverance pays off. {花|はな}よりだんご: the
  practical over the pretty.
- {急|いそ}がば{回|まわ}れ keeps old grammar: いそがば = {急|いそ}げば.
- Use proverbs about yourself, or with friends; aimed at someone senior they can sound like a
  lecture.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: -ish, tends to, full of: っぽい, 気味, がち, だらけ, 的, 向き / 向け
topics: っぽい and らしい
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 is about impressions, guesses and emphasis: how something looks to you, what you're
sure of and what you only suspect, and how to pile one point on another. It starts small, with
the little endings Japanese uses to sum up an impression in one word: childish, a touch of a
cold, always forgetting things, covered in mistakes, personally, made for beginners.

Each of these endings is a **[[suffix]]**: a piece that can't stand alone and is added to the end of
a word to make a new one. You met some in N4 (〜さ, 〜{方|かた}, 〜やすい). The ones here are about
how a person or thing comes across, so the theme is people: personality, looks, hair and clothes.

{彼|かれ}は{大人|おとな}なのに、ちょっと{子供|こども}っぽい。 — He's an adult, but he's a bit childish.
{最近|さいきん}、{疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ}です。 — I've been feeling a bit tired lately.
{忙|いそが}しいと、{食事|しょくじ}が{遅|おく}れがちになる。 — When I'm busy, my meals tend to get late.
この{作文|さくぶん}は{間違|まちが}いだらけだ。 — This essay is full of mistakes.

## -ish, -like: 〜っぽい

〜っぽい turns a word into an い-adjective meaning "-ish, -like, tending to". It's casual: common
in conversation and informal writing, less so in formal writing.

| Joins to | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| noun | {子供|こども}っぽい, {大人|おとな}っぽい | childish; grown-up (looking) |
| noun | {水|みず}っぽい, うそっぽい | watery; sounds like a lie |
| colour (noun or い-adj stem) | {黒|くろ}っぽい, {白|しろ}っぽい, {青|あお}っぽい | blackish, whitish, bluish |
| い-adjective stem | {安|やす}っぽい | cheap-looking, tacky |
| ます stem of a verb | {忘|わす}れっぽい, {怒|おこ}りっぽい | forgetful; quick to anger |

It conjugates like any い-adjective: {子供|こども}っぽくない, {安|やす}っぽかった, {黒|くろ}っぽい{服|ふく},
{大人|おとな}っぽく{見|み}える.

Three kinds of meaning come out of it:

1. Looks or feels like X (but isn't quite X). {黒|くろ}っぽい is not black but close to it;
   {大人|おとな}っぽい is said of a young person who seems older.
2. Has too much of X. {水|みず}っぽいスープ has too much water; {子供|こども}っぽい is said of
   an adult who behaves like a child, and it's a criticism.
3. After a ます stem: does X easily, as a habit of character. {忘|わす}れっぽい (always
   forgetting things), {怒|おこ}りっぽい (quick to get angry), あきっぽい (gets bored with things
   quickly).

{祖父|そふ}は{最近|さいきん}、{忘|わす}れっぽくなった。 — My grandfather has got forgetful lately.
このスープ、ちょっと{水|みず}っぽいね。 — This soup is a bit watery.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{十五歳|じゅうごさい}だけど、{大人|おとな}っぽく{見|み}える。 — She's fifteen, but she looks grown-up.
その{話|はなし}、なんだかうそっぽいなあ。 — That story sounds a bit made up.

In very casual speech, especially among young people, っぽい also follows a plain verb or adjective
and means "seems": {田中|たなか}さん、{今日|きょう}は{来|こ}ないっぽい (seems Tanaka isn't coming today).
Understand it, but use みたい or らしい when you aren't sure of the company.

### っぽい or らしい?

N4 showed you noun + らしい meaning "typical of, just like a real…": {春|はる}らしい{天気|てんき}
(real spring weather). Next to っぽい it makes a useful pair:

| | 〜らしい | 〜っぽい |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | has the qualities X should have | resembles X; has too much X |
| Feeling | usually praise | neutral or critical |
| {子供|こども} | {子供|こども}らしい: charmingly childlike (of a child) | {子供|こども}っぽい: childish (of an adult) |
| {学生|がくせい} | {学生|がくせい}らしい{服|ふく}: clothes fit for a student | {学生|がくせい}っぽい: looks like a student (may not be one) |

{子供|こども}は{子供|こども}らしく、{外|そと}で{元気|げんき}に{遊|あそ}んでほしい。 — I want children to be
children and play outside to their heart's content.
{三十歳|さんじゅっさい}にもなって、そんなことで{泣|な}くのは{子供|こども}っぽいよ。 — Crying over something
like that at thirty is childish.
そんなことを{言|い}うなんて、あなたらしくない。— It's not like you to say that. (なんて: lesson 20.)

Both often go with words like {男|おとこ} and {女|おんな}: {男|おとこ}らしい (manly), {女|おんな}らしい
(ladylike). They're still common, but many people now find them old-fashioned when they tell
someone how a man or a woman ought to be. {男|おとこ}っぽい{字|じ} (handwriting that looks like a
man's) is a plain description.

Context also has to separate N + らしい "typical" from N4's らしい "apparently":
あの{人|ひと}は{学生|がくせい}らしい can be "apparently he's a student". {学生|がくせい}らしい + noun
is often "typical of a student", but it can still be "who seems to be a student": the reading
below has {大学生|だいがくせい}らしい{男|おとこ}の{子|こ}, a young man who looked like a university student.

## A touch of: 〜{気味|ぎみ}

〜{気味|ぎみ} (read ぎみ, with a voiced ぎ) means "a touch of, slightly, a bit on the … side". It
follows a noun or a ます stem, and it's almost always about something unwelcome: health, tiredness,
weight, delays.

| Joins to | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| noun | かぜ{気味|ぎみ}, {寝不足|ねぶそく}{気味|ぎみ} | a slight cold; a bit short of sleep |
| ます stem | {疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ}, {太|ふと}り{気味|ぎみ}, {遅|おく}れ{気味|ぎみ} | a bit tired; putting on weight; running late |

It behaves like a noun: 〜{気味|ぎみ}だ, 〜{気味|ぎみ}で, 〜{気味|ぎみ}の + noun.

ちょっとかぜ{気味|ぎみ}なので、{今日|きょう}は{早|はや}く{寝|ね}ます。 — I've got a bit of a cold, so I'm
going to bed early today.
{工事|こうじ}は{少|すこ}し{遅|おく}れ{気味|ぎみ}だそうだ。 — I hear the building work is running a little
behind.
{最近|さいきん}{太|ふと}り{気味|ぎみ}の{父|ちち}は、{毎朝|まいあさ}{歩|ある}くことにした。 — My father, who's been
putting on a bit of weight, has decided to walk every morning.

The degree is small and it's a feeling or a trend at the moment: {疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ} is "rather
tired" now, not a lifelong condition. ({気味|きみ}が{悪|わる}い, read きみ, is a separate phrase:
"creepy, eerie".)

## Tends to: 〜がち

〜がち says something happens often or easily, and that it's a pity: "tends to, is apt to". It
follows a ます stem or a few nouns.

| Joins to | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ます stem | {忘|わす}れがち, {遅|おく}れがち, {休|やす}みがち | tends to forget; to be late; to miss days |
| noun | {病気|びょうき}がち, くもりがち | often ill; often cloudy |

Forms: 〜がちだ, 〜がちな / 〜がちの + noun, 〜がちで, and often 〜がちになる.

{忙|いそが}しいと、れんらくするのを{忘|わす}れがちだ。 — When I'm busy, I tend to forget to
keep in touch. (れんらく is in kana: one of its kanji is outside N3.)
{子供|こども}のころは{病気|びょうき}がちで、よく{学校|がっこう}を{休|やす}んだ。 — As a child I was often
ill and missed a lot of school.
{一人|ひとり}っ{子|こ}はわがままだと{思|おも}われがちだが、そうとは{限|かぎ}らない。 — People tend to
think only children are spoilt, but that isn't necessarily so.

がち is for things you'd rather didn't happen. Good habits don't take it: not ×{毎日|まいにち}
{勉強|べんきょう}しがちだ, but {毎日|まいにち}{勉強|べんきょう}するようにしている.

### っぽい, {気味|ぎみ} and がち side by side

| | {忘|わす}れっぽい | {忘|わす}れがち | {疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ} |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it says | a trait of the person | a tendency in some situations | a slight state now |
| Example | {祖父|そふ}は{忘|わす}れっぽい (Grandpa is forgetful) | {忙|いそが}しいと{食事|しょくじ}を{忘|わす}れがちだ (when busy I tend to forget meals) | {今週|こんしゅう}は{疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ}だ (I'm a bit tired this week) |

A good test: がち usually comes with a situation (when…, in winter…, people…), っぽい describes
someone, and {気味|ぎみ} describes how things are right now.

## Covered in, full of: 〜だらけ

Noun + だらけ means "covered in, full of" something unpleasant, and it suggests a mess: too much,
everywhere.

{部屋|へや}がごみだらけだ。 — The room is full of rubbish.
{雨|あめ}の{中|なか}でサッカーをして、{子供|こども}たちはどろだらけになった。 — The children played
football in the rain and got covered in mud. (どろ: mud.)
この{作文|さくぶん}は{間違|まちが}いだらけだから、もう{一度|いちど}{書|か}き{直|なお}しなさい。 — This essay is
full of mistakes, so write it again.

Forms: 〜だらけだ, 〜だらけの + noun ({間違|まちが}いだらけのレポート, a report full of mistakes),
〜だらけになる.

Because だらけ is negative, it doesn't suit things you like: a garden full of lovely flowers is
{花|はな}でいっぱいだ (いっぱい: full, neutral), not ×{花|はな}だらけだ, which would sound as if the
flowers were a nuisance.

## -ic, -al, in terms of: 〜{的|てき}

〜{的|てき} after a noun (usually a word written with two kanji) makes a な-adjective, like
English "-ic, -al": {個人的|こじんてき} (personal), {社交的|しゃこうてき} (sociable), {具体的|ぐたいてき}
(concrete), {理想的|りそうてき} (ideal), {国際的|こくさいてき} (international).

| Form | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 〜{的|てき}な + noun | {社交的|しゃこうてき}な{人|ひと} | a sociable person |
| 〜{的|てき}に + verb or adjective | {具体的|ぐたいてき}に{説明|せつめい}する | explain specifically |
| 〜{的|てき}だ | この{部屋|へや}は{理想的|りそうてき}だ | this room is ideal |
| 〜{的|てき}には | {個人的|こじんてき}には | personally, as far as I'm concerned |

〜{的|てき}に also means "in terms of, from the point of view of": {性格的|せいかくてき}に (in terms of
personality), {時間的|じかんてき}に (time-wise), {経済的|けいざいてき}に (financially).

{個人的|こじんてき}には、{長|なが}い{髪|かみ}のほうが{好|す}きだ。 — Personally, I prefer long hair.
{二人|ふたり}は{性格的|せいかくてき}に{合|あ}わないらしい。 — Apparently the two of them don't get on,
personality-wise.
{時間的|じかんてき}に{無理|むり}なら、{来週|らいしゅう}でもかまいません。 — If it's not possible time-wise,
next week is fine too.

Not every noun takes {的|てき}, so learn the common ones as words. In casual speech young people
also say {私|わたし}{的|てき}には (for me, as for me); you'll hear it, but some people find it
sloppy, so keep it out of polite speech.

On its own, {的|まと} is a target: {的|まと}に{当|あ}たる (hit the target).

## Suited to and aimed at: 〜{向|む}き, 〜{向|む}け

{向|む}く means "to face" and "to suit" (〜に{向|む}いている: is suited to). Two nouns come from it,
and they're easy to mix up:

| | 〜{向|む}き | 〜{向|む}け |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | suited to (by its nature) | made for, aimed at (on purpose) |
| Example | {初心者|しょしんしゃ}{向|む}きの{山|やま}: a mountain that suits beginners | {初心者|しょしんしゃ}{向|む}けの{本|ほん}: a book written for beginners |
| Forms | {向|む}きだ, {向|む}きの + N, {向|む}きではない | {向|む}けだ, {向|む}けの + N, {向|む}けに |

この{山|やま}は{道|みち}が{広|ひろ}くて、{初心者|しょしんしゃ}{向|む}きだ。 — This mountain has wide paths, so
it's good for beginners.
これは{子供|こども}{向|む}けの{番組|ばんぐみ}だが、{大人|おとな}が{見|み}ても{面白|おもしろ}い。 — This programme is
made for children, but it's fun for adults too.
{若者|わかもの}{向|む}けの{服|ふく}ばかりで、{母|はは}に{合|あ}うものがなかった。 — There were only clothes
aimed at young people, nothing that suited my mother.

The same thing can be both: {大人|おとな}{向|む}けの{絵本|えほん} is a picture book written for adults;
{大人|おとな}{向|む}きの{絵本|えほん} is one that suits adults, whoever it was made for. {向|む}き also
keeps its plain meaning, "facing": {南向|みなみむ}きの{部屋|へや} (a south-facing room).

## Describing people: character, looks and clothes

### Character

| Good | Neutral or either | Hard to live with |
|---|---|---|
| {正直|しょうじき} honest | おとなしい calm, quiet | わがまま spoilt, selfish |
| すなお open, accepting | {内気|うちき} shy | {自分勝手|じぶんかって} self-centred |
| {社交的|しゃこうてき} sociable | {人見知|ひとみし}り shy with strangers | {意地悪|いじわる} mean |
| {落|お}ち{着|つ}いている calm | {大人|おとな}っぽい grown-up | {生意気|なまいき} cheeky |
| {偉|えら}い admirable | {個性|こせい}がある has individuality | {短気|たんき}, {怒|おこ}りっぽい short-tempered |

{長所|ちょうしょ} (strong point) and {短所|たんしょ} (weak point) are the words of job interviews and
self-introductions: {私|わたし}の{長所|ちょうしょ}は{明|あか}るいところです. {性格|せいかく} is someone's
personality, {性質|せいしつ} their (or a thing's) basic nature, {才能|さいのう} a natural gift and
{能力|のうりょく} ability in general. たいど is the attitude someone shows, くせ a habit they can't
help.

### Looks and hair

{外見|がいけん} (appearance, formal), {顔|かお}つき (the look of someone's face), {表情|ひょうじょう}
(facial expression), スタイル (figure). {髪|かみ} is the hair on your head; かみのけ (in kana: its last kanji is
outside N3) is the same in everyday speech, and also a single hair. {前髪|まえがみ} is a fringe, {白髪|しらが}
grey hair, {長髪|ちょうはつ} long hair (mostly of men, formal), ひげ a beard or moustache. You get
your hair cut at a {美容院|びよういん} by a {美容師|びようし}.

{似|に}る (to resemble) is usually 〜に{似|に}ている: {私|わたし}は{母|はは}に{似|に}ている. Exactly alike
is そっくりだ: {声|こえ}が{父|ちち}にそっくりだ.

### Clothes and fashion

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {格好|かっこう} | how someone is dressed, the look | ふくそう | attire, dress (formal) |
| おしゃれ | stylish | {身|み}だしなみ | being neat and presentable |
| はで | flashy, loud | {地味|じみ} | plain, understated |
| {流行|りゅうこう}, {流行|はや}る | a trend; to be in fashion | ファッション | fashion |
| {無地|むじ} | plain (no pattern) | {上着|うわぎ} | jacket, outer layer |
| ワンピース | a dress | ジーンズ, ブーツ | jeans, boots |
| アクセサリー | accessories, jewellery | きがえる | to change clothes |

Note the two readings of {流行|りゅうこう}: {流行|はや}る (verb) but {流行|りゅうこう} (noun). けしょう is make-up.

Thirteen kanji for what people are like and how they look. Only the readings you meet at N3 are
listed.

Carried words you can now write with kanji: {美|うつく}しい, {美術館|びじゅつかん}, {形|かたち},

Readings to watch:

- 直 has two on'yomi: チョク in most words ({直前|ちょくぜん}), ジキ in {正直|しょうじき}. Its kun
  なお(す) means "fix, correct" ({間違|まちが}いを{直|なお}す); illness uses another kanji (lesson 22).
- {白髪|しらが} is a special reading: しら + が for {白|しろ} + {髪|かみ}. The formal はくはつ also exists.
- 形 is ギョウ only in a few words, the most common being {人形|にんぎょう}.
- 雑 also hides in ざっし (magazine), left in kana because its second kanji is outside N3.

Memory notes (hooks, not etymology):

- 美: a sheep's head with its horns on top of 大 (big): a big, fine sheep was the picture of
  beauty.
- 似: a person (亻) beside another shape: one person doing just as another does.
- 髪: long hair (the 彡 strokes) hanging down over 友 (friend).
- 靴: leather on the left (the part that means hide) and 化 (change) on the right: leather changed
  into a shoe.
- 偉: a person (亻) with a big, busy shape beside them: a person who stands out.
- 消: water (氵) next to "small": water makes a fire small until it's gone.
- 直: ten (十) eyes (目) looking straight ahead, with a line to keep it straight.
- 的: white (白) on the left: the white centre of a target.

## Dialogue: shopping for a dress

Ayaka and Mio are friends from university, shopping on a Saturday. Casual speech, with
contractions.

```dialogue
# At the clothes shop
あやか: ねえ、このワンピース、どう？
= Hey, what about this dress?
みお: うーん、ちょっと{子供|こども}っぽくない？ピンクだし、リボンもついてるし。
= Hmm, isn't it a bit childish? It's pink, and it's got a ribbon on it too.
あやか: そうかな。じゃあ、こっちの{黒|くろ}っぽいのは？
= You think? Then what about this blackish one?
みお: それはいいね。{大人|おとな}っぽいし、あやかに{似合|にあ}いそう。
= That one's nice. It's grown-up, and I think it'd suit you.
あやか: でも、{黒|くろ}って{地味|じみ}に{見|み}えがちじゃない？
= But don't black things tend to look a bit plain?
みお: アクセサリーをつければだいじょうぶだよ。{試着|しちゃく}してみたら？
= If you wear some jewellery, it's fine. Why don't you try it on?
あやか: どう？…あ、{最近|さいきん}{太|ふと}り{気味|ぎみ}だから、ちょっときついかも。
= How is it? Oh, I've put on a bit of weight lately, so it might be a bit tight.
みお: そんなことないって。ぴったりだよ。
= Don't be silly. It fits perfectly.
あやか: {値段|ねだん}は…えっ、{一万二千円|いちまんにせんえん}！
= And the price is... what, twelve thousand yen!
みお: {高|たか}いね。でも、{安|やす}っぽい{服|ふく}を{何着|なんちゃく}も{買|か}うより、いいのを{一着|いっちゃく}{買|か}ったほうがいいと{思|おも}うよ。
= It's pricey. But I think it's better to buy one good one than lots of cheap-looking ones.
あやか: みおって、{個人的|こじんてき}な{意見|いけん}をはっきり{言|い}うよね。
= You really say what you think, don't you, Mio.
みお: {正直|しょうじき}なのが{私|わたし}の{長所|ちょうしょ}だから。
= Being honest is my strong point.
あやか: {短所|たんしょ}でもあるけどね。じゃ、これにする。
= It's your weak point too. OK, I'll take it.
```

ついてる = ついている (lesson 25 gathers the contractions); 〜かも = かもしれない; そんなことないって
= "no way, that's not true" (って adds insistence); ぴったり = a perfect fit; {値段|ねだん} = price
({値|ね}: lesson 7).

## Reading: what clothes say

A post on a shop worker's blog, in the plain だ style of blogs.

> {私|わたし}は{駅前|えきまえ}の{小|ちい}さな{服屋|ふくや}で{働|はたら}いている。{毎日|まいにち}お{客|きゃく}さんを{見|み}ていると、{服|ふく}の{選|えら}び{方|かた}にはその{人|ひと}の{性格|せいかく}がよく{出|で}ると{思|おも}う。{黒|くろ}っぽい{服|ふく}や{無地|むじ}のシャツばかり{選|えら}ぶ{人|ひと}は、{落|お}ち{着|つ}いていて{真面目|まじめ}そうに{見|み}える。はでな{色|いろ}が{好|す}きな{人|ひと}は{社交的|しゃこうてき}で、よく{話|はな}しかけてくれる。もちろん、{個人的|こじんてき}にそう{感|かん}じるだけだが。
>
> {先週|せんしゅう}、{大学生|だいがくせい}らしい{男|おとこ}の{子|こ}が{来|き}た。「めんせつに{着|き}ていく{服|ふく}が{欲|ほ}しいんです。でも、ぼくは{子供|こども}っぽく{見|み}られがちで…」と{言|い}う。{来週|らいしゅう}、{初|はじ}めてのめんせつがあるそうだ。{確|たし}かに{顔|かお}つきがやさしくて、{年|とし}より{若|わか}く{見|み}える。{本人|ほんにん}も{最近|さいきん}は{寝不足|ねぶそく}{気味|ぎみ}で、{自信|じしん}がないらしい。{私|わたし}は{地味|じみ}すぎない{青|あお}っぽいスーツと{白|しろ}いシャツをすすめた。{店|みせ}には{若者|わかもの}{向|む}けのはでな{服|ふく}が{多|おお}いが、めんせつには{向|む}かない。
>
> きがえて{出|で}てきた{彼|かれ}は、{急|きゅう}に{大人|おとな}っぽくなっていた。「{自分|じぶん}じゃないみたいだ」と{笑|わら}い、{背|せ}をのばした。その{顔|かお}を{見|み}て、{私|わたし}もうれしくなった。そのとき、{服|ふく}は{性格|せいかく}を{見|み}せるものだが、{性格|せいかく}を{少|すこ}し{変|か}えることもあるのかもしれないと{思|おも}った。{彼|かれ}が{帰|かえ}ったあと、{試着室|しちゃくしつ}は{服|ふく}だらけだったけれど。

ぼく = "I" (said by men; in kana because its kanji is outside N3); めんせつ = job interview (N4);
{本人|ほんにん} = the person himself; {自信|じしん} = confidence; すすめる = to recommend (N4);
{向|む}かない = isn't suited; {背|せ}をのばす = to straighten up; 〜ものだ = that's how things are
(lesson 9).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What does the writer think clothes show? — The wearer's personality: people who choose
   blackish or plain clothes seem calm and serious; people who like flashy colours are sociable.
   She admits it's only her personal feeling (〜{個人的|こじんてき}にそう{感|かん}じるだけ).
2. What was the student's problem? — He needed clothes for a job interview, but people tend to see
   him as childish-looking ({子供|こども}っぽく{見|み}られがち), and he lacked confidence.
3. Why didn't the writer suggest the clothes the shop has most of? — They're flashy clothes aimed
   at young people, which don't suit an interview.
4. What happened to the fitting room? — It was covered in clothes (〜だらけ) after he left: the
   one bad point in a good day.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

I work in a small clothes shop in front of the station. Watching customers every day, I think the
way people choose clothes shows a lot about their personality. People who only choose blackish
clothes or plain shirts look calm and serious. People who like flashy colours are sociable and
often start chatting with me. Of course, that's just my personal impression.

Last week a young man who looked like a university student came in. "I want something to wear to
a job interview. But people tend to think I look like a kid," he said. It was true: his face was
gentle, and he looked younger than his age. He had his first interview next week. He'd been a bit short of sleep lately too, and he
didn't seem very confident. I recommended a bluish suit that wasn't too plain, and a white shirt.
The shop has a lot of flashy clothes aimed at young people, but they don't suit an interview.

When he came out after changing, he suddenly looked grown-up. "It doesn't look like me," he
laughed, and stood up straight. Seeing his face, I felt happy too. At that moment I thought: clothes show your personality, but
maybe they can change it a little too. Though after he left, the fitting room was covered in
clothes.

</details>

## Pronunciation

- っぽい starts with a small っ: a full beat of silence before ぽ. {子供|こども}っぽい is six morae,
  こ・ど・も・っ・ぽ・い, and the pitch falls after the ぽ: [こどもっぽい:5]. The same goes for
  [わすれっぽい:5] and [おとなっぽい:5].
- {気味|ぎみ} as a suffix is voiced: かぜぎみ, {疲|つか}れぎみ. Plain {気味|きみ} (as in
  {気味|きみ}が{悪|わる}い) isn't.
- {美容院|びよういん:2} has five morae, び・よ・う・い・ん; {病院|びょういん:0} has four, びょ・う・い・ん.
  Say the よ as a full beat or you'll be sent to the hospital.
- {髪|かみ:2} (hair) and {紙|かみ:2} (paper) sound the same; {神|かみ:1} (god) falls after the first mora.

```speak
{彼|かれ}はちょっと{子供|こども}っぽいね。
= He's a bit childish, isn't he?
{最近|さいきん}、{疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ}なんです。
= I've been feeling a bit tired lately.
{冬|ふゆ}は{運動|うんどう}{不足|ぶそく}になりがちだ。
= In winter you tend not to get enough exercise.
{部屋|へや}がごみだらけだよ。
= The room's full of rubbish.
{個人的|こじんてき}には、こっちのほうが{好|す}きです。
= Personally, I like this one better.
これは{初心者|しょしんしゃ}{向|む}けの{本|ほん}です。
= This book is for beginners.
```

## Common mistakes

- Using がち for good habits: ×{毎朝|まいあさ}{走|はし}りがちだ. がち is for things you'd rather
  didn't happen. Say {毎朝|まいあさ}{走|はし}るようにしている.
- だらけ with things you like: ×{花|はな}だらけの{庭|にわ} (sounds like a nuisance). Use
  {花|はな}でいっぱいの{庭|にわ}.
- Using {子供|こども}っぽい as praise for a child. For a child acting as children do, say
  {子供|こども}らしい; っぽい usually criticizes an adult.
- Joining {気味|ぎみ} to an い-adjective: ×{痛|いた}い{気味|ぎみ}. It follows nouns and ます stems:
  かぜ{気味|ぎみ}, {疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ}. ({痛|いた}みがある or ちょっと{痛|いた}い instead.)
- Forgetting that 〜{的|てき} makes a な-adjective: ×{個人的|こじんてき}の{意見|いけん}. It's
  {個人的|こじんてき}な{意見|いけん}.
- Mixing up {向|む}き and {向|む}け: a TV programme made for children is {子供|こども}{向|む}け;
  {子供|こども}{向|む}き says only that it suits them.
- Reading {流行|はや}る as りゅうこうる. It's {流行|はや}る; {流行|りゅうこう} is the noun.

## Key points

- A **[[suffix]]** joins the end of a word to make a new one. This lesson's suffixes sum up
  impressions.
- 〜っぽい (noun, colour, い-adj stem, ます stem): -ish, too much of, does easily. Casual,
  often critical. N + らしい: typical of, as X should be, usually praise.
- 〜{気味|ぎみ} (noun, ます stem): a touch of, slightly, now: かぜ{気味|ぎみ}, {疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ}.
- 〜がち (ます stem, some nouns): tends to (unwelcome): {忘|わす}れがち, {病気|びょうき}がち.
- 〜だらけ (noun): covered in, full of (bad, messy): {間違|まちが}いだらけ.
- 〜{的|てき}: makes な-adjectives ({個人的|こじんてき}な, {具体的|ぐたいてき}に); 〜{的|てき}に: in terms of.
- 〜{向|む}き: suited to; 〜{向|む}け: made for, aimed at.
- New kanji: 格 能 美 形 似 靴 髪 偉 単 雑 的 消 直, and the special reading {白|しら}{髪|が}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Impressions and certainty: 気がする, ように見える, に違いない, っけ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 summed up impressions in one word. This lesson puts them into whole sentences and sorts
them by how sure you are: a vague feeling (I've a feeling that…), what something looks like (he
looks as if…), a firm conclusion (it must be…), and, in casual talk, the thing you're trying to
remember (what time was it again?).

The theme is people together: friends, dating, love, marriage, weddings, married life and the
family occasions that bring everyone round one table.

{何|なん}となく、{前|まえ}に{会|あ}ったことがあるような{気|き}がする。 — Somehow I feel as if we've met
before.
{二人|ふたり}はとても{幸|しあわ}せそうに{見|み}えた。 — The two of them looked very happy.
あの{二人|ふたり}は{付|つ}き{合|あ}っているに{違|ちが}いない。 — Those two must be going out.
{結婚式|けっこんしき}、{何時|なんじ}からだっけ？ — What time's the wedding again?

## I've a feeling that: 〜ような{気|き}がする

> **Review (N4).** Plain form + {気|き}がする: I have a feeling that.
> {何|なに}か{忘|わす}れている{気|き}がする (I've a feeling I've forgotten something).

Adding ような (from N4's ようだ) makes the feeling vaguer and softer: "somehow it feels as
if". It joins exactly like ようだ:

| Before ような{気|き}がする | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb (plain) | {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}るような{気|き}がする | I've a feeling it'll rain |
| い-adjective | {少|すこ}し{寒|さむ}いような{気|き}がする | it feels a bit cold, somehow |
| な-adjective + な | {彼|かれ}は{元気|げんき}なような{気|き}がする | I've a feeling he's fine |
| noun + の | {前|まえ}に{会|あ}った{人|ひと}のような{気|き}がする | I feel it's someone I've met before |

In casual speech, みたいな{気|き}がする: {夢|ゆめ}みたいな{気|き}がする (it feels like a dream).

{彼女|かのじょ}とは、{初|はじ}めて{会|あ}ったときから{気|き}が{合|あ}うような{気|き}がした。 — From the first
time I met her, I felt we'd get on.
{最近|さいきん}、{夫|おっと}が{少|すこ}し{冷|つめ}たいような{気|き}がする。{気|き}のせいかな。 — Lately I feel my
husband's a bit cold towards me. Maybe it's just my imagination.

### Why use it

- For a feeling without evidence. {何|なん}となく (somehow, for no clear reason) goes well
  with it.
- To soften an opinion. こっちのほうがいいような{気|き}がします sounds less pushy than
  こっちのほうがいいと{思|おも}います. Japanese speakers do this a lot in polite talk.
- {気|き}のせい (just my imagination) is its natural partner: {気|き}のせいかもしれない.

Strong words of certainty such as {絶対|ぜったい} (definitely) don't sit well with it: the
sentence ends up half sure, half not. For a firm view, use と{思|おも}う or the endings further down.

## Looks as if: 〜ように{見|み}える, 〜みたいに{見|み}える

N4 taught {見|み}える after adjectives and nouns: {若|わか}く{見|み}える, {学生|がくせい}に{見|み}える.
〜ように{見|み}える takes a whole clause, so you can say what someone looks as if they're doing,
have done or feel. It joins like ようだ again: verb or い-adjective + ように{見|み}える, な-adjective +
なように{見|み}える, noun + のように{見|み}える. Casual: 〜みたいに{見|み}える, with な-adjectives and
nouns joining directly.

{田中|たなか}さんは{怒|おこ}っているように{見|み}える。 — Tanaka looks as if he's angry.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{泣|な}いたように{見|み}えた。{目|め}が{赤|あか}かったから。 — She looked as if she'd been
crying: her eyes were red.
{二人|ふたり}はとても{幸|しあわ}せなように{見|み}える。 — The two of them seem very happy.
あの{人|ひと}、{先生|せんせい}みたいに{見|み}えるね。 — That person looks like a teacher, doesn't he?

What you say is how it looks to you, and it often leaves room for "but really…":

{楽|たの}しそうに{見|み}えるけど、{本当|ほんとう}は{疲|つか}れているのかもしれない。 — She looks as if
she's enjoying herself, but maybe she's actually tired.

### ように{見|み}える or そう?

N4's 〜そう (looks like) goes on a stem and is about the look of a quality or of something about
to happen: おいしそう, {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}りそう. It can't take a past or a full clause. ように{見|み}える
can:

| You want to say | そう | ように{見|み}える |
|---|---|---|
| It looks delicious. | おいしそうだ ✓ | おいしいように{見|み}える (possible, but stiff) |
| It looks like it's about to rain. | {降|ふ}りそうだ ✓ | — |
| She looks as if she's been crying. | — | {泣|な}いたように{見|み}える ✓ |
| He looks as if he isn't listening. | — | {聞|き}いていないように{見|み}える ✓ |

## It must be: 〜に{違|ちが}いない

〜に{違|ちが}いない says you're convinced: "it must be, I'm sure that". It follows the plain form;
な-adjectives and nouns join without だ.

| Before に{違|ちが}いない | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb | {二人|ふたり}は{結婚|けっこん}するに{違|ちが}いない | they're sure to get married |
| verb (past) | {彼|かれ}はもう{知|し}っていたに{違|ちが}いない | he must already have known |
| い-adjective | あの{店|みせ}は{高|たか}いに{違|ちが}いない | that shop must be expensive |
| な-adjective | {二人|ふたり}は{幸|しあわ}せに{違|ちが}いない | they must be happy |
| noun | あれは{彼|かれ}のお{父|とう}さんに{違|ちが}いない | that must be his father |

Polite: 〜に{違|ちが}いありません. The meaning comes from {違|ちが}う (to be wrong): "there can't be
a mistake about it".

{彼|かれ}の{顔|かお}を{見|み}て、{何|なに}かいいことがあったに{違|ちが}いないと{思|おも}った。 — When I saw his
face, I thought something good must have happened.
こんなにきれいな{花|はな}を{選|えら}んだのは、{妻|つま}に{違|ちが}いない。 — It must have been my wife
who chose such pretty flowers.

It's common in writing, stories and news commentary. In conversation it's fine, but it can
sound a little dramatic; friends often say きっと〜と{思|おも}う or 〜はずだ instead.

### に{違|ちが}いない or はず?

Both are sure, but the source differs. はず (N4) is a conclusion from facts, logic, schedules
and how things normally work: "it should be (that's how it's supposed to be)". に{違|ちが}いない is
your own strong conviction, often from a clue or a hunch: "I'm sure, it must be".

| | はず | に{違|ちが}いない |
|---|---|---|
| A known plan or rule | {式|しき}は{二時|にじ}からのはずです ✓ | ×{式|しき}は{二時|にじ}からに{違|ちが}いない (odd: nobody needs convincing) |
| Expected, but it didn't happen | {来|く}るはずなのに{来|こ}ない ✓ | ×{来|く}るに{違|ちが}いないのに |
| A hunch from a clue | ({何|なに}かあったはずだ: sounds like a deduction) | {何|なに}かあったに{違|ちが}いない ✓ |

## Judging by the signs: 〜とみえる (recognition)

In writing, and in slightly old-fashioned speech, plain form + とみえる / とみえて means "it
appears that, judging by what you can see":

{夫|おっと}はよほど{疲|つか}れていたとみえて、{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}でずっと{寝|ね}ていた。 — My husband
must have been very tired: he slept the whole way on the train. (よほど: very, extremely.)

You only need to understand it. In your own speech, ようだ or らしい does the same job.

## As if: まるで〜ようだ (review) and 〜かのように

> **Review (N4).** まるで〜ようだ / みたいだ: just like, as if.
> {彼女|かのじょ}の{家|いえ}は、まるでホテルのようだ (Her house is just like a hotel).

〜かのように (and 〜かのようだ) also means "as if", for something that isn't really so. It follows
the plain form (a noun or な-adjective takes である or だった), and it belongs mostly to writing and
stories. Recognize it:

{二人|ふたり}は、まるで{何|なに}もなかったかのように{話|はな}し{始|はじ}めた。 — The two of them started talking
as if nothing had happened.

## Remind me: 〜っけ

〜っけ at the end of a casual sentence means you're trying to remember something you once knew, or
checking it: "…again?", "wasn't it…?". Often you're half talking to yourself.

| Before っけ | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| noun / な-adj + だ | {式|しき}は{何曜日|なんようび}だっけ？ | What day is the ceremony again? |
| noun / な-adj + だった | {彼|かれ}の{名前|なまえ}、{何|なん}だったっけ？ | What was his name again? |
| verb or い-adj (past) | {窓|まど}、{閉|し}めたっけ？ | Did I shut the window? |
| んだ + っけ | {二人|ふたり}はどこで{出会|であ}ったんだっけ？ | Where did they meet again? |

Polite forms exist and are common at work: {会議|かいぎ}は{何時|なんじ}からでしたっけ？ (What time is
the meeting again?), {前|まえ}にお{会|あ}いしましたっけ？ (Have we met before?).

Two limits:

- It's for things you knew, or should know. Asking a stranger the way, you can't say
  ×{駅|えき}はどこだっけ？; it's {駅|えき}はどこですか.
- With verbs and い-adjectives it usually takes the past (〜たっけ) or んだっけ:
  {明日|あした}{来|く}るんだっけ？ (You're coming tomorrow, right?).

In the past tense, said to yourself, っけ can also be nostalgic: {子供|こども}のころ、よくこの{川|かわ}で
{遊|あそ}んだっけ (We used to play by this river a lot when we were kids, didn't we).

## How sure are you?

Drawing a conclusion from what you notice is **[[inference]]**; passing on what someone told you is
**[[hearsay]]**. Put this lesson's endings next to N4's and you get a rough scale (speakers don't all
draw the lines in the same places):

| Ending | What it's based on | How sure |
|---|---|---|
| 〜に{違|ちが}いない | your own conviction, from clues | very sure |
| 〜はずだ | facts, logic, plans | sure: "it should be" |
| 〜だろう / でしょう | your judgment | fairly sure |
| 〜ようだ / みたいだ | what you notice (inference) | it seems |
| 〜ように{見|み}える | how it looks to you | an impression, maybe wrong |
| 〜ような{気|き}がする | a feeling | vague |
| 〜そうだ / らしい | what you heard or read (hearsay) | passing it on |
| 〜かもしれない | a possibility | maybe |

## Relationships and family events

### Friends and love

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {親友|しんゆう} | best friend | {友人|ゆうじん} | friend (formal) |
| なかま | group of friends, teammates | なかよし | good friends |
| {友情|ゆうじょう} | friendship | {付|つ}き{合|あ}い | relationship, socializing |
| {気|き}が{合|あ}う | to get on well | なかなおりする | to make up |
| {出会|であ}う, {出会|であ}い | to meet (first time); a meeting | さそう, {断|ことわ}る | to invite (ask out); to turn down |
| こい, れんあい | love; romance | かたおもい | unrequited love |
| かれし | boyfriend | デート | date |
| {告白|こくはく}する | to tell someone you love them | うらぎる | to betray |
| {愛|あい}, {愛|あい}する, {愛情|あいじょう} | love (deep); to love; affection | {抱|だ}く, {抱|だ}きしめる | to hold; to hug tight |

なか (relationship) is written in kana in this course, since its kanji is outside N3: なかがいい
(get on well), なかなおり, なかよし, なかま.

### Marriage and the family

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| プロポーズ | proposal | {婚約|こんやく}, {婚約者|こんやくしゃ} | engagement; fiancé(e) |
| お{見合|みあ}い | arranged meeting | どくしん | single |
| {結婚|けっこん}{相手|あいて} | marriage partner | {新婚|しんこん}, {新婚旅行|しんこんりょこう} | newly married; honeymoon |
| {夫婦|ふうふ} | married couple | {夫妻|ふさい}, {夫人|ふじん} | Mr and Mrs; Mrs (formal) |
| {共働|ともばたら}き | both working | {家庭|かてい} | household, home |
| りこんする | to get divorced | {別|わか}れ | parting, break-up |
| {長男|ちょうなん}, {長女|ちょうじょ} | eldest son, daughter | {末|すえ}っ{子|こ} | youngest child |
| しんせき | relatives | {記念日|きねんび} | anniversary |

{夫|おっと} and {妻|つま} (my husband, my wife) are N5 words that now have their kanji. Talking about
someone else's, ごしゅじん and おくさん are still the everyday words.

### At a wedding

{招待|しょうたい}する / {招待状|しょうたいじょう} (to invite / an invitation), {式|しき} and {式場|しきじょう}
(the ceremony and the venue), ひろうえん (the reception), はなよめ or, formally, {新婦|しんぷ} (the
bride), しんろう (the groom), スピーチ, かんぱい (a toast), {引|ひ}き{出物|でもの} (the gift each
guest takes home), いわう (to celebrate). {幸福|こうふく} and {幸運|こううん} are the formal words for
happiness and good fortune.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for love, marriage and happiness.

### Love and marriage

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 愛 | love | アイ | | 13 | {愛|あい}, {愛|あい}する, {愛情|あいじょう} |
| 婚 | marriage | コン | | 11 | {結婚|けっこん}, {婚約|こんやく}, {新婚|しんこん} |
| 結 | tie, join | ケツ | むす(ぶ) | 12 | {結|むす}ぶ, {結婚|けっこん}, {結果|けっか} |
| 夫 | husband | フ, フウ | おっと | 4 | {夫|おっと}, {夫婦|ふうふ}, {夫人|ふじん} |
| 妻 | wife | サイ | つま | 8 | {妻|つま}, {夫妻|ふさい} |
| 婦 | woman, wife | フ | | 11 | {夫婦|ふうふ}, {主婦|しゅふ}, {新婦|しんぷ} |

### People and closeness

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 彼 | he, that | | かれ, かの | 8 | {彼|かれ}, {彼女|かのじょ}, かれし |
| 緒 | thread; together | ショ | | 14 | {一緒|いっしょ}に |
| 抱 | embrace | | だ(く) | 8 | {抱|だ}く, {抱|だ}きしめる |

### Invitations, welcomes and happiness

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 招 | invite | ショウ | まね(く) | 8 | {招|まね}く, {招待|しょうたい}, {招待状|しょうたいじょう} |
| 迎 | welcome, meet | ゲイ | むか(える) | 7 | {迎|むか}える, {迎|むか}え (pick-up), {送迎|そうげい} (pick-up and drop-off) |
| 幸 | happiness | コウ | しあわ(せ) | 8 | {幸|しあわ}せ, {幸福|こうふく}, {幸運|こううん} |
| 福 | blessing, fortune | フク | | 13 | {幸福|こうふく} |

Carried words you can now write with kanji: {結婚|けっこん}する, {結婚式|けっこんしき}, {結果|けっか},
{夫|おっと}, {妻|つま}, {主婦|しゅふ}, {彼|かれ}, {彼女|かのじょ}, {一緒|いっしょ}に, {迎|むか}える, {幸|しあわ}せ,
and {付|つ}き{合|あ}う (付 is lesson 21's).

Readings to watch:

- 夫 is フ in {夫妻|ふさい} and {夫人|ふじん} but フウ in {夫婦|ふうふ}.
- 婦 is プ after ん: {新婦|しんぷ}.
- 彼 is かの only in {彼女|かのじょ}. In かれし (boyfriend) the second kanji is outside N3.
- 抱 is also いだ(く) in writing: {夢|ゆめ}を{抱|いだ}く (to cherish a dream). You'll meet it; だ(く) is
  the everyday reading.
- 幸 has a second kun, さいわ(い) (fortunately), which you'll meet later.

Memory notes (hooks, not etymology):

- 愛: a heart (心) in the middle, with a roof of hands above and walking legs below: love is a
  heart you carry with you.
- 婚: a woman (女) and the sun (日) going down: weddings were once held at dusk.
- 結 and 緒 both start with the thread radical on the left: 結 ties a lucky knot; 緒 is the
  thread that keeps people {一緒|いっしょ}, together.
- 夫: 大 (a grown person) with an extra line across the top, a hairpin: a married man with his
  hair tied up.
- 妻 and 婦 both have a woman (女) at the bottom or on the left, with a hand holding a broom or a
  hairpin: old pictures of married life.
- 抱 and 招 both start with the hand radical (扌): hands that hold and hands that wave you in.
- 迎: the road radical (辶): going out along the road to meet someone.
- 幸: it looks like a pair of handcuffs; being free of them is happiness.
- 福: the altar radical (礻) and a full jar: blessings are a full jar on the altar.

```trace
愛婚結彼抱緒招迎夫妻婦幸福
```

## Dialogue: whose wedding was it again?

Rie and her brother Daiki talk at home about their cousin's wedding. Casual: っけ shows up a lot
when family members check things with each other.

```dialogue
# Our cousin's wedding
りえ: ねえ、まゆみちゃんの{結婚式|けっこんしき}って、いつだっけ？
= Hey, when's Mayumi's wedding again?
だいき: {来月|らいげつ}の{十日|とおか}じゃなかったっけ。{招待状|しょうたいじょう}、{来|き}てたよ。
= Wasn't it the tenth of next month? The invitation came.
りえ: そうそう。{相手|あいて}の{人|ひと}に{会|あ}ったことある？
= Right, right. Have you met the guy?
だいき: {一回|いっかい}だけ。{落|お}ち{着|つ}いてて、{優|やさ}しそうな{人|ひと}に{見|み}えたよ。
= Just once. He seemed calm and kind.
りえ: まゆみちゃん、{昔|むかし}は「{一生|いっしょう}{結婚|けっこん}しない」って{言|い}ってたのにね。
= And Mayumi used to say she'd never get married.
だいき: {二人|ふたり}はどこで{出会|であ}ったんだっけ？
= Where did they meet again?
りえ: たしか、{山登|やまのぼ}りのサークル。{最初|さいしょ}から{気|き}が{合|あ}ったんだって。
= A hiking club, I think. Apparently they hit it off from the start.
だいき: {最近|さいきん}のまゆみちゃん、{前|まえ}より{明|あか}るくなったような{気|き}がしない？
= Don't you feel Mayumi's got more cheerful lately?
りえ: する、する。{幸|しあわ}せなんだろうね。
= I do, I do. She must be happy.
だいき: で、りえ、{式|しき}でスピーチするって{聞|き}いたけど。
= So, Rie, I heard you're giving a speech at the ceremony.
りえ: そうなの。もう{何|なに}を{話|はな}すか{考|かんが}えてるんだけど、{絶対|ぜったい}{泣|な}いちゃう。いや、{泣|な}くに{違|ちが}いない。
= Yes. I'm already thinking about what to say, but I'm bound to cry. No, I'm sure I will.
だいき: りえはすぐ{泣|な}くからなあ。ハンカチ、{忘|わす}れないようにね。
= You always cry. Don't forget a handkerchief.
りえ: うん。あ、{新婚旅行|しんこんりょこう}はどこに{行|い}くって{言|い}ってたっけ？
= OK. Oh, where did she say they're going on their honeymoon?
だいき: ハワイだったような{気|き}がするけど…{本人|ほんにん}に{聞|き}いて。
= I've a feeling it was Hawaii, but... ask her yourself.
```

{落|お}ち{着|つ}いてて = {落|お}ち{着|つ}いていて (lesson 25); {一生|いっしょう} = all one's life (lesson 1);
{山登|やまのぼ}り = hiking, climbing; 〜んだって (they say, apparently) is lesson 22's, recognized here;
{絶対|ぜったい} = definitely; {泣|な}いちゃう = {泣|な}いてしまう (N4); {本人|ほんにん} = the person herself.

## Reading: a speech at the reception

The cousin's speech at the reception, in polite style. It's the kind of speech guests read from a
card: warm, a little formal, with a story or two.

> {皆様|みなさま}、{本日|ほんじつ}はおめでとうございます。{新婦|しんぷ}まゆみさんのいとこの、{山下|やました}りえです。ひと{言|こと}ごあいさつ{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます。
>
> まゆみさんと{私|わたし}は{同|おな}じ{年|とし}で、{子供|こども}のころはまるで{姉妹|しまい}のように、いつも{一緒|いっしょ}でした。まゆみさんは{小|ちい}さいころから{正直|しょうじき}で、{少|すこ}し{短気|たんき}なところもありましたが、{困|こま}っている{人|ひと}を{見|み}ると、{何|なに}かせずにはいられない{性格|せいかく}でした。
>
> {三年前|さんねんまえ}、まゆみさんから「{山|やま}のサークルで、{気|き}が{合|あ}う{人|ひと}に{出会|であ}った」と{聞|き}きました。そのときのうれしそうな{顔|かお}を、{今|いま}でもよく{覚|おぼ}えています。{私|わたし}は、この{人|ひと}こそまゆみさんの{運命|うんめい}の{相手|あいて}に{違|ちが}いないと{思|おも}いました。{初|はじ}めて{直人|なおと}さんに{会|あ}ったとき、{少|すこ}し{内気|うちき}な{方|かた}のように{見|み}えましたが、{話|はな}してみると、とても{落|お}ち{着|つ}いていて、まゆみさんをいつも{笑|わら}わせてくれる{方|かた}でした。
>
> {最近|さいきん}のまゆみさんは、{前|まえ}より{優|やさ}しくなったような{気|き}がします。きっと{直人|なおと}さんのおかげでしょう。お{二人|ふたり}とも、お{互|たが}いを{大切|たいせつ}にして、{笑顔|えがお}の{多|おお}い{家庭|かてい}を{作|つく}ってください。そして、けんかをしたら、その{日|ひ}のうちになかなおりしてくださいね。お{二人|ふたり}の{幸|しあわ}せを{心|こころ}から{願|ねが}っています。

{皆様|みなさま} = everyone (polite, lesson 24); {本日|ほんじつ} = today (formal); {申|もう}し{上|あ}げる =
humble "say" (N4); {姉妹|しまい} = sisters; 〜せずにはいられない = can't help doing (lesson 10);
こそ = the very… (lesson 15); {運命|うんめい} = fate, destiny; {方|かた} = person (polite);
{笑顔|えがお} = smiling face (lesson 10).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. How does Rie describe Mayumi as a child? — Honest, a little short-tempered, and unable to leave
   alone anyone who was in trouble.
2. What did Rie think when she first heard about Naoto? — That he must be Mayumi's destined
   partner (〜に{違|ちが}いないと{思|おも}いました), because Mayumi looked so happy.
3. What was Rie's first impression of Naoto, and was it right? — He looked a little shy
   (〜のように{見|み}えました), but once they talked he turned out to be calm and to make Mayumi laugh.
4. What two pieces of advice does Rie give the couple? — To treasure each other and make a home
   full of smiles, and to make up on the same day if they quarrel.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Ladies and gentlemen, congratulations on this happy day. I'm Rie Yamashita, the bride Mayumi's
cousin. Please allow me to say a few words.

Mayumi and I are the same age, and as children we were always together, just like sisters. Even
when she was little, Mayumi was honest. She could be a bit short-tempered, but when she saw
someone in trouble, she couldn't help doing something about it.

Three years ago Mayumi told me, "I've met someone I really get on with at the hiking club." I can
still picture how happy she looked. I thought this man must be the one she was destined to be
with. When I first met Naoto, he seemed a little shy, but once we talked I found he was very calm
and always made Mayumi laugh.

I feel Mayumi has grown kinder lately. That must be thanks to Naoto. I hope you'll both treasure
each other and make a home full of smiles. And if you quarrel, please make up before the day is
over. From the bottom of my heart, I wish you every happiness.

</details>

## Pronunciation

- っけ has a small っ before it, a full beat: だっけ is three morae, だ・っ・け. Say it with a light,
  slightly rising or flat tone; it's a question to yourself, not a demand.
- に{違|ちが}いない is said as one smooth phrase, with no pause after に. In fast speech the
  polite に{違|ちが}いありません keeps all its morae; don't drop the い.
- {夫婦|ふうふ:1} has a long ふう: ふ・う・ふ, three morae, falling after the first. Don't shorten it
  to ふふ.
- {愛|あい:1} is two morae and falls after the あ. {相手|あいて:3} stays high to its last mora and
  drops on a particle after it: あいてが.

```speak
{前|まえ}にどこかで{会|あ}ったような{気|き}がします。
= I've a feeling we've met somewhere before.
{彼|かれ}は{疲|つか}れているように{見|み}えますね。
= He looks as if he's tired, doesn't he?
あの{二人|ふたり}は{結婚|けっこん}するに{違|ちが}いない。
= Those two are sure to get married.
{式|しき}は{何時|なんじ}からだっけ？
= What time does the ceremony start again?
{会議|かいぎ}は{三時|さんじ}からでしたっけ？
= The meeting was from three, wasn't it?
おめでとうございます。お{幸|しあわ}せに。
= Congratulations. I wish you every happiness.
```

## Common mistakes

- Joining ような{気|き}がする like みたい: ×{静|しず}かような{気|き}がする. It's {静|しず}かなような
  {気|き}がする (or casual {静|しず}かみたいな{気|き}がする).
- Putting だ before に{違|ちが}いない: ×{犯人|はんにん}だに{違|ちが}いない. It's {犯人|はんにん}に{違|ちが}いない.
- Using に{違|ちが}いない for timetables and plans: ×{電車|でんしゃ}は{九時|くじ}に{出|で}るに{違|ちが}いない. A known
  schedule is はず: {九時|くじ}に{出|で}るはずだ.
- Using っけ for new information: ×(to a stranger) トイレはどこだっけ？ っけ is for things you
  knew and forgot.
- Mixing up {見|み}える patterns: ×{若|わか}いに{見|み}える. Adjective alone: {若|わか}く{見|み}える; with a
  clause: {若|わか}いように{見|み}える (stiffer).
- Writing {夫婦|ふうふ} as ふふ or reading {新婦|しんぷ} as しんふ.

## Key points

- 〜ような{気|き}がする: a vague feeling; softens opinions. Joins like ようだ (な-adj な, noun の).
- 〜ように{見|み}える / みたいに{見|み}える: looks as if (a clause, any tense). そう can't take a past.
- 〜に{違|ちが}いない: must be, I'm sure (own conviction). No だ before it. はず is for facts and plans.
- 〜とみえる and 〜かのように: recognize them in writing.
- 〜っけ: casual "…again?" for things you knew: だっけ, たっけ, んだっけ; polite でしたっけ.
- **[[Inference]]** draws a conclusion from what you notice; **[[hearsay]]** passes on what you were told.
- New kanji: 愛 婚 結 彼 抱 緒 招 迎 夫 妻 婦 幸 福.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Against expectations: くせに, にしては, 割に, ながらも, ば〜のに
topics: にしては and 割に
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Things often don't turn out the way you'd expect from the facts: he's clever but never studies;
she's only a beginner but plays like a pro; the restaurant is cheap, yet the food is good. This
lesson gathers the ways Japanese says "although", "for a…", "considering" and "if only", each
with its own feeling: annoyance, surprise, fairness or regret.

The theme is school: pupils and teachers, lessons and homework, tests and grades, being there and
being absent, and the long road of entrance exams.

{知|し}っているくせに、{教|おし}えてくれない。 — He knows, but he won't tell me.
{初|はじ}めてにしては、よくできた。 — For a first try, that was really good.
この{店|みせ}は{安|やす}い{割|わり}に、おいしい。 — This restaurant is good, considering how cheap it is.
もっと{早|はや}く{言|い}ってくれればよかったのに。 — If only you'd told me sooner.

## Even though (and I don't like it): 〜くせに

〜くせに means "even though", and it complains. The speaker is criticizing, blaming or looking down
on someone, or, between close friends, teasing. It joins the plain form like a noun does:

| Before くせに | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb | {知|し}っているくせに | even though he knows |
| い-adjective | {若|わか}いくせに | young as he is |
| な-adjective + な | {下手|へた}なくせに | even though she's no good at it |
| noun + の | {子供|こども}のくせに | when he's only a child |

{弟|おとうと}は{勉強|べんきょう}しなかったくせに、{点数|てんすう}が{悪|わる}いと{先生|せんせい}のせいにする。 — My
brother didn't study, and yet he blames the teacher for his bad marks.
{受験生|じゅけんせい}のくせに、{毎晩|まいばん}ゲームばかりしている。 — He's supposed to be preparing for
exams, and he plays games every night.

It can end a sentence, leaving the complaint unsaid: {本当|ほんとう}は{知|し}ってるくせに！ (You know
perfectly well!). Between friends this can be playful: {好|す}きなくせに (you like it really).

### くせに or のに?

N4's のに also means "even though", but it's more neutral:

| | のに | くせに |
|---|---|---|
| Feeling | surprise, disappointment, regret | blame, contempt, teasing |
| About yourself | ✓ {勉強|べんきょう}したのに、{落|お}ちた | ✗ (you don't scold yourself this way) |
| Two different people | ✓ {母|はは}が{作|つく}ったのに、{弟|おとうと}は{食|た}べなかった | ✗: the person in both halves is usually the same |
| To a superior | fine in polite form | rude |

{一生|いっしょう}けんめい{勉強|べんきょう}したのに、{試験|しけん}に{落|お}ちてしまった。 — I studied as hard as I
could, and I still failed the exam. (Not ×{勉強|べんきょう}したくせに: it's about me.)

## For a…: 〜にしては

〜にしては says "for a…, considering that it's…": the result is not what you'd expect from X.
It follows a noun, or the plain form of a verb.

{初|はじ}めてにしては、{上手|じょうず}ですね。 — That's good for a first time.
{十一月|じゅういちがつ}にしては、{今日|きょう}は{暑|あつ}い。 — It's hot
today, for November.
{毎日|まいにち}{練習|れんしゅう}しているにしては、なかなか{上手|じょうず}にならない。 — For someone who
practises every day, he isn't getting much better.
{小学生|しょうがくせい}にしては、{難|むずか}しい{本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでいる。 — He reads difficult books for a
primary school pupil.

It's an evaluation by the speaker: good or bad, but not your own plan or request. It doesn't
normally follow an adjective directly (×{高|たか}いにしては): use 〜{割|わり}に for that.

## Considering: 〜{割|わり}に(は)

〜{割|わり}に(は) compares two amounts: "considering, for (the price, the age…)". The result is more
or less than X would lead you to expect.

| Before {割|わり}に | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| noun + の | {値段|ねだん}の{割|わり}に | considering the price |
| verb | {勉強|べんきょう}した{割|わり}に | considering how much I studied |
| い-adjective | {高|たか}い{割|わり}に | for something so expensive |
| な-adjective + な | {静|しず}かな{割|わり}に | for somewhere so quiet |

この{店|みせ}は{値段|ねだん}の{割|わり}に、{量|りょう}が{多|おお}い。 — This place gives you a lot for the price.
{勉強|べんきょう}した{割|わり}には、{点数|てんすう}が{悪|わる}かった。 — My score was bad, considering how much I
studied.
{祖母|そぼ}は{年|とし}の{割|わり}に{若|わか}く{見|み}える。 — My grandmother looks young for her age.
この{学校|がっこう}はこうそくがきびしい{割|わり}に、{生徒|せいと}は{自由|じゆう}そうだ。 — For a school with
strict rules, the pupils seem quite free.

You'll often see it in kana, わりに. On its own, {割|わり}に / わりと is also an adverb,
"comparatively, fairly": {今日|きょう}はわりと{静|しず}かだ (it's fairly quiet
today).

### にしては or {割|わり}に?

With a noun they often swap: {子供|こども}にしては / {子供|こども}の{割|わり}に{上手|じょうず}だ. The
differences:

- Adjectives take only {割|わり}に: {高|たか}い{割|わり}に ✓, ×{高|たか}いにしては.
- Amounts and degrees ({値段|ねだん}, {年|とし}, {大|おお}きさ) sound most natural with {割|わり}に:
  {値段|ねだん}の{割|わり}に.
- A fact or a role ("for someone who is a…") suits にしては: プロにしては{下手|へた}だ (for a
  professional, he's bad).

## Although: 〜ながら(も)

N4's ながら joined two actions done at the same time: {音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きながら{勉強|べんきょう}する. With
words for a state, not an action, ながら(も) means "although, while (admitting)". It's mostly
written or formal, and も adds weight.

| Joins to | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ます stem of a state verb | {知|し}りながら, {知|し}っていながら | although (he) knows |
| い-adjective (dictionary form) | せまいながらも | small as it is |
| な-adjective stem | {残念|ざんねん}ながら, {不便|ふべん}ながら | unfortunately; inconvenient as it is |
| noun | {子供|こども}ながら | though only a child |

{彼|かれ}は{間違|まちが}いだと{知|し}っていながら、{何|なに}も{言|い}わなかった。 — He knew it was a mistake, yet
he said nothing.
せまいながらも、{家族|かぞく}みんなが{集|あつ}まれる{家|いえ}だ。 — Small as it is, it's a home where
the whole family can get together.
{卒業式|そつぎょうしき}で、{先生|せんせい}は{泣|な}きながらも{笑|わら}っていた。 — At the graduation ceremony
our teacher was smiling, even through her tears.

The last one sits on the border: {泣|な}く is an action, but with も it reads "although crying".
Set phrases are common: {残念|ざんねん}ながら (unfortunately), {小|ちい}さいながら (small though it is).

Saying "although X, still Y" is a **[[concession]]**: you grant a point, then say the result holds
anyway. くせに, のに, ながらも and the ても forms below are all concessions with different
feelings.

## Wishes and regret: 〜ば〜のに, 〜たらいいのに

A ば or たら clause with のに at the end talks about what isn't so, and wishes it were:

| Pattern | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 〜ば〜のに (if… then… but it isn't so) | {時間|じかん}があれば{行|い}けるのに | I could go if I had time (but I don't) |
| 〜ばいいのに / 〜たらいいのに | {雨|あめ}がやめばいいのに | I wish the rain would stop |
| 〜ばよかったのに | もっと{早|はや}く{言|い}えばよかったのに | you should have said so sooner |

もう{少|すこ}し{安|やす}ければ、{買|か}うのに。 — If it were a bit cheaper, I'd buy it.
{夏休|なつやす}みがもっと{長|なが}ければいいのに。 — I wish the summer holidays were longer.
{毎日|まいにち}{少|すこ}しずつ{勉強|べんきょう}すればよかったのに。 — You should have studied a little every
day.

N4's 〜ばよかった (I should have…) is plain regret. Adding のに adds a sigh: disappointment, or
blame when it's about someone else.

## Even if, no matter how: たとえ〜ても, どんなに〜ても

> **Review (N4).** 〜ても / 〜でも: even if. いくら〜ても: however much.

たとえ in front makes the "even if" hypothetical and firm: "even supposing". どんなに in front
stresses degree: "no matter how (much)".

たとえ{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っても、{運動会|うんどうかい}はあるそうだ。 — Apparently sports day is on even if it
rains.
たとえ{親|おや}に{反対|はんたい}されても、{美術|びじゅつ}の{大学|だいがく}に{行|い}きたい。 — Even if my
parents are against it, I want to go to art school.
どんなに{練習|れんしゅう}しても、{速|はや}く{走|はし}れない。 — No matter how much I practise, I can't run fast.

## Even so: それにしても

それにしても starts a sentence: "I accept that, but even so". It also opens a remark about
something striking: "My, (it's)…".

{忙|いそが}しいのは{分|わ}かる。それにしても、れんらくくらいしてほしい。 — I know you're busy. Even so, I'd
like you to at least get in touch.
それにしても、{今日|きょう}は{暑|あつ}いね。 — My, it's hot today.

## Casual: 〜たって, 〜だって

In casual speech, 〜たって and 〜だって mean 〜ても and 〜でも. They're made from the た form:

| Word | ても form | Casual |
|---|---|---|
| {走|はし}る | {走|はし}っても | {走|はし}ったって |
| {読|よ}む | {読|よ}んでも | {読|よ}んだって |
| {高|たか}い | {高|たか}くても | {高|たか}くたって |
| {静|しず}か / {子供|こども} | {静|しず}かでも / {子供|こども}でも | {静|しず}かだって / {子供|こども}だって |

{今|いま}から{走|はし}ったって、{間|ま}に{合|あ}わないよ。 — Even if you run now, you won't make it.
そんなこと、{子供|こども}だって{知|し}ってるよ。 — Even a child knows that.

Two other だって will come up: at the start of a sentence, だって is a casual "but, because"
(だって、{眠|ねむ}かったんだもん: but I was sleepy!), and 〜んだって is hearsay, "I hear" (lesson 22).

## School words

### People and places

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {生徒|せいと} | pupil | {教師|きょうし}, {教員|きょういん} | teacher (job), teaching staff |
| {教|おし}え{子|ご} | a teacher's former pupil | {卒業生|そつぎょうせい} | graduate |
| {教頭|きょうとう} | deputy head | クラスメート | classmate |
| {受験生|じゅけんせい} | exam candidate | {小学校|しょうがっこう}, {中学校|ちゅうがっこう} | primary, junior high school |
| {体育館|たいいくかん} | gym | {予備校|よびこう} | prep school for entrance exams |

### Lessons, tests and grades

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {学期|がっき}, {学年|がくねん} | term; school year | {時間割|じかんわり} | timetable |
| {国語|こくご}, {数学|すうがく}, {理科|りか} | Japanese, maths, science | さんすう, {体育|たいいく} | arithmetic, PE |
| {教科書|きょうかしょ} | textbook | ていしゅつ | handing in |
| {満点|まんてん} | full marks | {赤点|あかてん} | a failing mark |
| {正解|せいかい} | correct answer | {誤|あやま}り | error (formal) |
| {難問|なんもん} | hard question | {通知表|つうちひょう} | report card |
| {学力|がくりょく} | academic level | ゆうしゅう | excellent |

### Being there, or not

{出席|しゅっせき} (attendance), {欠席|けっせき} (absence), {早退|そうたい} (leaving early), {登校|とうこう} and
{下校|げこう} (going to and leaving school), {不登校|ふとうこう} (not going to school for a long time),
サボる (to skip, casual), なまける (to slack). And the bad endings: {留年|りゅうねん} or {落第|らくだい}
(repeating a year, failing), {中退|ちゅうたい} (dropping out). The good ones: {進学|しんがく} (going on to
the next school) and {卒業式|そつぎょうしき}. Every school year starts with an {入学式|にゅうがくしき}, and
lunch at many state schools is {給食|きゅうしょく}.

### Learning

{学|まな}ぶ (to learn, formal), {教|おそ}わる (to be taught), やり{直|なお}す (to redo), {覚|おぼ}え
(memory, how fast you learn: {覚|おぼ}えが{早|はや}い), {苦労|くろう} (hardship), {苦|くる}しい and
{苦|くる}しむ (hard; to suffer), {誤解|ごかい} (a misunderstanding), {欠|か}ける (to lack: やる{気|き}に
{欠|か}ける), じゅぎょうりょう (tuition fees), {教育|きょういく} (education), いじめ (bullying).

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for school, memory and difficulty.

### People at school

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 徒 | follower; on foot | ト | | 10 | {生徒|せいと}, {徒歩|とほ} (on foot) |
| 師 | teacher, master | シ | | 10 | {教師|きょうし}, {美容師|びようし}, {医師|いし} (doctor, formal) |
| 育 | raise | イク | そだ(てる), そだ(つ) | 8 | {育|そだ}てる, {育|そだ}つ, {教育|きょういく}, {体育|たいいく} |
| 卒 | graduate | ソツ | | 8 | {卒業|そつぎょう}, {卒業式|そつぎょうしき} |
| 練 | train, practise | レン | | 14 | {練習|れんしゅう} |

### There or not there

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 欠 | lack | ケツ | か(ける) | 4 | {欠|か}ける, {欠席|けっせき}, {欠点|けってん} (fault) |
| 席 | seat | セキ | | 10 | {席|せき}, {出席|しゅっせき}, {座席|ざせき} |

### Memory and mistakes

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 覚 | remember; wake | カク | おぼ(える), さ(める) | 12 | {覚|おぼ}える, {覚|おぼ}え, {目|め}が{覚|さ}める (wake up), {感覚|かんかく} (sense) |
| 忘 | forget | ボウ | わす(れる) | 7 | {忘|わす}れる, {忘|わす}れ{物|もの}, {忘年会|ぼうねんかい} (year-end party) |
| 誤 | mistake | ゴ | あやま(る) | 14 | {誤|あやま}り, {誤解|ごかい} |

### Easy and hard

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 易 | easy | イ | やさ(しい) | 8 | {易|やさ}しい, {容易|ようい} (easy, formal) |
| 難 | difficult | ナン | むずか(しい) | 18 | {難|むずか}しい, {難問|なんもん} |
| 苦 | suffering; bitter | ク | くる(しい), にが(い) | 8 | {苦|くる}しい, {苦|にが}い, {苦手|にがて}, {苦労|くろう} |

Carried words you can now write with kanji: {育|そだ}てる, {卒業|そつぎょう}する, {練習|れんしゅう},
{席|せき}, {覚|おぼ}える, {忘|わす}れる, {忘|わす}れ{物|もの}, {易|やさ}しい, {難|むずか}しい, {苦|にが}い and
{苦手|にがて}.

Readings to watch:

- やさしい has two spellings: {易|やさ}しい is "easy (not difficult)"; {優|やさ}しい (lesson 20) is
  "kind, gentle". Same word in N5's list, different kanji for the two meanings.
- 易 is イ in {容易|ようい} but やさ(しい) on its own. (It's also エキ in some words you'll meet
  at N2.)
- 苦 has two kun readings: くる(しい) (painful, hard) and にが(い) (bitter). {苦手|にがて} uses にが.
- 誤 as a verb, {誤|あやま}る (to make an error), is written: in speech people say {間違|まちが}える.
  N4's あやまる (to apologize) is a different word, written with a kanji outside N3.
- 覚 is さ(める) in {目|め}が{覚|さ}める (to wake up).

Memory notes (hooks, not etymology):

- 徒: the "going" radical on the left (a person walking) and 走 (run) on the right: a pupil
  walking or running to school.
- 師: a heap of earth and a banner: the master who leads the troop.
- 育: a baby upside down (the top part) over flesh (月): a child being born and growing.
- 卒: 十 (ten) at the bottom of a soldier's coat: ten people done with their duty, graduated.
- 欠: a person with a wide-open mouth, yawning: something's missing.
- 覚: a roof with three strokes on top, over 見 (see): what you've seen stays under your roof.
- 忘: 亡 (gone, lesson 1) over 心 (heart): it's gone from your heart.
- 誤: 言 (words) on the left: a mistake in what was said.
- 難: 18 strokes, the longest in this lesson; the bird on the right can't fly because
  it's so hard.
- 苦: grass (艹) over 古 (old): old grass tastes bitter.

```trace
徒師育卒練欠席覚忘誤易難苦
```

## Dialogue: the report card

Saki and her mother look at Yuta's end-of-term report card. Casual, family speech.

```dialogue
# The report card
はは: ねえ、ゆうたの{通知表|つうちひょう}、{見|み}た？
= Hey, have you seen Yuta's report card?
さき: {見|み}た{見|み}た。{数学|すうがく}、すごくよくなってたね。
= I have. His maths has got really good.
はは: そうなの。{毎晩|まいばん}ゲームばかりしてる{割|わり}には、{点数|てんすう}がいいのよ。
= Yes. For someone who plays games every night, his marks are good.
さき: じゅくにも{行|い}ってないにしては、すごいよね。
= It's impressive for someone who doesn't even go to cram school.
はは: でも、{国語|こくご}はまた{赤点|あかてん}すれすれ。{本|ほん}を{全然|ぜんぜん}{読|よ}まないんだから。
= But Japanese was nearly a fail again. He never reads any books.
さき: {先生|せんせい}は{何|なん}て？
= What did the teacher say?
はは: 「{能力|のうりょく}はあるのに、{宿題|しゅくだい}をよく{忘|わす}れます」って。
= "He's capable, but he often forgets his homework."
さき: ゆうたって、{自分|じぶん}はすぐ{忘|わす}れるくせに、{私|わたし}が{約束|やくそく}を{忘|わす}れると{怒|おこ}るんだよね。
= You know, Yuta forgets everything himself, and yet he gets angry when I forget a promise.
はは: ふふ。{残念|ざんねん}ながら、そこはお{父|とう}さんに{似|に}たのね。
= Ha. Sadly, that's where he takes after your father.
さき: それにしても、{宿題|しゅくだい}くらいやればいいのに。
= Even so, he could at least do his homework.
はは: {言|い}ったって{聞|き}かないのよ。{私|わたし}が{子供|こども}のころは、たとえ{熱|ねつ}があっても{学校|がっこう}に{行|い}ったものよ。
= Telling him does no good. When I was a child, I went to school even if I had a temperature.
さき: それは{休|やす}んだほうがよかったと{思|おも}うけど…。
= I think you'd have been better off staying at home...
```

すれすれ = only just, nearly (a fail); {約束|やくそく} =
promise (N4); 〜たものだ = used to (lesson 9).

## Reading: the boy who got full marks

An essay by a junior-high-school teacher for a teachers' magazine, in the plain だ style.

> {教師|きょうし}になって{二十年|にじゅうねん}になる。{毎年|まいとし}たくさんの{生徒|せいと}に{出会|であ}うが、{今|いま}でもよく{思|おも}い{出|だ}す{生徒|せいと}がいる。{初|はじ}めてたんにんをしたクラスの、{健|けん}という{男|おとこ}の{子|こ}だ。
>
> {健|けん}は{頭|あたま}がいい{割|わり}に{勉強|べんきょう}をせず、{宿題|しゅくだい}もよく{忘|わす}れた。{欠席|けっせき}や{遅刻|ちこく}も{多|おお}かった。ほかの{先生|せんせい}たちは「{能力|のうりょく}があるくせに、やる{気|き}がない」と{言|い}っていた。{私|わたし}もそう{思|おも}っていた。
>
> ある{日|ひ}、{健|けん}が{理科|りか}のテストで{満点|まんてん}を{取|と}った。じゅぎょうにあまり{出|で}ていなかったにしては、{完全|かんぜん}な{答|こた}えだった。{話|はなし}を{聞|き}くと、{夜|よる}は{病気|びょうき}のお{母|かあ}さんの{世話|せわ}をしながら、{一人|ひとり}で{教科書|きょうかしょ}を{読|よ}んでいたという。{朝|あさ}{起|お}きられない{日|ひ}が{多|おお}かったのは、そのせいだった。{健|けん}は{苦|くる}しいながらも、{一人|ひとり}でがんばっていたのだ。{私|わたし}は{何|なに}も{知|し}らずに、{彼|かれ}を{誤解|ごかい}していた。
>
> 「{言|い}ってくれればよかったのに」と{言|い}うと、{健|けん}は「{言|い}ったって、どうにもならないから」と{笑|わら}った。
>
> {今|いま}、{健|けん}は{医者|いしゃ}として{働|はたら}いている。{卒業|そつぎょう}して{十五年|じゅうごねん}たつが、{毎年|まいとし}{手紙|てがみ}をくれる。たとえ{点数|てんすう}が{悪|わる}くても、{遅刻|ちこく}が{多|おお}くても、{理由|りゆう}を{聞|き}くまでは{生徒|せいと}を{判断|はんだん}しない。{健|けん}が{教|おし}えてくれたことだ。

たんにん = homeroom teacher (N4); {完全|かんぜん} = perfect, complete (lesson 23); {世話|せわ}をする = to look
after (N4); 〜という = they say, he said; {知|し}らずに = without knowing (lesson 10); として = as
(lesson 11); たつ = (time) passes; {判断|はんだん}する = to judge (lesson 28).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What did the other teachers think of Ken? — That he had ability but no motivation
   (〜くせに、やる{気|き}がない).
2. Why was the full mark surprising? — Because he had missed so many lessons (〜にしては).
3. Why was Ken often late or absent? — At night he looked after his sick mother and studied alone,
   so many mornings he couldn't get up.
4. What did the writer learn from Ken? — Not to judge a pupil, even one with bad marks or a lot of
   lateness, before hearing the reasons.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

It's twenty years since I became a teacher. Every year I meet a lot of pupils, but there's one I
still often think of: a boy called Ken, in the first class I was ever in charge of.

Ken was clever, but considering that, he didn't study, and he often forgot his homework. He was
often absent or late, too. The other teachers used to say, "He's got the ability, but no
motivation." I thought so too.

One day Ken got full marks in a science test. For someone who'd missed so many lessons, his
answers were perfect. When I asked him about it, he told me that at night he looked after his sick
mother and read the textbook on his own. That was why there were so many mornings when he
couldn't get up. Hard as it was, he'd been managing on his own. And I, knowing nothing, had
misjudged him.

"If only you'd told me," I said, and Ken laughed: "Telling you wouldn't have changed anything."

Ken works as a doctor now. Fifteen years after leaving school, he still writes to me every year.
Even if a pupil's marks are bad, even if they're often late, I don't judge them until I've heard
the reason. That's what Ken taught me.

</details>

## Pronunciation

- くせに: く・せ・に, three morae, with the pitch falling after the せ in most speech. In anger it
  comes out sharp and fast: {知|し}ってるくせに！
- {割|わり}に is わ・り・に; in quick speech it often becomes わりと or just わり.
- ながらも: don't drop the も; it's what turns "while" into "although" with a state verb.
- 〜たって: the っ is a full beat: た・っ・て. {高|たか}くたって is six morae, た・か・く・た・っ・て.

```speak
{知|し}ってるくせに、{教|おし}えてくれないんだ。
= You know, but you won't tell me.
{初|はじ}めてにしては、{上手|じょうず}ですね。
= That's good for a first time.
この{店|みせ}は{値段|ねだん}の{割|わり}においしい。
= This place is good for the price.
{残念|ざんねん}ながら、{中止|ちゅうし}になりました。
= Unfortunately, it's been cancelled.
もっと{早|はや}く{言|い}ってくれればよかったのに。
= If only you'd told me sooner.
{今|いま}から{走|はし}ったって{間|ま}に{合|あ}わないよ。
= Even if you run now, you won't make it.
```

## Common mistakes

- Using くせに about yourself: ×{私|わたし}は{練習|れんしゅう}したくせに、{負|ま}けた. Use のに:
  {練習|れんしゅう}したのに、{負|ま}けた.
- くせに to a superior: ×{先生|せんせい}は{知|し}っているくせに… It's openly critical, so it's rude to
  someone above you.
- にしては after an adjective: ×{高|たか}いにしては{小|ちい}さい. Use {割|わり}に: {高|たか}い{割|わり}に{小|ちい}さい.
- Forgetting の before {割|わり}に with a noun: ×{値段|ねだん}{割|わり}に. It's {値段|ねだん}の{割|わり}に.
- Reading ながら as "while" with a state: {知|し}っていながら is "although he knew", not "while
  knowing".
- Leaving out のに when you mean a wish about something that isn't so: {時間|じかん}があれば{行|い}ける
  is a plain condition ("if I have time, I can go"); {時間|じかん}があれば{行|い}けるのに says you
  don't have the time.
- Writing やさしい "kind" with 易: that's {優|やさ}しい.

## Key points

- 〜くせに: even though (blame, contempt, teasing); about someone else; not to superiors.
  のに is neutral and can be about yourself.
- 〜にしては (noun, verb): for a…, the result isn't what X would suggest.
- 〜{割|わり}に(は) (noun の, verb, い-adj, な-adj な): considering, in proportion to.
- 〜ながら(も) with states: although ({知|し}りながら, せまいながらも, {残念|ざんねん}ながら).
- 〜ば〜のに, 〜ばいいのに, 〜ばよかったのに: what isn't so, wishes and regret.
- たとえ〜ても (even supposing), どんなに〜ても (no matter how), それにしても (even so), casual
  〜たって / 〜だって.
- A **[[concession]]** grants a point and says the result holds anyway.
- New kanji: 徒 師 育 卒 練 欠 席 覚 忘 誤 易 難 苦.
