lessons.title: Who says what: role language and slang
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 25 showed what casual particles do. This lesson is about who uses them. Japanese lets a
speaker show a lot about themselves through small words: which "I" they choose, how they end a
sentence, which slang they use. Manga, anime, games and translated novels push this much further
than real life, giving each type of character a recognizable way of talking.

The goal here is to recognize these styles, understand what they suggest, and know which ones are
safe for you to use. Much of this is changing fast, and people's habits vary by age, region and
personality: treat everything below as tendencies, not rules.

## Words for "I"

| Word | Who uses it, typically | Feel |
|---|---|---|
| {私|わたくし} | anyone, in very formal speech | formal, humble |
| {私|わたし} | anyone; women in casual speech too | neutral, polite |
| あたし | women and girls, casually | soft, casual |
| ぼく | boys and men; also some men at work | gentle, a little boyish |
| おれ | men and boys, with friends and family | rough, casual, confident |
| うち | girls and young women in western Japan (and elsewhere) | casual, regional |
| わし | old men in stories; some older men in western Japan | elderly, gruff |
| {自分|じぶん} | some men in sports or the armed forces; in Kansai, "you" | stiff, or regional |

For a learner, {私|わたし} is always safe. Men can use ぼく with friends, and おれ with close friends,
but not at work with customers or in an interview: there, {私|わたし} (or {私|わたくし}).

## Endings and character

Lesson 25's sentence-final particles carry a gender and age flavour that's stronger in fiction
than in life:

| Ending | In fiction, typically | In real speech today |
|---|---|---|
| 〜わ↗, 〜わよ, 〜わね | a refined woman | rare among young Tokyo women; heard from some older women |
| 〜かしら | a woman, often older | rare among young speakers |
| 〜のよ, 〜なのよ | a woman | still heard, mostly from women |
| 〜ぞ, 〜ぜ | a tough young man | ぞ heard from men; ぜ rare outside fiction |
| 〜だぜ | a cool, cocky hero | mostly fiction |
| 〜じゃ, 〜のう | an old man, a wise master | regional in parts of western Japan |
| 〜ですわ, 〜ですの | a rich young lady | almost only fiction |
| 〜でござる | a samurai | only fiction and jokes |

These sets are **[[role language]]** ({役割語|やくわりご}): ways of speaking that don't belong to any real
group so much as to a character type in stories. The term comes from the work of the linguist
Satoshi Kinsui in the early 2000s. Role language lets a manga artist tell you who someone is from
one line:

- 「わしが{若|わか}いころはのう…」 — an old man (or a professor) telling a story.
- 「よろしくてよ」, 「〜ですわ」 — a rich young lady. Nobody really talks like this.
- 「せっしゃは〜でござる」 — a samurai (せっしゃ is an old word for "I"); you'll meet it in
  historical comedies.

Translators use role language too. In a Japanese translation of an English novel, a gruff old
farmer may speak with わし and 〜じゃ, while a young woman says 〜わ, even though the English had
none of that. When you read translated books, notice how the translator built each character's
voice.

## Young people's words

Slang changes every few years, but a handful of words have lasted and are now heard from people
of many ages in casual speech:

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| やばい | dangerous, bad; or amazing | やばい、{遅刻|ちこく}だ！ / このケーキ、やばい！ |
| マジ | seriously, for real | マジで？ |
| ウケる | that's hilarious | それ、ウケる！ |
| ガチ | seriously, for real (stronger) | ガチで{疲|つか}れた。 |
| すごい (adverb) | very (instead of すごく) | すごいおいしい |
| 〜みたいな | like, sort of | 「えっ？」みたいな |
| キモい | gross, creepy | (rude: don't use it about people) |
| ドタキャン | last-minute cancellation | (lesson 25) |

Notes:

- やばい started as "dangerous, risky": you'll hear it in every sense from "uh-oh" to "awesome".
  Tone and situation tell you which.
- ウケる is {受|う}ける (lesson 24's kanji) in a slang sense, "to go down well", usually written in
  katakana in this sense: "that's a hit with me", that's funny.
- すごいおいしい (すごい before an adjective) is very common in speech, but the standard form is
  すごくおいしい. Write すごく.
- Many dictionaries and teachers call these words "not correct". They're perfectly normal among
  friends, but they mark the speaker as casual or young.

Each year, a list of the year's buzzwords ({流行語|りゅうこうご}) is announced, and most of them are
forgotten a year or two later. Don't try to learn the latest ones from a list; pick them up from
your friends if you have Japanese friends of that age.

## When not to use them

The safest rule for a learner: copy the style of the people you're talking to, one step more
polite. In particular:

- At work, with teachers, with customers and in any first meeting: {私|わたし}, です/ます, no slang.
- With friends: casual speech, and the slang your friends use themselves.
- Role-language endings (〜わよ, 〜ぜ, 〜じゃ, 〜でござる): never in earnest. They sound like a
  character in a cartoon, or like a joke.
- Gendered words: Japanese listeners notice when a learner picks a style that doesn't seem to fit.
  Neutral choices ({私|わたし}, plain casual without わ or ぜ) are never wrong.

Your ことばづかい (choice of words) is part of how people see you. A learner who speaks clear,
neutral Japanese sounds far better than one who mixes keigo with slang.

## Dialogue: reading manga together

Nana and Ken, university friends, are reading a manga. Nana explains the characters' speech.

```dialogue
# Who's speaking?
ケン: ねえ、この{人|ひと}、「わしは{知|し}らんのう」って{言|い}ってるけど、どういう{意味|いみ}？
= Hey, this guy says わしは{知|し}らんのう. What does that mean?
なな: 「{私|わたし}は{知|し}らないね」っていう{意味|いみ}。おじいさんの{話|はな}し{方|かた}だよ。
= It means "I don't know". It's how old men talk.
ケン: でも、この{人|ひと}、{若|わか}く{見|み}えるよ。
= But he looks young.
なな: あ、ほんとだ。じゃあ、{実|じつ}はすごい{年|とし}をとった{神様|かみさま}なのかも。マンガではよくあるんだよね。
= Oh, you're right. Then maybe he's actually a really old god. That happens a lot in manga.
ケン: そうなんだ。じゃあ、こっちの「{行|い}くわよ」って{言|い}ってる{女|おんな}の{人|ひと}は？
= I see. And this woman who says {行|い}くわよ?
なな: それは、ちょっとお{金持|かねも}ちっぽい{女性|じょせい}かな。{今|いま}、ふつうの{人|ひと}はあんまり{言|い}わないけど。
= She's probably meant to sound kind of rich. Ordinary people don't really say it now.
ケン: マジで？おれ、アニメで{覚|おぼ}えて、{友|とも}だちに{使|つか}っちゃったよ。
= Seriously? I learned it from anime and used it with my friends!
なな: え、ウケる！みんな、びっくりしたでしょ。
= What, that's hilarious! Everyone must have been surprised.
ケン: うん、すごい{笑|わら}われた。
= Yeah, they laughed a lot.
なな: ケンは「{行|い}くよ」でいいよ。それが{一番|いちばん}{自然|しぜん}。
= Just say {行|い}くよ, Ken. That's the most natural.
```

{知|し}らん = {知|し}らない (in western Japan and in role language); {年|とし}をとる = to grow old; 〜っぽい
= -ish, sort of (lesson 16); すごい{笑|わら}われた = casual for すごく{笑|わら}われた; {自然|しぜん} = natural.

## Reading: a column on how we speak

A short newspaper column. Plain だ style.

> 「やばい」という{言葉|ことば}を{聞|き}かない{日|ひ}はない。{昔|むかし}は「{危|あぶ}ない」という{意味|いみ}だけだったが、{今|いま}の{若者|わかもの}は、おいしい{物|もの}を{食|た}べても、きれいな{景色|けしき}を{見|み}ても「やばい」と{言|い}う。
>
> これを「{日本語|にほんご}がおかしくなった」と{言|い}う{人|ひと}もいる。しかし、{言葉|ことば}はいつの{時代|じだい}も{変|か}わってきた。{今|いま}ふつうに{使|つか}っている{言葉|ことば}にも、{昔|むかし}は{若者|わかもの}{言葉|ことば}だったものがたくさんある。
>
> {大切|たいせつ}なのは、{相手|あいて}と{場所|ばしょ}によって、{言葉|ことば}を{使|つか}い{分|わ}けることだろう。{友|とも}だちと「やばい」と{笑|わら}い{合|あ}う{若者|わかもの}も、めんせつでは「すばらしいと{思|おも}います」と{言|い}えるなら、{何|なに}も{問題|もんだい}はない。

めんせつ = job interview (N4; a kanji in it is outside N3); {危|あぶ}ない = dangerous (N5, now with lesson 26's kanji);
{使|つか}い{分|わ}ける = to use each one in the right place; {笑|わら}い{合|あ}う = to laugh together.

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. How has the meaning of やばい changed, according to the writer? — It used to mean only
   "dangerous", but young people now also say it about delicious food or beautiful scenery.
2. What is the writer's opinion of young people's language? — Language has always changed, and
   it's no problem as long as people choose their words to fit the person and the place.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Not a day goes by without hearing the word やばい. Once it only meant "dangerous", but young
people today say やばい when they eat something delicious or see beautiful scenery.

Some people say this shows that Japanese has gone wrong. But language has changed in every age.
Many words we use normally today were once young people's slang.

What matters is probably using different words depending on who you're with and where you are.
If young people who laugh together with friends saying やばい can say "I think it's wonderful" at
a job interview, there's no problem at all.

</details>

## Key points

- Words for "I": {私|わたし} (safe for everyone), ぼく and おれ (men, casual), あたし (women, casual),
  わし (old men, mainly in stories).
- **[[Role language]]** ({役割語|やくわりご}): speech styles that mark character types in fiction and
  translation (〜わよ, 〜ぜ, 〜じゃ, 〜でござる). Recognize them; don't use them in earnest.
- Slang to recognize: やばい, マジ, ウケる, ガチ, すごい + adjective. Casual only.
- Copy the style of the people you're talking to, one step more polite; neutral Japanese is never
  wrong.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Written Japanese: である, 〜ず and joining with the stem
topics: のである and opinions in writing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last module of the course is about Japanese on the page: how it is written, how longer
texts are connected, and how the JLPT N3 tests your reading. This lesson starts with the style
itself.

So far you've met two styles: polite (です / ます) and casual (the plain form, with だ after
nouns). There is a third, which you've seen in headlines, notices and a few readings: the
**[[written style]]**, also called the である style. Reports, essays, textbooks, scientific
articles, newspaper editorials and many columns are written in it. It uses the plain form, puts
である where speech has だ, and joins clauses in its own way.

{地球|ちきゅう}の{気温|きおん}は{上|あ}がり{続|つづ}けている。 — The Earth's temperature keeps rising.
{原因|げんいん}の{一|ひと}つは{人間|にんげん}の{活動|かつどう}である。 — One of the causes is human activity.
{問題|もんだい}は{深刻|しんこく}であり、{今後|こんご}も{続|つづ}くと{考|かんが}えられる。 — The problem is serious, and it is thought that it will continue.

The theme is science and the environment: the climate, energy, pollution, wild and farm animals,
plants and the future. From this lesson on, the readings in this module are written in the
である style.

## Three styles side by side

| | Polite | Casual / plain (だ style) | Written (である style) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noun | {原因|げんいん}です | {原因|げんいん}だ | {原因|げんいん}である |
| な-adjective | {深刻|しんこく}です | {深刻|しんこく}だ | {深刻|しんこく}である |
| い-adjective | {高|たか}いです | {高|たか}い | {高|たか}い |
| Verb | {増|ふ}えています | {増|ふ}えている | {増|ふ}えている |
| Guess | {増|ふ}えるでしょう | {増|ふ}えるだろう | {増|ふ}えるだろう / {増|ふ}えるであろう |
| Explaining | {増|ふ}えているんです | {増|ふ}えているんだ | {増|ふ}えているのである |

Two things to notice. First, verbs and い-adjectives look the same in the casual and the written
styles: the difference is in the words around them (しかし, not でも; {非常|ひじょう}に, not
すごく) and in the endings after nouns. Second, the plain だ style is also a written style:
diaries, blogs, novels and news articles mostly use it. である is heavier and more impersonal,
the voice of reports and opinion pieces. Many writers mix the two, ending most sentences in the
plain form and using である for definitions and conclusions. What careful writers avoid is mixing
です / ます with either of them in the same text.

The Japanese names are です・ます{調|ちょう} (the です / ます style) and だ・である{調|ちょう}
(the だ / である style); 〜{調|ちょう} here means "tone, style".

## The forms of である

である replaces だ after nouns and な-adjectives. It conjugates like the verb ある, so its forms
are easy to guess:

| だ style | である style | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {原因|げんいん}だ | {原因|げんいん}である | it is the cause |
| {原因|げんいん}ではない (じゃない in speech) | {原因|げんいん}ではない | it is not the cause |
| {原因|げんいん}だった | {原因|げんいん}であった | it was the cause |
| {原因|げんいん}ではなかった | {原因|げんいん}ではなかった | it was not the cause |
| {原因|げんいん}だろう | {原因|げんいん}であろう / だろう | it is probably the cause |
| {原因|げんいん}で、 | {原因|げんいん}であり、 | it is the cause, and… |
| {原因|げんいん}なら | {原因|げんいん}であれば | if it is the cause |
| {学生|がくせい}の{私|わたし} | {学生|がくせい}である{私|わたし} | I, who am a student |

- じゃない is speech. In formal writing the negative is ではない.
- である can also modify a noun: {大切|たいせつ}な{存在|そんざい}である{馬|うま} (the horse, which is
  an important presence). With a な-adjective before a noun, the ordinary な is still usual:
  {深刻|しんこく}な{問題|もんだい}.
- Never put である after a verb or an い-adjective: ×{高|たか}いである, ×{増|ふ}えるである. Those
  words already end the sentence. (After のだ → のである, see below, it's fine:
  {高|たか}いのである.)
- であろう is the formal guess of essays and editorials. In ordinary writing だろう is just as
  correct: {今後|こんご}も{増|ふ}えるだろう.

## Joining clauses in writing: the stem and 〜ず

In speech you join two clauses with the て form: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}って、{風|かぜ}が{吹|ふ}いた. In
writing the ます stem does the same job, followed by a comma. This is called the **continuative
form** (or stem joining):

| Word | Speech (て form) | Writing (stem) |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}って、 | {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}り、 |
| Verb + いる | {増|ふ}えていて、 | {増|ふ}えており、 |
| い-adjective | {気温|きおん}が{高|たか}くて、 | {気温|きおん}が{高|たか}く、 |
| Noun, な-adjective | {問題|もんだい}で、 | {問題|もんだい}であり、 |
| Negative | {降|ふ}らないで / {降|ふ}らなくて、 | {降|ふ}らず、 |
| Negative い-adjective | {高|たか}くなくて、 | {高|たか}くなく、 |
| Negative noun | {原因|げんいん}ではなくて、 | {原因|げんいん}ではなく、 |

{夏|なつ}は{気温|きおん}が{高|たか}く、{雨|あめ}が{多|おお}い。 — In summer temperatures are high and there is a lot of rain.
{馬|うま}は{昔|むかし}から{人|ひと}を{運|はこ}び、はたけで{働|はたら}いてきた。 — Since long ago, horses have carried people and worked in the fields.
{地球|ちきゅう}の{気温|きおん}は{上|あ}がっており、{海面|かいめん}も{上|あ}がっている。 — The Earth's temperature is rising, and so is the sea level.
{原因|げんいん}は{一|ひと}つではなく、{様々|さまざま}である。 — The causes are not one but many.

Notes:

- 〜ている becomes 〜ており (from おる, the humble いる you met in N4), never ×〜てい、. This おり
  isn't humble here: it's simply the written stem of いる.
- する → し、({研究|けんきゅう}し、), {来|く}る → {来|き}、 (rare; writers prefer {来|き}て). ある → あり、;
  いる → おり、 (the bare stem い、 is hardly ever used for joining).
- The ず form from lesson 10 is the written negative join: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}らず (not raining),
  する → せず, {来|く}る → {来|こ}ず. 〜ずに still means "without": {何|なに}も{食|た}べずに{出|で}かけた.
- The stem and the て form mean the same here, and good writing mixes them. A paragraph with
  four 〜り、 in a row sounds mechanical, so writers use the て form too, especially where the
  first action leads into the second ({調|しら}べて{分|わ}かった).

## のである: explaining in writing

You know んです from N4: it explains, gives the background, or insists. Its written form is
のである (and the plain のだ). It often comes at the end of a paragraph, where the writer states
what the facts above add up to:

{夜|よる}になっても{気温|きおん}が{下|さ}がらない。{町|まち}そのものが{熱|ねつ}をためているのである。 — Even at night the temperature doesn't drop. (The reason is that) the town itself is storing heat.
{馬|うま}は{車|くるま}がない{時代|じだい}の「エンジン」だったのである。 — The horse was, in fact, the "engine" of the age before cars.

The negative is のではない ("it isn't that…"), and the soft question のではないだろうか
("isn't it the case that…?", lesson 19) is the most common way to give your own opinion
modestly in writing:

{問題|もんだい}はぎじゅつではなく、{私|わたし}たちの{生活|せいかつ}なのではないだろうか。 — Isn't the problem our way of life rather than technology?

(ぎじゅつ, technology, has a kanji outside the N3 list, so this course writes it in kana.)

## Opinions in writing: と{考|かんが}えられる, べきである

Written Japanese avoids "I think" (と{思|おも}います) in serious texts. Instead the writer lets the
idea "be thought":

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜と{考|かんが}えられる | it is thought that, it can be considered that | {原因|げんいん}はCO2だと{考|かんが}えられる。 |
| 〜と{思|おも}われる | it seems that, one would think | {今後|こんご}も{増|ふ}えると{思|おも}われる。 |
| 〜と{言|い}える | one can say that | {大|おお}きな{進歩|しんぽ}と{言|い}える。 |
| 〜のではないだろうか | isn't it the case that…? | {見直|みなお}すべきなのではないだろうか。 |
| 〜べきである | ought to, should | {一人|ひとり}{一人|ひとり}が{考|かんが}えるべきである。 |
| 〜{必要|ひつよう}がある | it is necessary to | エネルギーを{減|へ}らす{必要|ひつよう}がある。 |

と{考|かんが}えられる and と{思|おも}われる look like passives, but they are the "spontaneous"
use of the passive form: the thought arises by itself. と{考|かんが}えられる sounds more reasoned
(based on facts); と{思|おも}われる is more of an impression. Lesson 22 introduced them for
recognition; in writing you will see them in almost every paragraph. べきである is lesson 9's
べきだ in written dress, and it is strong: it tells the reader what ought to be done.

## Written words

Some everyday words are too casual for a report. Swap them:

| Speech | Writing | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| でも, だけど | しかし, 〜が | but, however |
| だから | そのため, したがって (lesson 28) | so, therefore |
| それに | また, {更|さら}に | also, moreover |
| AとB | AおよびB | A and B |
| すごく, とても | {非常|ひじょう}に, かなり | very |
| ちょっと | {少|すこ}し, やや | a little |
| {色々|いろいろ}な | {様々|さまざま}な | various |
| やっぱり | やはり | as expected |
| 〜けど | 〜が | …, but |
| 〜なくて / 〜ないで | 〜ず(に) | not…, without |
| 〜みたいだ | 〜ようだ | it seems |
| 〜って | 〜という / 〜とは | called…, (as for) … |
| 〜など | 〜{等|とう} / 〜など | and so on |
| {私|わたし}たち | {私|わたし}たち / われわれ | we |

- および joins nouns only, like と: {馬|うま}および{牛|うし}. It sounds official; また joins
  sentences.
- 〜{等|とう} (and so on) is written after nouns in reports and notices: {馬|うま}、{牛|うし}{等|とう}.
  In ordinary text など is fine, and など can also be written {等|など}, so read the context.
- われわれ is the "we" of speeches and essays that speak for a group ("we humans"); {私|わたし}たち
  is the ordinary written "we".

## Numbers in writing

- **Horizontal text** (books with Western-style lines, the web, most reports) uses Arabic
  numerals: 2026{年|ねん}, {約|やく}30%, 1,500{万人|まんにん}.
- **Vertical text** (novels, newspapers) uses **[[kanji numerals]]**, often digit by digit with 〇:
  {二〇二六年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}, {三〇|さんじゅう}パーセント. Fixed words always keep their
  kanji: {一人|ひとり}, {一部|いちぶ} (a part), {一方|いっぽう}, {第一|だいいち}.
- Large numbers count in {万|まん} (ten thousand), then おく (a hundred million; its kanji is outside
  N3), then ちょう (a trillion). {一|いち}おく{二千万人|にせんまんにん} is 120 million.
- Limits: 〜{以上|いじょう} (… or more), 〜{以下|いか} (… or less), and **〜{未満|みまん} (under,
  less than)**, which doesn't include the number itself: {十八歳|じゅうはっさい}{未満|みまん} means
  17 and below; {十八歳|じゅうはっさい}{以下|いか} includes 18.
- {約|やく} (about) is the written word for ぐらい: {約|やく}{三度|さんど} (about three degrees).
  〜{割|わり} (tenths) and 〜パーセント are lesson 4's.

## Headlines: a reminder

Headlines are even shorter than the である style. They drop particles and endings and finish on
a noun or on a する noun: 「{地球|ちきゅう}の{気温|きおん}、{過去|かこ}{最高|さいこう}に」 (The Earth's
temperature at a record high), 「{野生|やせい}の{馬|うま}、{百年|ひゃくねん}ぶりに{発見|はっけん}」 (A wild
horse found for the first time in a hundred years). Read the missing parts back in:
{気温|きおん}が{過去|かこ}{最高|さいこう}になった, {馬|うま}が{発見|はっけん}された.

## Words for science and the environment

These are the words of articles about the planet: most are new in this lesson, and a few
({実験|じっけん}, {人類|じんるい}, えいきょう, しょくぶつ, {減|へ}らす) come from earlier lessons. Many have a
kanji outside the N3 list, so this course writes them in kana; in real texts you'll see them in
kanji.

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| The planet | {地球|ちきゅう} (the Earth), うちゅう (space), ほし (star), {人類|じんるい} (humankind), {未来|みらい} (the future), {今後|こんご} (from now on) |
| Climate | かんきょう (environment), {気候変動|きこうへんどう} (climate change), {地球|ちきゅう}おんだんか (global warming), {温室|おんしつ} (greenhouse), にさんかたんそ (carbon dioxide), {温度|おんど} (temperature) |
| Energy | エネルギー, {電力|でんりょく} (electric power), {発電|はつでん} (power generation), {原子力|げんしりょく} (nuclear power), せきゆ (oil), しげん (natural resources) |
| Pollution and waste | おせん (pollution), プラスチック, つかいすて (single-use), リサイクル, {物質|ぶっしつ} (substance), {原料|げんりょう} (raw material) |
| Living things | {生物|せいぶつ} (organism), {生|い}き{物|もの} (creature), しょくぶつ (plant), {野生|やせい} (wild), {馬|うま}, {牛|うし}, ぶた (pig), ひつじ (sheep), {子猫|こねこ} (kitten), ぜつめつ (extinction), {進化|しんか} (evolution) |
| Science | {実験|じっけん} (experiment), {観察|かんさつ}する (to observe), {進歩|しんぽ} (progress), {予想|よそう} (prediction), {人工|じんこう} (artificial), {天然|てんねん} (natural) |
| Problems and answers | {原因|げんいん} (cause), えいきょう (effect), {危険性|きけんせい} (risk), かのうせい (possibility), {深刻|しんこく} (serious), たいさく (measures), {減|へ}らす (to reduce), {活用|かつよう} (making good use of), {活動|かつどう} (activity), {存在|そんざい} (existence), {無事|ぶじ} (safe) |

{野生|やせい}の{馬|うま}は、この{百年|ひゃくねん}でぜつめつしかけたが、{今|いま}は{少|すこ}しずつ{増|ふ}えている。 — Wild horses almost died out over the last hundred years, but now they are slowly increasing.
{人工|じんこう}の{光|ひかり}が{多|おお}い{町|まち}では、ほしがほとんど{見|み}えない。 — In towns with a lot of artificial light, you can hardly see the stars.
{牛|うし}やぶた、ひつじを{育|そだ}てるにも、{多|おお}くの{水|みず}と{土地|とち}が{必要|ひつよう}である。 — Raising cows, pigs and sheep takes a lot of water and land too.
プラスチックの{原料|げんりょう}はせきゆであり、もやすとにさんかたんそが{出|で}る。 — The raw material of plastic is oil, and burning it gives off carbon dioxide.
つかいすての{物|もの}を{減|へ}らすことは、{一人|ひとり}でもできるたいさくである。 — Cutting down on single-use things is a measure even one person can take.
{子猫|こねこ}の{動|うご}きを{観察|かんさつ}し、{毎日|まいにち}きろくした。 — I observed the kitten's movements and recorded them every day.
うちゅうの{研究|けんきゅう}は{今後|こんご}{大|おお}きく{進歩|しんぽ}すると{予想|よそう}されている。 — Space research is expected to make great progress from now on.

The words for language itself are here too: {書|か}き{言葉|ことば} (written language) and
{話|はな}し{言葉|ことば} (spoken language), {横書|よこが}き and たてがき (horizontal and vertical
writing), {漢数字|かんすうじ} (kanji numerals).

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for causes, dangers, life and the natural world.

### Cause and being

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 原 | origin; field | ゲン | はら | 10 | {原因|げんいん} (cause), {原料|げんりょう} (raw material), {原子力|げんしりょく} (nuclear power), {野原|のはら} (field) |
| 因 | cause | イン | | 6 | {原因|げんいん} |
| 在 | exist, be in a place | ザイ | | 6 | {存在|そんざい} (existence), {現在|げんざい} (the present) |
| 未 | not yet | ミ | | 5 | {未来|みらい} (the future), {未満|みまん} (under, less than) |
| 無 | nothing, without | ム, ブ | な(い) | 12 | {無事|ぶじ} (safe and sound), {無料|むりょう} (free of charge), {無理|むり} (impossible) |

### Danger and depth

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 危 | danger | キ | あぶ(ない) | 6 | {危|あぶ}ない, {危険|きけん}, {危険性|きけんせい} (risk) |
| 険 | steep; risky | ケン | | 11 | {危険|きけん}, {保険|ほけん} (insurance) |
| 刻 | carve; time | コク | きざ(む) | 8 | {深刻|しんこく} (serious), {時刻|じこく} (time, hour), {遅刻|ちこく} (lateness) |

### Life, warmth and animals

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 活 | lively; life | カツ | | 9 | {生活|せいかつ} (daily life), {活動|かつどう} (activity), {活用|かつよう} (making use of) |
| 温 | warm | オン | あたた(かい), あたた(める) | 12 | {温度|おんど}, {気温|きおん}, {体温|たいおん}, {温|あたた}かい (warm, of things), {温室|おんしつ} (greenhouse) |
| 等 | equal; and so on | トウ | ひと(しい) | 12 | 〜{等|とう} (and so on), {平等|びょうどう} (equality), {等|ひと}しい (equal) |
| 馬 | horse | バ | うま | 10 | {馬|うま}, {馬車|ばしゃ} (carriage) |
| 猫 | cat | | ねこ | 11 | {猫|ねこ}, {子猫|こねこ} (kitten) |

Carried words you can now write with kanji: {危|あぶ}ない, {危険|きけん}, {保険|ほけん}, {無料|むりょう},
{無理|むり}, {生活|せいかつ}, {遅刻|ちこく}, {気温|きおん}, {体温|たいおん}, {猫|ねこ}, and
{温|あたた}かい for things that are warm to the touch (soup, a bath, a welcome). Warm weather is
written with another kanji outside N3, so in this course it stays あたたかい.

Notes:

- 無 is ム in {無理|むり} and {無料|むりょう} and ブ in {無事|ぶじ}. Its kun な(い) is the ない of "there
  is no…", but in modern writing ない is almost always kana.
- 等 has three faces: トウ in {平等|びょうどう} and 〜{等|とう}, ひと(しい) "equal", and a written
  spelling of など. 猫's on'yomi ビョウ is rare; at N3 you need only ねこ.
- 刻 is きざ(む), "to carve, to chop finely" (lesson 3's kitchen word). {深刻|しんこく} is "cut
  deep": serious.
- Don't confuse {未来|みらい} (the future, of the world) with しょうらい (your own future: a job,
  a family), which you know from N4.

Memory notes:

- 原 is a cliff (厂) with a spring (白 + 小) coming out from under it: the source, the origin.
- 因 is 大 (a person lying spread out) inside a box: something that leads to what happens next.
- 未 looks like 木 (tree) with one more short branch at the top: a tree that hasn't finished
  growing, "not yet". 末 (the end), with the long branch on top, is the opposite.
- 危 is a person (the top) on a cliff (厂) above someone crouching (㔾): danger.
- 温 has water (氵) on the left: warm water, a bath.
- 馬 is a picture: the mane at the top, the legs as four dots below.
- 猫 has the animal side (犭) on the left: one of the animals.

```trace
原因馬猫未無危険活刻在等温
```

## Dialogue: rewriting a report

Nanami and Sota are classmates. Sota has written his report on the environment in the polite
style. (Casual speech between friends; the report sentences they quote are in the written
style.)

```dialogue
# The report
ナナミ: ソウタくん、かんきょうのレポート、もう{書|か}いた？
= Sota, have you written the environment report yet?
ソウタ: うん、{昨日|きのう}{書|か}き{終|お}わった。ほら。
= Yeah, I finished it yesterday. Look.
ナナミ: あれ、「{地球|ちきゅう}の{温度|おんど}が{上|あ}がっています」？{先生|せんせい}、である{調|ちょう}で{書|か}くようにって{言|い}ってたよ。
= Hang on, "the Earth's temperature is rising" with です and ます? The teacher said to write it in the である style.
ソウタ: えっ、そうだっけ。じゃあ「{上|あ}がっています」はどうなるの？
= What, did she? So what does "is rising" become?
ナナミ: 「{上|あ}がっている」。{動|うご}きを{表|あらわ}す{言葉|ことば}は、ふつうの{形|かたち}にするだけ。
= 「{上|あ}がっている」. Words for actions just go into the plain form.
ソウタ: 「{大|おお}きな{問題|もんだい}です」は？
= And "it's a big problem"?
ナナミ: 「{大|おお}きな{問題|もんだい}である」。「だ」でもいいけど、レポートなら「である」のほうがかたい{感|かん}じがする。
= "It is a big problem", with である. だ is OK too, but for a report である sounds more formal.
ソウタ: 「{原因|げんいん}はよく{分|わ}かりません」は「{分|わ}からない」か。
= So "the cause isn't well understood" becomes 「{分|わ}からない」.
ナナミ: そう。それから「CO2を{出|だ}して、{気温|きおん}が{上|あ}がる」の「て」は、「{出|だ}し、」にすると{書|か}き{言葉|ことば}っぽくなるよ。
= Right. And the て in "we emit CO2 and the temperature rises" sounds more like writing if you make it 「{出|だ}し、」.
ソウタ: 「CO2を{出|だ}し、{気温|きおん}を{上|あ}げている」…なるほど。じゃあ、{最後|さいご}の「みんなでがんばりましょう」は？
= "Emits CO2 and raises the temperature"… I see. Then what about the last line, "let's all do our best"?
ナナミ: それは「{私|わたし}たち{一人|ひとり}{一人|ひとり}が{努力|どりょく}するべきである」とか。
= That would be something like "each one of us should make an effort".
ソウタ: なんか{急|きゅう}に{偉|えら}い{人|ひと}が{書|か}いたみたいだな。
= Somehow it suddenly sounds like an important person wrote it.
ナナミ: それがである{調|ちょう}だよ。
= That's the である style for you.
```

{表|あらわ}す = to express (lesson 12); {書|か}き{言葉|ことば} = written language, the opposite of
{話|はな}し{言葉|ことば} (spoken language); かたい = stiff, formal (of a style).

## Reading: why towns get hot

An explanatory column from a science magazine for general readers, in the である style.

> {夏|なつ}の{夜|よる}、{都会|とかい}の{気温|きおん}がなかなか{下|さ}がらないと{感|かん}じる{人|ひと}は{多|おお}いのではないだろうか。{実際|じっさい}、{東京|とうきょう}のへいきん{気温|きおん}はこの{百年|ひゃくねん}で{約|やく}{三度|さんど}{上|あ}がったと{言|い}われている。{地球|ちきゅう}{全体|ぜんたい}の{上|あ}がり{方|かた}と{比|くら}べると、かなり{大|おお}きな{数字|すうじ}である。つまり、{地球|ちきゅう}おんだんかだけでは{説明|せつめい}できない{変化|へんか}なのである。このように{都市|とし}の{気温|きおん}がまわりより{高|たか}くなることは「ヒートアイランド」と{呼|よ}ばれ、{世界|せかい}の{多|おお}くの{大都市|だいとし}で{見|み}られる。
>
> {原因|げんいん}は{一|ひと}つではない。まず、{都市|とし}の{地面|じめん}の{多|おお}くはアスファルトやコンクリートでおおわれており、{昼間|ひるま}に{太陽|たいよう}の{熱|ねつ}をため、{夜|よる}になってもそれを{出|だ}し{続|つづ}ける。{次|つぎ}に、{木|き}や{草|くさ}が{少|すく}ない。しょくぶつは{葉|は}から{水|みず}を{出|だ}し、まわりの{温度|おんど}を{下|さ}げる{働|はたら}きをしているが、ビルの{多|おお}い{町|まち}ではその{働|はたら}きがあまり{期待|きたい}できない。{更|さら}に、エアコンや{車|くるま}など、{人間|にんげん}の{活動|かつどう}から{出|で}る{熱|ねつ}も{多|おお}い。{暑|あつ}いからエアコンを{使|つか}い、その{熱|ねつ}でまた{外|そと}が{暑|あつ}くなるのである。
>
> {問題|もんだい}は{暑|あつ}さだけではない。{夜|よる}の{最低|さいてい}{気温|きおん}が25{度|ど}{以上|いじょう}の{日|ひ}も、{昔|むかし}に{比|くら}べてずっと{増|ふ}えている。{夜|よる}も{気温|きおん}が{下|さ}がらず、{体|からだ}が{十分|じゅうぶん}に{休|やす}まらないと、{病気|びょうき}になる{危険性|きけんせい}も{高|たか}くなる。{特|とく}にお{年寄|としよ}りや{小|ちい}さな{子供|こども}にとっては{深刻|しんこく}な{問題|もんだい}であると{考|かんが}えられる。
>
> では、どうすればよいのか。{屋上|おくじょう}でしょくぶつを{育|そだ}てる、{道|みち}に{水|みず}をまく、やねを{白|しろ}っぽい{色|いろ}にする、といった{方法|ほうほう}がすでに{試|ため}されている。{一|ひと}つ{一|ひと}つのこうかは{小|ちい}さくても、{町|まち}{全体|ぜんたい}で{取|と}り{組|く}めば、{温度|おんど}を{下|さ}げることはできないことではない。{未来|みらい}の{町|まち}を{住|す}みやすい{場所|ばしょ}にするために、{私|わたし}たち{一人|ひとり}{一人|ひとり}が{自分|じぶん}にできることを{考|かんが}えるべきである。

おおう (to cover; its kanji is outside N3) → おおわれており, "is covered, and"; ためる = to store
up; {期待|きたい} = expectation, hope; まく = to sprinkle; こうか = effect; {取|と}り{組|く}む =
to tackle (a problem). Find the written-style features: である after nouns ({数字|すうじ}である,
{問題|もんだい}であると), two のである, one 〜ず、, stem joins such as ため、, {使|つか}い、 and
おおわれており、, と{考|かんが}えられる and べきである.

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. Why does the writer say the change in Tokyo can't be explained by global warming alone? —
   Because Tokyo's average temperature has risen by about three degrees in a hundred years,
   much more than the Earth as a whole.
2. What are the three causes? — Asphalt and concrete store the sun's heat by day and give it
   off at night; there are few trees and plants to cool the air; and human activity (air
   conditioners, cars) produces heat.
3. What vicious circle does the writer describe with air conditioners? — People use air conditioners
   because it is hot, and their heat makes the outside even hotter
   (その{熱|ねつ}でまた{外|そと}が{暑|あつ}くなる).
4. What does the writer conclude? — That small measures add up if a whole town takes part, and
   that each of us should think about what we can do (〜べきである).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Many people probably feel that on summer nights the temperature in the city just won't come
down. In fact, Tokyo's average temperature is said to have risen by about three degrees over
the last hundred years. Compared with the rise for the Earth as a whole, that is a rather large
figure. In other words, it is a change that global warming alone can't explain. This way in
which a city becomes hotter than its surroundings is called the "heat island", and it is seen
in many of the world's large cities.

There is not just one cause. First, much of the ground in a city is covered with asphalt and
concrete, which stores the sun's heat in the daytime and goes on giving it off after dark.
Next, there are few trees and little grass. Plants release water from their leaves and work to
lower the temperature around them, but in a town full of buildings you can't expect much of
that. On top of that, a lot of heat comes from human activity, such as air conditioners and
cars. We use air conditioners because it is hot, and their heat makes it hotter outside again.

The problem isn't only the heat. The number of nights when the temperature stays at 25 degrees or above has also risen sharply compared with the past. If the temperature doesn't fall at night and the body can't
rest properly, the risk of falling ill rises too. It is thought to be a serious problem
especially for elderly people and small children.

So what should be done? Methods such as growing plants on rooftops, sprinkling water on the
streets and painting roofs a whitish colour are already being tried. Even if the effect of
each one is small, if a whole town takes them up, bringing the temperature down is not
impossible. To make the towns of the future pleasant places to live, each of us should think
about what we ourselves can do.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{原因|げんいん}は{一|ひと}つではない。
= There is not just one cause.
{問題|もんだい}は{深刻|しんこく}であり、{今後|こんご}も{続|つづ}くと{考|かんが}えられる。
= The problem is serious, and it is thought that it will continue.
{気温|きおん}が{下|さ}がらず、{眠|ねむ}れない{夜|よる}が{続|つづ}いた。
= The temperature didn't fall, and sleepless nights followed one after another.
{私|わたし}たち{一人|ひとり}{一人|ひとり}が{考|かんが}えるべきである。
= Each one of us should think about it.
{未来|みらい}の{地球|ちきゅう}のために、エネルギーを{減|へ}らす{必要|ひつよう}がある。
= For the Earth of the future, we need to cut our energy use.
```

When you read a written text aloud, read it as written: keep である (it is never shortened)
and don't turn it into です.

## Common mistakes

- ×{高|たか}いである, ×{増|ふ}えるである. である follows nouns and な-adjectives only. Verbs and
  い-adjectives end the sentence as they are: {高|たか}い, {増|ふ}える (or {高|たか}いのである).
- ×{原因|げんいん}じゃない in a report. Write ではない.
- ×{増|ふ}えてい、{減|へ}っている. The written stem of 〜ている is 〜ており: {増|ふ}えており、.
- ×しず. The ず form of する is せず: {何|なに}もせず.
- Mixing styles: a report that ends one sentence in である and the next in です. Choose one
  style for the whole text (だ and である may share a text; です / ます may not join them).
- ×{十八歳|じゅうはっさい}{未満|みまん} for "18 and under". {未満|みまん} excludes the number; use
  {以下|いか} to include it.

## Key points

- The written style: plain forms, である after nouns and な-adjectives (である, ではない, であった,
  であろう, であり, であれば). じゃない doesn't belong in formal writing.
- Clauses join with the stem in writing: {降|ふ}り、, {高|たか}く、, 〜であり、, 〜ており、, and in the
  negative 〜ず、 (する → せず).
- のである (= んです) explains or concludes; のではないだろうか gives a modest opinion.
- Opinions: 〜と{考|かんが}えられる, 〜と{思|おも}われる, 〜と{言|い}える, 〜べきである, 〜{必要|ひつよう}がある.
- Written words: しかし, また, および, {非常|ひじょう}に, {様々|さまざま}な, やはり, 〜{等|とう}, われわれ.
- Numbers: Arabic in horizontal text, kanji in vertical text; {約|やく}, {以上|いじょう},
  {以下|いか}, {未満|みまん} (under, excluding the number).
- New kanji: 原 因 馬 猫 未 無 危 険 活 刻 在 等 温.

The reference sheet "Written style" puts the polite, casual and written forms side by side. The
words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Compound verbs: 〜出す, 〜込む, 〜切る, 〜直す, 〜合う, 〜っぱなし
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Written Japanese, the subject of this module, is full of verbs made of two verbs: {取|と}り{出|だ}す
(take out), {思|おも}い{込|こ}む (be convinced), {使|つか}い{切|き}る (use up), {見直|みなお}す (look
at again). You've used a few since N4: 〜{始|はじ}める, 〜{終|お}わる, 〜{続|つづ}ける, 〜すぎる,
and lesson 3's 〜かける. This lesson takes the most useful second halves one by one, shows what
each adds, and sorts the compounds you can build yourself from the ones you learn as words.

{雨|あめ}が{急|きゅう}に{降|ふ}り{出|だ}した。 — It suddenly started to rain.
{古|ふる}い{手紙|てがみ}を{押|お}し{入|い}れから{取|と}り{出|だ}した。 — I took some old letters out of the closet.
{一度|いちど}{書|か}いた{作文|さくぶん}を{書|か}き{直|なお}した。 — I rewrote the essay I'd written.
{電気|でんき}をつけっぱなしで{寝|ね}てしまった。 — I fell asleep with the light left on.

The theme is the home: rooms and furniture, housework and cleaning, repairs and DIY, moving and
storage.

## How compound verbs are built

A **[[compound verb]]** is the ます stem of one verb + a second verb: {書|か}きます → {書|か}き +
{直|なお}す = {書|か}き{直|なお}す. The second verb does the conjugating, so the compound belongs to
the second verb's group: {取|と}り{出|だ}す is group 1 like {出|だ}す, {組|く}み{立|た}てる is group 2
like {立|た}てる.

{書|か}き{直|なお}します · {書|か}き{直|なお}して · {書|か}き{直|なお}さない — just like {直|なお}す.

Which half carries the meaning? It depends on the compound:

| Kind | Example | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| The first verb is the action, the second adds a direction or an aspect | {書|か}き{直|なお}す (write + again), {食|た}べ{切|き}る (eat + completely) | You can build these yourself from many verbs. They are patterns. |
| Both halves together make a new meaning | {思|おも}い{込|こ}む (think + into → be convinced), {見直|みなお}す (look + fix → reconsider; think better of someone) | You learn these as words. |

The productive patterns are below. The compounds that have become words of their own are
vocabulary items in this lesson ({取|と}り{出|だ}す, {思|おも}い{込|こ}む, {見直|みなお}す,
{話|はな}し{合|あ}う…), and lesson 24's {取|と}り{消|け}す (to cancel) is one of them too. A good
dictionary lists the lexicalized ones as words; the patterns it doesn't need to list.

## 〜{出|だ}す: suddenly, or out

**1. Start suddenly.** Stem + 〜{出|だ}す means something starts without warning, often
something the speaker didn't plan or control:

{赤|あか}ちゃんが{急|きゅう}に{泣|な}き{出|だ}した。 — The baby suddenly burst into tears.
{話|はなし}を{聞|き}いて、みんなが{笑|わら}い{出|だ}した。 — When they heard the story, everyone started laughing.
{犬|いぬ}がドアの{音|おと}を{聞|き}いて{走|はし}り{出|だ}した。 — The dog heard the door and started running.

〜{始|はじ}める is the neutral "begin": {四月|しがつ}から{日記|にっき}を{書|か}き{始|はじ}めた (I
started keeping a diary in April). Use 〜{出|だ}す for a sudden start and 〜{始|はじ}める for a
planned one; {日記|にっき}を{書|か}き{出|だ}した would sound as if the urge came over you.

**2. Out.** With verbs of moving and taking, 〜{出|だ}す is "out (of somewhere)":

{子供|こども}が{道|みち}に{飛|と}び{出|だ}した。 — A child ran out into the road.
れいぞうこからぎゅうにゅうを{取|と}り{出|だ}した。 — I took the milk out of the fridge.
{会社|かいしゃ}の{書類|しょるい}を{家|いえ}に{持|も}ち{出|だ}してはいけない。 — You mustn't take company documents home.

## 〜{込|こ}む: into, or deeply

**1. Into.** 〜{込|こ}む (lesson 8's kanji {込|こ}) adds "in, into":

{池|いけ}に{飛|と}び{込|こ}む (to jump into a pond) · {部屋|へや}にソファーを{運|はこ}び{込|こ}む (to carry a sofa into the room) · {飛行機|ひこうき}に{水|みず}を{持|も}ち{込|こ}む (to take water onto a plane) · {深|ふか}く{息|いき}を{吸|す}い{込|こ}む (to breathe in deeply).

{書|か}き{込|こ}む is "to write in": on a form, in a margin, or a post on a website:
{申込書|もうしこみしょ}に{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}き{込|こ}んでください.

**2. Deeply, for a long time.** With some verbs it means the action goes deep or goes on:

{友|とも}だちと{夜|よる}まで{話|はな}し{込|こ}んだ。 — I got deep into conversation with my friend until night.
{今夜|こんや}はかなり{冷|ひ}え{込|こ}むそうだ。 — They say it's going to get really cold tonight.

**3. Words of their own.** {思|おも}い{込|こ}む is "to be convinced of (usually something that
isn't true)", and {落|お}ち{込|こ}む (lesson 10) is "to feel down":

{今日|きょう}は{日曜日|にちようび}だと{思|おも}い{込|こ}んでいた。 — I was sure today was Sunday.

## 〜{切|き}る and 〜{切|き}れない: completely, or can't finish

〜{切|き}る means doing something to the end, completely. 〜{切|き}れない is the potential
negative: "can't finish, too much to…".

{一週間|いっしゅうかん}で{本|ほん}を{読|よ}み{切|き}った。 — I read the whole book in a week.
{買|か}った{野菜|やさい}は、{悪|わる}くなる{前|まえ}に{使|つか}い{切|き}ろう。 — Let's use up the vegetables we bought before they go bad.
{仕事|しごと}のあと、{疲|つか}れ{切|き}って{何|なに}もできなかった。 — After work I was so exhausted I couldn't do anything.
こんなにたくさんは{食|た}べ{切|き}れない。 — I can't eat all of this.
{空|そら}には{数|かぞ}え{切|き}れないほどのほしがあった。 — There were more stars in the sky than you could count.

Be careful with {切|き}る on its own: it means "to cut". Only after a stem does it mean
"completely".

## 〜{直|なお}す: again, properly

〜{直|なお}す (lesson 16's kanji {直|なお}) is "do again (and better)":

{間違|まちが}いが{多|おお}かったので、{手紙|てがみ}を{書|か}き{直|なお}した。 — There were a lot of mistakes, so I rewrote the letter.
もう{一度|いちど}{考|かんが}え{直|なお}してください。 — Please think it over again.
{失敗|しっぱい}しても、また{最初|さいしょ}からやり{直|なお}せばいい。 — Even if you fail, you can just start again from the beginning.

{見直|みなお}す is both "to look over again, to review" ({答|こた}えを{見直|みなお}す, check your
answers; {生活|せいかつ}を{見直|みなお}す, rethink your way of life) and "to see someone in a better
light" ({彼|かれ}を{見直|みなお}した, I think better of him now).

## 〜{合|あ}う: each other

〜{合|あ}う makes the action mutual: both sides do it to each other.

{困|こま}ったときは{助|たす}け{合|あ}おう。 — Let's help each other when we're in trouble.
{家族|かぞく}で{話|はな}し{合|あ}って、{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}すことに{決|き}めた。 — We talked it over as a family and decided to move.

{話|はな}し{合|あ}う (to discuss, to talk things through) is a word of its own; so are
{知|し}り{合|あ}い (an acquaintance) and {似合|にあ}う (to suit), which you know from N4.

## 〜{上|あ}げる and 〜{上|あ}がる: up, or finished

With verbs of movement, 〜{上|あ}げる (transitive) and 〜{上|あ}がる (intransitive) mean "up":
{重|おも}い{箱|はこ}を{持|も}ち{上|あ}げる (to lift a heavy box), いすから{立|た}ち{上|あ}がる (to stand
up from a chair). With verbs of making, they mean "finish, complete":

{一晩|ひとばん}でレポートを{書|か}き{上|あ}げた。 — I finished writing the report in one night.
{料理|りょうり}ができあがった。 — The meal is ready.

## Reminders: 〜{続|つづ}ける, 〜すぎる, 〜かける

> You know these already: 〜{続|つづ}ける "keep on" ({雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}り{続|つづ}けている),
> 〜すぎる "too much" ({食|た}べすぎた), and lesson 3's 〜かける "start to, half-done"
> ({読|よ}みかけの{本|ほん}). They are the same kind of compound: stem + a verb that adds an
> aspect.

## 〜っぱなし: left that way

Stem + っぱなし means "left in that state", when it should have been changed back: the light
left on, the door left open, the tap left running. It usually complains.

{電気|でんき}をつけっぱなしにしないで。 — Don't leave the light on.
{窓|まど}を{開|あ}けっぱなしで{出|で}かけてしまった。 — I went out and left the window open.
{水|みず}を{出|だ}しっぱなしにしていた。 — I'd left the water running.

〜っぱなしにする (to leave something…), 〜っぱなしで (with… left…) and 〜っぱなしだ are the usual
frames. It's an everyday spoken word; it's fine in writing but not in a formal report. (It
sometimes means "the whole time": {一日中|いちにちじゅう}{立|た}ちっぱなしだった, I was on my feet all
day.)

## Words for the home

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| The house | {住宅|じゅうたく} (housing), {住|す}まい (home, where you live), {家庭|かてい} (household, family home), {一戸建|いっこだ}て (detached house), {二階建|にかいだ}て (two-storey), {庭|にわ} (garden), やね (roof), {戸|と} (door), {雨戸|あまど} (storm shutter), {段|だん} (step) |
| Rooms | {居間|いま} (living room), {洋室|ようしつ} (Western-style room), {寝室|しんしつ} (bedroom), てんじょう (ceiling), かべ (wall), たな (shelf), クローゼット, {物置|ものおき} (storage shed), {置|お}き{場|ば} (a place to keep something) |
| Furniture | {家具|かぐ}, ソファー, カーテン, じゅうたん (carpet), {電球|でんきゅう} (light bulb) |
| Cleaning | そうじき (vacuum cleaner), ぞうきん (cleaning cloth), ほこり (dust), よごれ (dirt, a stain), よごれる (to get dirty), せんたくき (washing machine), せんたくもの (the laundry), せいり (sorting out), しゅうのう (storage space), とじまり (locking up) |
| Repairs and DIY | {日曜大工|にちようだいく} (DIY), {大工|だいく} (carpenter), {工具|こうぐ} (tools), ねじ (screw), くぎ (nail), ペンキ (paint), ぬる (to paint, to spread), {手入|てい}れ (care, upkeep) |
| Verbs | {折|お}る / {折|お}れる (to break, fold / be broken), {抜|ぬ}く / {抜|ぬ}ける (to pull out / come out), {除|のぞ}く (to remove, exclude), {取|と}り{除|のぞ}く (to remove), {散|ち}らす (to scatter), {散|ち}らかす (to make a mess of), {備|そな}える (to prepare for), {外|はず}す (to take off, remove), {取|と}り{付|つ}ける (to install), {組|く}み{立|た}てる (to assemble), {持|も}ち{上|あ}げる (to lift) |

てんじょう, かべ, たな, やね and the other words in kana have a kanji outside N3, so this course
writes them in kana.

てんじょうの{電球|でんきゅう}を{取|と}りかえた。 — I changed the light bulb in the ceiling.
{台風|たいふう}に{備|そな}えて、{雨戸|あまど}を{閉|し}めた。 — I shut the storm shutters to get ready for the typhoon.
{風|かぜ}で{庭|にわ}の{木|き}が{折|お}れてしまった。 — The tree in the garden broke in the wind.
{子供|こども}がおもちゃを{部屋中|へやじゅう}に{散|ち}らかした。 — The children scattered their toys all over the room.
{歯|は}が{一本|いっぽん}{抜|ぬ}けた。 — One of my teeth came out.

## Kanji

Thirteen kanji for the house and what you do in it.

### Parts of the house

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 庭 | garden, yard | テイ | にわ | 10 | {庭|にわ}, {家庭|かてい} (household) |
| 窓 | window | ソウ | まど | 11 | {窓|まど}, {窓口|まどぐち} (service counter) |
| 戸 | door | コ | と (ど) | 4 | {戸|と}, {雨戸|あまど} (storm shutter), {一戸建|いっこだ}て (detached house) |
| 階 | floor, storey | カイ (ガイ) | | 12 | 〜{階|かい}, {階段|かいだん} (stairs), {二階建|にかいだ}て |
| 段 | step, level | ダン | | 9 | {段|だん} (a step), {階段|かいだん}, {値段|ねだん} (price), {段|だん}ボール (cardboard box) |
| 居 | be, stay | キョ | い(る) | 8 | {居間|いま} (living room), {居眠|いねむ}り (dozing off), {居酒屋|いざかや} (pub) |

### Putting, hanging, preparing

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 置 | put, place | チ | お(く) | 13 | {置|お}く, {置|お}き{場|ば}, {物置|ものおき} (storage shed), {位置|いち} (position) |
| 掛 | hang | | か(ける) | 11 | {掛|か}ける (to hang), {掛|か}け{時計|どけい} (wall clock) |
| 備 | prepare, equip | ビ | そな(える) | 12 | {備|そな}える (to prepare for), {予備|よび} (spare) |

### Breaking, pulling out, clearing away

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 折 | fold, break | セツ | お(る), お(れる) | 7 | {折|お}る, {折|お}れる, {折|お}り{紙|がみ} (origami) |
| 抜 | pull out | | ぬ(く), ぬ(ける) | 7 | {抜|ぬ}く, {抜|ぬ}ける |
| 除 | remove | ジョ | のぞ(く) | 10 | {除|のぞ}く, {取|と}り{除|のぞ}く, そうじ (cleaning: its first kanji is outside N3, so it stays in kana) |
| 散 | scatter | サン | ち(る), ち(らす), ち(らかる), ち(らかす) | 12 | {散歩|さんぽ} (a walk), {散|ち}らかる, {散|ち}らかす, {散|ち}らす, {散|ち}る (to fall, of petals and leaves) |

Carried words you can now write with kanji: {窓|まど}, {窓口|まどぐち}, {階段|かいだん}, 〜{階|かい},
{値段|ねだん}, {置|お}く, {散歩|さんぽ}, {散|ち}らかる, and {掛|か}ける in the sense "to hang"
({絵|え}を{掛|か}ける). In its other senses かける usually stays in kana: {電話|でんわ}をかける, めがねを
かける, いすにかける.

Notes:

- 戸 is と on its own and ど after another word ({雨戸|あまど}, {引|ひ}き{戸|ど}, a sliding door), and
  コ in counting houses ({一戸建|いっこだ}て).
- 階 is ガイ after さん: {三階|さんがい}; elsewhere カイ ({二階|にかい}, {四階|よんかい}). Some speakers
  say さんかい too.
- 居 is the kanji of いる "to be", but the verb いる is written in kana. It keeps its kanji in nouns:
  {居間|いま}, {居眠|いねむ}り.
- {折|お}る (transitive) / {折|お}れる (intransitive) and {抜|ぬ}く / {抜|ぬ}ける are pairs like the ones
  in N4: {紙|かみ}を{折|お}る (to fold paper), {木|き}が{折|お}れる (a tree breaks); {歯|は}を{抜|ぬ}く (to
  pull a tooth), {歯|は}が{抜|ぬ}ける (a tooth comes out).

Memory notes:

- 窓 has a hole at the top (the "cave" part) over a heart (心): the opening in the wall you look
  out of.
- 戸 is a picture of a one-leaf door hanging from a frame.
- 置 has a net (罒) on top: you put something down under it.
- 抜 has the hand (扌) on the left: pulling something out by hand.
- 散 has 月 at the bottom left and a hand hitting (攵) on the right: knocking things so they scatter.

```trace
庭窓戸階段掛折抜除居散置備
```

## Dialogue: putting the shelf together

Mei and her younger brother Riku are assembling a bookshelf in her new flat. (Casual speech
between siblings.)

```dialogue
# The bookshelf
メイ: リク、ちょっと{手伝|てつだ}って。このたな、{組|く}み{立|た}てなきゃいけないの。
= Riku, give me a hand. I've got to put this shelf together.
リク: いいよ。{説明書|せつめいしょ}は？
= Sure. Where are the instructions?
メイ: はい、これ。ねじが{三十本|さんじゅっぽん}もあるんだよ。
= Here. There are thirty screws!
リク: {説明書|せつめいしょ}の{通|とお}りにやれば{大|たい}したことないって。……あれ、この{部分|ぶぶん}、ぎゃくじゃない？
= If you do what the instructions say, it's no big deal. …Hang on, isn't this part the wrong way round?
メイ: え、{本当|ほんと}？さっき{取|と}り{付|つ}けたばかりなのに。
= What, really? I've only just put it on.
リク: うん、{上|うえ}と{下|した}が{反対|はんたい}。{一回|いっかい}{外|はず}して、やり{直|なお}そう。
= Yeah, the top and bottom are the wrong way round. Let's take it off and do it again.
メイ: もう、{最初|さいしょ}からちゃんと{読|よ}めばよかった。
= Ugh, I should have read it properly from the start.
リク: よし、できた。{持|も}ち{上|あ}げるから、そっち{持|も}って。
= Right, done. I'm going to lift it, so hold that end.
メイ: ありがとう。{本|ほん}、{全部|ぜんぶ}{入|はい}りきるかな。{段|だん}ボール{五箱|ごはこ}{分|ぶん}あるんだけど。
= Thanks. I wonder if all the books will fit. There are five boxes' worth.
リク: それは{無理|むり}だよ。もう{読|よ}まない{本|ほん}を{見直|みなお}して、{減|へ}らしたら？
= No way. Why not go through the ones you won't read again and get rid of some?
メイ: そうだね。あ、それから、ドライバー、{出|だ}しっぱなしにしないでね。
= I suppose so. Oh, and don't leave the screwdriver lying around.
リク: はいはい。{手伝|てつだ}ってあげたのに……。
= Yes, yes. And after I helped you…
```

{説明書|せつめいしょ} = instructions; {大|たい}したことない = no big deal; {部分|ぶぶん} = part;
ぎゃく = the wrong way round (its kanji is outside N3); {入|はい}りきる = to fit in completely; 〜{分|ぶん} = the amount of: {五箱|ごはこ}{分|ぶん},
five boxes' worth.

## Reading: living with fewer things

An essay by a reader of a lifestyle magazine, in the である style.

> {去年|きょねん}の{春|はる}、{私|わたし}は{十年|じゅうねん}{住|す}んだアパートを{出|で}て、{小|ちい}さな{一戸建|いっこだ}てに{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}した。じゅんびを{始|はじ}めてまずおどろいたのは、{物|もの}の{多|おお}さである。{押|お}し{入|い}れから{取|と}り{出|だ}してみると、{何年|なんねん}も{使|つか}っていない{物|もの}が{次々|つぎつぎ}に{出|で}てきた。{一度|いちど}{着|き}たきりの{服|ふく}、{読|よ}みかけの{本|ほん}、いつか{直|なお}そうと{思|おも}っていたこわれたいす。{全部|ぜんぶ}{段|だん}ボールに{入|い}れると、{三十箱|さんじゅっぱこ}{以上|いじょう}になった。{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}しの{日|ひ}、トラックに{運|はこ}び{込|こ}まれる{箱|はこ}の{山|やま}を{見|み}て、{私|わたし}は{少|すこ}し{恥|は}ずかしくなった。
>
> {私|わたし}はずっと、{物|もの}が{多|おお}いのは{家|いえ}がせまいからだと{思|おも}い{込|こ}んでいた。しかし、{問題|もんだい}は{家|いえ}の{広|ひろ}さではなかった。「いつか{使|つか}うかもしれない」と{考|かんが}え、{何|なに}もすてずに{取|と}っておいた{私|わたし}の{習慣|しゅうかん}だったのである。
>
> そこで、{新|あたら}しい{家|いえ}では{三|みっ}つのルールを{決|き}めた。{一年|いちねん}{使|つか}わなかった{物|もの}は{家|いえ}に{置|お}かない。{必要|ひつよう}な{物|もの}には{必|かなら}ず{置|お}き{場|ば}を{決|き}める。{置|お}き{場|ば}のない{物|もの}は{買|か}わない。{最初|さいしょ}は{難|むずか}しかったが、{半年|はんとし}{続|つづ}けると、{部屋|へや}が{散|ち}らからなくなった。{物|もの}が{少|すく}ないので、そうじも{十分|じゅっぷん}で{終|お}わる。{探|さが}し{物|もの}をする{時間|じかん}も{減|へ}り、{朝|あさ}{出|で}かける{前|まえ}にあわてることもなくなった。
>
> {物|もの}を{減|へ}らして{分|わ}かったことが、もう{一|ひと}つある。{物|もの}を{大切|たいせつ}にするようになったのである。{食|た}べ{物|もの}は{使|つか}い{切|き}れるだけ{買|か}い、{物|もの}がこわれたら、まず{自分|じぶん}で{直|なお}してみる。{先週|せんしゅう}は、{庭|にわ}に{置|お}いてある{古|ふる}いいすにペンキをぬり{直|なお}した。{日曜大工|にちようだいく}は{初|はじ}めてだったが、{家族|かぞく}にほめられ、{今|いま}では{一番|いちばん}{好|す}きないすになっている。
>
> {物|もの}を{持|も}たない{生活|せいかつ}が、だれにでも{合|あ}うわけではない。しかし、{一度|いちど}{自分|じぶん}の{持|も}ち{物|もの}を{見直|みなお}してみることは、{生活|せいかつ}そのものを{見直|みなお}すことにつながるのではないだろうか。

おどろく = to be surprised (its kanji is outside N3); {習慣|しゅうかん} = habit; つながる = to lead
to, to be connected to. Find the compound verbs: {取|と}り{出|だ}す, {思|おも}い{込|こ}む,
{使|つか}い{切|き}る, ぬり{直|なお}す, {見直|みなお}す; and the lesson 3 forms {着|き}たきり and
{読|よ}みかけ.

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. What surprised the writer when getting ready to move? — How many things there were: things
   not used for years kept coming out of the closet, and they filled more than thirty boxes.
2. What had the writer wrongly believed, and what was the real problem? — That there were too
   many things because the house was small ({思|おも}い{込|こ}んでいた); the real problem was the
   habit of keeping everything in case it might be useful one day.
3. What are the three rules? — Don't keep anything not used for a year; give every necessary
   thing a fixed place; don't buy anything that has no place.
4. What else changed? — The writer began to take care of things: buying only as much food as can
   be used up, mending things before replacing them, and repainting an old garden chair.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Last spring I left the flat I had lived in for ten years and moved into a small detached house.
When I started getting ready, the first thing that surprised me was the sheer number of things.
When I took things out of the closet, one thing after another came out that I hadn't used for
years: clothes I'd worn only once, books I'd half read, a broken chair I'd always meant to fix
some day. When I put it all in cardboard boxes, it came to more than thirty. On moving day, watching the mountain of boxes being loaded into the lorry, I felt a little ashamed.

I had always been convinced that I had too many things because the house was small. But the
problem wasn't the size of the house. It was my habit of thinking "I might use it one day" and
keeping everything without throwing anything away.

So in the new house I set three rules. Things I haven't used for a year don't stay in the house.
Everything I need must have a fixed place. I don't buy anything that has no place. At first it
was hard, but after keeping it up for six months, my rooms stopped getting messy. Because there
are few things, cleaning takes only ten minutes. I spend less time looking for things, and I
no longer rush around in the morning before going out.

There's one more thing I found out by having fewer things: I've started to take care of them. I
buy only as much food as I can use up, and when something breaks, I first try to repair it
myself. Last week I repainted an old chair that stands in the garden. It was my first try at
DIY, but my family praised it, and now it's my favourite chair.

A life without many possessions doesn't suit everyone. But taking a fresh look at your
belongings just once may well lead you to take a fresh look at your life itself.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{雨|あめ}が{急|きゅう}に{降|ふ}り{出|だ}した。
= It suddenly started to rain.
こんなにたくさんは{食|た}べ{切|き}れません。
= I can't eat all of this.
もう{一度|いちど}{書|か}き{直|なお}します。
= I'll write it again.
{家族|かぞく}で{話|はな}し{合|あ}って{決|き}めました。
= We talked it over as a family and decided.
{電気|でんき}をつけっぱなしにしないでね。
= Don't leave the light on, OK?
```

A compound verb is said as one word, with at most one fall in pitch, usually near the end
({書|か}き{直|なお}す: かきなお\す; many, such as {見直|みなお}す, are also said flat). Don't say it as
two separate words.

## Common mistakes

- ×{書|か}く{直|なお}す, ×{書|か}いて{直|なお}す. The first verb is the ます stem: {書|か}き{直|なお}す.
- 〜{出|だ}す for a planned start: ×{来月|らいげつ}からジムに{通|かよ}い{出|だ}す. Use 〜{始|はじ}める:
  {通|かよ}い{始|はじ}める.
- ×{食|た}べ{切|き}らない for "can't finish eating". The potential negative is
  {食|た}べ{切|き}れない; {食|た}べ{切|き}らない means "don't (choose to) eat it all".
- ×{思|おも}い{込|こ}む for an ordinary "think". It means being convinced, usually wrongly:
  {明日|あした}だと{思|おも}い{込|こ}んでいた (I was sure it was tomorrow).
- ×{電気|でんき}をつけっぱなす. っぱなし is a noun: {電気|でんき}をつけっぱなしにする.

## Key points

- Compound verb = ます stem + verb; it conjugates like the second verb.
- Patterns you can build: 〜{出|だ}す (suddenly; out), 〜{込|こ}む (into; deeply), 〜{切|き}る /
  〜{切|き}れない (completely; can't finish), 〜{直|なお}す (again), 〜{合|あ}う (each other),
  〜{上|あ}げる / 〜{上|あ}がる (up; finished), 〜{続|つづ}ける, 〜すぎる, 〜かける.
- Words of their own: {取|と}り{出|だ}す, {思|おも}い{込|こ}む, {見直|みなお}す, {話|はな}し{合|あ}う,
  {取|と}り{付|つ}ける, {組|く}み{立|た}てる, {取|と}り{除|のぞ}く, {取|と}り{消|け}す (lesson 24).
- Stem + っぱなし: left on, left open (usually a complaint).
- New kanji: 庭 窓 戸 階 段 掛 折 抜 除 居 散 置 備.

The reference sheet "Compound verbs" lists the patterns with more examples. The words from this
lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Connecting ideas: ところが, 一方, その上, 結局, むしろ, 上で
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 26 gave you the forms of written Japanese, and lesson 27 its verbs. This lesson gives you
the joints: the words that link one sentence to the next and tell the reader where the argument
is going. A **[[conjunction]]** such as しかし or その{上|うえ} at the start of a sentence says "now
comes a contrast" or "and there's more". On the JLPT N3, "text grammar" questions ask you to
choose exactly these words in a passage, and the long readings are built with them.

{雨|あめ}がやむのを{待|ま}った。ところが、{雨|あめ}はますます{強|つよ}くなった。 — I waited for the rain to stop. But, contrary to what I hoped, it got heavier.
この{店|みせ}は{安|やす}い。その{上|うえ}、{味|あじ}もいい。 — This place is cheap. What's more, the food is good.
{一時間|いちじかん}{話|はな}し{合|あ}ったが、{結局|けっきょく}{何|なに}も{決|き}まらなかった。 — We talked for an hour, but in the end nothing was decided.

The theme is opinions and debate: agreeing and disagreeing, pros and cons, choices about how to
live, and judging and deciding.

## Contrast: しかし, でも, ところが

All three are "but", and they are not interchangeable.

| Word | Style | Use |
|---|---|---|
| でも | speech | any contrast, in conversation |
| しかし | writing, speeches | any contrast; can introduce your own opinion |
| ところが | speech and writing | what actually happened went against what you expected |

{天気予報|てんきよほう}では{晴|は}れだった。ところが、{午後|ごご}から{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}り{出|だ}した。 — The forecast said sunny. But then it started raining in the afternoon.
この{方法|ほうほう}は{便利|べんり}だ。しかし、{問題|もんだい}もある。 — This method is convenient. However, it has problems too.

ところが reports a surprising fact, so the sentence after it is usually in the past and is never
your own request, plan or opinion: ×ところが、{家|いえ}にいましょう. Use しかし or でも for those.

Two milder relatives: それでも (even so, nevertheless) says the second fact holds in spite of the
first: {何度|なんど}も{失敗|しっぱい}した。それでも、あきらめなかった. ただ (but, the only thing is) adds a small
reservation: いい{部屋|へや}だ。ただ、{駅|えき}から{少|すこ}し{遠|とお}い.

### Reminders: つまり, さて, ところで

> You know three of these words from N4. つまり (in other words, so) sums up or restates:
> {彼|かれ}は{母|はは}の{兄|あに}、つまり{私|わたし}のおじだ. さて (now, well then) moves to the
> main point or the next step. ところで (by the way) changes the subject; don't confuse it with
> ところが. すなわち (that is, namely) is the formal, written つまり: recognize it in texts.

## Reasons: なぜなら〜からだ, そのため, したがって

なぜなら starts a sentence that gives the reason for the one before, and that sentence ends in
〜からだ (written: からである; polite: からです):

{私|わたし}はこの{計画|けいかく}に{反対|はんたい}だ。なぜなら、{費用|ひよう}がかかりすぎるからだ。 — I'm against this plan. The reason is that it costs too much.

Going the other way, from cause to result, writing uses そのため (because of that) and したがって
(therefore, so; logical and formal); speech uses だから.

{道|みち}が{工事中|こうじちゅう}だった。そのため、バスが{三十分|さんじゅっぷん}{遅|おく}れた。 — The road was under construction. Because of that, the bus was thirty minutes late.

そこで (so, and so) is a little different: something happened, and so someone did something
about it. {部屋|へや}が{暗|くら}かった。そこで、{窓|まど}を{大|おお}きくした (The room was dark, so we
made the window bigger).

## Adding: その{上|うえ}, しかも, {更|さら}に

| Word | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| その{上|うえ} | on top of that (same direction) | {仕事|しごと}が{多|おお}い。その{上|うえ}、{給料|きゅうりょう}も{安|やす}い。 |
| しかも | and what's more (often stronger, or surprising) | {安|やす}い。しかも、おいしい。 |
| {更|さら}に | further, in addition (also "even more") | {値段|ねだん}が{更|さら}に{上|あ}がった。 |
| また | also (lesson 26) | また、{次|つぎ}のような{例|れい}もある。 |

あやまらなかった (He came late. And on top of that, he didn't apologize). あやまる (to
apologize) has its kanji outside N3; it's written in kana in this course.

The clause-joining 〜{上|うえ}に (on top of, lesson 20) does the same job inside one sentence:
{安|やす}い{上|うえ}に、おいしい.

## Two sides: {一方|いっぽう}, それに{対|たい}して, ぎゃくに

{一方|いっぽう}(で) puts a second side next to the first ("meanwhile, on the other hand"). それに
{対|たい}して (lesson 11's に{対|たい}して) contrasts two things point by point. ぎゃくに (on the
contrary; the other way round) says the second fact is the opposite of what you'd expect:

{都会|とかい}は{便利|べんり}だ。{一方|いっぽう}、{物|もの}の{値段|ねだん}は{高|たか}い。 — The city is convenient. On the other hand, things are expensive.
{兄|あに}は{外|そと}で{遊|あそ}ぶのが{好|す}きだった。それに{対|たい}して、{弟|おとうと}は{本|ほん}ばかり{読|よ}んでいた。 — My older brother loved playing outside. By contrast, my younger brother was always reading.
{薬|くすり}を{飲|の}みすぎると、ぎゃくに{体|からだ}に{悪|わる}い。 — If you take too much medicine, it does you harm instead.

## In the end: {結局|けっきょく}, ついに, とうとう, やっと

| Word | Meaning | Feeling |
|---|---|---|
| {結局|けっきょく} | in the end, after all | after all the talk or effort, this was the outcome (often a let-down or "back to the start") |
| やっと | at last | relief: something you wanted finally happened |
| とうとう | finally, in the end | after a long time; for good or bad results |
| ついに | at last, finally | like とうとう, more dramatic and written |

{三回目|さんかいめ}の{試験|しけん}で、やっと{合格|ごうかく}した。 — I finally passed on my third try.
{何年|なんねん}も{使|つか}った{車|くるま}が、とうとう{動|うご}かなくなった。 — The car I'd used for years finally stopped running.
{人類|じんるい}はついに{月|つき}に{立|た}った。 — Humankind at last stood on the Moon.
{色々|いろいろ}{考|かんが}えたが、{結局|けっきょく}{行|い}かなかった。 — I thought about it a lot, but in the end I didn't go.

やっと is for results you were waiting for: ×やっと{車|くるま}がこわれた sounds as if you wanted it
to break. Use とうとう for a long-feared result.

## Rather: むしろ

むしろ says "rather, if anything": the truth is closer to the second option than to the first,
often the opposite of what people assume. It often comes with 〜より.

{雨|あめ}の{日|ひ}の{京都|きょうと}は{悪|わる}くない。むしろ、{静|しず}かで{好|す}きだ。 — Kyoto on a rainy day isn't bad. If anything, I like it because it's quiet.
{失敗|しっぱい}は{恥|は}ずかしいことではなく、むしろ{大切|たいせつ}な{経験|けいけん}だ。 — Failing isn't something to be ashamed of; rather, it's a valuable experience.

かえって (on the contrary, instead) is similar but describes a result that went against
your intention: {急|いそ}いだら、かえって{時間|じかん}がかかった (I hurried, and it took longer
instead).

## Admitting a point: {確|たし}かに〜が

A good argument admits the other side before answering it. {確|たし}かに (it's true that, certainly)
opens the admission, and が, けれども or しかし turns back to your view:

{確|たし}かに{車|くるま}は{便利|べんり}だ。しかし、{町|まち}の{中|なか}なら{自転車|じてんしゃ}で{十分|じゅうぶん}である。 — Cars are certainly convenient. But in town a bicycle is enough.

(N4's たしか means "if I remember rightly"; {確|たし}かに is the adverb "certainly, admittedly", from
the same word {確|たし}か "sure, certain".)

## 〜{上|うえ}で: after doing; in doing

{上|うえ}で has two uses, both with a meaning of their own, so it keeps its kanji.

| Form | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb (た form) + {上|うえ}で | after doing (and on that basis) | よく{考|かんが}えた{上|うえ}で{決|き}めます。 (I'll decide after thinking it over carefully.) |
| Noun + の + {上|うえ}で | after (formal) | {相談|そうだん}の{上|うえ}で{決|き}めます。 |
| Verb (dictionary form) + {上|うえ}で | in doing, for the purpose of | {外国語|がいこくご}を{学|まな}ぶ{上|うえ}で{大切|たいせつ}なのは、{毎日|まいにち}{続|つづ}けることだ。 |

The first is stronger than 〜てから: the second action depends on the first. {両親|りょうしん}と
{話|はな}し{合|あ}った{上|うえ}で、{留学|りゅうがく}を{決|き}めた (I decided to study abroad after talking
it through with my parents).

## Writing an argument

An opinion essay in Japanese usually has four moves, and each move has its own words:

| Move | Words |
|---|---|
| Your view | {私|わたし}は〜に{賛成|さんせい} / {反対|はんたい}である。 |
| Reasons | {第一|だいいち}に、〜。{第二|だいに}に、〜。 / まず、〜。{次|つぎ}に、〜。 / なぜなら〜からだ。 |
| The other side | {確|たし}かに〜。しかし、〜。 / 〜という{意見|いけん}もある。{一方|いっぽう}で、〜。 |
| Conclusion | このように、〜。 / つまり、〜。 / {以上|いじょう}のことから、〜と{考|かんが}える。 |

Memory notes:

- 賛 has two 夫 (husband) side by side on top of a shell, an old sign for money: two people
  putting their money in together, "agreeing".
- 対 has the "hand" part on the right, holding something up opposite you.
- 判 has 刂 (a knife) on the right: cutting things into right and wrong, judging.
- 断 has an axe on the right: cutting off, refusing.
- 決 has water (氵): a river that breaks through a bank goes one way. Decided.
- 然 has 灬 (fire) at the bottom and a dog (犬) on top right: the meaning grew from "burn", then
  "so, like that". A story helps: a dog by the fire, naturally.
- 努 has 力 (power) under it: putting your strength into something, effort.
