<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Recently, it seems, more and more young people are leaving the city and choosing to live in the
countryside. This is because, with the internet, there is now a lot of work that can be done
without going to the office. I am in favour of this way of life.

First, life in the countryside has many advantages. Rent is cheap and the air is clean. On top
of that, because there is no commute, people have more time to spend with their families.
Being able to bring up children close to nature is another great strength. Second, it is a gain for the regions whose populations are falling too. The reason is that if
young people come, towns become lively again.

It's true that country life has its inconvenient side. Shops and hospitals are far away, and
there are quite a few places where you can't live without a car. For elderly people in
particular, this can become a serious problem. In fact, a friend of mine moved
to a mountain village with great hopes. But the winter snow was much harder than expected, and in
the end the friend came back to town after two years.

However, this story doesn't show that country life is bad. Rather, it teaches us how important
it is, when choosing where to live, to look into it carefully in advance. My friend also says,
"I should have decided after living through one winter."

Both the city and the country have their strengths and weaknesses. In other words, what
matters is not whether it's the city or the country, but what you want to
value. Do you choose convenience, or quiet time? It's fine for that judgement to differ from
person to person. I would like ours to be a society in which each of us can freely choose the
way of life that suits us.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{私|わたし}はこの{意見|いけん}に{賛成|さんせい}です。
= I agree with this opinion.
{確|たし}かにそうですね。でも、{欠点|けってん}もあると{思|おも}います。
= That's certainly true. But I think there are drawbacks too.
なぜなら、{時間|じかん}がかかりすぎるからです。
= The reason is that it takes too long.
よく{考|かんが}えた{上|うえ}で{決|き}めます。
= I'll decide after thinking it over carefully.
{結局|けっきょく}、{何|なに}も{決|き}まりませんでした。
= In the end, nothing was decided.
```

In a debate, a conjunction at the start of a sentence is usually followed by a short pause
(しかし、… / {確|たし}かに、…), which the comma shows in writing.

## Common mistakes

- ×ところが、{明日|あした}{行|い}きましょう. ところが reports an unexpected fact; it can't introduce a
  suggestion. Use でも or しかし.
- ×ところで for "but". ところで (by the way) changes the subject; ところが is "but, to my
  surprise".
- ×なぜなら、{高|たか}いです. A なぜなら sentence ends in 〜からだ / からです: なぜなら、{高|たか}いからです.
- ×やっと{車|くるま}がこわれた. やっと is for something you were waiting for;
  a long-feared result takes とうとう.
- ×{考|かんが}える{上|うえ}で{決|き}める for "decide after thinking". "After" needs the た form:
  {考|かんが}えた{上|うえ}で.
- Using {適当|てきとう} as praise in conversation: {適当|てきとう}な{人|ひと} often sounds like "a careless
  person". Say {適切|てきせつ} or ちょうどいい for "just right".

## Key points

- Contrast: でも (speech), しかし (writing), ところが (what happened went against expectations;
  not before a request or plan).
- Reasons and results: なぜなら〜からだ; そのため, したがって (writing), そこで (and so someone acted).
- Adding: その{上|うえ}, しかも, {更|さら}に, また. Two sides: {一方|いっぽう}, それに{対|たい}して, ぎゃくに.
- In the end: {結局|けっきょく} (outcome), やっと (relief), とうとう / ついに (after a long time).
- むしろ (rather); {確|たし}かに〜が (admitting a point); {要|よう}するに, つまり (in short).
- 〜た{上|うえ}で (after, on that basis); 〜る{上|うえ}で (in doing).
- An argument: view → reasons → the other side → conclusion.
- New kanji: 賛 対 利 由 断 得 判 然 絶 決 努 適 程.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Reading and listening practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is practice for the two skills the JLPT N3 scores separately from vocabulary and
grammar: reading and listening. It has five original texts of the sizes and kinds the test
uses (two short ones, a mid-length article, a long story and an **[[information retrieval]]** task
with a price list), then listening at natural speed. It teaches the last six kanji of the course,
the ones you meet on notices and tickets, and about thirty words for notices and exam tasks.

Nothing here is new grammar. Everything comes from lessons 1 to 28, and the questions at the end
are written like the test's.

## Reading strategies

**Read the question first.** Before a text, look at what you'll be asked. On the test, the
question is printed under the passage: read it, then read the text with that one thing in mind.

**Short texts (notices, emails, memos).** These answer one practical question: what should
I do, by when, where? Look for the request (〜てください, 〜ようにお{願|ねが}いします), dates and times,
and the small words that change the rule:

| Word | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ただし (N4) | adds a condition or exception | ただし、{日曜日|にちようび}は{休|やす}みです。 |
| なお | adds a further note ("please also note") | なお、{参加費|さんかひ}は{当日|とうじつ}お{払|はら}いください。 |
| 〜を{除|のぞ}いて, 〜{以外|いがい} | except | {月曜日|げつようび}を{除|のぞ}いて{毎日|まいにち}{開|あ}いています。 |
| 〜{以降|いこう} | from … on | {午後|ごご}{六時|ろくじ}{以降|いこう}は{料金|りょうきん}が{半分|はんぶん}になります。 |
| 〜の{際|さい}は | when, in case of (formal) | ご{利用|りよう}の{際|さい}は、{受付|うけつけ}でお{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いてください。 |
| 〜{必着|ひっちゃく} | must arrive by | {三月|さんがつ}{一日|ついたち}{必着|ひっちゃく} |
| {先着|せんちゃく}〜{名|めい} | the first … people | {先着|せんちゃく}{三十名|さんじゅうめい} |

**Mid-length texts (explanations, essays).** Find the topic in the first paragraph and the
writer's point in the last. Conjunctions are signposts (lesson 28): しかし and ところが turn the
argument, つまり and このように sum it up, {確|たし}かに admits the other side. The question "what
does the writer most want to say?" is almost always answered after one of them.

**Long texts.** At N3 a long passage is about a thousand characters. Don't translate as you go:
read a paragraph, then say to yourself in a few words what it was about. Questions usually follow
the order of the text. Questions about a feeling ("why did she say…?") are answered by the
sentences just before and after the line.

**Information retrieval.** A timetable, price list or notice, and a person with a situation. The
work is matching: write down the person's conditions first (day, time, age, number of people),
then go through the table and apply each rule, including the small print under it.

**Time.** In the 70-minute grammar and reading section, the reading part usually needs the
larger share of the time. Don't spend more than a minute or two on any one grammar question.

## Kanji

The last six kanji of the course, all common on notices, tickets and in exam instructions.

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 指 | finger; point to | シ | ゆび, さ(す) | 9 | {指|ゆび}, {指|さ}す (to point), {指定席|していせき} (reserved seat), {指示|しじ} (instructions) |
| 留 | stay; fasten | リュウ, ル | と(める) | 10 | {留学|りゅうがく} (study abroad), {留守|るす} (being out), {書留|かきとめ} (registered mail), {留|と}める (to fasten) |
| 構 | structure; mind | コウ | かま(う) | 14 | {結構|けっこう} (quite; fine), {構内|こうない} (on the premises), {構|かま}わない (it doesn't matter) |
| 破 | tear, break | ハ | やぶ(る), やぶ(れる) | 10 | {破|やぶ}る (to tear; to break a rule), {破|やぶ}れる (to tear) |
| 際 | occasion; edge | サイ | | 14 | 〜の{際|さい} (when, on the occasion of), {国際|こくさい} (international), {実際|じっさい} (in fact) |
| 積 | pile up | セキ | つ(む), つ(もる) | 16 | {積|つ}む (to load, pile), {積|つ}もる (to pile up, of snow), {見積|みつ}もり (estimate) |

Carried words you can now write with kanji: {指|ゆび}, {留学|りゅうがく}, {留守|るす}, {留|と}める
in the sense "to fasten, to pin" ({紙|かみ}をクリップで{留|と}める; "to stop" is still {止|と}める),
{構|かま}わない (from N4's 〜てもかまわない), and {結構|けっこう}です (no, thank you).

Notes:

- {結構|けっこう} has three uses: "quite, fairly" ({結構|けっこう}{高|たか}い), "fine, good" (それで
  {結構|けっこう}です) and, in {結構|けっこう}です said to an offer, a polite "no, thank you". Context
  decides.
- {破|やぶ}る is both "to tear (paper)" and "to break (a promise, a rule, a record)":
  {約束|やくそく}を{破|やぶ}る. {破|やぶ}れる is "to be torn". ({敗|やぶ}れる, "to be beaten" in lesson 15,
  sounds the same.)
- 〜の{際|さい}(は) is the formal "when": ご{利用|りよう}の{際|さい}は = when you use (this).
- {指|さ}す (to point at) is written with 指; N4's さす "to sting" is a different verb.

Memory notes:

- 指 has the hand (扌) on the left: the part of the hand you point with.
- 積 has the grain plant (禾) on the left: sheaves of grain piled up.
- 破 has 石 (stone) on the left: a stone that breaks things.

```trace
指留構破際積
```

## Text 1: a station notice

> **{東口|ひがしぐち}{工事|こうじ}のお{知|し}らせ**
>
> {駅|えき}をご{利用|りよう}の{皆様|みなさま}へ
>
> {十一月|じゅういちがつ}{十六日|じゅうろくにち}から{三十日|さんじゅうにち}まで、{東口|ひがしぐち}の{階段|かいだん}の{工事|こうじ}を{行|おこな}います。{工事|こうじ}の{間|あいだ}、{毎日|まいにち}{夜|よる}{十時|じゅうじ}から{次|つぎ}の{日|ひ}の{朝|あさ}{五時|ごじ}まで、{東口|ひがしぐち}は{通|とお}れません。この{時間|じかん}は{西口|にしぐち}をご{利用|りよう}ください。なお、{構内|こうない}のエレベーターは{工事|こうじ}{中|ちゅう}も{使|つか}えます。{工事|こうじ}の{際|さい}は{大|おお}きな{音|おと}が{出|で}ることがあります。ご{不便|ふべん}をおかけしますが、よろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。
>
> {東町駅|ひがしまちえき}

{工事|こうじ} = construction work; {行|おこな}う = to carry out (formal); ご{不便|ふべん}をおかけします = we
apologize for the inconvenience.

<details>
<summary>Question (answer inside)</summary>

On 20 November you arrive at the station at 11 p.m. Which exit can you use, and can you take
the lift? — Only the west exit (the east exit is closed from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. during the work);
the lift inside the station can still be used (なお、{構内|こうない}のエレベーターは…{使|つか}えます).

</details>

## Text 2: an email from a teacher

> {件名|けんめい}：{来週|らいしゅう}のクラスについて
>
> クラスの{皆|みな}さんへ
>
> {来週|らいしゅう}{水曜日|すいようび}のクラスは、{私|わたし}の{都合|つごう}で、{木曜日|もくようび}の{同|おな}じ{時間|じかん}に{変|か}わります。{教室|きょうしつ}は{三階|さんがい}の{第二|だいに}{教室|きょうしつ}です。{木曜日|もくようび}に{来|こ}られない{人|ひと}は、{月曜日|げつようび}までにメールで{知|し}らせてください。また、{先週|せんしゅう}{配|くば}った{作文|さくぶん}の{用紙|ようし}は、クラスの{際|さい}に{必|かなら}ず{持|も}ってきてください。{用紙|ようし}を{破|やぶ}ってしまった{人|ひと}やなくした{人|ひと}には、{新|あたら}しいものを{渡|わた}します。
>
> {田村|たむら}

{件名|けんめい} = subject (of an email); {都合|つごう} = convenience, circumstances; {用紙|ようし} = form,
sheet of paper.

<details>
<summary>Question (answer inside)</summary>

A student has lost the essay sheet and can come on Thursday. What should she do? — Nothing
before the class: she just comes on Thursday to classroom 2 on the third floor, and the teacher
will give her a new sheet. (Only students who *can't* come on Thursday need to email by Monday.)

</details>

## Text 3: pointing and calling

An explanatory article in the である style (about 400 characters).

> {日本|にほん}の{駅|えき}で、{運転手|うんてんしゅ}や{駅員|えきいん}が{電車|でんしゃ}や{信号|しんごう}を{指|ゆび}でさしながら、「{出発|しゅっぱつ}{進行|しんこう}！」などと{大|おお}きな{声|こえ}を{出|だ}しているのを{見|み}たことがあるだろうか。これは「{指|ゆび}さし{確認|かくにん}」と{呼|よ}ばれ、{鉄道|てつどう}だけでなく、{工場|こうじょう}や{工事|こうじ}の{現場|げんば}などでも{行|おこな}われている。
>
> {指|ゆび}さし{確認|かくにん}の{目的|もくてき}は、{間違|まちが}いを{減|へ}らすことである。{人|ひと}は{慣|な}れた{仕事|しごと}ほど、よく{見|み}ないで「だいじょうぶだ」と{思|おも}い{込|こ}んでしまう。{特|とく}に{毎日|まいにち}{同|おな}じ{作業|さぎょう}をしていると、{確認|かくにん}したつもりで{実|じつ}はしていない、ということが{起|お}こりやすい。{目|め}で{見|み}るだけでなく、{指|ゆび}を{動|うご}かし、{声|こえ}に{出|だ}し、その{声|こえ}を{自分|じぶん}の{耳|みみ}で{聞|き}くことで、{注意|ちゅうい}が{向|む}くのである。{実際|じっさい}、ある{研究|けんきゅう}では、{指|ゆび}さしと{声|こえ}を{合|あ}わせると、ただ{見|み}るだけの{場合|ばあい}より{間違|まちが}いがずっと{少|すく}なくなったという。
>
> {最初|さいしょ}は{少|すこ}し{恥|は}ずかしいかもしれないが、この{方法|ほうほう}は{家|いえ}でも{使|つか}える。{出|で}かける{前|まえ}に、ガスの{火|ひ}や{窓|まど}を{一|ひと}つずつ{指|ゆび}さして、「よし」と{言|い}ってみてはどうだろうか。

{出発|しゅっぱつ}{進行|しんこう} = "departure, proceed" (a railway call); {目的|もくてき} = aim; {現場|げんば}
= site; {注意|ちゅうい}が{向|む}く = your attention turns (to it).

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. According to the writer, why do people make mistakes in work they know well? — Because the
   more used to a job they are, the more they assume all is well without really looking
   (よく{見|み}ないで…{思|おも}い{込|こ}んでしまう).
2. What does pointing and calling add to just looking? — Moving your finger, saying it aloud and
   hearing your own voice, which makes you pay attention.
3. What does the writer suggest at the end? — Trying it at home: pointing at the gas and the
   windows one by one before going out and saying よし.

</details>

## Text 4: the reserved seat

A short story (about 1,000 characters). Stories are told in the plain style; in this one, nouns
at the end of a sentence take である.

> {年末|ねんまつ}、{私|わたし}は{実家|じっか}に{帰|かえ}るため、{特急|とっきゅう}の{指定席|していせき}を{取|と}った。{三号車|さんごうしゃ}の{十二番|じゅうにばん}A、{窓側|まどがわ}の{席|せき}である。{年末|ねんまつ}の{電車|でんしゃ}はいつも{満員|まんいん}なので、{一|いっ}か{月|げつ}も{前|まえ}に{予約|よやく}しておいたのだ。
>
> ところが、{電車|でんしゃ}に{乗|の}ってみると、その{席|せき}にはもう{小|ちい}さなおばあさんが{座|すわ}っていた。{足元|あしもと}には、{大|おお}きな{紙|かみ}ぶくろが{二|ふた}つ{置|お}いてある。
>
> 「あの、すみません。そこ、{私|わたし}の{席|せき}だと{思|おも}うんですが……」
>
> {私|わたし}がきっぷを{見|み}せると、おばあさんはあわてて{自分|じぶん}のきっぷを{取|と}り{出|だ}した。それは{自由席|じゆうせき}のきっぷだった。{自由席|じゆうせき}と{指定席|していせき}の{違|ちが}いを{知|し}らなかったらしい。
>
> 「まあ、ごめんなさいね。すぐ{立|た}ちますから」
>
> おばあさんは{重|おも}そうなふくろを{持|も}ち{上|あ}げようとした。{自由席|じゆうせき}は{一号車|いちごうしゃ}と{二号車|にごうしゃ}だが、{通路|つうろ}まで{人|ひと}でいっぱいで、そこまで{歩|ある}いていくのは{大変|たいへん}そうだった。
>
> 「いいですよ、{座|すわ}っていてください。{私|わたし}は{若|わか}いですから」
>
> 「{本当|ほんとう}にいいの？{悪|わる}いわねえ」
>
> 「{平気|へいき}です。{立|た}っているのには{慣|な}れていますから」
>
> {気|き}がつくと、{私|わたし}はそう{言|い}っていた。{三時間|さんじかん}も{立|た}ち{続|つづ}けるのは{楽|らく}ではない。それでも、そのときは、そうするのが{当然|とうぜん}のような{気|き}がしたのである。
>
> {電車|でんしゃ}が{走|はし}り{出|だ}すと、おばあさんは{少|すこ}しずつ{話|はな}し{始|はじ}めた。{雪|ゆき}の{多|おお}い{町|まち}に{住|す}む{娘|むすめ}さんに{赤|あか}ちゃんが{生|う}まれ、{今日|きょう}{初|はじ}めて{会|あ}いに{行|い}くのだという。ふくろの{中|なか}は、{自分|じぶん}で{作|つく}った{料理|りょうり}と、{赤|あか}ちゃんの{小|ちい}さな{服|ふく}だった。「{夜|よる}も{眠|ねむ}れないくらい{楽|たの}しみでね」と{笑|わら}う{顔|かお}を{見|み}ているうちに、{足|あし}の{疲|つか}れもあまり{気|き}にならなくなった。{窓|まど}の{外|そと}の{景色|けしき}が{町|まち}から{山|やま}へ、{山|やま}から{雪|ゆき}の{野原|のはら}へと{変|か}わっていくのも、ほとんど{見|み}ていなかった。{気|き}がつくと、{私|わたし}も{自分|じぶん}の{家族|かぞく}の{話|はなし}をしていたのである。
>
> {二時間|にじかん}ほどたったころ、{車内|しゃない}のアナウンスが{次|つぎ}の{駅|えき}の{名前|なまえ}を{告|つ}げた。おばあさんが{降|お}りる{駅|えき}である。おばあさんはふくろの{中|なか}から{何|なに}かを{取|と}り{出|だ}して、{私|わたし}の{手|て}にのせた。{赤|あか}い{紙|かみ}で{折|お}った、{小|ちい}さなつるだった。
>
> 「{赤|あか}ちゃんにあげようと{思|おも}って、たくさん{折|お}ってきたの。{一|ひと}つはあなたに」
>
> おばあさんはそう{言|い}うと、{何度|なんど}も{頭|あたま}を{下|さ}げて{降|お}りていった。
>
> {空|あ}いた{席|せき}に{座|すわ}って、{私|わたし}は{窓|まど}の{外|そと}を{見|み}た。{雪|ゆき}の{積|つ}もった{田|た}んぼが、どこまでも{続|つづ}いている。{手|て}の{中|なか}の{赤|あか}いつるを{見|み}ながら、{私|わたし}は{思|おも}った。{最初|さいしょ}から{予約|よやく}した{席|せき}に{座|すわ}っていたら、この{景色|けしき}もきっと、ただの{雪|ゆき}の{景色|けしき}だっただろう。{家|いえ}に{着|つ}いたら、このつるを{母|はは}に{見|み}せて、{今日|きょう}のことを{話|はな}そうと{思|おも}う。

{実家|じっか} = your parents' home; {窓側|まどがわ} = window side; {足元|あしもと} = at your feet; つる =
a crane (the bird; origami cranes are a symbol of good wishes); {告|つ}げる = to announce.

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. Why was the old woman in the writer's seat? — She had an unreserved-seat ticket and didn't
   know the difference between reserved and unreserved seats ({違|ちが}いを{知|し}らなかったらしい).
2. Why did the writer let her keep the seat? — The unreserved cars were packed right into the
   aisles, and walking there with her heavy bags looked hard; at that moment it felt like the
   natural thing to do.
3. Why did the writer stop minding the tiredness? — While listening to her talk happily about
   meeting her new grandchild and watching her smile, the writer forgot about it (〜うちに).
4. What does the last sentence mean? — That because of the meeting, the snowy view had become
   special; from the reserved seat it would have been just a view of snow.

</details>

## Text 5: a price list (information retrieval)

> **{市民|しみん}プールのご{利用|りよう}について**
>
> | | {平日|へいじつ} | {土日|どにち}・{休日|きゅうじつ} |
> |---|---|---|
> | {大人|おとな} | 400{円|えん} | 500{円|えん} |
> | {中学生|ちゅうがくせい}・{高校生|こうこうせい} | 200{円|えん} | 250{円|えん} |
> | {小学生|しょうがくせい} | 100{円|えん} | 150{円|えん} |
> | {小学生|しょうがくせい}{未満|みまん} | {無料|むりょう} | {無料|むりょう} |
>
> - えいぎょう{時間|じかん}：{午前|ごぜん}{九時|くじ}〜{午後|ごご}{九時|くじ}（{入場|にゅうじょう}は{午後|ごご}{八時|はちじ}まで）
> - {定休日|ていきゅうび}：{毎週|まいしゅう}{月曜日|げつようび}（{月曜日|げつようび}が{休日|きゅうじつ}の{場合|ばあい}は、{次|つぎ}の{日|ひ}）
> - {午後|ごご}{六時|ろくじ}{以降|いこう}に{入場|にゅうじょう}する{方|かた}は、{料金|りょうきん}が{半分|はんぶん}になります。
> - {小学生|しょうがくせい}{未満|みまん}のお{子|こ}さんは、{必|かなら}ず{大人|おとな}と{一緒|いっしょ}に{入場|にゅうじょう}してください。

{休日|きゅうじつ} = a day off, a public holiday; {入場|にゅうじょう} = admission, going in.

<details>
<summary>Questions (answers inside)</summary>

1. Mr Kato and his nine-year-old daughter go in at 6.30 p.m. on a Saturday. How much do they pay
   in all? — 325 yen. On a Saturday the adult price is 500 yen and the primary-school price
   150 yen; after 6 p.m. both are halved: 250 + 75 = 325.
2. Can a four-year-old go in on her own on a Wednesday afternoon? — No. It would be free, but
   children under primary-school age must go in with an adult.
3. It's a Monday that is also a public holiday. Is the pool open? — Yes; when Monday is a
   holiday, the pool closes on the next day (Tuesday) instead.

</details>

## Listening strategies

The N3 listening section has five kinds of task. Three need a strategy:

- **Task-based** (what will the person do next?). The first plan in a conversation is often
  changed: listen for でも, じゃあ, やっぱり and the last decision.
- **Key points** (why, what is the main reason?). You see the question and the choices before
  you hear the conversation: read them during the pause, and listen for から, ので, {実|じつ}は and
  なぜかというと.
- **Quick response** (choose the right reply to one line). There's no picture and no time to
  think: decide what kind of line it is (a request, an apology, an offer, a question) and pick a
  reply of the matching kind.

Natural speech is fast and full of fillers (えーと, あのう, まあ, なんか) and contractions
(〜てる, 〜ちゃう, 〜なきゃ, 〜って: lesson 25). Don't try to catch every word. Fillers carry no
meaning; the content comes after them.

```dialogue
# At the pool counter
{受付|うけつけ}: こんばんは。
= Good evening.
{中村|なかむら}: あ、こんばんは。えーと、{大人|おとな}{一人|ひとり}と{子供|こども}{一人|ひとり}なんですけど。
= Oh, good evening. Er, one adult and one child, please.
{受付|うけつけ}: お{子|こ}さんは{小学生|しょうがくせい}ですか。
= Is your child at primary school?
{中村|なかむら}: はい、{三年生|さんねんせい}です。あの、{六時|ろくじ}{過|す}ぎたら{半分|はんぶん}になるって{聞|き}いたんですけど……。
= Yes, in the third year. Um, I heard it's half price after six…
{受付|うけつけ}: はい。{今日|きょう}は{土曜日|どようび}で、{今|いま}{六時|ろくじ}{半|はん}ですので、お{二人|ふたり}で{三百二十五円|さんびゃくにじゅうごえん}です。
= That's right. It's Saturday and half past six now, so that's 325 yen for the two of you.
{中村|なかむら}: よかった。じゃあ、これで。あ、それから、{来週|らいしゅう}の{月曜日|げつようび}って{開|あ}いてます？
= Great. Here you are. Oh, and are you open next Monday?
{受付|うけつけ}: {来週|らいしゅう}の{月曜日|げつようび}は{休日|きゅうじつ}ですので、{開|あ}いております。そのかわり、{火曜日|かようび}がお{休|やす}みになります。
= Next Monday is a public holiday, so we're open. Instead, we're closed on the Tuesday.
{中村|なかむら}: そっか、{火曜日|かようび}か。じゃあ、{月曜日|げつようび}にまた{来|く}るね、ユイ。
= Oh right, Tuesday. Then we'll come again on Monday, Yui.
```

Notice: {半分|はんぶん}になるって{聞|き}いた (〜って = と, lesson 22), {開|あ}いてます (〜ています →
〜てます), そっか (そうか, said quickly), and the polite {開|あ}いております from the counter
(lesson 24). そのかわり is "instead, in exchange" (lesson 13's {代|か}わりに, here written in kana
as a set phrase). Answering a task question here ("When can they come next week?") depends on the
last two lines, not the first ones.

## Words for notices and exam tasks

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| Tickets and places | {指定席|していせき} (reserved seat), {構内|こうない} (in the station, on the premises), {書留|かきとめ} (registered mail) |
| Notices | {開始|かいし} (start), しゅうりょう (end, close), えいぎょう (business, being open), {定休日|ていきゅうび} (regular closing day), {先着|せんちゃく} (first come, first served), {参加費|さんかひ} (participation fee), たいしょう (who something is for), {当日|とうじつ} (on the day), {事前|じぜん} (in advance), 〜{以降|いこう} (from … on), {必着|ひっちゃく} (must arrive by), なお (please also note), 〜の{際|さい} (when), {指示|しじ} (instructions), {開館|かいかん} / {閉館|へいかん} (opening / closing, of a library or museum), {入場料|にゅうじょうりょう} (admission fee), {利用者|りようしゃ} (users) |
| Verbs | {指|さ}す (to point at), {破|やぶ}る (to tear; to break a promise), {破|やぶ}れる (to tear), {積|つ}む (to load, to pile), {積|つ}もる (to pile up), {構|かま}う (to mind, to care) |
| Other | {結構|けっこう} (quite; fine), {見積|みつ}もり (estimate, quote) |
| Exam tasks | ひっしゃ (the writer of a text), {本文|ほんぶん} (the main text), {段落|だんらく} (paragraph), {要点|ようてん} (main point), {聞|き}き{取|と}る (to catch, to make out by ear), {読|よ}み{取|と}る (to read, to grasp from a text) |

{本文|ほんぶん}の{内容|ないよう}と{合|あ}っているものを{選|えら}びなさい。 — Choose the one that matches the content of the text.
ひっしゃが{一番|いちばん}{言|い}いたいことは{何|なん}ですか。 — What does the writer most want to say?
{第二|だいに}{段落|だんらく}の{要点|ようてん}をまとめなさい。 — Sum up the main point of the second paragraph.
{雪|ゆき}が{三十|さんじゅう}センチも{積|つ}もった。 — Thirty centimetres of snow piled up.
トラックに{段|だん}ボールを{積|つ}んだ。 — We loaded the cardboard boxes onto the lorry.
{約束|やくそく}を{破|やぶ}ってはいけない。 — You mustn't break a promise.
{時間|じかん}はかかっても{構|かま}いません。 — I don't mind if it takes time.

## Say it

```speak
{指定席|していせき}をお{願|ねが}いします。
= A reserved seat, please.
ご{利用|りよう}の{際|さい}は、{受付|うけつけ}でお{名前|なまえ}を{書|か}いてください。
= When you use it, please write your name at reception.
{本文|ほんぶん}の{内容|ないよう}と{合|あ}っているものを{選|えら}びなさい。
= Choose the one that matches the content of the text.
{結構|けっこう}です。
= No, thank you. (to an offer)
{雪|ゆき}が{積|つ}もっていますね。
= The snow has piled up, hasn't it.
```

## Key points

- Read the question before the text. Short texts: find the request, the date and the exceptions
  (ただし, なお, 〜を{除|のぞ}いて, 〜{以降|いこう}, 〜の{際|さい}は). Mid and long texts: the writer's point
  comes after a signpost (しかし, つまり, このように).
- Information retrieval: list the person's conditions, then apply every rule, including the
  small print.
- Listening: in task questions the last decision counts; in key-point questions, read the choices
  first; in quick response, match the kind of line. Fillers carry no meaning.
- New kanji: 指 留 構 破 際 積. That's all 370 N3 kanji (649 in all); the list is in the
  reference sheet "The N3 kanji".

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The JLPT N3 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last core lesson of the course. It explains the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test
at level N3: what the level means, how the test is built and scored, and how to prepare. It then
reviews the grammar of the whole course by what it does, so you can see where to go back before
the test. It ends with a plan for the last month and the road towards N2. There are no new kanji;
the new words are the vocabulary of the test itself. The quiz mixes questions from every module:
treat it as a final check.

## The JLPT and the level N3

The **[[JLPT]]** ({日本語|にほんご}{能力|のうりょく}{試験|しけん}) has five levels, from N5 to N1. N3 is the
middle one, and the official description calls it a bridge between the basic levels (N5, N4) and
the advanced ones (N2, N1).

The official summary is that N3 learners can understand Japanese used in everyday situations to a
certain degree. In this course's own words:

- they can read texts on everyday topics with concrete content, get the gist of newspaper
  headlines, and follow a slightly harder text when it's put another way;
- they can follow everyday conversations at close to natural speed and understand what is said
  and how the speakers are related.

Compared with N4, the texts are longer (N3 is the first level with a long passage), the speech is
faster, and the grammar includes the formal phrases and judgements of written Japanese. As at
N4, there is no speaking or writing section: every question is multiple choice.

The JLPT has published no official lists of words, kanji or grammar since the test was revised
in 2010. This course follows the scope that has become standard: about 3,700 words and about 650
kanji in all, counting N5's and N4's.

## How the N3 test is built

The test is taken in one sitting, in three timed parts. Times can change, and the listening time
depends a little on the recordings, so check jlpt.jp before your test.

| Test section | Time | What's in it |
|---|---|---|
| Language knowledge (vocabulary) | 30 minutes | kanji reading, orthography, contextually defined expressions, paraphrases, usage |
| Language knowledge (grammar) and reading | 70 minutes | selecting a grammar form, sentence composition, text grammar; short, mid-size and long passages, information retrieval |
| Listening | 40 minutes | task-based comprehension, key points, general outline, verbal expressions, quick response |

### Vocabulary

- **Kanji reading**: a word in kanji in a sentence; choose its reading. Watch for long vowels,
  small っ and voicing ({決心|けっしん}, {雨戸|あまど}).
- **Orthography**: a word in hiragana; choose the kanji. The wrong choices use real kanji with the
  same sound, such as {期|き} or {機|き} offered for the キ of {気温|きおん}.
- **Contextually defined expressions**: a sentence with a blank; choose the word that fits.
- **Paraphrases**: choose the expression closest in meaning to the underlined one
  ({結構|けっこう}{高|たか}い ≈ かなり{高|たか}い).
- **Usage**: choose the sentence in which a word is used correctly (as in this course's
  "Which sentence uses … correctly?" questions).

### Grammar and reading

- **Selecting a grammar form**: one blank, four forms (〜わけがない or 〜はずがない?).
- **[[Sentence composition]]**: four blanks, one marked ★, and four words to put in order. You
  choose the word that goes in the ★ position. This course's "build the sentence" questions
  train exactly this skill. An original example:

  これは ＿＿ ＿＿ ★ ＿＿ です。
  1 くれた　2 {母|はは}が　3 セーター　4 {作|つく}って

  The sentence is これは{母|はは}が{作|つく}ってくれたセーターです (this is a sweater my mother made for
  me), so the order is 2 4 1 3 and the ★ word is 1, くれた. Build the whole sentence first, on
  paper, then find the ★. If two orders seem possible, read both aloud: on the test only one is
  natural Japanese.
- **[[Text grammar]]**: a passage with several blanks; choose the conjunction, the grammar form or
  the word that fits the flow (lesson 28).
- **Reading**: short passages (notices, emails, memos), mid-size passages (explanations,
  essays), a long passage of about a thousand characters, and **[[information retrieval]]** (find
  what one person needs in a timetable, a price list or a notice). Lesson 29 has one of each.

### Listening

- **Task-based**: what will the person do next? Listen for the final decision.
- **Key points**: why, what is the main point? Read the choices in the pause before the
  conversation.
- **General outline**: what is the speaker's main point? There are no printed choices before
  you listen; take short notes.
- **Verbal expressions**: a picture and a situation; choose what the person should say
  (a request, an apology, an offer, a greeting).
- **Quick response**: one line, then three replies; choose the natural one. You hear everything
  only once.

## Scoring

| Scoring section | Score range | Sectional pass mark |
|---|---|---|
| Language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar) | 0–60 | 19 |
| Reading | 0–60 | 19 |
| Listening | 0–60 | 19 |
| Total | 0–180 | 95 (overall pass mark) |

Three points matter:

- Grammar is scored with vocabulary, but reading has a score of its own, even though grammar and
  reading share one 70-minute test section.
- To pass you need both the overall pass mark (95) and at least 19 in each of the three scoring
  sections. 120 in all with 18 in listening is a fail.
- Missing any test section means failing, and then no scores are shown at all.

The scores are scaled, not simply counted, so you can't turn a number of right answers into
points yourself. In practice: aim well above the pass marks in your strong sections and make
sure your weakest one is safely over 19.

## Strategies

### Before the test

- **Know the format.** Do the official sample questions on jlpt.jp under timed conditions,
  once early and once in the last week (see the reading list).
- **Practise the weak section.** Look at your quiz results in this course: the topics you miss
  most show where to go back. For many learners it's listening; then listen every day, even
  for ten minutes.
- **Read every day.** Reading is a section of its own at N3, and it takes most of the 70 minutes.
  Speed comes from volume: graded readers and NHK NEWS WEB EASY (reading list).
- **Review words with their kanji.** The vocabulary section is half kanji: the readings of
  carried words in kanji ({危険|きけん}, {窓口|まどぐち}, {散歩|さんぽ}) are typical questions.
- **Bring what the test asks for**: the test voucher (じゅけんひょう), pencils and an eraser
  (answers are marked on a マークシート), a watch. Check the rules on jlpt.jp; they can change.

### During the test

- **Vocabulary (30 minutes)**: a few dozen short questions; don't stop on one. If you don't know
  a reading, choose and move on: there's no penalty for wrong answers.
- **Grammar and reading (70 minutes)**: do the grammar quickly (a minute or less each) to keep
  the time for reading. Read each reading question first. Keep about fifteen minutes for the long
  passage and the information retrieval.
- **Listening (40 minutes)**: read the printed choices in the pauses. Don't go back to a missed
  question: the next one has already started.
- **Mark every answer.** Blank answers score nothing.

## The whole course by function

| Function | Patterns | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| While, during, every time | 〜うちに, 〜{最中|さいちゅう}に, 〜{途中|とちゅう}で, 〜{中|ちゅう} / {中|じゅう}; 〜たびに, 〜ごとに, 〜たとたん, 〜てはじめて, 〜ついでに, 〜ぶりに | 1, 2 |
| Moments and change | 〜ところに / ところを, 〜たところ, 〜かける, 〜たて, 〜きり; 〜につれて, 〜にしたがって, 〜とともに, 〜{一方|いっぽう}だ, 〜ば〜ほど | 3, 4 |
| Trying and pretending | 〜ようとする / しない, 〜つもりで / たつもり, 〜ふりをする, 〜たことにする | 5 |
| Reasons and results | 〜おかげで, 〜せいで, 〜ため(に), 〜ことから, 〜{結果|けっか}; 〜わけだ, 〜わけではない, 〜わけがない, 〜わけにはいかない | 6, 7 |
| No need, should, no choice | 〜ことはない, 〜とは{限|かぎ}らない, 〜て{済|す}む; 〜べきだ, 〜ものだ, 〜ことだ; 〜ずに, 〜しかない, 〜てしょうがない, 〜ずにはいられない, 〜ようがない | 8, 9, 10 |
| The formal phrases | として, にとって, に{対|たい}して; について, に{関|かん}して, を{中心|ちゅうしん}に, をはじめ, において; によって, 〜{代|か}わりに, に{反|はん}して; に{比|くら}べて, から〜にかけて, を{通|とお}して | 11–14 |
| Degree and emphasis | 〜ほど, 〜くらい, 〜さえ, 〜こそ, 〜あまり | 15 |
| Impressions and guesses | 〜っぽい, 〜{気味|ぎみ}, 〜がち, 〜だらけ, 〜{的|てき}, 〜{向|む}き / {向|む}け; 〜ような{気|き}がする, 〜ように{見|み}える, 〜に{違|ちが}いない, 〜っけ; 〜としたら, まさか, もしかしたら, 〜のではないか | 16, 17, 19 |
| Against expectations; and more | 〜くせに, 〜にしては, 〜{割|わり}に, 〜ながらも, 〜ば〜のに; 〜だけでなく, 〜ばかりか, 〜はもちろん, 〜{上|うえ}に, 〜ことか, 〜なんて | 18, 20 |
| Passing on words | 〜ように{言|い}う, 〜てもらいたい, 〜とおりに; 〜ということだ, 〜とのことだ, 〜んだって; 〜というのは, 〜と{言|い}えば, 〜といっても, 〜というより | 21–23 |
| Keigo and casual speech | 〜させていただく, お〜です, お〜いたす, 〜ております; 〜ちゃう, 〜とく, 〜なきゃ, 〜じゃん, 〜もん | 24, 25 |
| Writing | である, 〜ず、, stem joining, のである, 〜と{考|かんが}えられる; compound verbs, 〜っぱなし; conjunctions, 〜{上|うえ}で | 26–28 |

### Seven pairs to check

These are the contrasts the test likes best. If any of them is unclear, go back to its lesson.

1. **わけがない and はずがない** (lessons 7, 19): both "can't be", but はずがない is about what you
   expect from facts; わけがない is a stronger, more emotional "no way".
2. **おかげで and せいで** (lesson 6): a good result and a bad one.
3. **として and にとって** (lesson 11): として is a role ("as a teacher"); にとって is a viewpoint
   for evaluations ("for me, it's important").
4. **くせに and のに** (lesson 18): both "even though"; くせに blames a person, often rudely.
5. **ところが and しかし** (lesson 28): ところが is an unexpected fact, never before a request or
   plan.
6. **〜{出|だ}す and 〜{始|はじ}める** (lesson 27): a sudden start and a planned one.
7. **{未満|みまん} and {以下|いか}** (lesson 26): {未満|みまん} doesn't include the number.

## Words for the exam

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| On the day | {受験料|じゅけんりょう} (exam fee), {受験者|じゅけんしゃ} (test taker), じゅけんひょう (test voucher), {試験官|しけんかん} (invigilator), {問題用紙|もんだいようし} (question booklet), {解答用紙|かいとうようし} (answer sheet), マークシート (machine-marked answer sheet), きゅうけい (break), {音声|おんせい} (recording, audio), {直前|ちょくぜん} (just before), {前日|ぜんじつ} (the day before), {本番|ほんばん} (the real thing) |
| Answers | {問|と}い (question), せんたくし (answer choices), {解答|かいとう} (answer), {正解|せいかい} (correct answer), {答|こた}え{合|あ}わせ (checking answers) |
| Results | {満点|まんてん} (full marks), {合格点|ごうかくてん} (pass mark), {合格者|ごうかくしゃ} (successful candidate), {不合格|ふごうかく} (failing), {認定|にんてい} (certification), レベル, {目安|めやす} (rough guide) |
| Preparing | {過去問|かこもん} (past papers), もぎしけん (mock exam), {問題集|もんだいしゅう} (workbook), {時間配分|じかんはいぶん} (managing your time), {弱点|じゃくてん} (weak point), {集中力|しゅうちゅうりょく} (concentration), くりかえす (to repeat) |

You know many test words already: {試験|しけん}, {受験|じゅけん}する, {合格|ごうかく}する, {文法|ぶんぽう},
ごい (vocabulary), {読解|どっかい} (reading comprehension), ちょうかい (listening comprehension),
{得点|とくてん} (score, lesson 15), {本文|ほんぶん}, {段落|だんらく} and ひっしゃ (lesson 29).

{本番|ほんばん}では、{時間配分|じかんはいぶん}に{気|き}をつけよう。 — In the real test, watch how you use your time.
{公式|こうしき}の{問題集|もんだいしゅう}を{三回|さんかい}くりかえして{解|と}いた。 — I worked through the official workbook three times.
{答|こた}え{合|あ}わせをして、{自分|じぶん}の{弱点|じゃくてん}が{分|わ}かった。 — When I checked my answers, I found my weak points.
{合格点|ごうかくてん}は{九十五点|きゅうじゅうごてん}だが、{三|みっ}つの{得点|とくてん}がそれぞれ{十九点|じゅうきゅうてん}{以上|いじょう}でなければならない。 — The pass mark is 95, but each of the three scores has to be at least 19.

A word of caution about {過去問|かこもん}: complete JLPT papers aren't sold year by year. The
official workbooks ({公式|こうしき}{問題集|もんだいしゅう}) contain full practice tests in the real
format, and the sample questions on jlpt.jp show every question type.

## A study plan for the last month

| When | What to do |
|---|---|
| Four weeks before | Do one full practice test with the real times. Mark it and find your weakest section. |
| Weeks 4–2 | Every day: 20 minutes of words and kanji (this course's reviews), one reading (one of the course's readings or a graded reader), 15 minutes of listening. Twice a week, go back to the lessons behind the pairs you miss. |
| Week 2 | A second practice test. Compare the sections with the first one. |
| The last week | Light review only: the reference sheets, the seven pairs above, the readings of carried words in kanji. Check the test centre, the time and what to bring. |
| The day before | Rest. Pack the voucher, pencils, an eraser and a watch. Go to bed early. |

## After N3: towards N2

N2 is the level of Japanese used in a wider range of situations: newspaper articles and
explanations on general topics, and conversations and news at natural speed. Courses commonly
put it at about 6,000 words and 1,000 kanji in all (no official figures). Three things change:

- **Reading.** Real texts with fewer helps: start NHK's ordinary news site, columns, and novels
  written for young readers. Read a lot, and look up only what blocks the meaning.
- **Grammar.** N2 grammar is mostly written and formal, and many N2 patterns are close cousins
  of N3 ones: 〜にわたって (throughout), 〜をめぐって (over, concerning), 〜ものの (although), 〜しだい
  (as soon as; depending on). Grammar words like these are usually written in kana.
- **Listening.** Longer talks and news reports with no printed choices: practise summarizing what
  you heard in one sentence.

Keep the habits of this course: reviews every day, a reading every day, and the written style
for anything you write.

## Dialogue: after the test

Two friends who took the N3 together meet outside the test centre. (Casual speech.)

```dialogue
# After the test
ケン: おつかれ！どうだった？
= Well done! How did it go?
アヤ: うーん、{読解|どっかい}は{結構|けっこう}できたと{思|おも}う。でも、{長文|ちょうぶん}で{時間|じかん}が{足|た}りなくなっちゃって。
= Hmm, I think the reading went pretty well. But I ran out of time on the long passage.
ケン: {分|わ}かる。ぼくは{文法|ぶんぽう}のところでなやみすぎて、{最後|さいご}の{二問|にもん}は{適当|てきとう}に{選|えら}んじゃった。
= I know what you mean. I spent too long agonizing over the grammar, and I just picked any old answer for the last two.
アヤ: {適当|てきとう}にって……。でも、{何|なに}も{書|か}かないよりはいいよね。ちょうかいは？

ケン: {最初|さいしょ}のほうは{聞|き}き{取|と}れたんだけど、{最後|さいご}の、すぐ{答|こた}える{問題|もんだい}が{速|はや}くて……。
= I could follow the first part, but the last one, where you answer straight away, was so fast…
アヤ: あれ、{考|かんが}えてるうちに{次|つぎ}の{問題|もんだい}が{始|はじ}まっちゃうよね。
= With those, the next question starts while you're still thinking.
ケン: そうそう。{結果|けっか}が{出|で}るまで、{落|お}ち{着|つ}かないなあ。
= Exactly. I won't be able to relax until the results come out.
アヤ: まあ、もう{終|お}わったことだし、{考|かんが}えてもしかたないよ。{今日|きょう}は{何|なに}かおいしいものでも{食|た}べに{行|い}こう。
= Well, it's over now, so there's no point worrying. Let's go and eat something nice today.
ケン: {賛成|さんせい}！そのあとで、{答|こた}え{合|あ}わせしない？
= Agreed! Shall we check our answers afterwards?
```

Notice the casual forms from lesson 25 (〜ちゃって, 〜ちゃった, {考|かんが}えてる), {適当|てきとう} in its
everyday sense "any old way" (lesson 28), and 〜てもしかたない (lesson 10).

## Can you do this?

Before the test, check that you can:

- read a notice and say what to do, by when, and what the exceptions are (lesson 29);
- follow a 900-character essay and say what the writer most wants to say (lessons 26–28);
- choose between pairs like おかげで / せいで, わけがない / はずがない, として / にとって;
- put four words in order around a ★ (the build questions);
- read the carried words in kanji: {危険|きけん}, {値段|ねだん}, {窓口|まどぐち}, {理由|りゆう}, {自由|じゆう};
- follow a conversation at natural speed with fillers and contractions, and pick out the final
  decision.

## Common mistakes

- Counting raw answers as points. JLPT scores are scaled; use practice tests to see your level,
  not to calculate a score.
- Forgetting the sectional pass marks: a high total doesn't pass if one section is under 19.
- Spending too long on grammar questions and running out of time for the long passage.
- Leaving answers blank. There's no penalty for a wrong answer.
- Trying to understand every word in listening. Listen for the decision, the reason, the kind of
  line.

## Key points

- JLPT N3: vocabulary 30 minutes; grammar and reading 70 minutes; listening 40 minutes.
- Three scoring sections, each 0–60: language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar), reading,
  listening. Pass: 95 of 180 and at least 19 in each section.
- Question types include sentence composition (★, this course's build questions), text grammar,
  a long passage and information retrieval.
- Review by function, and check the seven pairs.
- The last month: two practice tests, daily words, reading and listening, then rest.
- No new kanji. The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews
  when you complete the lesson.

## What this lesson is for

This honors lesson is one longer story, about 3,000 characters in six parts: three times the
length of the JLPT N3's long passage. Every grammar point in it comes from this course, and the
questions afterwards check both the story and the grammar that carries it.

Read each part twice: once straight through for the story, without stopping for words, and once
slowly, noticing how it's built. A translation of each part is in a box you can open. The story
is told in the plain past style; its few new words are listed before it and join your
vocabulary reviews when you finish the lesson.

## Before you read

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {時計屋|とけいや} | watch and clock shop, watchmaker |
| {掛|か}け{時計|どけい} | wall clock |
| かいちゅうどけい | pocket watch (its first kanji is outside N3) |
| はり | hand (of a clock); needle (its kanji is outside N3) |
| まく | to wind (a spring): ねじをまく, to wind a clock (its kanji is outside N3) |
| {形見|かたみ} | keepsake (something left by someone who has died) |
| {老人|ろうじん}ホーム | care home for the elderly |
| {果|は}たす | to fulfil (a promise, a duty) |

Also: {平成|へいせい}{八年|はちねん}, the eighth year of the Heisei era, which is 1996; ねじ (here: the
winding crown); {受付|うけつけ} on a tag: "received".

## 1. The stopped clocks

> {祖父|そふ}が{亡|な}くなったのは、{今年|ことし}の{春|はる}のことだった。{祖父|そふ}は{海|うみ}の{近|ちか}くの{小|ちい}さな{町|まち}で、{五十年|ごじゅうねん}{以上|いじょう}{時計屋|とけいや}をしていた。{店|みせ}をどうするか、{家族|かぞく}で{何度|なんど}も{話|はな}し{合|あ}ったが、{結局|けっきょく}、{閉|し}めることに{決|き}まった。{東京|とうきょう}で{働|はたら}いている{私|わたし}が、{夏|なつ}{休|やす}みを{使|つか}って{店|みせ}の{中|なか}をせいりすることになった。
>
> {駅|えき}を{降|お}りると、{海|うみ}のにおいがした。{駅前|えきまえ}の{店|みせ}はいくつか{変|か}わっていたが、{港|みなと}へ{続|つづ}く{道|みち}は{昔|むかし}と{同|おな}じだった。{十年|じゅうねん}ぶりに{店|みせ}の{戸|と}を{開|あ}けると、{古|ふる}い{木|き}のにおいがした。かべには{大小|だいしょう}{様々|さまざま}な{掛|か}け{時計|どけい}が{掛|か}かっている。けれど、どの{時計|とけい}のはりも{止|と}まっていた。{祖父|そふ}が{入院|にゅういん}してから、ねじをまく{人|ひと}がだれもいなかったのだ。
>
> {子供|こども}のころ、この{店|みせ}は{時計|とけい}の{音|おと}でいっぱいだった。{遊|あそ}びに{来|く}るたびに、{私|わたし}は{祖父|そふ}のひざに{座|すわ}って、その{音|おと}を{聞|き}いたものだ。{祖父|そふ}は{細|こま}かい{部品|ぶひん}を{一|ひと}つずつ{取|と}り{出|だ}しては、また{組|く}み{立|た}てた。その{手|て}の{動|うご}きは、まるで{手品|てじな}のようだった。{祖父|そふ}はあまり{話|はな}さない{人|ひと}だったが、{時計|とけい}の{話|はなし}になると、{急|きゅう}に{楽|たの}しそうな{顔|かお}をした。「{時計|とけい}は、{大切|たいせつ}にすれば{人|ひと}より{長|なが}く{生|い}きるんだよ」というのが、{祖父|そふ}の{口|くち}ぐせだった。
>
> {今|いま}、{店|みせ}の{中|なか}では{何|なに}も{聞|き}こえない。{私|わたし}は{窓|まど}を{開|あ}け、{一|ひと}つ{一|ひと}つの{時計|とけい}のほこりを{落|お}とすことから{始|はじ}めた。

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

It was this spring that my grandfather died. For more than fifty years he had run a watch and
clock shop in a small town by the sea. My family talked again and again about what to do with
the shop, but in the end it was decided to close it. I work in Tokyo, and it fell to me to use
my summer holiday to sort out the inside of the shop.

When I got off the train, I could smell the sea. A few of the shops in front of the station had
changed, but the road down to the harbour was just as it used to be. When I opened the shop door
for the first time in ten years, there was a smell of old wood. All
kinds of wall clocks, big and small, hung on the walls. But the hands of every one of them had
stopped. Since my grandfather went into hospital, there had been nobody to wind them.

When I was a child, the shop was full of the sound of clocks. Every time I came to play, I used
to sit on my grandfather's knee and listen to it. He would take the tiny parts out one by one and
then put them back together; his hands moved as if he were doing a magic trick. He wasn't a man
of many words, but when the talk turned to clocks his face would suddenly light up. "Look after a
clock and it'll live longer than a person": that was what he always said.

Now, nothing could be heard in the shop. I opened the window and began by dusting the clocks,
one by one.

</details>

## 2. The watch in the drawer

> {三日目|みっかめ}の{午後|ごご}、{祖父|そふ}の{仕事台|しごとだい}の{引|ひ}き{出|だ}しを{開|あ}けたところ、{小|ちい}さな{箱|はこ}が{出|で}てきた。{中|なか}には、{古|ふる}いかいちゅうどけいが{一|ひと}つ{入|はい}っていた。{手|て}に{取|と}ると、{思|おも}ったより{重|おも}い。ふたには{小|ちい}さな{花|はな}の{絵|え}があり、{箱|はこ}には{紙|かみ}が{付|つ}いていた。{祖父|そふ}の{字|じ}で、こう{書|か}いてある。
>
> 「{森田様|もりたさま}。{平成|へいせい}{八年|はちねん}{八月|はちがつ}{三日|みっか}{受付|うけつけ}。{直|なお}し{終|お}わり。{取|と}りに{来|こ}られるまで、あずかること。」
>
> {紙|かみ}は{少|すこ}し{色|いろ}が{変|か}わっていたが、{祖父|そふ}らしい、{小|ちい}さくてていねいな{字|じ}だった。
>
> {平成|へいせい}{八年|はちねん}と{言|い}えば、{三十年|さんじゅうねん}も{前|まえ}である。そんなに{長|なが}い{間|あいだ}、{祖父|そふ}はこの{時計|とけい}を{取|と}っておいたのだ。{直|なお}してあるのに、{森田|もりた}さんはなぜ{取|と}りに{来|こ}なかったのだろう。そして{祖父|そふ}は、なぜすてずに{待|ま}ち{続|つづ}けたのだろうか。
>
> {祖父|そふ}は、{直|なお}した{時計|とけい}をすべてノートに{書|か}いていた。{平成|へいせい}{八年|はちねん}のページを{探|さが}すと、{確|たし}かに{森田|もりた}という{名前|なまえ}があった。しかし、{電話番号|でんわばんごう}は{書|か}いていない。{住所|じゅうしょ}のところには、{港|みなと}の{近|ちか}くの{町名|ちょうめい}だけがあった。その{日|ひ}の{夕方|ゆうがた}、{私|わたし}は{港|みなと}まで{歩|ある}いて{行|い}ってみた。ところが、そのあたりには{新|あたら}しいマンションが{建|た}っていて、{森田|もりた}という{名前|なまえ}はどこにも{見|み}つからなかった。
>
> {店|みせ}に{戻|もど}って、{私|わたし}はその{時計|とけい}を{耳|みみ}に{当|あ}ててみた。もちろん、{何|なに}も{聞|き}こえなかった。

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

On the afternoon of the third day, when I opened the drawer of my grandfather's workbench, a
small box turned up. Inside was an old pocket watch. When I picked it up, it was heavier than I'd expected. Its lid had a little picture of a flower,
and there was a piece of paper attached to the box. It said, in my grandfather's handwriting:

"Mr Morita. Received 3 August, Heisei 8. Repair finished. Keep until collected."

The paper had changed colour a little, but the writing was small and careful, just like my
grandfather.

Heisei 8 was thirty years ago. All that time, my grandfather had kept this watch. It had been
repaired, so why hadn't Mr Morita come for it? And why had my grandfather gone on waiting
instead of throwing it away?

My grandfather had written every watch and clock he repaired in a notebook. When I looked for the
page for Heisei 8, there was the name Morita. But there was no phone number, and where the address
should have been there was only the name of a district near the harbour. That evening I walked to
the harbour. But new blocks of flats stood there now, and the name Morita was nowhere to be found.

Back at the shop, I held the watch to my ear. Of course, I heard nothing.

</details>

## 3. Looking for Mr Morita

> {次|つぎ}の{日|ひ}、{私|わたし}は{近所|きんじょ}の{人|ひと}に{森田|もりた}さんのことを{聞|き}いて{回|まわ}った。{向|む}かいのパン{屋|や}のおばさんが、{森田|もりた}さんを{覚|おぼ}えていた。
>
> 「ああ、{森田|もりた}さんね。{港|みなと}の{近|ちか}くに{住|す}んでいて、{船|ふね}に{乗|の}る{仕事|しごと}をしていた{人|ひと}よ。{確|たし}か、{三十年|さんじゅうねん}ぐらい{前|まえ}に、{急|きゅう}に{遠|とお}くの{町|まち}へ{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}していったわ。おくさんが{亡|な}くなってすぐだったから、つらかったんでしょうね。それに、{森田|もりた}さんはよくこのお{店|みせ}に{来|き}ていたわよ。おじいさんとは{古|ふる}い{友|とも}だちで、{夜|よる}おそくまで{話|はな}し{込|こ}んでいることもあったわ」
>
> {二人|ふたり}が{友|とも}だちだったとは、{知|し}らなかった。だからこそ、{祖父|そふ}はこの{時計|とけい}をすてられなかったのかもしれない。
>
> {私|わたし}は{町|まち}の{公民館|こうみんかん}にお{願|ねが}いして、{知|し}らせを{出|だ}してもらった。「{森田様|もりたさま}、または{森田様|もりたさま}をご{存|ぞん}じの{方|かた}。{時計|とけい}をお{返|かえ}ししたいので、お{電話|でんわ}ください。」{知|し}らせには、{時計|とけい}の{写真|しゃしん}も{付|つ}けた。
>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

The next day I went round asking the neighbours about Mr Morita. The woman at the bakery across
the street remembered him.

"Oh, Mr Morita. He lived near the harbour and worked on the boats. If I remember rightly, he
suddenly moved far away about thirty years ago. It was just after his wife died, so it must have
been hard for him. And Mr Morita often came to the shop, you know. He and your grandfather were
old friends; sometimes they'd sit talking till late at night."

I hadn't known they were friends. Perhaps that was exactly why my grandfather couldn't throw the
watch away.

I asked the town's community centre to put up a notice for me: "To Mr Morita, or anyone who
knows him. We would like to return a watch; please telephone." I added a photo of the watch to the notice.

A week went by and the phone didn't ring. The day I had to go back to Tokyo was getting closer,
and just as I was beginning to think it was hopeless, a letter came. It was from Mr Morita's
daughter.

"My father is now in a care home in a nearby city. When I told him about the notice, he said
nothing for a while. Then he said, 'That watch is my wife's keepsake,' and burst into tears.
After my mother died, my father apparently wanted to have her watch repaired. But his work made
him move suddenly, and time went by without his being able to collect it."

</details>

## 4. The night before

> {手紙|てがみ}には、{娘|むすめ}さんの{電話番号|でんわばんごう}が{書|か}いてあった。{私|わたし}はすぐに{電話|でんわ}をかけた。{娘|むすめ}さんの{声|こえ}は{明|あか}るかったが、{少|すこ}し{心配|しんぱい}そうでもあった。
>
> 「{父|ちち}はもう{九十歳|きゅうじゅっさい}{近|ちか}いので、{長|なが}い{話|はなし}をすると{疲|つか}れてしまうかもしれません。でも、{時計|とけい}のことを{聞|き}いてから、{毎日|まいにち}{楽|たの}しみにしているんです。{今度|こんど}の{日曜日|にちようび}はいかがですか」

>

>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

The letter gave the daughter's phone number, and I called her straight away. Her voice was
cheerful, but a little worried too.

"My father is nearly ninety, so a long conversation may tire him. But since he heard about the
watch, he's been looking forward to it every day. How would next Sunday suit you?"

After I hung up, I read her letter again and again.

I decided to put off going back to Tokyo by a week. I had to ask rather a lot of my company, but
I felt I couldn't just go home like this.

On the night before the Sunday, I took the watch out of its box and put it on my grandfather's
workbench. As he always used to, I laid it on a clean sheet of paper and gently wiped the dirt
from the glass. For an old watch, it was much cleaner than I'd expected. Perhaps, over those
thirty years, my grandfather had opened the box now and then to look after it.

I thought about winding it. But I didn't. I felt that the person who set this watch going again
should be Mr Morita, not me.

</details>

## 5. Once more

> {次|つぎ}の{日曜日|にちようび}、{私|わたし}は{時計|とけい}を{持|も}って{老人|ろうじん}ホームを{訪|たず}ねた。{森田|もりた}さんは、{窓|まど}のそばのいすに{座|すわ}っていた。{思|おも}っていたより{小|ちい}さな{人|ひと}だった。{部屋|へや}の{入|い}り{口|ぐち}では、{娘|むすめ}さんが{静|しず}かに{見|み}ていた。
>
> {箱|はこ}を{開|あ}けたとたん、{森田|もりた}さんの{顔|かお}が{変|か}わった。ゆっくりと{時計|とけい}を{取|と}り{出|だ}し、ふたを{開|あ}けて、{花|はな}の{絵|え}を{指|ゆび}でなでた。
>
> 「{三十年|さんじゅうねん}も……。{君|きみ}のおじいさんは、ずっと{待|ま}っていてくれたんだね。この{時計|とけい}はね、{結婚|けっこん}したときに{私|わたし}が{妻|つま}にあげた{物|もの}なんだ。{給料|きゅうりょう}の{三|さん}か{月分|げつぶん}もしたんだよ。{妻|つま}は{毎朝|まいあさ}、{私|わたし}より{先|さき}に{起|お}きて、このねじをまいていた」

> {森田|もりた}さんは、ねじを{何回|なんかい}かまいた。すると、{止|と}まっていたはりが、{少|すこ}しずつ{動|うご}き{出|だ}した。チッ、チッ、チッ。{小|ちい}さな{音|おと}が、{静|しず}かな{部屋|へや}の{中|なか}に{聞|き}こえた。
>
> 「あのとき{取|と}りに{行|い}けなかったことが、ずっと{心|こころ}に{残|のこ}っていたんだ。{行|い}くべきだったのに、{行|い}けば{妻|つま}のことを{思|おも}い{出|だ}してしまう{気|き}がしてね。{妻|つま}と{約束|やくそく}したんだよ。この{時計|とけい}は、ずっと{動|うご}かしておくって。これでやっと、その{約束|やくそく}が{果|は}たせる」
>
> {森田|もりた}さんは{時計|とけい}を{耳|みみ}に{当|あ}てて、{目|め}を{閉|と}じた。それから、{祖父|そふ}のことを{聞|き}いた。{今年|ことし}の{春|はる}に{亡|な}くなったと{言|い}うと、{森田|もりた}さんは{小|ちい}さくうなずいた。
>
> 「そうか……。{会|あ}って、お{礼|れい}を{言|い}いたかったな。{君|きみ}から{伝|つた}えてくれないか。{時計|とけい}は{今|いま}も、ちゃんと{動|うご}いているって」

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

The next Sunday I took the watch and visited the care home. Mr Morita was sitting in a chair by
the window. He was smaller than I had imagined. His daughter watched quietly from the doorway.

The moment I opened the box, his expression changed. Slowly he took out the watch, opened the
lid and stroked the picture of the flower with his finger.

"Thirty years… Your grandfather waited for me all this time. You know, I gave this watch to my
wife when we got married. It cost three months' pay. Every morning she got up before me and
wound it."

Mr Morita wound the watch a few times. Then the hands, which had stopped, began little by little
to move. Tick, tick, tick. A tiny sound could be heard in the quiet room.

"Not being able to go and collect it back then has stayed on my mind all these years. I should
have gone, but I felt that if I did, I'd think of my wife. I made her a promise, you know: that
I'd always keep this watch going. Now at last I can keep that promise."

Mr Morita held the watch to his ear and closed his eyes. Then he asked about my grandfather. When
I told him he had died this spring, Mr Morita gave a small nod.

"I see… I wish I could have met him and thanked him. Will you tell him for me? That the watch is
still going, just as it should."

</details>

## 6. Time moves again

> {帰|かえ}りの{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}で、{私|わたし}は{祖父|そふ}のことを{考|かんが}えていた。{祖父|そふ}にとって、{時計|とけい}を{直|なお}すことは、ただの{仕事|しごと}ではなかったのだろう。{一|ひと}つ{一|ひと}つの{時計|とけい}に、だれかの{大切|たいせつ}な{時間|じかん}が{入|はい}っている。だからこそ、{三十年|さんじゅうねん}も{待|ま}ち{続|つづ}けることができたのではないだろうか。
>
> {店|みせ}に{戻|もど}ると、{私|わたし}は{一番|いちばん}{大|おお}きな{掛|か}け{時計|どけい}のねじをまいてみた。{祖父|そふ}がするのを{子供|こども}のころに{何度|なんど}も{見|み}ていたので、やり{方|かた}は{覚|おぼ}えていた。カチ、カチ、となつかしい{音|おと}が{戻|もど}ってきた。「{時計|とけい}は、{大切|たいせつ}にすれば{人|ひと}より{長|なが}く{生|い}きるんだよ」。{祖父|そふ}の{声|こえ}が{聞|き}こえたような{気|き}がした。{一|ひと}つが{動|うご}き{出|だ}しただけで、{店|みせ}の{中|なか}が{急|きゅう}に{明|あか}るくなったように{感|かん}じた。
>
> その{夜|よる}、{私|わたし}は{東京|とうきょう}の{母|はは}に{電話|でんわ}をかけた。{店|みせ}をしばらく{閉|し}めずに、{週末|しゅうまつ}だけでも{開|あ}けてみたい。{時計|とけい}のことを、{近|ちか}くの{時計屋|とけいや}さんに{習|なら}ってみたい。そう{話|はな}すと、{母|はは}は「あなたが{時計|とけい}を？」と{笑|わら}ったが、{反対|はんたい}はしなかった。
>
> {店|みせ}を{閉|し}めるのは、もう{少|すこ}し{先|さき}にしてもいいかもしれない。{私|わたし}はそう{思|おも}いながら、{次|つぎ}の{時計|とけい}を{手|て}に{取|と}った。

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

On the train home, I thought about my grandfather. For him, mending clocks and watches must have
been more than just a job. Every one of them holds someone's precious time. Wasn't that exactly
why he was able to go on waiting for thirty years?

Back at the shop, I tried winding the biggest wall clock. As a child I had watched my grandfather
do it many times, so I remembered how. Tick-tock, tick-tock: the old, familiar sound came back. "Look after a clock and it'll live
longer than a person." I felt as if I could hear my grandfather's voice. With just one clock
going, the shop suddenly seemed brighter.

That night I phoned my mother in Tokyo. I told her I'd like to keep the shop open for a while,
even if only at weekends, and to learn about clocks from a watchmaker nearby. My mother laughed,
"You, with clocks?", but she didn't say no.

Perhaps closing the shop could wait a little longer. With that thought, I picked up the next
clock.

</details>

## Grammar to notice

| In the story | Pattern | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| {遊|あそ}びに{来|く}るたびに | every time | 2 |
| {聞|き}いたものだ | used to (nostalgic) | 9 |
| {引|ひ}き{出|だ}しを{開|あ}けたところ | when I did…, I found | 3 |
| {取|と}りに{行|い}けないまま | while still not… | N4 |
| {思|おも}いかけたとき | was beginning to think | 3 |
| {平成|へいせい}{八年|はちねん}と{言|い}えば | speaking of… | 23 |
| 〜ということです | (the letter) reports | 22 |
| {開|あ}けたとたん | the moment | 2 |
| {動|うご}き{出|だ}した, {待|ま}ち{続|つづ}けた, {話|はな}し{合|あ}った | compound verbs | 27 |
| {行|い}くべきだったのに | should have, but | 9, N4 |
| {祖父|そふ}にとって | for (a viewpoint) | 11 |
| だからこそ | precisely because of that | 15 |
| 〜のではないだろうか | isn't it the case that…? | 19, 26 |
| {帰|かえ}るわけにはいかない | can't (in good conscience) | 7 |
| {森田|もりた}さんであるべきだ | ought to be (written style) | 9, 26 |

Notice how the story builds its suspense with questions the narrator asks herself at the end of
part 2 (なぜ〜のだろう, なぜ〜のだろうか), and answers them only in parts 3 and 4.

lessons.title: Writing an opinion piece: さくぶん and げんこうようし
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The JLPT tests only reading and listening, but writing is how you find out what you really
know. Japanese schools teach essay writing on squared manuscript paper, げんこうようし (its
second kanji is outside N3), and school essays and essay tests often have a limit of 400
characters: one sheet of 20 × 20 squares. This honors lesson brings together lessons 26 to 28:
the である style, the conjunctions and the four moves of an argument, in a {作文|さくぶん} of
about 400 characters.

## The rules of げんこうようし

These are the usual school rules for vertical manuscript paper. Details vary a little between
schools and teachers, so follow your teacher's or the test's instructions when they differ.

| Where | Rule |
|---|---|
| {題名|だいめい} (title) | On the first line, starting a few squares down (two or three are common). |
| Name | On the second line, ending one square before the bottom. Leave a square between family name and given name. |
| Paragraphs | Start each {段落|だんらく} on a new line, leaving the first square blank. Don't leave empty lines between paragraphs. |
| One square each | Every character takes one square, including small kana (ゃ, っ), the long-vowel mark ー, 「 」 and the punctuation 。 and 、. |
| Small kana and punctuation | In vertical writing they go in the top right of their square. |
| The top of a line | 。、 and a closing 」 never start a line. If one falls at the top, write it in the last square of the line before, together with the last character (or just below the last square). |
| 。 and 」 | When a quotation ends a sentence, 。 and 」 share one square. |
| Numbers | In vertical writing, kanji numerals ({二〇二六年|にせんにじゅうろくねん}); in horizontal writing, Arabic numerals, two digits to a square. |

Horizontal げんこうようし follows the same rules, turned on their side.

A note on {字数|じすう}, the character count: blank squares at the start of a paragraph and at
the end of a line usually count, because the limit is the number of squares. A common rule of thumb in
schools is to fill at least 80 percent of the limit; a 400-character essay of 200 characters
looks unfinished.

## The plan of a 400-character essay

Lesson 28's four moves fit into three paragraphs:

| Part | About | What it does | Words |
|---|---|---|---|
| {書|か}き{出|だ}し (opening) | 60–80 characters | The topic and your view | 〜が{増|ふ}えている。{私|わたし}は〜と{考|かんが}える。 |
| Body | 200–260 characters | Two reasons with an example each; the other side | {第一|だいいち}に、{第二|だいに}に、〜からである。もちろん / {確|たし}かに〜。 |
| {結|むす}び (ending) | 60–80 characters | The conclusion, in other words than the opening | つまり、 / このように、〜べきではないだろうか。 |

Write it in the である style from start to finish ({文体|ぶんたい}, the style, must not change),
and use written words: しかし, not でも; {非常|ひじょう}に, not すごく; と{考|かんが}える, not
と{思|おも}います.

## A model essay

The topic: 「{紙|かみ}の{本|ほん}と{電子|でんし}の{本|ほん}」 (Paper books and e-books). The essay is
shown in lines here; on げんこうようし each paragraph would start with a blank square.

> **{子供|こども}には{紙|かみ}の{本|ほん}を**
>
> {最近|さいきん}、スマートフォンで{本|ほん}を{読|よ}む{人|ひと}が{増|ふ}えている。{確|たし}かに、{電子|でんし}の{本|ほん}は{軽|かる}くて{便利|べんり}である。しかし、{私|わたし}は、{子供|こども}には{紙|かみ}の{本|ほん}をすすめたいと{考|かんが}える。
>
> {理由|りゆう}は{二|ふた}つある。{第一|だいいち}に、{紙|かみ}の{本|ほん}は{集中|しゅうちゅう}しやすい。スマートフォンで{読|よ}んでいると、メッセージやゲームが{気|き}になって、{途中|とちゅう}でやめてしまいがちだ。{実際|じっさい}、{私|わたし}も{電子|でんし}の{本|ほん}を{使|つか}い{始|はじ}めてから、{最後|さいご}まで{読|よ}み{切|き}った{本|ほん}が{減|へ}った。{第二|だいに}に、{紙|かみ}の{本|ほん}は{内容|ないよう}が{頭|あたま}に{残|のこ}りやすい。どのページのどのあたりに{何|なに}が{書|か}いてあったか、{手|て}と{目|め}で{覚|おぼ}えられるからである。もちろん、{電子|でんし}の{本|ほん}にも{利点|りてん}はある。{大人|おとな}が{通勤|つうきん}{中|ちゅう}に{読|よ}むのなら、むしろそのほうが{便利|べんり}だろう。
>
> {電子|でんし}か{紙|かみ}か、どちらか{一|ひと}つに{決|き}める{必要|ひつよう}はない。つまり、{大切|たいせつ}なのは、{目的|もくてき}に{合|あ}わせて{選|えら}ぶことである。{本|ほん}を{読|よ}む{習慣|しゅうかん}を{作|つく}る{子供|こども}の{時期|じき}には、{紙|かみ}の{本|ほん}を{選|えら}ぶべきではないだろうか。

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

**Paper books for children**

These days more and more people read books on their smartphones. E-books are certainly light
and convenient. Even so, for children I would recommend paper books.

There are two reasons. First, it's easier to concentrate on a paper book. When you read on a
smartphone, you tend to get distracted by messages and games and stop halfway. In fact, since I started
using e-books, I've finished fewer books to the end. Second, the
content of a paper book stays in your head more easily, because your hands and eyes remember on
which page, and where on the page, something was written. Of course, e-books have their
advantages too. For an adult reading on the way to work, they may well be more convenient.

There's no need to decide on just one of the two. In other words, what matters is choosing to suit the purpose. In childhood, when the habit of
reading is formed, shouldn't we choose paper books?

</details>

The essay is about 350 characters, close to 90 percent of a 400-square sheet once the blank
squares at the start of each paragraph are counted. Look at how it's built:

- **The opening** states the topic (more people read on phones), admits the other side
  ({確|たし}かに), and gives the view with しかし and と{考|かんが}える.
- **The body** has two reasons signposted {第一|だいいち}に and {第二|だいに}に, each with an
  example, and the second one explained with 〜からである. もちろん〜 gives the other side its due.
- **The ending** restates the view in new words (つまり, {目的|もくてき}に{合|あ}わせて) and closes with
  a modest べきではないだろうか.
- Grammar from the course: 〜がちだ (lesson 16), 〜やすい (N4), {読|よ}み{切|き}る (lesson 27), むしろ
  (lesson 28), 〜べき (lesson 9).

## How to write one

1. **Plan** for five minutes: your view in one sentence, two reasons, one example for each, and
   the other side.
2. **Write a draft** ({下書|したが}き) quickly, without stopping to count.
3. **Check** with the list below, then count the characters.
4. **Copy it out** neatly on the manuscript paper.

## Checklist

- Is the whole essay in the である style, with no です / ます and no casual words?
- Does the opening give your view, and does the ending repeat it in other words?
- Does each reason have an example, and is there a {確|たし}かに or もちろん for the other side?
- Does every paragraph start with one blank square, on a new line ({改行|かいぎょう})?
- Is there a 。 or 、 at the top of any line?
- Is the {字数|じすう} between about 80 and 100 percent of the limit?

## Common mistakes

- Starting sentences with でも or だから. Use しかし and そのため / したがって (lesson 28).
- ×{私|わたし}は〜と{思|おも}います。 in a である essay. Write 〜と{考|かんが}える or 〜と{思|おも}う.
- Writing the opening and the ending in the same words. Say the conclusion again, differently.
- Three reasons without examples. Two reasons, each with an example, persuade better than three
  bare ones.
- Leaving a blank line between paragraphs. Start a new line with one blank square instead.

## Key points

- げんこうようし: title a few squares down on line 1, name at the bottom of line 2, one blank square
  at the start of each paragraph, one character (or punctuation mark) per square, no 。、 at the
  top of a line.
- 400 characters: opening (view), body (two reasons with examples, the other side), ending
  (conclusion in new words).
- One style throughout: である, with written words.

sections.name: Passing on words, keigo and casual speech
Written Japanese and the N3 exam

questions.stem: スープは{温|あたた}かい___、{飲|の}んでください。 (Please drink the soup while it's warm.)
questions.explanation: The soup won't stay warm, so "drink it while it lasts" is 〜うちに: {温|あたた}かいうちに. {最中|さいちゅう} and {途中|とちゅう} follow actions and journeys, not a state like being warm, and ころ is "the time when", which doesn't give a request a time limit.

questions.stem: {暗|くら}く___うちに、{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}りましょう。 (Let's go home before it gets dark.)
questions.explanation: "Before (something unwanted) happens" is the negative + うちに: {暗|くら}くならないうちに, literally "while it hasn't got dark yet". {暗|くら}くなるうちに would mean "while it's getting dark", the opposite of the advice, and た and て forms don't go before うちに.

questions.stem: Which sentence is natural?
choices: {日本|にほん}に{来|こ}ないうちに、{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}しました。
{日本|にほん}に{来|く}る{前|まえ}に、{日本語|にほんご}を{勉強|べんきょう}しました。
{若|わか}い{最中|さいちゅう}に、たくさん{旅行|りょこう}しました。
{温|あたた}かい{途中|とちゅう}に、{食|た}べてください。
questions.explanation: Coming to Japan was a planned event in time order, so {前|まえ}に: {来|く}る{前|まえ}に. 〜ないうちに is for getting ahead of something unwanted, so {来|こ}ないうちに sounds as if coming to Japan were a danger. {最中|さいちゅう} needs an action with a peak (not a stage of life: {若|わか}いうちに), and {途中|とちゅう} needs a journey or a process.

questions.stem: {試合|しあい}の___に、{急|きゅう}に{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}りだしました。 (Right in the middle of the match, it suddenly started to rain.)
questions.explanation: "Right in the middle of" an event, followed by something unexpected, is 〜の{最中|さいちゅう}に. {前|まえ}に and あとに would put the rain before or after the match, and a noun + うちに needs a state that will end ({子供|こども}のうちに), not an event like a match.

questions.stem: {駅|えき}から{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}る{途中|とちゅう}___、{古|ふる}い{本屋|ほんや}があります。
questions.explanation: ある says where something is, so {途中|とちゅう}に: "on my way home there's an old bookshop". {途中|とちゅう}で is for an event that happens on the way ({途中|とちゅう}で{友|とも}だちに{会|あ}った), and を and が don't fit after {途中|とちゅう} here.

questions.stem: How is 一日中 read? {日曜日|にちようび}は一日中{雨|あめ}でした。
questions.explanation: After a stretch of time, 中 is じゅう, "all through": {一日中|いちにちじゅう}, all day. ちゅう is "in progress" after an activity ({会議中|かいぎちゅう}), and ついたち is the first day of a month, not "one day".

questions.stem: A: 「{部長|ぶちょう}とお{話|はな}ししたいんですが。」 B: 「すみません、{部長|ぶちょう}は{今|いま}、___。」
choices: {会議|かいぎ}の{最中|さいちゅう}です
{会議|かいぎ}の{途中|とちゅう}にいます
{会議|かいぎ}の{間|あいだ}です
questions.explanation: 〜の{最中|さいちゅう}です says an action is in progress right now, usually as a reason not to disturb: "he's in the middle of a meeting". うちです and {間|あいだ}です can't end a sentence like this, and {途中|とちゅう}にいます treats the meeting as a road.

questions.stem: What does this sentence mean? {本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでいるうちに、{眠|ねむ}くなってきました。
choices: I read a book so that I would get sleepy.
I read the book before I got sleepy.
While I was reading, I started to get sleepy.
I got sleepy, so I stopped reading.
questions.explanation: 〜ているうちに + a change: while one thing goes on, something else comes about without your planning it. Here the sleepiness crept up during the reading. "So that" would be ように or ために, and "before" would be {前|まえ}に.

questions.stem: {祖母|そぼ}は{百歳|ひゃくさい}まで___しました。
questions.explanation: {長生|ながい}きする is to live a long life: "my grandmother lived to a hundred". {成長|せいちょう}する is to grow up (a child, a company), {期待|きたい}する is to expect, and {一生|いっしょう} (a whole life) is a noun that doesn't take する.

questions.stem: Which is closest in meaning to the underlined word? {当時|とうじ}は、{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}に{何|なに}もありませんでした。 (underlined: {当時|とうじ})
questions.explanation: {当時|とうじ} is "back then, at that time", so そのころ (in those days) is closest. {今|いま}でも (even now) and これから (from now on) are the wrong time, and ときどき is "sometimes".

questions.stem: Which sentence uses {成長|せいちょう} correctly?
choices: {雨|あめ}がだんだん{成長|せいちょう}してきました。
{店|みせ}の{値段|ねだん}が{去年|きょねん}より{成長|せいちょう}しました。
{私|わたし}は{先月|せんげつ}、{髪|かみ}を{成長|せいちょう}しました。
{子供|こども}たちは{毎年|まいとし}{大|おお}きく{成長|せいちょう}しています。
questions.explanation: {成長|せいちょう}する is for living things growing up (children, animals) or for things that develop, such as a company. Rain gets heavier ({強|つよ}くなる), prices go up ({上|あ}がる), and you grow your hair out with のばす, not {成長|せいちょう}.

questions.stem: How is 若者 read? この{町|まち}は若者が{少|すく}なくなりました。
questions.explanation: {若者|わかもの} (young people) uses two kun readings: わか + もの. ジャク is the on'yomi of 若, but it isn't used in this word, and the い of {若|わか}い disappears in the compound.

questions.stem: Which kanji is right for the word in brackets? {祖父|そふ}は{去年|きょねん}［なくなりました］。
questions.explanation: For a person who has died, なくなる is written 亡くなる (pass away). 無くなる is "to run out, to be lost" (of things), and 泣く (cry) and 鳴く (of animals, call) are other verbs that can't take なる like this.

questions.stem: Listen. What will the speaker do?

audio.text: わすれないうちに、いまメモしておきます。

choices: Make a note later, when they remember.
Make a note now, before they forget.
Ask someone else to make a note.
questions.explanation: {忘|わす}れないうちに、{今|いま}メモしておきます: "before I forget, I'll make a note now". 〜ないうちに is "before it happens", and 〜ておく is doing something in advance.

questions.stem: Listen. Why can't the speaker talk now?

audio.text: ごめん、いましょくじのさいちゅうなんだ。あとでかけなおすね。

choices: They are on the way to a restaurant.
They are in the middle of a meal.
questions.explanation: {今|いま}{食事|しょくじ}の{最中|さいちゅう}なんだ: "I'm right in the middle of a meal". かけなおす is to call back. "On the way" would be {途中|とちゅう}, and "just finished" would be {食|た}べたところ or {食|た}べたばかり.

questions.stem: Listen. Which is the best reply?

audio.text: さめないうちに、どうぞ。

questions.explanation: {冷|さ}めないうちに、どうぞ: "please have it before it gets cold", said when serving food or tea. The natural answer is いただきます. どういたしまして answers thanks, おかげさまで answers a question about your health or success, and いってきます is said when leaving home.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
distractors: {若|わか}い{最中|さいちゅう}に
questions.prompt: While I'm young, I want to see all sorts of countries in the world.
questions.explanation: {若|わか}いうちに{世界|せかい}のいろいろな{国|くに}を{見|み}てみたいです. The time phrase usually comes first, though it can also stand just before the verb. {最中|さいちゅう} can't follow a stage of life.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: I fell asleep halfway through the film.
questions.explanation: Falling asleep is an event, so {途中|とちゅう}で, not {途中|とちゅう}に (which says where something is). 〜てしまう adds that it happened without meaning to.

questions.stem:
Read the email and answer.

{先週|せんしゅう}、{二十年|にじゅうねん}ぶりに{小学校|しょうがっこう}の{同窓会|どうそうかい}がありました。{初|はじ}めはだれがだれか{分|わ}かりませんでしたが、{話|はな}しているうちに、みんなの{子供|こども}のころの{顔|かお}を{思|おも}い{出|だ}しました。{途中|とちゅう}で{先生|せんせい}も{来|き}てくださって、みんなで{昔|むかし}の{写真|しゃしん}を{見|み}ました。{先生|せんせい}は{今年|ことし}{七十歳|ななじゅっさい}になったそうですが、{昔|むかし}と{同|おな}じように{元気|げんき}でした。{帰|かえ}りに{先生|せんせい}は「みんなが{元気|げんき}なうちに、また{会|あ}いましょう」とおっしゃいました。

({同窓会|どうそうかい}: class reunion)

What happened as the writer talked with old classmates?
choices: The writer forgot who everyone was.
The writer remembered what everyone looked like as children.
The writer showed everyone some old photos.
The writer decided to organize another reunion.
questions.explanation: {話|はな}しているうちに、みんなの{子供|こども}のころの{顔|かお}を{思|おも}い{出|だ}しました: while they talked, the writer came to remember everyone's childhood faces. At first ({初|はじ}めは) the writer didn't know who was who. They all looked at the photos together, and it was the teacher who suggested meeting again.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with one kanji (or its reading in hiragana): {今週|こんしゅう}___に{返事|へんじ}をください。 (Please reply some time this week.)
questions.explanation: {今週中|こんしゅうちゅう}に: "within this week, some time this week". 〜{中|ちゅう}に after a period you're in now sets a deadline. Note the reading: {今週中|こんしゅうちゅう}, but {今日中|きょうじゅう}.

questions.topic: たびに and ごとに
questions.stem: この{写真|しゃしん}を{見|み}る___、{祖父|そふ}のことを{思|おも}い{出|だ}します。 (Every time I look at this photo, I remember my grandfather.)
questions.explanation: "Every time (an event happens)" with a verb is dictionary form + たびに, and a memory is the typical second half. ごとに follows a number or a noun ({一時間|いちじかん}ごとに), とたん follows the た form and means "the moment", and ついでに is "while you're at it".

questions.topic: たびに and ごとに
questions.stem: この{駅|えき}には、{二十分|にじゅっぷん}___バスが{来|き}ます。 (Buses come to this station every twenty minutes.)
questions.explanation: A regular interval after a number is ごとに: {二十分|にじゅっぷん}ごとに, every twenty minutes. たびに follows a verb or a noun + の for repeated events, ぶりに is "for the first time in…", and うちに is "while".

questions.topic: たとたん and てはじめて
questions.stem: {電車|でんしゃ}を{降|お}りた___、{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}りだしました。 (The moment I got off the train, it started to rain.)
questions.explanation: た form + とたん: the very moment one thing happened, something unexpected followed. ついでに would mean the rain was an extra errand, たびに needs the dictionary form (and a repeated event), and うちに can't follow a た form.

questions.topic: ついでに and ぶりに
questions.stem: Which sentence is natural?
choices: {駅|えき}に{着|つ}いたとたん、{電話|でんわ}してください。
{明日|あした}{東京|とうきょう}に{行|い}くたびに、{友|とも}だちに{会|あ}います。
{駅|えき}に{行|い}くついでに、{手紙|てがみ}を{出|だ}してきます。
この{駅|えき}には、めったに{急行|きゅうこう}が{止|と}まります。
questions.explanation: 〜ついでに: going to the station anyway, I'll post the letter too. たとたん reports a past surprise and can't end in a request (use {着|つ}いたら), たびに needs something that happens again and again (not one trip tomorrow), and めったに needs a negative ({止|と}まりません).

questions.topic: たとたん and てはじめて
questions.stem: {日本|にほん}に{住|す}んで___、{電車|でんしゃ}がどんなに{便利|べんり}か{分|わ}かりました。 (It was only after living in Japan that I understood how convenient the trains are.)
questions.explanation: 〜てはじめて: only after A did you realize B. 〜てからでないと needs a negative second half ("you can't… until"), とたん follows the た form, not the て form, and ついでに would make the understanding an errand.

questions.topic: たとたん and てはじめて
questions.stem: きっぷを{買|か}って___、ホームには{入|はい}れません。 (You can't go onto the platform until you've bought a ticket.)
questions.explanation: "Not until A" with a negative second half is 〜てからでないと: {買|か}ってからでないと{入|はい}れません. 〜てはじめて is a realization after the fact, 〜ているうちに is "while doing", and ばかり needs た (たばかり, just did).

questions.topic: ついでに and ぶりに
questions.stem: Fill in the blank in hiragana: {三年|さんねん}___に{国|くに}へ{帰|かえ}りました。 (I went back to my country for the first time in three years.)
questions.explanation: A length of time + ぶりに: "for the first time in…", something happening again after a gap. It's the same ぶり as in ひさしぶり.

questions.stem:
Read and answer.

{私|わたし}は{毎朝|まいあさ}、{自転車|じてんしゃ}で{駅|えき}まで{行|い}きます。{家|いえ}から{駅|えき}までは{十分|じゅっぷん}ぐらいで、{帰|かえ}りもたいてい{自転車|じてんしゃ}です。{雨|あめ}の{日|ひ}はたまにバスに{乗|の}りますが、タクシーにはめったに{乗|の}りません。{駅|えき}からは{地下鉄|ちかてつ}で{会社|かいしゃ}まで{二十分|にじゅっぷん}です。{地下鉄|ちかてつ}はしょっちゅうこんでいて、{座|すわ}れるのは{一週間|いっしゅうかん}に{一回|いっかい}ぐらいです。{去年|きょねん}までは{車|くるま}で{通|かよ}っていましたが、{朝|あさ}は{道路|どうろ}がひどくこむので、やめました。

Which does the writer use least often now?
questions.explanation: タクシーにはめったに{乗|の}りません: the writer hardly ever takes a taxi. The bicycle and the underground are every day, and the bus is たまに, now and then. The car isn't used at all any more, but it isn't one of the choices.

questions.stem: {朝|あさ}の{電車|でんしゃ}は___で、{全然|ぜんぜん}{座|すわ}れませんでした。
questions.explanation: {満員|まんいん} is "packed, full of people", the reason you couldn't sit. {終点|しゅうてん} is the end of the line, {始発|しはつ} the first train of the day (often the easiest to get a seat on), and {運休|うんきゅう} means the train wasn't running at all.

questions.stem: Which is closest in meaning? {本|ほん}を{読|よ}んでいて、{降|お}りる{駅|えき}を{乗|の}り{越|こ}してしまいました。
choices: {降|お}りる{駅|えき}より{先|さき}まで{行|い}ってしまいました。
{降|お}りる{駅|えき}の{前|まえ}の{駅|えき}で{降|お}りてしまいました。
{電車|でんしゃ}に{乗|の}り{遅|おく}れてしまいました。
{電車|でんしゃ}が{駅|えき}に{止|と}まりませんでした。
questions.explanation: {乗|の}り{越|こ}す is to ride past your stop, so you went further than your station. Getting off too early is the opposite, {乗|の}り{遅|おく}れる is to miss the train, and a train that doesn't stop {通過|つうか}します.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses {寄|よ}る correctly?
choices: {毎朝|まいあさ}{七時|しちじ}に{寄|よ}って、{会社|かいしゃ}へ{行|い}きます。
{会社|かいしゃ}の{帰|かえ}りに、{本屋|ほんや}に{寄|よ}りました。
{借|か}りた{本|ほん}を{友|とも}だちに{寄|よ}りました。
{急|きゅう}に{雨|あめ}が{寄|よ}りだしました。
questions.explanation: {寄|よ}る is to drop in somewhere on the way: 〜に{寄|よ}る. A time can't be "dropped in on" (you'd get up: {起|お}きる), giving back a book is {返|かえ}す, and rain {降|ふ}る.

questions.stem: How is 遅れ read? {雪|ゆき}のため、{電車|でんしゃ}に{十分|じゅっぷん}の遅れが{出|で}ています。
questions.explanation: {遅|おく}れ (a delay) is the noun of {遅|おく}れる, so it's read おくれ. おそ is the reading in {遅|おそ}い (slow, late), チ is the on'yomi ({遅刻|ちこく}), and おそれ is a different word (fear).

questions.stem: Which kanji is right? {新|あたら}しい{電車|でんしゃ}はとても［はやい］です。 (The new trains are very fast.)
questions.explanation: はやい about speed is 速い. 早い is early or soon in time ({朝|あさ}が{早|はや}い), 遠い is far and 遅い is slow.

questions.stem: How is 船便 read?
questions.explanation: {船便|ふなびん} (sea mail): 船 becomes ふな before another word, and 便 is ビン in post and flights. ベン is its reading in {便利|べんり}.

questions.stem: Listen to the announcement. Which is true?

audio.text: まもなく、さんばんせんに、とうきょうゆきのでんしゃがまいります。

choices: A train for Tokyo is about to arrive at platform 3.
A train from Tokyo has just left platform 3.
The train for Tokyo will leave from platform 8.
Platform 3 is closed until Tokyo trains arrive.
questions.explanation: まもなく (shortly), {三番線|さんばんせん}に (at platform 3), {東京|とうきょう}{行|ゆ}き (bound for Tokyo), まいります (humble "come"): a train for Tokyo will arrive shortly at platform 3.

questions.stem: Listen. What kind of train is it?

audio.text: このでんしゃは、えきごとにとまります。

choices: A train that doesn't stop until the end of the line.
A train that stops every hour.
A train that stops at every station.
A train that stops only at large stations.
questions.explanation: {駅|えき}ごとに{止|と}まります: it stops at each station, like a かくえきていしゃ. ごとに after a noun is "at each one".

questions.stem: Listen. Which is the best reply?

audio.text: ひさしぶり！げんきだった？

choices: うん、{元気|げんき}だったよ。そっちは？
はじめまして。よろしく。
questions.explanation: ひさしぶり！{元気|げんき}だった？ is "long time no see, how have you been?", so you answer about how you've been and ask back. はじめまして is for a first meeting, which this isn't.

questions.topic: たとたん and てはじめて
questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: The moment I opened the door, the cat ran outside.
questions.explanation: た form + とたん, then what happened at that moment. たびに can't follow a た form, and opening a door once isn't a repeated event.

questions.topic: ついでに and ぶりに
questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: While I'm going to the station, I'll drop in at the bank.
questions.explanation: The main errand comes first, then ついでに, then the extra: {駅|えき}に{行|い}くついでに{銀行|ぎんこう}に {寄|よ}ってきます. 〜てくる here is "go and come back".

questions.stem:
Read the station notice and answer.

お{知|し}らせ

{四月|しがつ}{一日|ついたち}から{時刻表|じこくひょう}が{変|か}わります。{朝|あさ}{七時|しちじ}から{九時|くじ}までは、{電車|でんしゃ}が{五分|ごふん}ごとに{来|き}ます。{昼|ひる}は{十五分|じゅうごふん}ごとです。また、{夜|よる}{十一時|じゅういちじ}{以降|いこう}はかいそくが{運休|うんきゅう}になり、かくえきていしゃだけが{走|はし}ります。{最終|さいしゅう}{電車|でんしゃ}の{時刻|じこく}は{変|か}わりません。ご{利用|りよう}のみなさまにはごめいわくをおかけしますが、よろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。くわしくは{駅|えき}の{窓口|まどぐち}でお{聞|き}きください。

({以降|いこう}: from … on)

From April, what happens after 11 p.m.?
choices: Rapid trains run every fifteen minutes.
questions.explanation:
{夜|よる}{十一時|じゅういちじ}{以降|いこう}はかいそくが{運休|うんきゅう}になり、かくえきていしゃだけが
{走|はし}ります: after 11 p.m. rapid trains are cancelled and only local trains run. Every five minutes is the morning rush, and the last train's time doesn't change.

questions.topic: ところに and ところを
questions.stem: {出|で}かけようとしている___、{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}ってきました。 (Just as I was about to go out, it started to rain.)
questions.explanation: "Just as I was (about to) do A, B came along" is 〜ところに. ところを needs a verb of seeing, catching or helping after it ({見|み}られた), たところ needs a past verb before it, and ところだ ends a sentence.

questions.topic: ところに and ところを
questions.stem: {教室|きょうしつ}で{寝|ね}ているところ___、{先生|せんせい}に{見|み}られてしまいました。
questions.explanation: The scene someone saw or caught is the object of {見|み}られる: {寝|ね}ているところを{見|み}られた, "I was caught sleeping". ところに would need something arriving ({先生|せんせい}が{来|き}た), and で and が don't fit.

questions.stem: {駅|えき}で{聞|き}いた___、{電車|でんしゃ}は{運休|うんきゅう}だそうです。 (I asked at the station, and apparently the trains aren't running.)
questions.explanation: 〜たところ + a result: "when I did A, I found B". Asking at the station led to finding out about the cancellation. とたん is for a sudden event at that very moment, たびに needs the dictionary form and a repeated event, and ついでに is "while I was at it".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "When I tried eating it, it was delicious"?
choices: {食|た}べてみるところ、おいしかったです。
{食|た}べているところ、おいしかったです。
{食|た}べてみたところ、おいしかったです。
questions.explanation: 〜たところ followed by a past result: {食|た}べてみたところ、おいしかったです. {食|た}べてみたところです ends the sentence and means "I've just tried it". The dictionary form and 〜ている before ところ don't give "when I did, I found".

questions.stem: テーブルの{上|うえ}に{飲|の}み___のコーヒーが{置|お}いてあります。 (There's a half-drunk coffee on the table.)
questions.explanation: The ます stem + かけ + の is "half done": {飲|の}みかけのコーヒー. {飲|の}みたて isn't a word (たて works with only a few verbs such as {焼|や}く and できる), and きり and ところ don't follow the ます stem.

questions.stem: このパンは{焼|や}き___で、まだ{温|あたた}かいですよ。 (This bread is fresh out of the oven and still warm.)
questions.explanation: The ます stem + たて is "freshly done": {焼|や}きたて. {焼|や}きかけ would be half-baked, and ばかり needs the た form ({焼|や}いたばかり), as does きり.

questions.stem: {弟|おとうと}は{朝|あさ}{出|で}かけた___、まだ{帰|かえ}ってきません。 (My brother went out this morning and still hasn't come back.)
questions.explanation: 〜たきり + a negative: "did A, and nothing has changed since". ところに would need something arriving just then, たて doesn't follow the た form, and うちに can't follow a past form.

questions.stem: Which sentence is natural?
choices: {食|た}べたてのケーキがあります。
{二人|ふたり}きりで、ゆっくり{話|はな}しました。
{電話|でんわ}したところ、{店|みせ}に{行|い}きました。
{兄|あに}は{出|で}かけたきり、すぐ{帰|かえ}ってきました。
questions.explanation: {二人|ふたり}きり is "just the two of us". たて doesn't go with {食|た}べる (use {食|た}べたばかり), 〜たところ must be followed by what you found, not your next action, and 〜たきり means nothing changed afterwards, so it can't be followed by "came straight back".

questions.stem: スープに{入|い}れる{野菜|やさい}は、___ください。 (Chop the vegetables for the soup finely.)
questions.explanation: {細|こま}かく{切|き}る is to chop finely, into small pieces. {丸|まる}く is "into a round shape", and {冷|つめ}たく and {熱|あつ}く are about temperature, not cutting.

questions.stem: Which is closest in meaning? スープが{冷|さ}めてしまいました。
choices: スープがこげてしまいました。
スープがなくなってしまいました。
スープが{熱|あつ}くなくなってしまいました。
スープが{熱|あつ}くなりすぎてしまいました。
questions.explanation: {冷|さ}める is for something hot cooling down: the soup is no longer hot. こげる is to burn, なくなる is to run out, and {熱|あつ}くなりすぎる is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses {冷|ひ}やす correctly?
choices: {冬|ふゆ}になって、{天気|てんき}が{冷|ひ}やしました。
お{湯|ゆ}が{冷|ひ}やして、{水|みず}になりました。
{熱|ねつ}が{冷|ひ}やして、{元気|げんき}になりました。
ビールをれいぞうこで{冷|ひ}やしておきました。
questions.explanation: {冷|ひ}やす is transitive: you chill something (〜を{冷|ひ}やす). Things that get cold by themselves take the intransitive {冷|ひ}える (weather) or {冷|さ}める (hot water), and a fever {下|さ}がる.

questions.stem: How is 湯 read? お湯をわかしてください。
questions.explanation: お{湯|ゆ} (hot water) uses the kun reading ゆ. トウ is the on'yomi ({熱湯|ねっとう}), and みず is {水|みず}, cold water.

questions.stem: Which kanji is right? たまねぎを［こまかく］{切|き}ります。
questions.explanation: こまかい (fine, small) is 細かい. 小 and 少 are read ちい(さい) and すく(ない)/すこ(し), not こま, and 短 is みじか(い), short.

questions.stem: How is 日本酒 read?
questions.explanation: In the compound, 酒 uses its on'yomi シュ: {日本酒|にほんしゅ}. The kun reading さけ is the word on its own, and さか comes before another word ({酒屋|さかや}).

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker's situation?

audio.text: いま、ちょうどごはんをたべおわったところです。

choices: They are in the middle of eating.
questions.explanation: {食|た}べ{終|お}わったところです: 〜たところだ is "have just done". "About to eat" would be {食|た}べるところ, and "in the middle of" {食|た}べているところ.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say about the bread?

audio.text: このパン、やきたてですよ。あたたかいうちにどうぞ。

choices: It needs to be warmed up.
questions.explanation: {焼|や}きたて is "fresh from the oven", and {温|あたた}かいうちにどうぞ is "have some while it's warm". Half-eaten would be {食|た}べかけ.

questions.stem: Listen. Which is the best reply?

audio.text: おいそがしいところ、すみません。

choices: いいえ、だいじょうぶですよ。
はい、{忙|いそが}しくてすみません。
