vocab.example: {途中|とちゅう}で{文体|ぶんたい}を{変|か}えないように{気|き}をつけよう。
vocab.exampleEn: Be careful not to change style halfway through.

vocab.note: Also {下書|したが}きする.
vocab.example: まず{下書|したが}きをして、それから{字数|じすう}を{数|かぞ}えた。
vocab.exampleEn: First I wrote a draft, then I counted the characters.

vocab.note: Also {改行|かいぎょう}する. On げんこうようし a new paragraph starts on a new line with one blank square.
vocab.example: {話|はなし}が{変|か}わるところで{改行|かいぎょう}しましょう。
vocab.exampleEn: Start a new line where the topic changes.

readingList.title: Free Tadoku Books
readingList.level: Level 0 to level 5; levels 3 and 4 suit N3
readingList.note: Short graded readers written for learners of Japanese, free to read in the browser or to download, some with an audio recording. At N3, read level 2 fast for fluency and levels 3 and 4 for new words and longer stories. Level 5 is the step towards N2.

readingList.title: Japanese Graded Readers (Nihongo Yomu Yomu Bunko)
readingList.level: Levels 0 to 4; levels 3 and 4 suit N3
readingList.note: A long-running series of small graded readers sold in packs, each with an audio recording. At levels 3 and 4 the books are short novels, biographies and adapted classics, a good bridge to lesson 30h1's length. Paid; many university and public libraries have them.

readingList.title: Taishukan Japanese Readers (にほんご多読ブックス)
readingList.level: Levels 0 to 5; levels 3 and 4 suit N3
readingList.note: A second series of graded readers sold in packs, on the same principles as the Ask series. Paid.

readingList.title: NHK NEWS WEB EASY
readingList.note: A selection of each day's news rewritten in simpler Japanese, with furigana you can turn off, a pop-up dictionary in Japanese and audio read by a synthesized voice. At N3, read without furigana first, then check; read the headline and say what the article will be about before you start (lesson 26's headline rules).

readingList.title: YomuJP
readingList.level: N6 (easier than N5) to N1; the N3 articles suit this course
readingList.note: Short articles about life in Japan sorted by JLPT level, with pictures and a recording by a native speaker. Read the N4 articles fast, the N3 ones carefully, and listen to them again without the text as listening practice.

readingList.title: MATCHA (easy Japanese edition)
readingList.note: A travel and culture magazine for visitors to Japan with an edition in simple Japanese, with furigana on every kanji and English for some words. Good for lesson 14's travel words and for real explanatory articles.

readingList.title: Watanoc
readingList.level: Roughly N5 to N3 (each article gives its level)
readingList.note: A free web magazine in simple Japanese about food, culture, events and everyday news, with an approximate JLPT level for each article and English glosses on words. Re-check that the site is still online.

readingList.title: Satori Reader
readingList.level: Several difficulty levels; the middle series suit N3
readingList.note: Serialized stories and articles written for learners, read by Japanese voice actors, with notes on grammar and words, and furigana you can set to match the kanji you know. Paid subscription for the full library, with some content free to try.

readingList.title: JLPT sample questions
readingList.publisher: The Japan Foundation and Japan Educational Exchanges and Services
readingList.note: The official examples of every question type, with audio for listening. Do them under timed conditions in the last weeks before the test (lesson 30). The official practice workbooks, sold separately, contain full practice tests.

readingList.title: NHK NEWS WEB
readingList.note: NHK's ordinary news site, for the step after this course. Start with the short articles on topics you already know from NEWS WEB EASY, and read for the gist; many kanji will be new.

readingList.title: Aozora Bunko (青空文庫)
readingList.level: Mostly N2 and above; some children's stories are manageable after N3
readingList.note: A volunteer library of Japanese literature whose copyright has expired, free to read online. The language is often old-fashioned; at the end of this course, try short children's stories, with a dictionary, as a challenge rather than for fluency.
